PREFACE 

Organic chemistry is a mass of details, an immense collection of facts relative to hundreds of thousands of compounds, yet the relation of these facts to each other is so logical and their sequences so orderly that to understand the system is to remember the whole, as one remembers a cathedral without memorizing the stones of which it is built. Nearly all of the chemistry of carbon compounds can be deduced from a few simple postulates, all of which are connected with the position of carbon in the periodic table: (1) the quadrivalency of carbon (except in a very few cases) regardless of the nature of the elements with which it is combined; (2) its ability to combine with elements of diverse kinds; (3) the independency of its valencies, that is, its ability to hold diverse elements simultaneously or to exchange an atom or group held by one valence for one of some other kind without interference with the atoms held by the other valencies; (4) the remarkable fixedness of its bonds, which means that complicated and permanent molecular structures may be built up according to an orderly plan; (5) the exceptional ability that a carbon atom has of combining with other carbon atoms to form chains or rings.

The aim of this book is to present organic chemistry as a coordinated whole, to develop it logically, depending on the reasoning powers of the student and not to tax his memory. 

Many facts and details are presented, as it takes many bricks to build a house, but they are put in as parts of the whole. 

There has been no hesitancy in using physical chemistry where it is necessary to an understanding of the matter in hand. 

The aim has been to utilize the capabilities of the best students and yet to present the subject in such a way that the less well prepared can grasp it. Throughout much of the book the series has been taken as a unit, the object of study, and emphasis being put on the change of the physical properties as one goes up or iii

iv 

PREFACE 

down a series; one series is contrasted with another to show the effects of the different substituents. To this end great effort has been made to obtain accurate physical data. 

The book has been written to aid teachers by putting in the hands of the student a large assortment of related facts which can be used as desired in teaching the subject. By having these facts the student can be partially relieved of note-taking so as to give more attention to the thought.

CHAPTER I INTRODUCTION 

1. Like most names, the designation "organic" as applied to a division of chemistry is historical rather than descriptive. Substances derived from plants and animals appeared to the chemists of a century ago to be fundamentally different from minerals and the compounds that could be prepared from them. Sugar, starch, alcohol and oil of peppermint did not seem to be constituted like sulphuric acid, iron sulphide and copper sulphate. It was early found that animal and plant substances are made up, for the most part, of only a few elements, carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen. Furthermore, it was a simple matter to char sugar and prove the presence of carbon, but to get the carbon back into sugar appeared utterly hopeless.

Lemery¹ divided his famous Cours de Chymie, published in 1675, "into three parts: the first on minerals, the second on animals and the third on plants." The term organic came into use about two centuries later to describe animal and vegetable substances, since they were produced by organisms. It was adopted by 

Berzelius in his book published in 1806 to describe that part of physiology which deals with the chemical composition and processes of living bodies. In 1812 he divided chemistry into mineral and organic. At that time it was generally assumed that the laws of chemical combination and reaction are suspended, or at least greatly modified by the "vital force" that was assumed to be operative in the living organism. The synthesis in the laboratory 

¹ Nicolas Lemery (1645-1715), is known as a teacher and author of the "Cours de Chymie." This was so widely used that the author himself lived to see thirteen editions published and five translations in other languages. 

2 J. J. Berzelius (1779-1848), the great Swedish chemist, famous as a writer and theorist as well as an experimenter. 1

from dead matter of any of these typical organic substances was regarded as impossible or at least extremely unlikely. As long as such views were held, there could be no scientific development of organic chemistry, although in this period much was accomplished in accumulating facts which later were woven into the science. 

The great Scheele¹ was particularly successful in separating and characterizing acids from plants. The year 1928 was quite generally celebrated as the centenary of organic chemistry since it was in 1828 that Wöhler2 observed that ammonium cyanate could be transformed into urea, a typical animal product. He had previously prepared oxalic acid, a well known plant constituent, from cyanogen in 1824.

These discoveries created a sensation in their day and made a breach in the wall that separated organic chemistry from inorganic. From that time to this, one organic substance after another has yielded to the efforts of chemists. Many hundreds of the substances that occur in animals and plants have been produced in the laboratory from the elements, some directly, others from compounds that can be so produced. In addition, tens of thousands of compounds more or less similar to those that occur naturally have been prepared. There remain many natural substances such as rubber and cellulose that have not yet been synthesized, but the conquest of these is believed to be only a question of labor and time. .

It must be admitted, however, that we are still far from a complete understanding of plant and animal processes and a long way from a comprehension of how they are initiated and carried to completion. It is not yet known how the leaf assimilates water and carbon dioxide and fabricates sugar and starch. These have not yet been produced in the laboratory, but it is certain that they are chemical compounds the atoms of which are held together by the same forces and obey the same laws as are operative in copper sulphate or calcium carbonate. 

2. The Significance of the Term Organic. There is no longer any significance in the term " organic" as it was originally 

1 Carl Wilhelm Scheele (1742-1786), a Swedish apothecary, was the greatest chemical discoverer of his time. He isolated and identified oxygen and many other elements and compounds. 

2 Friedrich Wöhler (1800-1882) was Professor of Chemistry at the University of Göttingen, which he made famous as a school of chemistry.

INTRODUCTION 

3 employed, since of the hundreds of thousands of compounds now comprised in organic chemistry only a small percentage are connected in any way with animals or plants. The term organic is retained as a convenient designation for the chemistry of the compounds of carbon. As books on general chemistry include the simpler compounds of carbon such as carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, and the carbonates of the metals these are left out of organic texts. There is, however, no logical division and no two writers draw the line at exactly the same place; some substances such as acetic and oxalic acids usually appear in both divisions. 

The question naturally arises why the compounds of carbon should be singled out for such elaborate treatment rather than those of some other element such as nitrogen, sulphur or iron. 

There are several reasons. Up to the present time about 300,000 carbon compounds have been studied; in the entire scope of chemistry the known compounds that do not contain carbon are only a fraction of this number. The compounds of carbon exceed those of all the other elements not only in number but also in variety. 

Among them are acids, bases, salts, oxides, peroxides, hydroxides, halides, sulphides and polysulphides analogous to those of the other elements but far more numerous and, in addition, dozens of classes of compounds which are peculiar to carbon. If a book were written devoting one volume to each of the elements, these volumes would vary greatly in size and the one on carbon compounds would be several times thicker than all the others put together. Carbon atoms have in a remarkable degree the power of combining with each other to form chains and even rings. 

3. The Scope of Carbon Chemistry. The tremendous importance of carbon chemistry appears when one considers that our bodies are made up of carbon compounds and that the processes which go on in them are the reactions of carbon compounds. When these reactions take their normal course, there is digestion, assimilation, elaboration of tissue, production of heat and energy, maintenance of body temperature and elimination of waste. Under these conditions there is life and health; but when these do not function properly, there is sickness and death. The secretions of the ductless glands, toxins and antitoxins are carbon compounds, so are the vitamins and all foods. The physician is in truth an

organic chemist, as the processes which he is called upon to restore to their natural course are the reactions of organic compounds. 

The reactions with which he has to deal are far more complicated than those met in the laboratory and are much more difficult to follow than those which can be carried out in glass, but the hope of conquering the complex is through the understanding of the simple. Likewise, pharmacology is a branch of organic chemistry. 

This is true in a double sense, for nearly all of the drugs now in use are organic compounds and their preparation involves organic chemistry, while on the other hand, the processes in the body which the drugs are intended to modify or control are reactions between organic compounds.

Plants, no less than animals, are made up of carbon compounds. 

Even their skeletons are usually woody fibre, while those of animals are calcium phosphate.

It is an interesting fact that carbon and silicon, two elements in the fourth group of the periodic table, although they are not so abundant as some others, so largely dominate the earth. Carbon is the central and characteristic element in all substances associated with life, while the silicates, such as granite, feldspar, slate, sand and clay, make up the great bulk of the earth's crust. In this the carbonates are associated with the silicates. The vast number of carbon compounds are almost all related to the hydrides of carbon, although marble, limestone and dolomite, compounds of carbon dioxide, make up the largest mass. In sharp contrast with this, the hydrides of silicon are unimportant while the almost countless varieties of silicates are related to silicon dioxide. 

4. Carbon Compounds as Carriers of Energy. The daily need of man is energy; first for his body to carry on its functions, to maintain its temperature and activate its muscles; second, for his external needs for light, for electricity and for driving factories, railroads and motor cars. The sun supplies energy in abundance to the earth but distributes it in such a way that man cannot use it directly. It is true that sunlight may be concentrated by mirrors or lenses and made to run an engine, but this has not proved practicable. Streams descending from the mountains give up to waterwheels a small portion of the energy that lifted the water from the ocean, and air currents deliver a trifling amount of energy

INTRODUCTION 

5 LO to windmills, but food and fuel on which man depends for energy, come from plants, whether from herbs brought fresh to the table or from coal, the fossil remains of vegetation of past ages. Essentially the plant is a machine operated by the energy of sunlight to decompose carbon dioxide, liberating the oxygen and building up the carbon into organic compounds. This organic chemical reaction, so simple in statement but so elusive in fact, is the source of almost all of the energy now available to man. The needs of man for power are increasing in geometrical progression. The coal and oil that have been accumulated through geological periods are being depleted and a shortage of fuel may be anticipated even if it is not near. The food demands of the earth's ever increasing population will soon tax the productivity of the available tillable land. 

Apparently the hope of the future depends upon understanding the reactions that take place so silently in the green leaf and discovering how to carry them out artificially. 

The almost universal characteristic of organic compounds is combustibility. In contact with air they form unstable systems; they are prone to revert to carbon dioxide and water, from whence they came, and in doing so they give up the energy which was stored in them. 

5. Sources of Carbon Compounds. A few organic compounds are manufactured from carbon and inorganic materials. Coke and lime, in the electric furnace, give calcium carbide, from which acetylene is made by the action of water. From acetylene can be produced a number of important substances, among them acetaldehyde, acetic acid, oxalic acid, alcohol and ethyl acetate. 

Methanol and other alcohols are now manufactured by passing carbon monoxide and hydrogen over catalysts at high pressures. 

Many other compounds can be built up in similar ways but more often recourse is had to the stores of substances which are elaborated by plants. There are a vast number of these, and many of them are of great commercial importance. Sugar is obtained from sugar cane, from beets and the maple tree; starch from potatoes and Indian corn; cellulose in almost pure form is obtained from cotton fibre and wood pulp. Citric acid is found in limes and lemons; turpentine and rubber come from the sap of trees. Gum camphor, many tons of which are used in the manufacture of cellu-

loid, is extracted from the camphor tree. From the remotest antiquity spices and perfumes of plant origin have been important articles of commerce. Many characteristic and important substances are found in the essential oils; eugenol in cloves, geraniol and citronellol in rose, anethol in anise, linalyl acetate in bergamot, limonene and citral in lemon, carvone in caraway. Numerous alkaloids, some of which are of great medicinal importance such as quinine, strychnine, morphine, caffeine and nicotine, are obtained from plants. A smaller number of substances is furnished by animals.

Many of the substances that are originally present in plants are transformed by natural processes, such as decay and fermentation, into new substances. In this way alcohol is obtained from sugar, and acetic acid from alcohol, lactic acid from milk sugar, indigo from indican, glucose and fructose from sugar. By heating natural substances changes are brought about and new substances are produced; wood yields methanol, acetone and acetic acid, and bones give an oil from which a number of compounds have been isolated. The most important example is the distillation of coal that is carried on both for the coke, which is the residue left in the retort, and for illuminating gas which is given off. The tar that is separated from the gas is the source of benzene, toluene, xylene, naphthalene, anthracene, phenol and other substances on which has been founded the great artificial dye industry. Each of these numerous substances may be the starting point for the preparation by chemical methods of yet other compounds. Thus from alcohol ethyl chloride, ethylene, ether, chloroform, iodoform and hundreds of other compounds are obtained. 

Petroleum, which is found in large quantities in the earth, is a complicated mixture of scores of compounds of carbon and hydrogen, but there are so many of these and their properties are so nearly alike that their complete separation is practically impossible. 

6. Separation of Organic Compounds. Organic compounds exist in great abundance; every twig, every leaf, every flower, every fruit and seed consist not of one or two compounds but of many of them, and great difficulties arise when an attempt is made to obtain individual compounds from these mixtures. All of the constituents of any one fruit or flower have never been isolated, but

INTRODUCTION 

7 the chief ones can commonly be obtained in pure condition. Since separations depend on differences, advantage must be taken of all possible differences, chemical as well as physical. Of the physical properties, differences in volatility and solubility are the most useful. By distillation, a volatile substance is readily separated from a non-volatile as pure water is separated from the salts in sea water. By fractional distillation a more volatile compound can be separated from a less volatile, as alcohol is obtained from mixtures containing it and water. The extraction of a soluble substance from admixture with an insoluble is a simple matter, but mixtures of soluble substances must be dealt with and it is necessary to resort to partial solution and fractional crystallization as methods of separation. An understanding of these processes is of the utmost importance to the organic chemist, since either to study or to market a product the first requisite is to obtain it pure. 

7. Fractional Distillation. Notable advances have been made in the theory and practice of distillation within the last few years. 

Many of the chemical industries are looking to improved fractionation for purer products than have heretofore been available. 

For an adequate treatment reference must be made to physical chemistries and to books and articles on distillation,¹ as only the underlying principles can be given here. The simplest case is that of two mutually soluble liquids. VAPOR

Let us consider two liquids, A and B, and their mixture, A + B in the vessels, 1, 2 and 3, represented diagramatically in Fig. 1.

For simplicity it will be assumed that no air is present. At any

sures. given temperature the vapors in 1 and 3 will have certain pressures characteristic of the liquids A and B. In the space above the mixture of liquids in 2 there is present vapor of A and vapor of B, the total pressure being, of course, the sum of the two vapor pres- Each of these partial pressures is less than the pressure of the corresponding pure liquid in 1 or 3 since each liquid has something dissolved in it and its vapor pressure is lowered in accordance with Raoult's law. Experience with a great many pairs of liquids has shown that there are two cases: 1. The sum of the vapor pressures of A and B over all mixtures of A and B is less than that of A, the more volatile, and greater than that of B, the less volatile. 

2. The sum of the two vapor pressures over certain mixtures of A and B may, with certain pairs of liquids (Case 2a), be greater than that of the more volatile pure compound A or, with certain other pairs of liquids (Case 2b), less than that of the less volatile pure component B. 

8. Boiling Points of Mixtures. Case 1. It is best to think in terms of vapor pressures, but for practical purposes boiling points are used, as they are so much easier to determine. If the vessels 

1, 2 and 3 are heated the vapor pressures will be correspondingly raised, and under standard conditions when they reach 760 mm. of mercury the liquids will be at their boiling points. In 2 it is the sum of the two partial pressures that must reach 760 mm. In 

Case 1, the boiling points of all mixtures of A and B are between those of the pure components. In Case 2 some mixtures of A and B boil lower than either A or B (Case 2a) or higher than either A or B (Case 2b). 

Case 1. Mixtures of two similar liquids, such as two members of a homologous series (Chapter V) usually belong to this class. 

In general, a mixture of any two hydrocarbons, two alcohols, two ethers, two alkyl chlorides or bromides will fall into this class.

As an example, the case of carbon disulphide and carbon tetrachloride will be considered in detail. A number of mixtures of these two liquids were made up and their boiling points carefully determined. The results are given in Table I, the percentages being in moles rather than in grams.

73 will show the composition of the vapor in equilibrium, at that temperature, with the liquid of the composition represented by N, the intersection of this line with the liquid curve. 

From the diagram it is seen that the vapor always contains a greater proportion of the more volatile component than the liquid with which it is in equilibrium. On this simple statement hangs the whole theory of the separation of volatile liquids by fractionation. If a part of a mixture of two liquids is distilled, the distillate contains a higher proportion of the more volatile component, and the residue contains a smaller percentage than the original mixture. 

Conversely if a portion of vapor is condensed that part contains less of the more volatile constituent than the remainder of the vapor.

The problem is to find the amount and composition of the portions of the distillate that go into the several flasks. These data were plotted on large scale and the following values obtained. The 50-50 mixture is found to boil at 56.40° so flasks 1, 2 and 3 are not needed and the first distillate goes into No. 4. The cut is made at 58.48°, at which the liquid remaining has 42.1 per cent and the vapor has 66.2 per cent of the disulphide. The average composition of the vapor is 69.3 per cent.

The distillate is caught in flasks 2, 3, 4 and 5, the changes being

made as before at the chosen temperatures. When the liquid reaches the temperature of 61.51°, the contents of flask 6 is emptied into the distilling flask and the above process repeated. This is continued systematically to the end, each of the original fractions being put in at the proper temperature and each portion of the distillate being caught in the appropriate flask.

15 to accumulate in the end fractions. Experiments are on record in which such systematic fractionations were repeated a hundred times or more, the separation becoming progressively more complete but never quite perfect. As the separation progresses it is customary to widen the temperature intervals for the dwindling intermediate cuts and to narrow those for the end cuts. 

11. Automatic Fractionation. Obviously the separation of liquids by repeated fractionation as described above is extremely tedious. Many devices have been proposed for cutting down the number of fractionations necessary for obtaining a certain degree of separation. Nails were formerly hammered out on the anvil one at a time but are now made by a machine that takes a bar of steel at one end and drops the nails into a keg at the other. So a modern fractionating column accomplishes on an enormous scale with a minimum of attention a more perfect separation of mixtures than can be effected in the laboratory by a hundred fractionations in the hands of the most skillful operator. 

There are variations in the details of construction of these columns, but the principle is always the same. Usually there are 

40 to 60 plates one above the other in the column. These are shallow dishes, each one of which serves as a distillation flask sending vapor, richer in the more volatile constituent up to the plate above it and discharging the poorer residual liquid to the plate below it. The vapor from each plate is made to bubble through the liquid in the one above it and the descending liquid is made to come in the most intimate contact with the ascending vapor. As the efficiency of a column depends on contact of liquid with vapor, there must be descending liquid to meet the ascending vapor. This is provided by placing the condenser above the column and dividing the condensate, one part being sent back to the top of the column and the other to the receiver. The ratio of these is spoken of as the reflux ratio. For efficient operation 5 to 

10 parts are returned to one collected.

Formerly few constant boiling mixtures were known but now hundreds have been discovered. Some of the first were regarded as chemical compounds, but it was later found that the composition of the minimum boiling mixture changes with change of pressure. 

The most important of such mixtures is that formed by alcohol with water. The fact that the strongest alcohol which can be obtained by distillation contains only about 95 per cent of alcohol is sometimes spoken of as a failure of this process. On the contrary, the fact that this strength of alcohol is produced with such uniformity in quality is a triumph. Absolute alcohol boils at 

78.33° while a mixture of it and water containing 4.43 per cent by weight of water boils at 78.15° and it is this mixture which comes over first when any mixture of alcohol and water is distilled.

14. Steam Distillation. A commonly employed method of separating oils from non-volatile material is steam distillation. 

For instance, pine wood chips are placed in a still with water and the mixture is either boiled, or better, steam from a separate boiler is blown through the vessel containing the chips, and the vapors are passed through a cooling coil. The turpentine, being insoluble in water, separates as a layer and is drawn off.

15. Crystallization. In the separation and purification of solids, recourse is had to crystallization. If equal amounts of two solids, one of which is less soluble than the other, are present in a solution and the solvent is gradually evaporated off, the first crystals to separate will contain a larger proportion of the less soluble substance than the original mixture. The less soluble solid is concentrated in the portion that separates out just as the more volatile constituent of a liquid mixture is concentrated in the vapor that is given off. If the evaporation is continued, the suc-

INTRODUCTION 

21 ceeding crops of crystals which are obtained contain increasing amounts of the more soluble substance, just as the vapors given off in the latter part of a distillation are richer in the less volatile constituent. By re-solution of the crystals and recrystallization crystals of higher purity are obtained. This process may be repeated time after time until no difference can be detected between crystals from succeeding crystallizations. By systematically recrystallizing, uniting the crops of crystals of approximately the same composition and working up the mother liquors, two substances of different degrees of solubility can usually be separated. This process is closely analogous to systematic fractionation. It is always difficult and sometimes impossible to obtain the more soluble substance in a state of purity. Changes of solvent and other expedients are resorted to in difficult cases. 

16. Criteria of Purity. In practice, any substance is accepted as pure when all efforts at further purification fail to alter its properties. All properties may be included in this statement, but certain are chosen, partly because they are easy to measure and to state numerically and partly because they change markedly on the introduction of impurities. The most commonly used are the melting point of a solid and the boiling point of a liquid. When a solid is obtained its melting point is taken. After each recrystallization, or other purification, the melting point is again taken. As impurities are eliminated, the melting point of the substance rises, rapidly at first and then very slowly, until it becomes constant. 

This is in accordance with Raoult's law. A liquid is fractionally distilled until a portion is obtained that goes over at a constant temperature. In case the substances have been prepared previously and their properties recorded, the melting and boiling points that are obtained are compared with the data that are on record. 

Of course, a constant boiling mixture would be taken for a pure compound if only the above test were made. Mixtures are occasionally found, the melting points of which remain constant through a series of crystallizations. Such have sometimes been mistaken for individual substances. The chemist must be on his guard and apply other tests in suspicious cases. 

17. Qualitative Analysis. Naturally, the first thing is to determine what elements are present, but the methods are entirely

different from those of qualitative analysis for the metals. Instead of a systematic procedure for separating all possible elements, tests for particular elements which are suspected of being present are usually made. The most common characteristic of carbon compounds is their combustibility, although some of them burn with difficulty. Instead of burning the substance in air, it is frequently mixed with copper oxide and heated in a tube. The presence of carbon dioxide among the products of combustion is proof of the presence of carbon in the compound. Hydrogen nearly always accompanies carbon and betrays its presence by the formation of water in the burning. Next to carbon and hydrogen, the element most commonly encountered is oxygen, but its presence is frequently difficult to prove. Commonly, all the other elements are determined quantitatively and the difference between the sum of their percentages and 100 per cent is taken as oxygen " by difference." At best this throws all of the analytical errors onto the oxygen content and one must be sure that no other constituent has been overlooked. A positive test for the presence of oxygen is the formation of water vapor when the substance is heated strongly in an atmosphere of nitrogen. 

Nitrogen, sulphur and the halogens are frequently found in carbon compounds. These are found by Lassaigne's test. Sodium or potassium is, heated in a hard glass test tube and the substance dropped into the hot metal, which forms a cyanide, sulphide or halide if one of these elements is present. These can be detected by the ordinary methods of qualitative analysis. Compounds containing the above elements only burn completely, leaving no residue.

Phosphorus, which is a comparatively rare element in organic compounds, is detected by igniting the material with a mixture of sodium or potassium carbonate and nitrate, dissolving the residue in water and testing for the phosphate ion. An arsenic compound similarly treated gives the arsenate ion.

Silicon and the metals are more rarely present. When an organic compound containing any of these is burned, their oxides remain in the ash which is analyzed by the usual methods. In the case of organic compounds of platinum and silver, the metal is left as such on burning off the carbon.

INTRODUCTION 

23 18. Quantitative Analysis of Carbon Compounds. Only the principles of the methods can be given here. Reference must be made to analytical manuals for details of the procedures. 

To determine carbon and hydrogen, a known weight of the compound is burned in a current of air or of oxygen, or with copper oxide, and the resulting carbon dioxide and hydrogen are absorbed and determined. From these the weights of carbon and hydrogen in the substance are obtained and then the percentage of each element is calculated. An example will make this plain. A sample of benzoic acid weighing 0.1712 g. is burned and the water and carbon dioxide obtained weigh 0.0758 g. and 0.4320 g. respectively. Since water contains 11.13 per cent of hydrogen, 0.0758 g. of water corresponds to 0.00844 g. of hydrogen in the substance. 

The carbon is 3/11 of the 0.4320 g. of carbon dioxide, or 0.1178 g. 

From these the percentage composition is calculated: 0.00844 X 100 0.1178 X 100 

4.93% H and 0.1712 

68.81% C 0.1712

Assuming that no element is present other than carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, the balance 100 (68.814.93) = 26.26 is taken as oxygen.

This method, which was proposed by Liebig¹ in 1831, brought about great advances in organic chemistry. It has been modified in many ways to meet special conditions, gas and electric furnaces have been substituted for the old charcoal heaters which required dextrous fanning with a turkey wing, lead chromate and other oxidising agents replace the copper oxide in special cases, but the principle remains the same.

Nitrogen is determined in two ways. According to the Dumas method, the compound is burned by heating it in a tube with copper oxide in an atmosphere of carbon dioxide. The nitrogen is set free and is either swept out by carbon dioxide or pumped out, collected over caustic potash solution and measured. From its 

1 Justus von Liebig (1803-1873), a great leader in the development of organic chemistry, was the first to introduce laboratory instruction in chemistry. Liebig's Annalen, founded in 1832, gave the chemists of the world an opportunity to state their results and discuss their views. It is still one of the important journals.

volume, corrected for temperature and pressure, the weight of the nitrogen is calculated. In the Kjeldahl¹ method, the organic substance is heated with concentrated sulphuric acid, with certain additions, until it is completely oxidised. The nitrogen is thus converted into ammonium sulphate. An excess of caustic soda is added and the liberated ammonia is distilled over into a measured amount of standard acid, the excess of which is later titrated. 

The Carius method has long been employed for sulphur. In this method the organic compound is oxidised completely by heating it with fuming nitric acid in a sealed tube and its sulphur content thereby converted into sulphuric acid which is determined in the usual way. Halogen compounds are oxidised in a similar way, except that silver nitrate is added to the nitric acid. When the oxidation is complete, the halogen is found as silver halide, which is weighed. Oxidation of sulphur and halogen compounds by ignition with sodium peroxide in the Parr³ bomb has recently come into wide use. By this means the carbon and hydrogen are completely oxidised and the sulphur and halogens left as inorganic sodium compounds, which can be handled by the usual methods. 

As silver and platinum are left in the metallic state when organic compounds containing them are burned, the deterimnation of these elements is usually a very simple matter. For instance, a sample of the silver salt of an organic acid is weighed into a porcelain or silica crucible and carefully ignited with full access of air. The residue is the pure metal which is weighed just as it is in the crucible. The chlorplatinates of organic bases are easily obtained and are similarly analyzed. 

19. Determination of Molecular Weight. In order to determine the formula of a compound it is necessary to know not only its percentage composition, but also its molecular weight, which is the weight in grams of 22.4 liters under standard conditions. 

Since most organic substances are not gases at ordinary tempera-

INTRODUCTION 

25 tures, it is necessary to weigh their vapors at some convenient temperature, above their boiling points and calculate down to 0°. 

Practically, the difficulty of making accurate weighings and measurements at high temperatures can be avoided in two ways.

In the Dumas¹ method the weight of a known volume of the vapor at the desired temperature is found. A bulb is blown on the end of a short tube. A quantity of a substance, such as benzoic acid, much larger than the amount that is expected to remain after it is vaporized is placed in the bulb. If the bulb is now placed in boiling benzophenone, 306°, the benzoic acid will vaporize. As the excess of benzoic acid boils off it drives out all the air that was in the bulb. When no more of the vapor escapes, the tip of the tube is sealed. The amount of the benzoic acid is subsequently determined by weighing the cooled bulb, making proper allowances for air displacement.

In the Victor Meyer2 method a known weight is volatilized and the volume of vapor produced is measured. A vertical tube, about 

60 cm. long, has a bulb blown on its lower end. This bulb is immersed in a bath of suitable known temperature, that is, one high enough to volatilize the substance but not high enough to decompose it. When equilibrium is reached, a weighed amount of the substance is dropped down the tube. This volatilizes quickly and its vapor displaces its own volume of air which escapes by way of a side arm near the top of the vertical tube and is caught in a eudiometer standing over water. By measuring the air the volume of the vapor is known.

The determination of the molecular weights of non-volatile substances is based on Raoult's law which states that the amounts of any two substances required to elevate the boiling point of a solvent equal amounts are proportional to their molecular weights. 

The same is true with regard to the depression of the freezing point. 

These statements apply only to undissociated compounds, but most 1 Jean Baptiste André Dumas (1800-1884), a well-known French chemist. 

He was prominent in laying the groundwork for subsequent development in organic chemistry. 

2 Victor Meyer (1848-1897), was Professor of Chemistry at Stuttgart and

Zürich and succeeded Wöhler to the chief chemical chair at Göttingen. He is famous for his method of determining vapor density and researches on nitroand iso-nitro compounds of the aliphatic series and as joint author of a famous text-book of organic chemistry.

organic substances belong to that class. For the details of the manipulations in these methods reference must be made to laboratory manuals. 

20. Calculation of Formula. The formula of any substance must represent the make-up of a molecule, that is, the kinds of atoms and number of each kind in it. Coming back to benzoic acid, the formula must represent the molecule of benzoic acid which has the weight 122. Knowing the percentage composition, 68.81 per cent carbon, 4.93 per cent hydrogen, and 26.21 per cent oxygen, it is a simple matter to calculate the parts by weight of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in 122.05 parts by weight of benzoic acid. 

In carbon this is 68.81 per cent of 122.05 or 84, which is C7.

Similarly for oxygen it is 32 or O2 and for hydrogen it is 6 or H6, and the formula of benzoic acid is written as C7H6O2. This is frequently called the molecular formula since it is the formula of a molecule, but the adjective is superfluous as a formula should be understood as representing the composition of a molecule. 

21. Empirical Formula. As brought out above, an analysis and a molecular weight determination are required for the calculation of the formula of a compound, but there are cases in which it is difficult to get the molecular weight. When the molecular weight is not known an empirical formula is the only thing that can be obtained. It is a formula based solely on the analysis. 

An analysis shows the relative weights of the elements found in the substances; the empirical formula gives the relative numbers of atoms of different kinds present. Glycol is found to contain 

58.68 per cent carbon, 9.75 per cent hydrogen and 51.57 per cent oxygen. Dividing these percentages by the atomic weights we have: 38.68 12 3.22, 9.75 1.01

Evidently these are 1:3: 1 and the empirical formula of glycol is CH3O. This is the simplest formula that can be found which expresses the composition in atoms. The molecu-

CHAPTER II METHANE 

22. When vegetable matter decays under water, a gas, known as marsh gas, is formed and rises in bubbles. This gas was observed by Volta¹ in 1778. In certain processes of sewage disposal, the gas from the ripened sludge may contain as high as 80 per cent of this gas along with carbon dioxide, and by the removal of the latter the marsh gas may be obtained 94-98 per cent pure. 

This has been proposed as a commercial source. 

The same gas is found in coal mines, where it has long been the cause of terrific explosions. The gas issuing from one mine has been estimated at over 8,000,000 cu. ft. per day. The miners call it fire damp, damp” being their term for a vapor or gas. Natural gas which 66 is encountered in pockets in the earth's crust contains methane as the chief constituent, the percentage usually being 70 to 90 per cent but sometimes as high as 99 per cent. The pressure in such pockets may be very high, even up to 100 atmospheres. For 

1926 the U. S. production of natural gas was 1,313,019,000,000 cu. ft. This and related gases are found along with petroleum. 

Coal gas, which is manufactured for use in cities by heating soft coal in retorts, contains 20 to 40 per cent of the same gas. In scientific writings this gas is called methane, the name connecting it with methyl alcohol. Its formula is CH4 and it is the simplest compound of carbon and hydrogen.

At lower temperatures the equilibrium is much more favorable to the methane but the reaction velocity is so low that it is not practicable to make it go without a catalyst. The indirect synthesis of methane is readily accomplished, so readily that the process has commercial possibilities in localities where natural gas is not available. Hydrogen and carbon monoxide or dioxide are passed over finely divided metals, particularly nickel, at temperatures from 150° to 350° and methane is formed quantitatively:

CO + 3H2 → CH4 + H2O CO2 + 4H2 →→ CH4 + 2H2O Platinum and palladium cause these reactions to take place at much lower temperatures. If the metal is omitted no reaction takes place. The metal is called a "catalyst "-which is a term applied to something which causes reactions to take place and yet seems to take no part itself in the reactions which it causes. 

Many explanations have been given as to how the metal brings about this reaction, but they cannot be discussed here. 

The earliest synthesis of methane was from carbon bisulphide and hydrogen sulphide passed over heated copper: CS2 + 2H2S + 8Cu→ CH4 + 4Cu₂S

31 When aluminum carbide is treated with water, methane is evolved:

24. Physical Properties of Methane. Methane is a colorless gas with a slight odor. It is very slightly soluble in water, 9 cc. in 

100 cc. of water at 20°. Its specific gravity is 0.5545 compared with air, 1 liter weighing 0.7163 g. at 0° and 760 mm. It is the lightest compound gas known, one of the so-called permanent gases which long resisted liquefaction. The critical temperature and pressure of the gas are-82.5° and 45.7 atm. It can be condensed readily to a liquid by liquid air. When liquid methane evaporates under reduced pressure, a portion of it solidifies. 

Methane melts at -185.8° and boils at -160°. The weight of 

22.4 liters of methane is 16 g. and therefore its molecular weight is 16. It contains 75 per cent of carbon and 25 per cent of hydrogen. As 75 per cent of 16 is 12 and 25 per cent of 16 is 4, a whole molecule contains 12 of carbon and 4 of hydrogen, from which the molecular formula CH4 is obtained. 

25. Chemical Properties of Methane. Chemically, methane is comparatively inert towards most substances. It is not an acid, as none of its hydrogens is ionizable-and neither is it a base. 

It is one of a class of hydrocarbons, that is, compounds of hydrogen and carbon, known as paraffins, the name meaning "little affinity from the Latin parvum and affinitas. Methane is relatively difficult to ignite, a mixture with air having to be heated to above 600°. Mixtures of methane and air containing more than 5.5 per cent and less than 14.5 per cent of methane explode when brought into contact with a flame or spark. Methane burns with a nonluminous but intensely hot flame, the amount of heat liberated being very large:

CH4 +202 → CO2 + 2H2O + 210,900 cal.

One thousand B.T.U. per cubic foot are obtained from methane as compared with about 550 for coal gas, and about 300 for unenriched water gas. Compared with its heat of combustion, its heat of formation is small: 

C+2H2 CH4 +20,800 cal. The partial oxidation of methane is an attractive problem, as several valuable products can be formed in this way. Unfortunately it is extremely difficult to stop the oxidation at the right place. The reaction starts only at a high temperature and when once started is difficult to control, the final product usually being one of the oxides of carbon. As is shown in the equation below, the part way oxidation is highly exothermic which makes it difficult to remove the heat generated sufficiently rapidly to keep the temperature within bounds. Under special conditions a small percentage of formaldehyde can be obtained: 

CH4+ O2CH2O + H2O + 76,900 cal. Methane 210,900 Formaldehyde 134,000 26. The Chlorination of Methane. Under the influence of light, or of certain catalysts, chlorine reacts with methane. One hydrogen of the methane is removed and combines with one of the chlorine atoms to form hydrogen chloride. The other chlorine atom enters the methane molecule. The action continues; the successive products contain less and less hydrogen and correspondingly more chlorine. The reactions that take place are represented by the following equations, the validity of each of which has been proved by separate experiments:

CH4 + Cl2 → CHзCl + HCI CH3Cl + Cl2 → CH2Cl2 + HCl CH2Cl2 + Cl2 → CHCl3 + HCl CHCl3 + Cl2 → CCl4 + HCI In a mixture of the two gases ali of the reactions go on and it is impossible to stop at the formation of any one of the products except the end one. The mixture that is obtained by partial action

METHANE 

333 is difficult to separate into its constituents. By using a large excess of methane, the mono-chloro-methane, CH3Cl, also known as methyl chloride, can be manufactured on a commercial scale, but the difficulties are so great that this process is not largely employed, in spite of the cheapness of natural gas and of chlorine. 

With larger proportions of chlorine, the substitution products containing more chlorine predominate. By treatment with so called nascent hydrogen, the process may be reversed, that is, the chlorine is progressively removed and hydrogen put in its place. 

Thus carbon tetrachloride can be converted to methane. 

27. Substitution. In its action on methane, as described above, chlorine is said to act by substitution since one atom of chlorine enters the molecule for each atom of hydrogen that is removed; thus chlorine is considered as taking the place of the hydrogen. So far as the number of atoms is concerned, this statement can not be questioned, but in what sense the chlorine atom takes the place of the hydrogen atom and to what extent it functions as did the hydrogen atom have caused much discussion. 

When the idea of substitution was first proposed, it met with intense opposition from those who held the then prevalent dualistic theory according to which the elements are divided into electropositive (hydrogen and the metals) and electro-negative (oxygen, sulphur and the halogens), all combinations depending on the oppositeness of the electric charges. It was inconceivable to most chemists of that time that chlorine, a strongly electro-negative element, could take the place of hydrogen, an electro-positive element. As facts accumulated the dualistic theory was abandoned and the idea of substitution was accepted. It is indeed remarkable to what extent the chlorinated methanes resemble the original methane, although with increases in the molecular weights the boiling points are raised.

Chemically all five of the compounds show considerable similarity, all being neutral and relatively indifferent to most reagents. 

All are slightly soluble in water but very soluble in alcohol and ether. The compounds containing chlorine have sweetish odors and are reactive towards many compounds containing the metals, particularly sodium or potassium. In each of them the one carbon atom appears to be combined with the four univalent atoms inde-

pendently. For instance, the two hydrogen atoms in methylene chloride, CH2Cl2, may be substituted either by chlorine or bromine atoms to form CHCl3 or CCl4 and CHC12Br or CCl₂Br2 without disturbing the two original chlorine atoms or the chlorine atoms may enter into reactions without regard to the two hydrogens. 

Similar statements may be made relative to the hydrogen or chlorine atoms in the other compounds of this group. The fact that any one of the hydrogen or chlorine atoms in methylene chloride may be replaced without disturbing the other three is taken to mean that each of the four is directly and independently joined or linked to the carbon atom. 

Substitution is one of the characteristic reactions of carbon compounds. Not that this or any other type of reaction is peculiar to carbon, but carbon is unique among the elements in respect to the number and variety of the ways in which substitution may be effected in its compounds. A multitude of the compounds of carbon are actually made by substitution and are substitution products in the strict sense, but the conception of substitution has proved to be so useful in classifying and naming carbon compounds that the most of them are spoken of as substitution products of the hydrocarbons. The complex hydrocarbons are regarded as obtained from certain simpler hydrocarbons by substitution. 

28. The Valence of Carbon. From the position of carbon in the fourth group, four would be expected to be both its maximum and minimum, or its positive and negative valence. A carbon atom can give up four electrons or it can receive four, but in most cases it more probably shares eight electrons with other atoms. Its valence is four in nearly all of its compounds. Carbon monoxide is a notable exception and one that is difficult to explain. In this and in the isonitriles (Chapter XVI) carbon appears to be bivalent. 

In recent years triphenyl-methyl and other so-called "free radicals" (Chapter XXXVI) have been discovered. These appear to contain trivalent carbon, but they are strikingly different from the rest of carbon compounds and are to be regarded rather as incomplete molecules with unsatisfied affinities.

The quadrivalence of carbon is well illustrated by the following compounds of carbon with hydrogen and the halogens:

METHANE 

35 CH4 CH3F CH3Cl CH3Br CHзI CH2F2 CH2Cl2 CH2Br2 CH2I2 CHF3 CHCl3 CHBг3 CHI3 CHFC12 CHC12Br CHBr₂I CHCII2 CHFCIBr CHCI2I CHBRI2 CF2Cl2 CC12Br2 CCIBг3 CBrI3 CFC13 CC12I2 CCl3Br CBrgI CClзI In each of these one carbon atom is present with four characteristically univalent atoms. The simplest assumption is that the carbon atom is quadrivalent in each case and binds the four univalent elements. All of the compounds represented by the above formulae are known and all bear a sort of family likeness to each other. Some of them have been very superficially studied but, so far as known, the halogen atoms of all of them may be progressively replaced by hydrogen until methane is reached. In general one halogen may be replaced by another; many of them can be made from others by the action of a halogen or of hydrogen. 

One carbon atom combines with two bivalent atoms as in carbon dioxide, disulphide and diselenide: CO2 CS2 CSE2 Or it may unite with a bivalent atom along with two hydrogens as in formaldehyde, phosgene and thiophosgene: COH2 COC12 CSC12 Or with one trivalent and one univalent atom as in hydrocyanic acid, cyanogen chloride and cyanogen bromide:

CNH CNCI CNBr 29. Equivalence of the Valencies of Carbon. It is conceivable that there might be some differences among the four valencies of carbon; one hydrogen in methane might be held more securely than the rest or perhaps two of them might be joined by primary valencies and the other two by secondary. The progressive substitution of chlorine for hydrogen as described above would appear to be contrary to such a supposition. If there were any marked difference in the way the four hydrogen atoms are held, there would

likely be a break in the continuity of the substitution; the process might go on rapidly until one-fourth or one-half of the hydrogen had been replaced and then slow up or stop entirely. The energy liberated in the successive steps would be quite different. 

There is another way of reaching the same conclusion. Methylene chloride, CH2Cl2, may be made by chlorinating methane or monochloromethane. On the other hand, it may be obtained by removing chlorine from carbon tetrachloride, CC, or chloroform, CHCl3. If the valencies of carbon were not alike, two or more varieties of methylene chloride might conceivably be produced, depending on the method of preparation. The same may be said of methyl chloride and chloroform. If one hydrogen were more readily replaceable than the others, the chlorine in CH3Cl made by chlorinating methane should be in its place. Likewise, the bromine in CH3Br similarly prepared should have its bromine in the same position. Now if the first compound be brominated, and the second chlorinated, the two compounds obtained may be represented by:

CH2BrCl and CH2CIBr If there were a difference in the valencies by which the chlorine and bromine atoms are held these compounds should be different in their properties, to some extent at least, but experiment shows that this is not the case.

The experience of a century all goes to show that there is but one compound represented by each of the formulae: CH2Cl2, CH3Cl,

CH3Br, CH2ClBr

Systematic and laborious attempts have been made to find differences in the valencies of carbon and, so far, none have been found. 

30. Representation of Carbon Bonds. Any method may be used so long as the number and equality of the four valencies are clearly portrayed. Several devices are more or less frequently employed. Methane is written:

H-C-H H.C.H

HCH

METHANE 

37 3 The first impresses the eye directly with the number and equality of the linkages. It is customary to use lines to represent forces. 

There must be forces between the atoms to hold them together, so lines are used for these forces. A line joins the hydrogen atom to the carbon atom, which pictures the idea that chemical union is an attachment of one individual atom to another individual atom, not a general attraction of one or more particles for a number of other particles. Each line represents a unit of valence. Each hydrogen atom has one of these lines which shows its univalency. 

Four of these lines, or bonds, as they are frequently called, extend to the one carbon atom which indicates its quadrivalency. The attachment of each hydrogen to the carbon atom is pictured as being independent of the other three. It was stated above that any of these can be replaced without disturbing the others. This diagram represents to the eye the experimental facts.

In looking at a formula of this sort care must be taken to get from it all that it is intended to convey, and to guard against being misled. When this diagram is drawn on paper or on a blackboard, all of the bonds are represented as in a plane and as perpendicular to each other. It is not intended to imply anything as to the direction of the bonds, but only to show their member and equality. 

The atoms of the actual molecule are of course in three dimensional space. It will be brought out later on (Chapter IX) that there is reason to believe that the hydrogen atoms of methane are equally spaced on the surface of a sphere at the center of which is the carbon atom. The lines joining them to the center make an angle of 

109° instead of 90° as on the blackboard. It must always be remembered that these formulae are conventional diagrams and not pictures. We must look at them as we do at maps on which state capitals are represented by stars, large towns by circles and small ones by dots. We get the impression of the importance of the cities and of the special function of the capital without being misled as to the shapes of the settlements. The lines are frequently replaced by dots which take less space. Sometimes the lines and dots are left out and the H's grouped around the C as in the third formula. Occasionally a bracket is used or the H's are written above one another. It is desirable for the student to form the habit of turning formulae around and writing them in various ways, in order to learn to recognize the essentials and not to be bothered by the incidentals.

In terms of electrons, the carbon bonds are commonly believed to be non-polar, that is each bond is represented by a pair of shared elections and the formula of methane is: ..

H:C:H 

..

31. Structural Formulae. Any of the above would be called a structural formula of methane, as the relation of each atom to the molecule is shown. A structural formula is one which shows the relation of each atom of the molecule to the other atoms, indicates the valence of each and designates the atom or atoms with which it is combined. The molecular formula CH4 represents only two facts: that methane has a molecular weight of 16 and that it contains four atoms of hydrogen to one of carbon. The structural formula tells much more. Structural formulae, as will appear more fully as their derivation and interpretation are considered, contain in symbols the record of multitudes of experimental facts all of which are revealed to one who can read the writing. It required years of patient research on the part of a number of the best experimenters to arrive at the structural formula of indigo. 

The structural formulae of many natural substances have baffled serveral generations of chemists. A large part of the endeavor of organic chemists has been directed towards the determination of structural formulae. When a structural formula of any substance is determined, its nature is known and chemists are a long way on the road to knowing how to build it up, just as a skillful mechanic takes a machine apart, measures its parts and builds one like it. 

The synthesis of indigo followed very quickly after the discovery of its structural formula. This has been the case with many other substances.

33. Naming the Halogen Derivatives. Each one of the above compounds has at least two names, each of which is based on a different way of looking at it and brings out different relationships. 

All of them may be thought of as being derived from methane by replacing one or more of its hydrogen atoms by the halogens; then they will be named as chlorine derivatives of methane: chloromethane or monochloromethane, dichloromethane, trichloromethane and tetrachloromethane. The fluroine, bromine and iodine derivatives will be named similarly. It will be seen that those in a horizontal line in Table II are alike in having the same group of carbon and hydrogen atoms. Those in the first line are

Using this device, the halogen derivatives are called methyl chloride, methyl bromide and methyl iodide. The group CH2: is bivalent and is known as methylene and the derivatives as methylene chloride, methylene bromide and methylene iodide. Those in the third line have a connection with formic acid (Chapter XIV) and are known as chloroform, bromoform and iodoform. The fully substituted compounds are named from their composition: carbon tetrachloride, carbon tetrabromide and carbon tetraiodide. 

34. Methyl Chloride. This can be obtained by substitution, as stated above but is made by the action of hydrochloric acid on methyl alcohol (48). It is a colorless gas with a pleasant odor and burns with a white flame bordered with green. It is used to introduce the methyl group, CH3-, into various compounds. 

35. Methyl Bromide, and Methyl Iodide. These are prepared by the action of hydrobromic or hydriodic acid or of phosphorus tribromide on methyl alcohol (91). The iodide, b.p. 42.6°, is a liquid at room temperature, while the bromide, b.p. 4.6° is an easily condensible gas. They have the same uses as methyl chloride. In large scale operations, where cost of materials is an important consideration, methyl chloride is employed, while in the laboratory, where small quantities are required, the ease of handling the liquid methyl iodide and its greater reactivity more than make up for its greater cost. 

36. Methylene Chloride, Bromide and Iodide. These are usually obtained by substitution of hydrogen for halogen in the corresponding trihalogen substitution products:

CHCl3 + 2H → CH2Cl2 + HCl The hydrogen must be in the so called "nascent" state, that is, must be produced as it reacts by some suitable chemical reaction as that between a metal and an acid. The only one of these that is of importance is methylene iodide. It has the highest density, 3.3326 at 15°, of any known organic liquid. Heavy minerals such as galena which has a density of 7.13 can be separated from silicates, the most of which have a density less than 3, by adding the

powdered rock to methylene iodide. By mixing lighter liquids with methylene iodide, a medium can be obtained in which one mineral will float and another will sink, although the densities of the two minerals may be close together. 

37. Chloroform, Bromoform, and Iodoform. All of these can be readily made by adding chlorine, bromine or iodine to a mildly alkaline water solution of alcohol or acetone. For the manufacture of chloroform a mixture of bleaching powder with six times its weight of water is run slowly into 20 per cent alcohol which has been heated to boiling (118). The chloroform distils over with some water and alcohol. It is separated by fractionation and the dilute alcohol mixed with the next batch. At the present time the larger part of the chloroform is obtained by the reduction of carbon tetrachloride by iron and water:

CCl4 + 2H → CHCl3 + HCI A portion of the chloroform is reduced still further to methylene chloride which is separated by fractionation. 

Since its first use by Dr. Simpson of Edinburgh in 1848, chloroform has been largely employed as an anaesthetic but has been replaced almost entirely by ether and ethylene. In contact with air and in the light, chloroform decomposes slightly into phosgene and hydrogen chloride:

HCCl3 + 02 → COCl2 + HCI. Phosgene This reaction appears to be retarded by alcohol, and for this reason about 1 per cent of alcohol is usually added to chloroform. Chloroform is a heavy, low boiling liquid with a pleasant odor and sweet burning taste. It is used as a solvent as many organic substances such as hydrocarbons and fats are very soluble in it. It is a strong antiseptic. As it contains 89 per cent of chlorine and only 11 per cent of carbon and hydrogen, it does not burn. 

Bromoform has slight importance in medicine and none in the industries. Iodoform has been an important agent in treating wounds and sores to combat infection. As its characteristic odor is objectionable, other more or less similar iodine compounds which have less odor are used in its stead.

METHANE 

43 38. Carbon Tetrachloride. This is the end product of the chlorination of methane but is not made in quantity by this method since a cheaper process is available. This is the chlorination of carbon disulphide:

CS2+3C12→ CCl4 + S2C12 Originally iodine was used as a catalyst, or chlorine carrier, but iron and antimony compounds may be used instead. The sulphur monochloride chlorinates carbon bisulphide in the presence of iron: CS2+2S2Cl2 → CCl4 + 6S Carbon tetrachloride is a colorless, volatile liquid with a pleasant odor, similar to that of chloroform. It is a valuable solvent for fats, heavy hydrocarbons and rubber, and finds large use in the extraction of many such substances from insoluble material. Its low boiling point, 76.74°, makes it very suitable for this purpose but its high density, 1.63, is a detriment, as such a large weight of it is required to make a suitable volume. It is used on the large scale in the dry cleaning of clothes. For this purpose a light hydrocarbon, such as can be obtained by the distillation of petroleum, is just as efficient but is dangerous to use on account of the fire hazard. Carbon tetrachloride is entirely non-inflammable, as 

92 per cent of it is chlorine. It is possible to mix a considerable amount of light hydrocarbon with it and still have a mixture that will not burn. Such a mixture may be used for cleaning clothes. 

The use of carbon tetrachloride in fire extinguishers is important. 

When a stream of this liquid impinges on the base of a fire, it evaporates rapidly and envelopes the burning material in a vapor that cannot burn, does not support combustion and is five times as heavy as its own volume of air. It has recently attained medical importance in the eradication of hook-worms.

39. In Chapter II it was shown that carbon monoxide and hydrogen react, under the influence of certain catalysts, to give methane, the reaction being accompanied by the evolution of a large amount of heat:

CO + 3H2 → CH4 + H2O + 60,100 cal. 

67,0001 204,000 210,900

The figures under the formulae are the amount of heat in calories given by the combustion of a gram mole of each of the compounds represented. It is noticed that 28 g. carbon monoxide and 6 g. hydrogen give 60,100 calories when burned while the 16 g. of methane formed from them give only 210,900 calories. From these figures it is calculated that the heat given off in the reaction is 60,100 calories. In most organic reactions it is difficult to determine directly the heat given off or absorbed. The simplest way to find how much higher one mountain is than another is to measure the heights of both of them from sea level. In the thermochemistry of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen compounds, carbon dioxide and water are taken as the final products of combustion and constitute the level from which all thermal heights are measured. 

The heats of combustion for gram molecules of methanol, carbon monoxide and hydrogen are 170,900, 67,000 and 68,000 cal. 

From these the following equation can be written:

CO + 2H2 CH40 + 32,100 The fact that calculation shows this reaction to be exothermic gave chemists reason to believe that it would take place provided 1 The values of the heat of combustion used throughout the book are given in calories per gram mole at 15°. 44

METHANOL 

45 the right conditions could be found. The chief requirement was to find a suitable catalyst. Unfortunately, as shown above the formation of methane is even more strongly exothermic. In general, the reaction which evolves the most heat is the one that takes place most readily. 

40. Methanol Synthesis. Various catalysts were found that caused the production of methane but for a long time the search for a catalyst for the second reaction seemed hopeless. Finding catalysts for this reaction and determining the conditions under which it may be carried out successfully, constitute one of the triumphs of modern synthetic chemistry. The solution of this difficult problem is due mainly to Patart (Pa-tár), a French chemist, though the Badische Company in Germany has been foremost in its commercial development. 

The methanol synthesis closely resembles the Haber ammonia synthesis which was a big factor in the World War and may be the mainstay of agriculture in the future. The two reactions look very much alike:

N2 + 3H2 CO + 2H2 

2NH3 + 24,400 cal. 

CH40 + 32,100 cal.

The heat liberated is nearly the same for both and, in both cases, there is no reaction in either direction without a catalyst. The ammonia synthesis is a far simpler problem. Only one reaction product is possible from nitrogen and hydrogen; if by any means they can be made to react, ammonia is the result. As has been shown above, carbon monoxide and hydrogen can react in two different ways, and unfortunately the more desirable reaction is the less exothermic. It was, therefore, necessary to find, not simply a catalyst that will make them react, but a selective catalyst, one which will speed up the formation of methanol without aiding the production of methane. Actually no catalyst is known that causes the production of methanol exclusively, but some have been found which direct the reaction so that methanol is the chief product. In both reactions there is a sharp reduction in volume, 4 to 2 in one case and 3 to 1 in the other. Hence both are favored by the use of high pressures.

41. Methanol Equilibrium. According to the law of mass action: [CH4O] 30 or K[CO] [H2] [H2] = K[CO]·[H2]² [CH4O] [CO] X [H2]² = K constant

This is read: the concentration of the methanol equals times the concentration of the carbon monoxide multiplied by the square of the concentration of the hydrogen. This means the reaction is reversible and that, in the presence of a catalyst, hydrogen, carbon monoxide and methanol will coexist, their relative concentrations being mathematically related. If a portion of one of them is added to the mixture or removed from it the equilibrium will be disturbed but will be readjusted. This equation holds only when opportunity has been given for the reactants to reach equilibrium. In the absence of a catalyst, equilibrium will not even be approached and in the presence of a catalyst it is reached only after a time. Instead of "concentration of " it may be read "partial pressure of " since reaction in the gas phase is being considered. By " partial pressure " is meant the pressure exerted by any one constituent. The mass action law will be taken up briefly under esterification (§ 222) but for a thorough discussion of it the student must consult works on physical chemistry. 

It is easy to see from the above equation that a large value of K means that much methanol will be in equilibrium with moderate amounts of carbon monoxide and hydrogen, that is, the equilibrium will be far to the right in the reversible reaction as written above. A small value of K will be unfavorable to the formation of methanol.
