44. Preferential Cataysts. A number of catalysts, notably mixtures of chromium and zinc compounds, have the desired preferential action and are used in the methanol synthesis, but it is not possible to avoid the formation of some methane. This methane remains in the residue of unreacted carbon monoxide and hydrogen. Each time this mixture is repassed over the catalyst still more methane is formed. It soon accumulates so that the mixture has to be discarded. Hydrocarbons and alcohols of higher molecular weight are produced along with the methanol. The amounts of these vary greatly with the catalyst and with the operating conditions.

METHANOL 

49 The similarity of the methanol and ammonia syntheses has been pointed out. The two are sometimes closely associated in practice; the carbon monoxide which is a harmful constituent of hydrogen destined for ammonia manufacture being turned into useful methanol. The hydrogen required for the ammonia synthesis is commonly made by the water gas reaction; that is, by passing steam over hot coke, which gives a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen. The most of the carbon monoxide is separated from this mixture by liquefaction; the remainder of it is caused to combine with a part of the hydrogen to form methanol. 

45. Methanol from Methane. Methyl chloride, which can be made by chlorinating (26) methane from natural gas, yields methanol on heating with a water solution of soda or by passing it over slaked lime at 300°: 2CH3C1+ Ca(OH)2 → CaCl2 + 2CH40 On account of the low cost of the materials this is a promising process, but because of the difficulties involved it has not yet become commercially important. Large quantities of methyl chloride are actually manufactured from methanol. 

46. Methanol from Wood. When wood is heated out of contact with air, it begins to decompose at about 160°; vapors and gases are given off until at about 450° only charcoal is left in the retort. This process has long been operated on the large scale, both for the sake of the charcoal and of the products that are obtained from the vapors. The vapors are condensed, while the gases are used as fuel. The condensate separates into a watery layer and tar. Different woods give different amounts of distillate, hardwoods such as birch, beach and oak giving the largest amount, about 30 per cent of their weight. The aqueous part of the distillate contains three valuable substances, 1 to 2 per cent of methanol, about 0.5 per cent of acetone (196) and about 10 per cent of acetic acid (205). Lime is added to convert the acetic acid into calcium acetate and the methanol and acetone separated by fractionation. A large part of the methanol is used in its crude state for “denaturing" alcohol and the rest is refined. Until the advent of the synthetic method described above, the distillation of wood was the only large scale source of methanol. In the

United States for 1928, the production of methanol from wood distillation was 5,850,000 gallons compared with 1,350,000 synthetic. This ratio is likely to change, as the synthetic process is still not much beyond the experimental stage. 

47. Properties and Uses of Methanol. By purification and distillation methanol is obtained as a colorless liquid boiling at 

64.5°, solidifying at -97.8° and having the density 0.7864125.

It is very similar to alcohol and has been known as wood alcohol in commerce and as methyl alcohol in scientific writings. As these names have led to its being mistaken for alcohol, sometimes with serious consequences, the name methanol has been adopted for popular use. Carbinol is another name for it, one which is employed particularly in naming its derivatives. Methanol is poisonous. Many cases of blindness or death have been caused by drinking mixtures containing it. Blindness may result also from prolonged exposure to its vapors. 

Methanol burns with a non-luminous flame. It is a valuable solvent, although its use is restricted by the poisonous character of its vapor. In its solvent power for various substances it stands between water and alcohol but much nearer the latter (125). Its largest single use is as a denaturant for alcohol for which purpose about 2,800,000 gallons of the crude wood spirit was employed in 1928. About the same quantity of it was oxidised to formaldehyde (189). Methanol is an important starting material in chemical synthesis, dimethyl-aniline requiring about 350,000 gallons. 

Its derivatives are used in great quantity for building up a vast number of compounds, among them many important dyes, drugs and perfumes. Derivatives of methanol are found in many natural products, such as oil of wintergreen which is methyl salicylate (526). It can be obtained from these but in relatively insignificant amounts. 

48. Structural Formula of Methanol. The molecular formula of methanol is CH4O, which differs from that of methane, CH4, by one atom of oxygen. Methane appears to be a saturated compound; that is, one that does not react by direct addition. It has been shown above that such energetic reagents as the halogens act upon methane only by substitution. In order to take up an atom

METHANOL 

51 of oxygen directly, the quadrivalent carbon atoms would have to become hexavalent, which is unlikely. The structural formula of methanol must represent the facts that are known about methanol. 

Sodium dissolves in methanol with the evolution of hydrogen. 

When the solution is evaporated in vacuum, a white solid is left which has the composition CH3ONa. No greater proportion of hydrogen can be replaced by sodium, no matter how much of the metal is used. This shows that one of the four hydrogen atoms bears a different relation to the molecule from the other four. 

When methanol is treated with phosphorus pentachloride, thionyl chloride, or even with hydrogen chloride, the product is methyl chloride:

CH40 + PC15 POCl3 + HCl + CH3Cl CH40 + SOCl2 → SO2 + HCl + CH3Cl CH40 + HCl → H2O + CH3Cl This methyl chloride proves to be identical with that obtained by chlorinating methane. 

49. Comparing CH3Cl with CH4O, it is evident that one atom of oxygen and one of hydrogen have been replaced by a single atom of chlorine. Chlorine is nearly always univalent except in combination with oxygen, and appears to be univalent in methyl chloride, which can be obtained from methane by replacing one atom of hydrogen by one of chlorine. Now when methyl chloride is brought in contact with sodium, no hydrogen is replaced. Hence the particular one of the atoms of hydrogen in methanol which is replaceable by sodium is the one that is removed along with the oxygen atom and must be the one that is associated with it. Furthermore, this hydrogen can be removed without disturbing the oxygen, but if the oxygen atom is taken out the hydrogen goes with it. These facts are explained by assuming that the oxygen and hydrogen together form the univalent hydroxyl group -OH, which is well-known in inorganic compounds, and that this group is combined with the carbon atom along with the three hydrogen atoms. The structural formulae of methane, methyl chloride and methanol are written:

H-C-H H-C-Cl H-C-O-H These structural formulae represent, in conventional symbols, the facts above enumerated and these facts may, in turn, be inferred from the formulae. The formulae are usually written: CH4, CH3C and CH3OH or CH3 Cl and CH3 OH as it is understood that the H's written next to the C are to be considered as grouped around it and combined directly with it. 

It is to be noted that the methyl group, CH3-, passes as a whole from methyl chloride to methanol, and vice versa. Other possible names for methanol are methyl hydroxide and hydroxy-methane, according to whether it is regarded as a combination of methyl, CH3-, with hydroxyl, --OH or as methane in which the univalent hydroxyl group has replaced a hydrogen atom. 

50. Looking at the same formula from another point of view, it is seen that it is water in which one atom of hydrogen has been replaced by the methyl group: H-C-H H-C-OH and HOH CH3-OH Methanol is hydroxy-methane, but is just as truly methylwater. In its properties and in its reactions it shows this dual nature. When the formulae are written CH3OH and CHзCl, and are read methyl hydroxide and methyl chloride, the formulae KOH and KCl and the names potassium hydroxide and potassium chloride naturally come to mind. The reaction between methanol and hydrochloric acid is written:

CH3OH + HCl → CH3Cl + HOH This closely resembles the reaction:

KOH + HCl → KCl + HOH

METHANOL 

53 The CH3- group appears to be a sort of compound metal atom like ammonium, NH4-, in ammonium hydroxide, NH4OH, and chloride, NH4Cl. Many have been misled by these equations and have considered methyl hydroxide as a real base and its reaction with hydrochloric acid as a case of neutralization. Hypochlorous and nitrous acids contain hydroxyl groups and react with hydrochloric acid with the formation of water, but they are not bases, neither are the reaction products salts:

CIOH + HCI → CICI + HOH 

ONOH + HCl → ONCI + HOH Methanol contains a hydroxyl group but is not a base; its water solution contains no more hydroxyl ions than does pure water. 

The reactions above, representing the action of hydrochloric acid on methanol and on caustic soda, look alike because the latter does not represent all the facts, but when it is put in its true ionic form, the resemblance vanishes: K+ OH + H+ Cl→K+ Cl + HOH The methanol does not neutralize the acid by furnishing hydroxyl ions. The two do not react in dilute solution. Apparently it is the molecular hydrogen chloride that reacts with the methanol. 

The methyl chloride which is formed is not a salt. It dissolves only slightly in water, 0.9 g. in 100 cc. Its solution is neutral, but from the absence of ions rather than from the equivalence of hydrogen and hydroxyl ions. Its solution does not contain chloride ions since it gives no precipitate with silver nitrate. Methanol is really more acidic than basic. The sodium compound, CH3ONa, which is known as sodium methylate, is readily formed but is hydrolyzed when it is dissolved in water, as is the case of a salt of a strong base and an extremely weak acid. 

51. Actions of Acids on Methanol. The neutralization of caustic potash by hydrochloric acid is a typical ionic reaction and as such is instantaneous. Measurements of the speed of a rifle bullet have been made but not of the union of hydroxyl and hydrogen ions. The combination is non-reversible and goes to completion in the most dilute solution. Hydrogen chloride is

readily absorbed by methanol, giving an acid solution resembling the familiar aqueous hydrochloric acid. This conducts electricity well, although not as well as a corresponding water solution. A base added to this methanol solution is neutralized instantly with the formation of a salt. If the strength of the methanol hydrochloric acid solution is accurately determined and then redetermined after an interval of a day or two, a slight decrease is noted. This loss of strength goes on for some weeks, the rate gradually diminishing with time. The solution never becomes neutral even if the methanol is in large excess. During this process, methyl chloride is evolved by the mixture. The reaction of hydrochloric acid with methanol is a typical organic reaction, one between the undissociated molecules rather than between the ions. Probably an addition compound, CH40 HCl, is formed as an intermediate product. For the rapid preparation of methyl chloride the reaction is speeded up by heating the mixture. The addition of zinc chloride increases the rate still more. 

Other mineral acids react with methanol similarly to hydrochloric. Hydrobromic reacts more rapidly to form methyl bromide, and hydriodic acid still more rapidly giving methyl iodide. Nitric acid reacts promptly. The reactions are: and

CH3OH + HBr→ H2O + CH3Br CH3OH + HI→ H2O + CH3I CH3OH + HNO3 →H2O + CH3NO3 

With sulphuric acid the reaction goes in two stages:

CH3OH + H2SO4 → CH3HSO4 + H2O CH3OH + CH3HSO4 →→ (CH3)2SO4 + H2O The reactions are written as if water were given off, but an excess of concentrated sulphuric acid must be used to complete even the first stage, and oleum is required for the second. The first product is methyl sulphuric acid or mono-methyl sulphate. The pure acid is better made by dissolving sulphur trioxide in very cold anhydrous methanol. The product is an oil which does not solidify at −30°, and a very strong monobasic acid, comparable with hydrochloric acid. The calcium, barium, and lead salts are readily

METHANOL 

55 soluble in water, which makes them easy to separate from the corresponding sulphates. By adding the calculated amount of sulphuric acid to a water solution of the barium salt, filtering off the barium sulphate and evaporating off the water, the pure acid may be obtained. Methyl sulphuric acid decomposes when heated. 

If this is done in a vacuum, dimethyl sulphate passes over and sulphuric acid is left behind: 2CH3HSO4 → (CH3)2SO4 + H2SO4 This methyl sulphate, commonly called di-methyl sulphate to distinguish it from the mono-, is a neutral, oily liquid solidifying at -31.8°, boiling at 188.8°, and having the density 1.338515. 

Both the mono- and di-methyl sulphates, particularly the latter, are extensively used as methylating agents. They give the same products as methyl chloride, or methyl iodide, but have the advantage that they can be used in water solution. 

52. Metal Derivatives. Magnesium and aluminum dissolve in anhydrous methanol as does sodium (59). On evaporating magnesium methylate, Mg(OCH3)2 3CH4O, transparent prisms, or aluminum methylate Al(OCH3)3, a powder, is left behind. These like sodium methylate, CH3ONa, are hydrolyzed by water. 

Other reactions of methanol will be found in Chapter IX.

CHAPTER IV BUILDING MOLECULES 

53. The great structures of ancient and modern times excite our admiration, but it requires more cunning to construct a watch than to build a pyramid. The mind of man has never achieved a greater triumph than the building of molecular structures. There are 10,100,000,000,000,000,000 molecules in a milligram of acetic acid, yet man essays to take one of these apart, see how it is constructed and build one like it from the parts of other molecules. 

This chapter will be devoted to the building of molecules and to structural formulae which show how the parts of molecules are put together. There are hundreds of ways of building molecules, but for the sake of simplicity only a few syntheses will be taken up in this chapter. Hydrocarbons can be built up in numerous other ways, some of which will be mentioned from time to time as the substances from which hydrocarbons are made are studied. 

54. The Wurtz¹ Synthesis. When sodium is added to methyl iodide dissolved in dry ether, a gas is evolved and sodium iodide remains. This reaction was discovered in 1855 and the gas was believed to be free methyl, CH3, the reaction being supposed to be: CHgI + Na → NaI + CH3 This was considered as analogous to the replacement of one metal by another, as when a strip of iron is placed in a copper sulphate solution. Much ado was made over obtaining a radical in free condition. The designation "radical" had been given to groups of elements which appear in a number of compounds and which go through various reactions as units. Thus the group CH3, called methyl is found in CHзCl, CHзBr, CHзI, CHзNO3 and CH3OH and figures in many reactions such as the following: 

1 Charles Adolf Wurtz (1817-1884) was a prominent French chemist known also for his history of chemistry and his encyclopedic dictionary of chemistry. 56

BUILDING MOLECULES 

57 CH3OH + HCl → CH3Cl + H2O CHзCI+KI → CHзI + KCl CHзI + AgOH→ CH3OH + AgI In those days great importance was attached to these radicals which were regarded as compound elements analogous to NH4, considered as a compound metal. As the compounds of inorganic chemistry are the combinations of the simple elements, organic compounds were supposed to be built up from compound elements; that is, groups of atoms reacting as single atoms somewhat as a corporation composed of a number of men trades as an individual. 

Organic chemistry was the study of the reactions of these compound elements or radicals. Aluminum had been isolated by heating aluminum chloride with sodium, so it was natural to attempt the isolation of a radical in a similar manner. Analysis of the gas obtained by Wurtz gave the empirical formula CH3 which seemed to prove it to be the desired free radical. 

This was before the general acceptance of Avogadro's hypothesis by which molecular weights can be determined. It was soon observed that this gaseous free radical, CH3, instead of having a density less than methane, CH4 (density 0.5545 compared with air), actually had a density of 1.0494, which is nearly twice as great. 

When the significance of the densities of gases was realized, it was seen that the molecular weight of this gas must be 30, consequently the empirical formula CH3 was doubled to give the molecular formula C2H6. Hence it proved to be dimethyl instead of the supposed free radical methyl, CH3. In the electrolysis of sodium chloride free chlorine atoms are not obtained, since when the chlorine ions lose their charges, the resulting atoms immediately unite to give diatomic chlorine gas, Cl2, having the molecular weight 70.92. Thus two methyl groups freed from their combination with iodine, unite to form dimethyl, CH3 CH3. The reaction between sodium and methyl iodide is actually: 2CH3I+2Na→ CH3 CH3 + 2NaI

Each carbon is quadrivalent, yet the C2 is not octavalent but hexavalent and the formula must be C2H6, not C2Hs. The ethane is made by uniting parts of two methane molecules. Methyl chloride may be regarded as part of a methane molecule united with part of a chlorine molecule, and methyl alcohol as part of a methane molecule and part of a water molecule. The melting and boiling points are -172.0° and -88.3°, respectively, and the density is 1.0494 compared with air. It is relatively indifferent to chemical agents but can be chlorinated or brominated under the same conditions as methane. Naturally the process is more complicated, as a greater number of products can be formed, all the way from C2H5Cl and C2H5Вr to C2C16 and C2Bг6. These closely resemble the corresponding derivatives of methane except that their boiling points are higher, which is to be expected on account of the heavier molecules. Methyl chloride and bromide, CH3Cl and CH3Br, boil at -23.73° and 4.5°, while the corresponding ethyl compounds, C2H5Cl and C2H5Br, boil at 12.5° and 38.40°.

For convenience in naming compounds, the univalent group C2H5 is called ethyl. The above compounds may be named mono-chlor-ethane and mono-brom-ethane. This system is extended to those which contain more halogen atoms. Di-chlor-, tri-chlor-, tetra-chlor-, penta-chlor- and hexa-chlor-ethane with analogous designations for the bromine derivatives. 

56. Butane. By brominating ethane, bromethane (ethyl bromide) can be prepared and used in the Wurtz synthesis: 2C2H5Br+2Na→ C4H10 + 2NaBr Here again, the product is a gas that is readily condensed to a liquid. It is known as butane from its relation to butyric acid which, in turn, gets its name from butter. The empirical formula is C2H5 but its molecular weight is 58, which shows its molecular formula to be C4H10. It liquefies at 0.6° and solidifies at -135°. 

In physical and chemical properties it closely resembles methane and ethane. The names are given the same endings to show this similarity. In case a mixture of two iodides, as methyl and ethyl

iodides, is treated with sodium, a mixture of ethane, C2H6, butane, C4H10 and propane, C3H8 is obtained. 

57. The Structure of Butane. The structural formula of ethane was deduced above from that of methane; similarly that of butane can be inferred from that of ethane: H H H H H—C—H → H—C—Br →H-C-C-H→ H—C—C—Br H H H H Butane is made by the union of the two residues which are left when the two bromine atoms are removed from two molecules of ethyl bromide, thus:

H H H-C-C H H H H 

Br+ Br

H H HHHH C—C—H → H-C-C-C-C-H HHHH Butane is di-ethyl, or two ethyl groups joined together, C2H5— C2H5, but too much stress must not be put on this, lest the reader conclude that the union is between the ethyl groups as a whole rather than between the carbon atoms. There is every reason to believe that all of the unions are atomic, as represented in the structural formula above. It is very convenient to employ the conception of radicals and use methyl and ethyl groups in building up formulae, but such radicals have no independent existence either alone or as discrete parts of larger molecules. They are simply groups of atoms held together as atoms usually are, and when they join to other groups or to elements, the union is an atomic one between one carbon of the radical and some other atom. 

Later on, (Chapter XXXVI) a few radicals will be found that apparently exist in the free condition. 

This process of synthesis can be carried further and much longer carbon chains built up. Cetyl iodide, which is C16H33I, has been treated in ether-alcohol solution with sodium amalgam and di-cetyl, C32H66 obtained. Likewise lacceryl iodide, C32H65I, has been heated to 140° with potassium and a product obtained which has the composition C64H130. This is a solid melting at 

102°. Its molecular weight corresponds to this formula. The

BUILDING MOLECULES 

61 name given this compound is tetrahexacontane, which comes from the Greek word for 64. It is known that the thirty-two carbon atoms in lacceryl iodide are joined together in a chain and that the iodine is at one end of this chain. It may be assumed that the two lacceryl radicals join end to end to form dilacceryl or tatrahexacontane, as the ethyl radicals do in the formation of butane. This gives the structure of the tetrahexacontane, which is the longest chain of carbon atoms that has so far been put together. 

From the above it is evident that carbon atoms have the property of uniting with each other to a remarkable degree. This property is not peculiar to carbon, as compounds are known in which sulphur is linked to sulphur. In fact the sulphur molecule itself is represented by Ss. Ammonia and hydrazine are believed to be represented by:

N-H and N-N Ammonia Hydrazine

These suggest the formulae of methane and ethane. No compound of nitrogen with hydrogen alone is known which contains more than two nitrogens joined together, but one is known which is composed of nitrogen, hydrogen and carbon in which eight nitrogen atoms form a continuous chain. This was built up by linking nitrogen to nitrogen in much the same way in which carbon compounds are built up. Possibly still longer chains of nitrogen and other atoms can be linked together, but so far as investigation has gone no other element has been found that even approaches carbon in its ability to form long chains with atoms of its own kind.

Here again the structure of the product follows from those of the compounds used in building it up. This is only one example of one of the most common synthetical methods. Unlike the Wurtz synthesis and the one in which the zinc compounds are employed, this method is used on the large scale for building up compounds. 

60. The Synthesis of Carbon Compounds. The synthetic methods described above are given as examples to show how the organic chemist proceeds in constructing molecules. Of the hundreds of thousands of organic compounds that are known, only a very few can be obtained simply by bringing the necessary elements together and causing them to combine. It is customary to build up organic molecules from ready formed parts, somewhat as an automobile is assembled by fastening together previously fabricated parts. In the case of the machine, not only the right

BUILDING MOLECULES 

63 parts must be selected, but each one must be put in its proper place. It will be shown in Chapter VI that the same molecular parts may be put together in different ways in order to produce quite different structures. The illustrations which have been given show how methanol, a primary synthetic product, can be made the starting point in building up more complicated molecules. There are a number of other simple organic compounds which are readily made from their elements and which likewise serve as starting materials in the syntheses of more complicated compounds. Nature furnishes us with many organic molecules from which parts may be taken and used in constructing more complicated molecules. It is possible to build up the cetyl iodide, C16H33I, used above, step by step from methyl iodide, which is readily made from methanol, but this process is exceedingly laborious. Advantage is taken of the fact that cetyl alcohol, C16H33OH, is readily obtained from spermaceti. This alcohol is converted into the iodide which by the Wurtz synthesis gives the dotriacontane. If large pieces of molecules are used as starting materials very complicated structures may be put together with only a few reactions. If the structure of the parts and how they are joined together are known, the structure of the whole may be easily deduced. 

61. Energy. From the energy standpoint, the formation of the sodium iodide in the Wurtz synthesis is the important reaction, and the bringing together of the two methyl groups is incidental. 

The energy liberated when the sodium and iodine unite is enormous, while that required to remove the iodine from combination with carbon is relatively small, which is also true of the energy set free when the two methyl groups unite. This and many other laboratory organic syntheses are very wasteful of energy. On the other hand, there are many reactions between organic compounds that are readily initiated and take place with small energy losses. 

62. The Permanence of Carbon Bonds. Sodium and chlorine unite with the evolution of a large amount of heat as is shown by the equation: 

NaCl NaCl + 97,900 Calories while the union of carbon to carbon, or of carbon to hydrogen

involves less energy. If the stability of the molecule were proportional to the energy set free during its formation, sodium chloride would be extremely stable and ethane less so. Experiment shows that sodium chloride does require a much higher temperature for its decomposition than ethane. However, as soon as sodium chloride is dissolved in water it is torn asunder into sodium and chloride ions. The molecules that are left are dissociating and in turn recombining. X-ray photographs have shown that in a crystal of sodium chloride, the sodium and chlorine atoms are packed so that each sodium is surrounded by six chlorines and each chlorine is likewise surrounded by six sodiums. The molecule, NaCl, may exist as such in the vapor state but neither in water solution nor in the solid state is there any such entity. The molecules of carbon compounds, on the other hand, do seem to exist as such, both in solution and in the solid state. Organic acids dissociate but to only a small extent, except in a few cases. The same is true of the bases, but the majority of organic compounds dissolve in water and in other liquids without measurable dissociation. When dissociation does take place, it commonly concerns only hydrogen or hydroxyl and only rarely affects the carbon to carbon bonds. So far as can be learned from X-ray examination of crystalline organic compounds, their molecules maintain their identity and their individuality. The molecules of carbon compounds are permanent structures. This does not mean that carbon compounds do not undergo changes; many of them are extremely reactive, but there is nevertheless a certain fixity about them that is unusual among the compounds not containing carbon. 

This will be more and more apparent as the study progresses. 

It is this stability of carbon structures that makes the building of them possible. A castle can be built of bricks because each brick is held by the mortar just where it is placed in the wall and because other bricks may be added to them. A part of the wall may be taken down and altered as desired. Organic chemistry is characteristically the study of the structure of molecules, and its highest achievements have come in building up edifices whose constituents are atoms. Molecules have been built consisting of as many as 500 atoms, each one of which was placed exactly according to a preconceived plan, and it is certain that each one of them remained in its relations to its fellows just as it was placed. This

BUILDING MOLECULES 

65 does not mean that organic molecules are rigid structures of motionless parts. The atoms of carbon and the other atoms that are joined to them are in motion, as are the atoms in other molecules. 

However, it does mean that the linking of one atom to another is not disturbed by the vibrations or rotations which may be taking place. A chain may be coiled, uncoiled and flung about but through it all each link maintains its relations to the adjoining links. So it is with carbon chains. The molecules may pass from solid to liquid and to gas and back to liquid and to solid, they may dissolve and crystallize out, yet through it all each carbon atom preserves its relations with its attendant hydrogens or other atoms and with its fellow carbons in the chain. CHAPTER V THE METHANE SERIES 

63. Emphasis has been put on the immense number of the compounds of carbon. It would be a hopeless task to undertake to learn 300,000 carbon compounds were they not connected with each other in some orderly fashion. It is easier to locate an address on Manhattan Island than it is to find some one's house in a village. 

The reason is that the houses in the large city are on streets and each house is numbered. The compounds of carbon fall into series, and to locate a particular compound all that is necessary is to know the name of its series and its number in that series. On the plan of a city, streets and avenues may appear miles beyond any present development and the place that will be occupied by the house bearing a certain number can be pointed out years before it is built. It is thus with the compounds of carbon. Not only are the 300,000 known compounds arranged but the plan arrangement is so comprehensive that places are provided for millions and even billions yet undiscovered. The system is so thorough that one can write out methods for the preparation of a compound, to fit into a particular place in the plan and can predict in a general way its properties. The qualities and reactions of unknown elements have been foretold from the periodic table of the elements. 

The system of organic chemistry resembles in some respects the periodic table but it is on a vaster scale. 

Of all the series known, the longest and most typical is the methane series. It has additional importance from the fact that it serves as the meridian for the location and naming of a large part of the carbon compounds. In this chapter little will be said about the preparation of the compounds, as the most of them have to be made by the use of compounds and reactions that will be taken up later on. In a broad sense all of the paraffins are derivatives of methane and belong to the methane group, but for simplicity only those having unbranched chains will be included in the methane series. 66

METHANE SERIES 

67 64. The Methane Series. Several of the lower members and the highest of this series have already been mentioned in Chapter IV. 

By extending the Wurtz synthesis it would be possible to fill in all of the hydrocarbons between methane, CH4, and tetrahexacontane, C64H130. Fortunately, nature provides many longer or shorter carbon chains already put together from which many hydrocarbons can be built up with far less labor than would be required if it were necessary to start each time with methane. Many hydrocarbons are found ready-made in nature. 

An examination of the composition of the hydrocarbons so far studied shows an interesting regularity in the formulae: HCH HH нн H C-C H H C-C-C-C-H HHHH HHHH HHH H C-C-C- HHH C-C-CH HHH HHH or HCH₂H HCH2CH₂H HCH2CH2CH2CH₂H HCH2CH2CH2... CH2CH2CH₂H 

By drawing vertical lines through these formulae, each molecule is cut up into one or more —CH2— groups, while at each end there is an extra hydrogen atom. The members differ from each other in the number of -CH2- groups. The hydrocarbons so far studied H(CH2)H, H(CH2)2H, H(CH2)4H or H(CH2)„H. 

By taking away the parenthesis, H(CH2),H becomes C₂H2n+2, which is the general formula for the whole series. The same general formula fits all of the other paraffins as well. Any member of the series differs from the next by the constant difference of CH2, + if ascending and if descending the series. Ethane can be looked at as methane in which one H is replaced by the group-CH3. So propane is methyl-ethane and butane is methylpropane. The series of hydrocarbons, from methane to hexacontane, can be regarded as being built up from methane by the successive substitution of methyl for hydrogen.

66. Melting Points. A study of the melting points discloses more complicated relationships. The upper part of the curve from eicosane on appears to be smooth, the irregularities present being less than the errors of observation, but the lower part of the curve is a curious zigzag. Starting with propane; there is a large jump from the melting point of any hydrocarbon containing an odd number of carbon atoms to the next higher, but only a short

METHANE SERIES 

71 step from the melting point of one with an even number of that of the next higher. There appear to be two curves, the melting points of the odd members being on one curve and those of the even on the other. This remarkable relationship has not been satisfactorily explained but probably has something to do with the packing of the atoms in the molecule in the solid form. Similar phenomena are observed in some other related series. The melting points of methane and ethane are higher than would be expected and do not lie on the curves. Both of these have symmetrical structures which may be the reason for the high melting points. 

67. Densities. The densities, like the boiling points, rise rapidly at first and then more and more slowly. If the densities are taken at the melting point, the increase is slow indeed. Thus dodecane, C12H26, has a density of 0.773 at its melting point and noneicosane, C29H60, has a density of 0.7797 at its melting point, the average difference being only 0.0004 between succeeding members of the series. Between the densities of hexane and dodecane at 20°, 0.6603 and 0.7682 there is a difference of 0.1079, or an average of 0.0180 between two adjacent members of the series. 

68. Chemical Properties. Chemically all of the hydrocarbons of this series resemble each other closely. Chemical properties cannot be compared numerically as can the physical, so there is no certainty that there is a progression. All of them are rather indifferent to most chemical reagents except the halogens. Many chemists have been misled by the designation paraffin and have not looked for reactions of these hydrocarbons. As has been mentioned in the case of methane, all of them are reactive with chlorine and bromine. They are indifferent towards oxygen at ordinary temperatures. At higher temperatures they are readily oxidised but the oxidation, when once started, is difficult to control. Only recently has a beginning been made in the manufacture of useful products by the direct oxidation of aliphatic hydrocarbons. 

Much emphasis has been put on the stability of carbon compounds and the permanence of the union of one carbon atom to another carbon or to another element. This stability is well exemplified in the hydrocarbons. They are non-polar compounds; that is, they are composed of two elements neither of which is

strongly positive or negative. The carbon hydrogen union is of the same kind as the carbon to carbon bond. The paraffin hydrocarbons are extremely stable at ordinary temperatures and even up to 300°, but much above that temperature all of them are more or less unstable. Methane withstands the highest temperature; the stability of the others decreases with the lengthening of the carbon chain. When butane is passed through a hot tube at 

600-700° and at atmospheric pressure, three distinct reactions take place: 1methane is split off, leaving an unsaturated hydrocarbon, 2hydrogen separates leaving an unsaturated hydrocarbon containing the original carbon chain, 3the carbon chain breaks in the middle, one-half being a saturated hydrocarbon and the other half an unsaturated hydrocarbon. For butane these reactions are: 1. CH, CH2 CH2 CH3 →CH, CH: CH₂+ CH4 Butane (682,300) Propylene 490,200 - 18,800 cal. Methane 210,900 2. (682,300) Ethane 368,400 Ethylene 331,600 17,700 The figures under the formulae are the heats of combustion in calories of gram moles of these compounds. The figures in parentheses have been obtained by averaging those for higher and lower hydrocarbons but are near the correct values. It appears that the heat changes involved in cracking are not large. As the reactions are endothermic, they should be favored by a high temperature which corresponds with experimental facts. Actually, some high boiling hydrocarbons are produced from the intercombination of these unsaturated hydrocarbons. Unsaturated hydrocarbons will be studied in Chapter XXVI; for the present it is sufficient to consider them as saturated hydrocarbons which have lost some of their hydrogen. At very high temperatures, all of the bonds of a hydrocarbon seem to be loosened up and all sorts of rearrangements take place. There are decompositions and recombinations, so that if a pure hydrocarbon is heated sufficiently, the final result is a

METHANE SERIES 

73 miscellaneous mixture of hydrocarbons, some gaseous, some low boiling liquids and some less volatile. Hydrocarbons belonging to other series and even to other classes will be formed together with some free hydrogen and free carbon. In the end, the products will not be greatly different, whether the original material is a low boiling hydrocarbon such as hexane, or a much higher one, such as eicosane. This process begins somewhere about 300°, the temperature varying somewhat with the hydrocarbon used, but it is not rapid until higher temperatures, 450-500°, are reached. This fact is taken advantage of in "cracking" processes in which heavy, high boiling hydrocarbons are heated to convert them into mixtures from which low boiling fractions may be separated. 

There are many patented processes for "cracking," the differences being in the conditions under which the hydrocarbon is heated, whether in gas or liquid phase, whether under low or high pressure, whether in large boilers or in narrow tubes, but all are based on the single fact of the instability of the hydrocarbons at high temperatures. More will be said on this subject below. 

69. Petroleum. Hydrocarbons are widely distributed throughout the earth's crust and are found concentrated in certain localities, usually in sand or porous material under domes of impervious rock. It is easy to trace the origin and development of a coal bed, since it is found just where the vegetation accumulated, and the once soft but now hard slate adjacent to the coal frequently preserves the most delicate tracings of primeval leaves and stems. 

Oil is probably never found in its original site, being liquid, it can penetrate through porous strata and through cracks in the harder rocks. In some cases, it has been forced upwards by the pressure of water. In certain places, it has reached the surface of the earth, and in others it has been trapped under an impervious layer. 

There are always present greater or less amounts of the gaseous hydrocarbons, methane to butane, dissolved in the liquid hydrocarbons as carbon dioxide in soda water. When the amounts of these are great, the oil comes out as a gusher when a well is drilled through the dome. In time the gas pressure is spent and the oil is no longer forced out. The well is then pumped and may continue to yield a small but steady amount of oil for a long time. 

If the oil were in a single cavity, all of it could eventually be gotten

out through one well, but it is disseminated in sand, gravel or porous rock. Any one well drains only a limited region. 

Petroleum as it comes from the earth is a liquid which varies greatly in properties. It may be thin and of a light amber color or it may be almost black and so thick that it will hardly flow. 

The density ranges from about 0.85 to nearly 1. It is always an exceedingly complex mixture of not only a large number of hydrocarbons but also dissolved or suspended asphalt material, which is usually a mixture of highly complex hydrocarbon compounds of sulphur or oxygen. Since it is a mixture, it always distils over a wide range. In some cases, there are quantities of the lower hydrocarbons that are gases at ordinary temperatures. These are dissolved in the liquid portion but evaporate rapidly when the pressure is released. They are collected in the casing head, compressed and cooled, or otherwise treated to recover the compounds in the range of butane and pentane. In addition to these, there may be large proportions of volatile liquid hydrocarbons. In other petroleums, such as heavy Mexican petroleum, there may be only a small fraction which distils below 200°. The density of crude oil is closely associated with the proportion of the more volatile constituents and with the predominant types of hydrocarbons present. In some fields, the price is regulated by the density, but since the crude oil buyer uses the American Petroleum Institute scale, low density sometimes is spoken of as "high gravity." It should be noted that on the American Petroleum 

Institute scale, as on the Baumé, higher figures denote lower specific gravity. Ozokerite contains a large proportion of the high molecular weight, solid paraffins along with complex oxygen and sulphur compounds.

Asphalt (from ảopáλros, unalterable) is a mixture of heavier non-volatile hydrocarbon, oxygen and sulphur compounds. In many cases, it seems to be the residue left by the evaporation of a surface pool of oil, which has been slowly acted on by the air. 

The largest deposit of it is the Pitch Lake of Trinidad. It is found also in Venezuela and Cuba. 

70. Origin of Petroleum. No positive statement can be made as to the origin of petroleum and one can only speculate as to the reactions which led to its formation and the possible changes it

METHANE SERIES 

75 has since undergone. Two chief theories have been proposed, organic and inorganic, and experiments have been made in support of both of them. If organic origin is assumed, the question remains as to whether it is from animal or vegetable sources. It is possible that the various petroleums that differ so much in properties and are found in such diverse geological situations may have been produced from more than one sort of material and in more than one way. One theory is that petroleum has been formed from animal remains. In order to support this idea, Engler¹ distilled fish oil under pressure and obtained a mixture of hydrocarbons which could pass as petroleum. Some maintain that it is from plants. 

Oils are found in many plants, particularly in the seed. An examination of soft coal shows the presence of oils. Oils are commercially obtained from plants by distillation with steam, as turpentine from wood chips or essential oils from leaves and flowers. 

Down in the earth distillation may have taken place, volatile oils being driven from a heated zone and condensing in a cooler zone. 

In some cases, steam frequently found in the earth may have assisted in this distillation. It is not necessary to limit the process to large animals or plants. There are in every stagnant fresh water pool, millions of tiny organisms, animal as well as vegetable. 

These are constantly dying and sinking to the bottom where their remains may accumulate. It is known that methane is produced in the decomposition of such material, and a mass of this might well furnish petroleum on heating. What such small organisms lack in size they make up in numbers. Deposits of millions of tons of diatomaceous earth, each microscopic particle of which is the siliceous skeleton of an alga, are known. The presence of nitrogen and sulphur compounds in petroleum suggests animal or plant origin. The chief argument for such origin is that it probably nearly always contains optically active substances (138). These are characteristic of materials formed by organisms and their presence cannot be accounted for by a theory of purely inorganic origin. Oil shale occurs in large quantities. On heating, it gives oils similar to petroleum and such a process may have gone on down in the earth.

Aluminum carbide gives methane when brought into contact 

1 Carl Engler (1842-1925) was Professor at the Technical College of Karls ruhe and is known for his extensive work on petroleum.

with water (23). Iron carbide gives oily hydrocarbons when it is dissolved in dilute acid. Calcium carbide yields acetylene (422) on contact with water. By passing acetylene and hydrogen over nickel at 200°, Sabatier¹ and Senderens² obtained a clear yellow fluorescent liquid of density 0.791 with odor similar to rectified petroleum. It was a mixture which began to distil at 45° but left a residue at 250°. It contained aromatic hydrocarbons but was chiefly paraffin hydrocarbons. Without added hydrogen, acetylene passed over hot nickel gave an oil which contained large amounts of aromatic hydrocarbons. By varying the ratio of hydrogen to acetylene and the reaction temperature, different kinds of oils corresponding to the known types of petroleums were produced.

Recent developments add two other possible sources of petroleum. In the Bergius process, which is being operated experimentally in Germany, powdered coal is heated to 450° in hydrogen at about 300 atmospheres pressure, and a mixture of hydrocarbons somewhat resembling petroleum is produced. In the methanol synthesis, a mixture of hydrocarbons is produced as a by-product when hydrogen and carbon monoxide are passed over a catalyst at high temperatures and pressures. Under some conditions, this hydrocarbon mixture may become the chief product. 

Hydrogen and carbon monoxide may have been produced by water coming in contact with heated rocks containing carbon. The conditions approximating those required by the Bergius process must have been present in some localities. 

71. Classification of Petroleums. The oil refiner classifies petroleum according to the character of the residue left on distilling. 

If this is waxy, the oil is said to have a "paraffin base," while if it is asphaltic, the oil is called "asphalt base." There are three classes of hydrocarbons in the various petroleums, which may be classified according to which of these they contain. The lower boiling portion of Pennsylvania petroleum is little else than a mixture of the paraffins, the most of which seem to have straight

77 chains. By fractionation, all of the members of the methane series from methane to C27 H56 have been obtained from it. Russian petroleums contain considerable quantities of naphthenes (449). 

Some California petroleums are characterized by the presence of a large proportion of aromatic hydrocarbons (Chapter XXXI and XXXIII). 

72. Refining Petroleum. Distillation is the principle method by which the crude petroleum is separated into fractions which pass over between certain temperatures. Each fraction is purified so as to fit it for its intended use. The chief fractions are: gasoline up to 210°, kerosene 210° to 275°, gas oil up to a little above 300°. A residue of heavy lubricating oil and petroleum or asphalt is left to be distilled in vacuum or with steam. The lowest fractions of the gasoline are sometimes separated and are called petroleum ether 40-60°, painter's naphtha and ligroin. These when purified are employed as solvents. Formerly kerosene had a wide market, while gasoline was of little use. Under those conditions, the cut between these two was made at a lower temperature, so as to increase the yield of kerosene. In order to protect the public against kerosene that contained low boiling hydrocarbons and would be dangerous to use in lamps, laws were enacted requiring the kerosene to have a flash point ¹ above a specified temperature. 

Since the demand for gasoline has become so great, all that distils up to 210° is included in this fraction. Unstable compounds, including certain hydrocarbons, sulphur, nitrogen and oxygen compounds, are removed or changed to unobjectionable ones by treatment first with sulphuric acid and then caustic soda solution. 

Paraffin wax is obtained by chilling and filter-pressing the higher boiling fractions of paraffin base oils. 

73. Cracking. It has already been stated (68) that hydrocarbons are more or less unstable at high temperatures. In order to obtain the fractions mentioned above, there is more or less decomposition during the distillation. This is usually increased by slowing up the distillation so as to prolong the time of heating. As the straight run gasoline is not sufficient to meet the present demand for motor fuel, the "cracking" of the heavier oils is carried out on 1 The flash point is the temperature to which the oil must be heated for its vapor to take fire under certain carefully specified conditions.

a very large scale. In the Burton¹ process, heavy oils, called "gas oil" were heated under pressure in large boilers until decomposition had taken place, and the low boiling oils distilled over. A considerable fraction of the oil was broken down into gases and free carbon. In present-day processes, the oil is usually forced through pipe coils, set in a fire box, into a digestion chamber and finally to a fractionating tower.

75. Shale Oil. In Scotland, and in France to a less extent, the distillation of oil shale is an important industry. This process yields an oil similar to petroleum, which may be worked up to give products similar to those obtained from petroleum. There are immense beds of oil shale in the United States. The utilization of these is being carefully considered at the present time and a beginning has been made in actual production.

CHAPTER VI ISOMERISM 

76. By condensing natural gas to a liquid and then fractionating this liquid either at low temperature or under high pressure, it can be separated into methane (b.p. 161.4°), ethane (b.p. -88.3°), propane (b.p. 44.5°) and a butane fraction along with higher boiling hydrocarbons. Close fractionation of the butane fraction separates it into two portions, the one boiling at -10.3°, and the other at 0.6°. Analysis shows that both have the empirical formula C2H5 and vapor density determinations give 58 as the molecular weight for both. Hence both are to be represented by the same molecular formula C4H10. This phenomenon of two distinct substances having the same molecular formula is called isomerism, the word being made up from two Greek words meaning "equal" and " parts." The possibility of two different structures being built up of the same parts is dependent on the permanence of the bonds which hold these parts together, which, has been mentioned as being characteristic of carbon compounds. 

77. Two Butanes. In Chapter IV it was shown that two ethyl groups can be coupled together to form butane. The butane so obtained is the one that boils at 0.6°. The compound 

C4H10 that boils at -10.3° is called isobutane to distinguish it from butane. Two compounds having the formula C4H10 are found in natural gas but nowhere in the world has another been found having this same formula, nor have the labors of the chemists of the world produced another. Isobutane (b.p. - 10.3°)

There is no hesitancy in assigning the straight chain formula to the one boiling at 0.6° since it is the one that is formed by the 

Wurtz synthesis from ethyl bromide. The prefix n- which stands for the adjective normal is used where all of the carbon atoms are in a straight chain, as in butane. The other C4H10 hydrocarbon is assigned the formula that is left, namely the one with the branched chain. 

78. Two Propyl Bromides. Propyl bromide, C3H7Bг, is readily made by the action of hydrobromic acid on propyl alcohol, which is obtained from fusel oil, a by-product of the fermentation which produces ordinary alcohol. That this propyl bromide has the straight chain structure shown in the equation below is proved by the fact that it gives n-butane with zinc methyl: 2CH3 CH2 CH2Br+Zn (CH3)2 → ZnBr2+2CH3 CH2 CH2-CH3 

Propyl bromide n-Butane 

This propyl bromide boils at 70.9° and has the density 1.3640 at 16°. It greatly resembles methyl bromide and ethyl bromide, as will be brought out in this chapter. The stability of linkages in carbon compounds has been emphasized in an earlier section (62) and propyl bromide has this characteristic stability under ordinary circumstances.

If, however, a relatively small amount of aluminum bromide is added to a quantity of propyl bromide, heat is liberated, which indicates that some change is taking place. The propyl bromide may be separated from the aluminum bromide with little or no loss in weight. The liquid, however, now boils at 59.6° and has a density 1.310 at 25°. Analysis shows it to have exactly the

Thus, there are two compounds both of which have the same molecular formula, but judged by their physical properties, are unmistakably different. The second is called isopropyl bromide to distinguish it from propyl bromide. Isopropyl bromide

As the first formula has been assigned to the original propyl bromide, the second must represent isopropyl bromide. They are also called 1-bromopropane and 2-bromopropane. No other compound having the formula C3H7Br is known. 

In one of these bromopropanes the heavy bromine atom is at the end of the chain of carbon atoms, while in the other it is in the center. Isobutane has a methyl group in the middle of the chain. 

A stick with a weight at one end and one with a weight in the middle behave quite differently when they are thrown or struck. 

A number of sticks with bulky objects at one end will pack quite differently from similar sticks with these objects in the middle. 

Little is known of the shape of either of the molecules represented above, but it can safely be assumed that they are different and that, in the liquid or solid states, they would pack together differently. In terms of electrons, it can readily be supposed that there will be differences in the grouping of the valence electrons in the two structures. Any such differences will manifest themselves in alterations in the external fields of force that surround the molecules. This should influence the reactivities of the molecules. 

The stronger the attraction between the molecules of a liquid, the smaller will be the number of molecules which escape from its surface under the same conditions. This is to say that the greater the mutual attraction of the particles composing a liquid, the less its vapor pressure at a given temperature. It is not surprising that normal propyl bromide and isopropyl bromide have quite different densities and boiling points. In all cases there are chemical as

well as physical differences between isomers, but the physical differences have been mentioned in the above, since physical properties can be stated numerically and are thus easier to contrast. 

79. Isomerism. Isomerism is conditioned by differences of arrangement of the parts of a molecule; the permanency of such differences depends on the stability of the bonds between the atoms. The stability of carbon bonds has been emphasized as an outstanding characteristic of this element. The existence of isomers is a consequence of this fixedness of the atomic unions and is the best evidence of its reality. Among the compounds of carbon, isomerism is met at every turn, while among the compounds of other elements it is extremely rare. 

80. Isomeric Hydrocarbons. In the series of hydrocarbons studied in Chapter V the carbons are arranged in single file, and except at the ends of the chain, each carbon is joined to two and only two other carbons, giving a skeleton such as this: 

If a carbon atom can unite with one other or with two others, there is no reason why it cannot unite with three or even four. This would give skeletons such as: _d_d_d_ and ddd For simplicity only the carbon skeletons are written, assuming that all the valencies not used up in holding carbon atoms together are occupied by hydrogen atoms. As a matter of fact, compounds of these types are known. A carbon atom that is united with only one other carbon atom is called a primary carbon, one that is joined to two is a secondary carbon and one that holds three is a tertiary carbon. In the second skeleton above, there are three primary carbons, one secondary carbon, and one tertiary carbon.

ISOMERISM 

83 On the assumption that a carbon atom can unite with one, two, three, or four other carbon atoms, the possible arrangements of any given number of carbon atoms can be worked out on paper. 

Having written out the formulae in advance chemists can set out to prepare the hydrocarbons corresponding to them. If the reasoning is correct, it should be possible to synthesize as many hydrocarbons as there are formulae. If perchance too many hydrocarbons are found, it will show that the reasoning has been incomplete. 

81. The Number of Possible Isomers for Some Hydrocarbons. 

Two carbons can be arranged in only one way. The same is true if there are three: and

Actually, only one substance has so far been discovered with the formula CH4, only one with C2H6, and only one with C3H8. 

There is known only one CCl4, only one C2Clé, and only one C3Cl8.

For four carbon atoms there are two possible arrangements which may be the skeletons of hydrocarbons: and

These represent the two butanes which were discussed above. 

With five carbon atoms, there are three possible arrangements: n-Pentane dddd Isopentane Neo-pentane

Thus the theory predicts three pentanes. As a matter of fact, three and only three have been discovered. They boil at 36.2°, 27.95° and 9.5°, and differ among themselves in other properties.

Of the hexanes, n-hexane comes first with all six carbons in a row, then pentane with one carbon as a side chain which may be on either the second or third carbon, and lastly butane with two side chains which may be arranged in two ways. In all, the theory predicts five hexanes and just five hexanes are known, n-hexane boiling at 69.05°, 2-methyl-pentane, called isohexane, b.p. 60°, 3-methyl-pentane, b.p. 64°, 2,3-dimethyl-butane, b.p. 58° and 

2,2-dimethyl-butane or neo-hexane, b.p. 49.7°.

The theory predicts 9 heptanes; just 9 have been prepared. 

Of the octanes, 18 are possible but only 15 have so far been prepared. Of the nonanes, 35 are possible but only 10 are known. The greater the number of carbons the more numerous are the hydrocarbons predicted by the theory and the fewer there are that have been studied; thus chemical experimentation gives way to mathematical calculation. The number of isomeric hydrocarbons possible and the number so far prepared are given in the table. At first the number of possible isomers increases irregularly, but from decane on it slightly more than doubles from one formula to the next higher. The ratio increases as the number of carbon atoms increases.

Doubling a number ten times, increases it more than a thousand fold (exactly 1024). Continuing this process the following astounding figures are obtained.

Several comparisons will make these figures somewhat more real. Richter's Lexikon which lists the 144,150 organic compounds known up to January 1, 1910, is published in 4 large octavo volumes containing 4751 pages with an average of 30 compounds on each page. If all of the possible hydrocarbons having the formula 

C20H42 were prepared, a book nearly the size of this would be required to describe them. For the isomers of C30H62 a thousand such books would be necessary, while for the iosmers of C40H82, a million. These would fill a building such as the New York Public 

Library. For the isomers of C60H122, a million such libraries would be needed to house the books. It is inconceivable that any such number of isomers will ever be studied, as time and labor are required to prepare each one. As the number of atoms and the complexity of the structures increase, the difficulties of synthesis and of characterization mount up, but there is no reason to doubt the possibility of putting together the necessary groups to build up almost any hydrocarbon whose formula can be written down. 

All of this is but the logical development of two simple assumptions which appear to be thoroughly established: (1) the quadrivalence of carbon and (2) the fixity of the linkage of one carbon atom to another.

So far as chemists have investigated, no bounds have been found to the application of these principles. There are other

series of hydrocarbons, in some of which there are more possibilities of isomers. Where other elements, as oxygen, sulphur and the halogens are substituted for some of the hydrogen atoms, still more complicated relationships and a far larger number of isomers for a given number of carbons result. 

82. The Naming of Hydrocarbons. Methane, ethane, propane and butane have individual names but all the rest are named numerically; that is, by adding the ending -ane to the proper Greek numeral. Thus C6H14 is hex-ane and C10H22 is dec-ane. This ending is reserved for hydrocarbons of the general formula CnH2n+2, and certain cyclic hydrocarbons that will be considered later (Chapter XXX). All of the hydrocarbons that have the formula C10H22 are spoken of as decanes, but when simply decane is used, it is understood that the one with the straight chain structure, normal decane, is meant. To name any other hydrocarbon, the longest chain in it is selected for the root and such prefixes as may be necessary are added to this. The position of each group or side chain is shown by a number which indicates to which one of the carbon atoms in the main chain it is attached. In doing this, care must be taken not to be confused by the way in which the structural formulae happen to be written. C C C odddc B cdodac -C- C C معظظم • cophhoo Į Į D C-

ISOMERISM 

87. up.

In the examples above, A is written so as to look like a derivative of pentane, but the longest chain in it contains seven carbons, so the root is heptane. Attached to this are five methyl groupsso the name is penta-methyl-heptane, to which numerals must be prefixed to show the location of the methyl groups. This gives 

3,3,4,5,5-pentamethyl-heptane. In B the longest chain contains six carbons, hence it is a hexane, but there is a choice when carbon No. 4 is reached; it is possible either to keep on to the right or go 

As carbon No. 5 carries a methyl group, it makes the naming simpler to include that carbon in the main chain. The name is then 2,2,5-trimethyl-4-ethyl-hexane. In this compound two kinds of groups appear, the methyl, CH3—, and the ethyl, C2H5—. 

The rule is that the smaller group is named first and the others follow in the order of their size. It follows that the carbons in the longest chain must be numbered in such a way as to give the smaller group the lower number. In this hydrocarbon the naming might have started at No. 6 as the reference carbon and continued in the other direction, which would have made the name 2,5,5trimethyl-3-ethyl-hexane. This shows also what the hydrocarbon is, but to have two versions of the same name would be confusing. 

In naming C, the numbering starts at the right end of the chain and gives 3,4-dimethyl-5-ethyl-heptane. D is 3-methyl-5-ethyl- 

4-propyl-heptane. It is extremely desirable that the rules of nomenclature be followed strictly, since at best there are difficulties enough in finding and recognizing the more complicated compounds. The finding of a word in a dictionary depends on its being spelled the same way every time. Likewise the possibility of finding an organic compound in various indexes is based on uniformity of nomenclature. 

83. Other Methods of Naming. Other methods of naming may be convenient for special purposes, particularly to show the relationships of members of a group, just as sometimes instead of the street and number, a location is given as the N.E. corner of 

Sixth Avenue and 42nd Street. Frequently hydrocarbons, particularly those with many branches, are spoken of as substitution products of methane. Such names as tetra-isopropyl-methane, di-isobutyl, tetra-propyl-ethane convey pictures of the hydrocarbons more directly than the systematic names.

84. Radicals. Mention was made in Chapter IV of the attempt to isolate free radicals. Although they are not now regarded as "compound elements" the atoms of which are held together in some peculiar way, the idea of using groups as units is most convenient. They are called radicals, and are given individual names and symbols. This is a great convenience in naming compounds. A radical is simply a hydrocarbon minus an atom of hydrogen. The name of a radical is made by changing the -ane of the hydrocarbon to -yl. Thus CH4 is methane and CH3- is methyl. For the higher hydrocarbons this is not sufficiently definite, since it makes a difference which hydrogen atom is left off. The following abbreviations are used in this book as prefixes, i- for iso, s- or sec- for secondary and t- or tert- for tertiary. 

The longer forms, sec- and tert-, are in common use, and iso- is frequently treated as a part of the name, as isobutane and isopropyl, which may be found in some indexes under I. The shorter forms as prefixes appear more desirable because they are

85. Influence of Structure on Physical Properties. At the beginning of this chapter attention was called to the fact that i-butane differs from n-butane and that i-propyl bromide differs from n-propyl bromide in boiling point and density. They likewise differ in refractive index, surface tension, viscosity, solubility in water and in all other properties chemical as well as physical. 

This is true of all other sets of isomers. In some cases the differences are slight and in others marked, but they are always real. 

As yet no mathematical formulae have been worked out which enable the calculation of the exact effect of substituting an atom or group in this place or in that, but there are many regularities on which predictions may be based. 

The group most thoroughly investigated is that of the nine heptanes, the properties of which are given in the Tables XI and XII below. The boiling points and densities of some of the octanes are in the following table. For the sake of clearness only the skeletons of the hydrocarbons are shown.

Of all the members of a group the normal hydrocarbon has the highest boiling point; those that have two branches, the dimethylpentanes and dimethyl-hexanes, have lower boiling points than those with single branches. 

The heats of combustion of the heptanes are nearly the same. 

This agrees with the generally recognized fact that carbon to carbon and carbon to hydrogen bonds are practically the same as far as energy is concerned. The two that give the highest figures are the most symmetrical, the three that give the lowest are those that contain tertiary carbons. 

The regularities are best brought out by considering the changes in boiling point and density of a given normal hydrocarbon by the substitution of methyl and ethyl groups in different positions. 

Thus taking heptane (b.p. 98.4°, d. 0.6836) the substitution of a methyl group on the first carbon atom raises the boiling point 26.3° and the density 0.0226, while if it is joined to the second carbon, the differences are 17.6° and 0.0193. For this purpose n-heptane is considered as 1-methyl-hexane and as 1-ethyl-pentane and n-octane as 1-methyl-heptane and 1-ethyl-hexane. 86. Influence of Structure on Chemical Properties. As the chemical properties of the paraffin hydrocarbons are not pronounced, it is not to be expected that one of the isomeric heptanes or octanes will differ greatly from the others. There actually are some differences which depend on the presence of primary, secon- 1 2 3 4 dary or tertiary carbons.

In isopentane, CH3-CH-CH2-CH3, CH3 5 the carbons of the three methyl groups, 1, 4 and 5 are primary, that in the -CH2-, 3, is secondary while No. 2 is tertiary. The valence electrons which hold the carbons together must be differently disposed depending on how the carbons are bunched together. 

The valence electrons that surround a carbon atom are certainly not mutually independent, though just how they affect each other is not known. Hydrogen atoms are held somewhat differently by primary, secondary and tertiary carbons. As hydrogen has to be broken loose from carbon in any reaction of a hydrocarbon, the strength with which the hydrogen is held will determine the reactivity of the hydrocarbons. When more reactive atoms are substituted for the hydrogen atoms, the differences are greatly accentuated. Thus a bromine atom substituted in a hydrocarbon behaves quite differently when it is joined to a primary, secondary or tertiary carbon (94).

CHAPTER VII HALOGEN DERIVATIVES 

88. It was brought out in Chapter II that halogen atoms may take the places of the hydrogen atoms of methane. The replacement of one univalent atom by another of like valency is the simplest case of substitution and does not disturb the structure of the molecule. Halogens act on other hydrocarbons of the methane series to give analogous halogenated hydrocarbons; there may be partial or complete replacement of hydrogen; for hexachlorethane,

C2Cl6, hexabromethane, C2Bre, and octachloropropane, C3 Cls, are known. The number of conceivable halogen substitution products is enormous but relatively few of the possibilities have been realized. After the ethane group is considered, little is known of the polyhalogen substitution products. Those containing one halogen are well known, as are three classes of the dihalogen group: those in which the two halogens are attached to the same carbon atom, to adjacent, or to the end carbon atoms, as CH3 CH2 CHC12, CH3 CC12 CH3, CH3 CHCI-CH2Cl, and CICH2 CH2 CH2Cl. 

Since the direct action of the halogens on the paraffin hydrocarbons commonly yields extremely complicated mixtures, very few halogen derivatives have been prepared in that way. It has been found practicable to chlorinate some of the lower hydrocarbons, such as butane, pentane and hexane, which are obtained in quantity by the fractionation of casing-head gasoline or from natural gas. The monochloro derivatives of several of these are being produced on a commercial scale, and more progress is to be expected in this direction. These chlorine derivatives may be used as such or may serve as intermediates in the manufacture of the corresponding alcohols. 89. Synthesis of the Halogen Derivatives by Addition. Halogen acids can be added to unsaturated hydrocarbons (Chapter 

XXVI) to give monohalogen products: 96

HALOGEN DERIVATIVES 

97 CH3-CH=CH2 → CH3-CH-CH3 BrH Br

CH3 CH3 -CH₂C CH3-CH2-C-CH2- → CH3-CH2-CH3 BrH Br

Since in this reaction the halogen acid is separated into its elements, it may be expected to go most readily when hydriodic acid is used and least readily with hydrochloric acid. This is the case. The addition is effected by shaking the hydrocarbon for hours with saturated aqueous halogen acid. The particular nature of the hydrocarbon used has much to do with the speed of the reaction. 

The halogen of the acid adds to the carbon atom which carries the smallest number of hydrogens. Or stating it another way, the bromine or iodine of the acid goes to a tertiary carbon in preference to a secondary carbon, or to a secondary carbon rather than to a primary carbon.

If the halogens are used instead of the halogen acids with the unsaturated hydrocarbons, dihalogen compounds are obtained in which the halogens are joined to adjacent carbon atoms: CH3-CH-CH2 CH3-CH-CH2 or CH3-CHBrCH2Br BrBr Propylene 

Br Br

1, 2-Dibromopropane

CH3-CH=CH2 → CH3-CH-CH2 or CH3 CHCI CH₂I CII Cl 

1-Iodo-2-chloropropane 

This reaction takes place easily with chlorine, bromine and iodine or with iodine chloride or bromide. The hydrocarbon is dissolved in chloroform or carbon tetrachloride and a solution of the halogen in the same solvent is added. The reaction is usually extremely rapid, even at room temperature or below, provided moisture is present; thus a gaseous unsaturated hydrocarbon may be bubbled through a water solution of bromine. It must be noted that although these dihalogen compounds are prepared by addition to unsaturated hydrocarbons, they are regarded as substitution products

of the saturated hydrocarbons. In the example given above, bromine is added to propylene, C3H6, but the compound formed is 1,2-di-bromo-propane, which is considered to be a substitution product of propane:

HHH HCC—CH 

H Br Br

This is an example of the way that the word "substitution" is used all through organic chemistry. All organic compounds are spoken of as substitution products of the hydrocarbons without any regard to whether they have actually been prepared by substitution" or not. All the compounds considered in this section are considered as having been made by "substituting " one or more chlorine, bromine, iodine atoms or hydroxyl groups for one or more hydrogen atoms of a saturated hydrocarbon. 

Saturated hydrocarbons are those, such as have been considered in Chapters V and VI, in which the carbons are joined by single bonds. Methane, ethane, propane and methyl-hexane are saturated hydrocarbons. 

90. Fluorine Derivatives. Fluorine attacks methane, ethane and other hydrocarbons violently, combining with the hydrogen and setting free the carbon instead of uniting with it. Fluorine derivatives are obtained by the action of silver fluoride on the corresponding chlorine, bromine or iodine compounds:

C2H5I + AgF →C2H5F+AgI Fluorine derivatives are very imperfectly known, since they are difficult to prepare and have found no commercial applications. 

They are not used for syntheses as are the compounds containing the other halogens. The organic, as well as the inorganic compounds of fluorine, stand apart from those of the other halogens. 

91. Preparation of Halogen Derivatives from Alcohols. As methyl chloride, bromide and iodide are most readily prepared in pure form from methanol, so their higher homologs are commonly obtained from the higher alcohols (Chapter IX) by replacing the hydroxyl group by the halogen. To accomplish this, either a hydrogen or a phosphorus halide may be used. The choice

HALOGEN DERIVATIVES 

99 between these depends on the alcohol used and the halogen to be introduced. The action of the halide acids on methanol has been mentioned (Chapter III). Similar reactions take place with other alcohols:

C2H5OH + HCl → C2H5Cl + H2O 

Ethyl alcohol 

Ethyl chloride

C2H5OH + HBr→ C2H5Вr + H2O C2H5OH + HI→ C2H5I + H2O In each case a molecule of water is formed. As much energy is liberated when the hydrogen and the hydroxyl unite to form water, there will be a strong tendency for this reaction to go to completion. 

This is opposed by the difficulty of separating the hydrogen from the halogen which diminishes from hydrochloric acid to hydrobromic acid and on to hydriodic acid. The order of reactivity is: HI>HBr>HCl. These reactions appear to be non-ionic. 

They take place when the alcohol is saturated with gaseous hydrogen halide or mixed with the strong aqueous acid and heated. 

With the less reactive hydrochloric acid, it is customary to assist the reaction by the addition of anhydrous zinc chloride, which is a strong dehydrating agent, although in this case it seems to act more as a catalyst. Thus hydrogen chloride is passed into a heated mixture of the alcohol and zinc chloride and the alkyl chloride distils over. The process may be made continuous by adding the alcohol gradually and keeping the temperature suffi ciently high so that the water distils over as it is formed. An alkyl bromide or iodide may be made by distilling an alcohol with concentrated aqueous hydrobromic or hydriodic acid. Sometimes the halogen acid is prepared in the mixture. Thus to obtain ethyl bromide, alcohol and sodium bromide are mixed and sulphuric acid added, or a mixture of alcohol and sulphuric acid is added to sodium bromide. In either case heating is required to complete the reaction.

Using the same halogen acid on different alcohols, great differences are found in the ease with which the reaction takes place. 

It goes most readily where the hydroxyl is joined to a tertiary carbon atom (123) and least readily when the hydroxyl is on a primary carbon atom. More or less isomerisation may take place in this reaction, a primary alcohol giving some secondary or tertiary

halide as well as the primary halide. This is particularly true when sulphuric acid or a zinc halide is used to assist the reaction. 

In making i-butyl bromide in presence of sulphuric acid as much as 

25 per cent of the product may be t-butyl bromide.

Alkyl halides are also prepared by the action of the halides of phosphorus on alcohols: 3C2H5OH + PCl3 →3C2H5Cl + P(OH)3 3C2H5OH + PBг3→ 3C2H5Br + P(OH)3 3C2H5OH + PI3→ 3C2H5I + P(OH)3 In making alkyl bromides and iodides by this method it is not necessary to prepare the phosphorus halide in advance; red or yellow phosphorus is mixed with the alcohol and bromine or iodine added slowly. Unfortunately the reaction represented by the equation above is not the only one that can take place, particularly with phosphorus trichloride. The chlorine may combine with the hydrogen of the hydroxyl group to form hydrogen chloride, leaving the C2H5O- group to unite with the phosphorus. This reaction may be partial or complete:

C2H5OH + CIPC12 → C2H5OPC12 + HCl 3C2H5OH + PCl3 → (C2H5O)3P + 3HCl The compound (C2H5O)зP is triethyl phosphite in which three ethyl groups take the place of the three hydrogens of phosphorus acid, (HO)зP. When any given alcohol is mixed with phosphorus trichloride, both reactions go on simultaneously to produce some alkyl chloride and some alkyl phosphite and some of the intermediate products. According to the alcohol used and depending on the temperature and other conditions, more of the one product or of the other may be obtained. It is characteristic of organic compounds that they react in many ways simultaneously. 

The art of the organic chemist is in fixing the conditions so as to favor the desired reaction and to repress others.

are 1-chloropropane, 2-bromopropane and 2-methyl-3-chlorobutane. The numbering is arranged so that methyl, ethyl, etc., if they are present, have the small numerals. Polyhalogen derivatives are named by an extension of the same system as in the examples above.
