When caustic soda is added to its water solution there is no sign of any reaction, since no volatile or insoluble product is formed, but silver hydroxide precipitates the iodide ion and leaves the solution strongly alkaline: (C2H5)4NI + AgOH → (C2H5)4NOH + AgI Tetraethyl-ammonium iodide Tetraethyl-ammonium hydroxide

When the water is evaporated off, the tetraethyl-ammonium hydroxide is left as a deliquescent solid. It is a very strong base

and forms well defined salts with acids, even the weak ones. It is not volatile but decomposes on heating to 190°. 

The above reactions have been given one after the other as they would take place if the product were isolated each time, the salt decomposed and the amine heated with a fresh portion of ethyl iodide. As a matter of fact when a quantity of ammonia is heated in a closed vessel with a quantity of ethyl iodide, all of the products that are described above are found in the reaction product. Each salt as it is formed is partially decomposed and the liberated amine undergoes further reaction until finally the quaternary salt is reached. 

172. Catalytic Preparation of Amines. When alcohol vapor and ammonia are passed over certain oxides at about 300°, substituted amines are formed:

C2H5OH + HNH2 → C2H5NH2 + H2O Alumina, the blue oxide of tungsten, and silica gel are good catalysts for this reaction. Ethylamine and diethylamine undergo the same reaction with alcohol vapor: 

C2H5OH + H NHC2H5→ (C2H5)2NH + H2O

C2H5OH + HN(C2H5)2 → (C2H5)3N + H2O Hence the final product is a mixture of all three amines with unreacted ammonia and alcohol.

Good yields of amines can be obtained by heating an alcohol with ammonia and zinc chloride in an autoclave at 300° for 8 hours. In the preparation of amines by either of these methods, the same difficulties are met as in the chlorination of methane. 

Neither reaction can be stopped at any desired point. Both yield mixtures that are difficult to separate. The three methylamines all boil within 14° but, as can be seen from the table below, the mono-, di- and tri-ethylamines as well as the derivatives containing the higher alkyls can be separated by distillation. In the reactions above ethyl derivatives have been used but these are only examples of the whole class. Ammonia reacts with the other alkyl halides to form the corresponding alkyl amines and their salts.

173. Classes of Amines. As stated in the above and as shown in the group of formulae near the first of this chapter, there may be one, two, three or four alkyl groups joined to one nitrogen atom. 

The amines are divided into primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary according to the number of the alkyl groups. Care has to be taken to prevent confusion since the alkyls which are present in the amines may be primary, secondary or tertiary, as is seen in the following examples:

CH3 CH-NH2, (CH3 CH2 CH2)2NH CH3 CH2 and 

CHCH) N CH3 CH2 3

The first of these is a primary amine although it contains a secondary butyl group, the second is a secondary amine although the alkyls are primary and the last is a tertiary amine containing secondary alkyls.

175. Preparation of Individual Amines. The general reactions given above lead to mixtures of amines, so that methods have been sought by which individual amines can be obtained. Methylamine can be obtained by heating formaldehyde (190) solution (40 per cent) with ammonium chloride: 3HCHO+2NH3 → 2CH3NH2 + CO2 + H2O Trimethylamine is made by heating the same reactants in an autoclave at 110°: 9HCHO+2NH3 → 2(CH3)3N + 3CO2 + 3H2O It is found in many natural substances and in various plants. The presence of it in herring brine gives the brine its odor. It is frequently produced on heating organic compounds. When beet sugar molasses is fermented and the alcohol distilled off, the liquid that remains is called "vinasse." If this is evaporated to dryness and the residue distilled, trimethylamine is obtained. 

Primary amines are commonly obtained by Hofmann's reaction on amides (254). They are also made by the reduction of the nitroparaffins:

CH3NO2 + 6H → CH3NH2 + 2H2O This method is of little use on account of the difficulty of obtaining the nitro-paraffins. Nitriles (238) may be reduced to primary amines. Zinc and dilute acid may be used or the nitrile vapor and hydrogen passed over a catalyst:

CH3 C N + 4H → CH3 CH2 NH2 It will be noted that by Hofmann's reaction an amine is obtained that has one less carbon atom than the original acid; by this reaction methyl cyanide, CH, CN, which can be prepared from a methyl halide yields ethylamine. In the one case there is an increase, in the other a decrease in the number of carbon atoms. 

Primary amines are also formed by the alkaline hydrolysis of alkyl isocyanates (249) and alkyl isocyanides: CH3 N CO→ CH3NH2 + CO2 + H2O

178. Separation and Identification. It has been stated above that ammonia is readily alkylated but the mixture of amines so obtained is difficult to separate into its components. The boiling points of those containing the higher alkyls are far enough apart for fractionation to be applicable, but this is difficult with the lower alkyls and is not convenient when only small quantities are concerned.

The most distinctive reactions of the different classes of amines are those with nitrous acid. In all cases there is first union of the nitrous acid with the ammonia or amine to form a nitrite which is unstable:

HNH2 + HONO→ HOH + N2 + H2O CH3NH2 + HONO → CH3OH + N2 + H2O (CH3)2NH+ HONO→ (CH3)2N NO + H2O With a primary amine an alcohol is formed, the result being the replacement of the amino group by the hydroxyl. This reaction is useful in the determination of structure, as it links together an alcohol and an amino derivative. The structure of one of these may be determined by other means. In the case of the secondary amine, the NO group, which is known as the nitroso group, replaces the one hydrogen. The product is nitroso-dimethylamine. 

This and all other nitrosoamines give Liebermann's reaction 

(Chapter XXXII). The tertiary amine has no active hydrogen and therefore there can be no reaction. Treatment with nitrous acid serves well to remove small amounts of other amines from tertiary amines.

179. Alkyl Compounds of Other Elements of the Fifth Group. 

Alkyl derivatives of phosphine, arsine and stibine are known as well as the tetra-alkyl phosphonium, arsonium and stibonium bases and their salts. The trialkyl bismuth compounds such as (CH3)3Bi are known, but these do not form quaternary bases. a general way, these derivatives resemble the corresponding nitrogen compounds, although in solubility and in oxidisability there are marked differences. Ammonia is extremely soluble in water, 1050 volumes at 0°, and methylamine is even more so, 1150 volumes at 12.5°. One of the arsenic derivatives has been important in chemical history. Bunsen2 investigated this liquid and found its chief constituent to be (CH3)2As—O—As(CH3)2 called cacodyl oxide and written Kd2O. The univalent radical (CH3)2As-was called cacodyl and given the symbol Kd, as it goes through many reactions unchanged.

KdH. Cacodyl was regarded as a fine example of a radical or compound element. By oxidation of cacodyl oxide, cacodylic acid (CH3)2ASO OH is obtained. 183. In all the derivatives of the hydrocarbons so far considered a univalent atom, Cl, Br or I, or a group -OH, -SH, or -NH2, takes the place of a single hydrogen atom. In this chapter oxo-compounds are encountered in which two hydrogen atoms belonging to the same carbon are replaced by a bivalent oxygen atom. An oxo-compound is quite different from an ether in which two hydrogens belonging to different carbon atoms are replaced by an oxygen atom. It is evident that from propane two different oxo-derivatives can be formed: HHH H H 

HC.C.CO and HC.C.CH 

H H 1-Oxo-propane HOH 2-Oxo-propane These differ somewhat as do n-propyl and i-propyl alcohol but more radically, so that they are given different class names, the 1-oxo-compound being called an aldehyde and the other a ketone. 

The important difference between the two is that in an aldehyde the carbon, to which the oxygen is bound, carries a hydrogen atom, and in a ketone this hydrogen is absent. Certain reactions of aldehydes depend on the presence of this hydrogen; such reactions cannot take place with ketones. 

The salts of carbonic acid are stable but the free acid breaks down into carbon dioxide and water:

ОН OC →0=C=0+ H2O OH This is an example of a general rule. Except in a few special cases, a single carbon atom with two hydroxyl groups is an unsta- 187

ble arrangement. Attention must be called to the fact that many compounds exist, in solution or otherwise, that cannot be isolated. 

There is no more doubt of the existence of carbonic acid than there is of calcium carbonate. It is believed that oxo-compounds in the presence of water are in equilibrium with the corresponding dihydroxy compounds:

OH C=0+ H2O C2H5 OH C2H5 1,1-Dihydroxy-propane 1-Oxo-propane CH3 OH CH3 C=O + H2O CH OH CH3 2-Oxo-propane 2,2-Dihydroxy-propane

It will be seen later that derivatives of both the 1,1and the 2,2-dihydroxy propanes and of similar dihydroxy compounds are stable. 

184. Formation and Structure of Aldehyde. When alcohol vapor is passed through a tube filled with copper gauze which is kept at 300° or above, hydrogen is set free, one molecule for each molecule of alcohol:

CH3 CH2OH→ H2 + C2H4O The product has the molecular weight 44 so C2H4O is its molecular formula. It is a very volatile liquid boiling at 20.8° and having the density 0.783418. It mixes in all proportions with water, alcohol and ether. It is called aldehyde, since it is derived from alcohol by the loss of hydrogen and this in Latin is alcohol dehydrogenatus, which has been shortened to aldehyde. 

The structure of alcohol is known and in order to determine the structure of aldehyde it is necessary only to determine which two of the six hydrogens of alcohol are lost. Aldehyde is readily oxidised to acetic acid, which can be shown to contain the methyl group (Chapter XIV). As a methyl group is present in alcohol, it may be concluded that it is also present in aldehyde: CH3 CH2OH → CH3 CHO→ Alcohol Aldehyde → CH3COOH 

Acetic acid

If the methyl group is untouched in the above reaction, the two

OXO DERIVATIVES 

189 hydrogen atoms that are given off must come from the -CH2OH group, which gives two possible formulae for aldehyde: CH3 COH→ CH3C : O → CH3CO or CH3.C.OH Aldehyde The fact that carbon usually appears to be quadrivalent rather than bivalent favors the first formula. The further fact that the oxygen atom of aldehyde may be removed without disturbing the hydrogen atom is conclusive. Still further evidence is given by the reactions of aldehyde and alcohol with phosphorus pentachloride: CH3CHO + PCl5 → CH3CHCl2 + POCl3 Aldehyde ->> Dichloro-ethane

CH3 CH2OH + PC15 → CH3CH2Cl + POCl3 + HCl Alcohol Mono-chlor-ethane

While one chlorine atom replaces the OH group in the case of alcohol, two chlorine atoms take the place of the single oxygen atom in aldehyde and the hydrogen is not disturbed. The conclusion is that the oxygen atom in aldehyde must be joined to carbon by its two valencies as in the formula above. 

Instead of passing alcohol vapors over hot copper an oxidising agent and gentle heat can be used with alcohol in water solution. 

It is probable in this case that the reagent used does not actually give oxygen to the alcohol but rather simply takes care of the hydrogen which the alcohol is ready to give off. It is more correct to say that the oxidising agent dehydrogenates the alcohol. 

It is only within the last few years that the catalytic dehydrogenation processes have been extensively used. Formerly aldehydes were always made by oxidation in water solution. 

Aldehyde is obtained when 1,1-dichlor-ethane is heated with water and a base:

CH3 CHC12 + 2HOH → CH3 ·CH(OH)2 CH3-CH(OH)2 → CH3 CHO The aldehyde may be obtained from the corresponding acid in case the alcohol is not available, by heating the calcium salt of the acid with calcium formate, as is explained later in this chapter (201).

186. Addition Reactions of Aldehyde. Aldehyde is extremely reactive and can react in a great variety of ways. Very slight changes in conditions may entirely alter the course of its reactions. 

The characteristic reactions of aldehyde are mostly addition reactions and are dependent upon the C=O group, which is known as the carbonyl group. Many inorganic compounds containing doubly bound oxygen react by addition. Calcium oxide and sulphur trioxide take up water and other substances: OH Ca : 0 + →Ca он OH OH O₂S: 0 + | он OH In these cases which are typical, the water molecule appears to be split into hydrogen, which adds to the oxygen of the oxide and hydroxyl, which adds to the calcium or sulphur. It is not meant that this is the mechanism of the reaction, but the result is as if it had taken place this way. It is more probable that the oxide and the water molecules unite by virtue of secondary attractions to form a complex which subsequently rearranges by readjustment of electron orbits to give the hydroxide. In the cases of calcium oxide and of sulphur trioxide the union is nearly complete and the two hydroxyls are strongly held by the single atom. 

In contrast to these, carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide in water

191 solution, combine with water to only a small extent, but these solutions are distinctly acid, which shows that some addition has taken place. 66 1. Aldehyde adds hydrogen, reversing the reaction given above:

As shown by the above figures, this reaction is exothermic at room temperature with the equilibrium in favor of the alcohol, which explains the fact that aldehyde is readily hydrogenated at low temperatures, while it is dehydrogenated at 300° and above.

Some of these can be recrystallized from water, which gives a means of purifying the aldehydes. This reaction is of great value, as it serves to separate aldehydes from mixtures of other substances.

It is decomposed by dilute acid with the regeneration of the aldehyde and reacts with many substances as free aldehyde.

In the Cannizzaro¹ reaction use is made of strong aqueous caustic soda, which probably causes the same reaction to take place, although the ester cannot be isolated, as it is hydrolyzed by the alkali as fast as it is formed. It is usually said that the caustic soda induces simultaneous oxidation and reduction as the products actually obtained are the alcohol and the acid. A recent method for manufacturing ethyl acetate probably involves the Tischtschenko reaction. In this method ethyl alcohol is pumped through a heated tube containing a catalyst and ethyl acetate and hydrogen are produced.

1 Stanislaw Cannizzaro (1826-1910) was Professor of Chemistry in the

University of Palermo, Italy (1861-1876) and held the chair of Chemistry in the New University at Rome (1871-1910).

When a drop of sulphuric acid is added to a quantity of aldehyde, this reaction takes place. Considerable heat is evolved and the aldehyde boils. Paraldehyde is a liquid which boils at 124°, solidifies at 10.5° and has the density 0.994320. It is soluble in 8 parts of water at 25° and mixes with alcohol and ether. 

Vapor density determinations show that it has the molecular weight 132, which is three times that of aldehyde and corresponds to C6H12O3. It does not show the addition reactions of aldehyde, hence cannot have the carbonyl group =C : 0. Neither does it have alcohol reactions. It is broken down by acids with the regeneration of aldehyde. The structural formula above, which represents it as a cyclic multiple ether, agrees with all of these facts and is generally accepted. Were the carbons directly linked, its decomposition would probably not be so easy. Aldehyde is sometimes turned into paraldehyde for transportation and storage. 

This is depolymerized into aldehyde when needed. 

11. Several molecules unite to form metaldehyde: 4CH3CHO→ (CH3CHO)4 If a trace of hydrogen chloride, sulphur dioxide, or other acid is added to aldehyde cooled below 0°, metaldehyde is formed. It is a solid which crystallizes in needles, that does not melt but sublimes above 150°. It is insoluble in water, and only soluble to the extent of 1.8 g. per 100 cc. in boiling alcohol and 0.5 g. per 100 cc. in boiling ether. From the lowering of the freezing point of phenol, metaldehyde appears to have the molecular weight 176, which indicates that four molecules of aldehyde have united to form it. 

Its structure is unknown. When it is heated with sulphuric acid, aldehyde is evolved. 

12. Aldehyde polymerizes into resins. This cannot be represented by an equation. Under the influence of alkali or of heat, aldehyde is transformed into brownish resinous substances of indefinite composition and unknown constitution.

19. Aldehyde is readily oxidised to acetic acid:

CH3C +0-CH3 C OH This is the way the reaction is usually written, but it is more probable that it is the dehydrogenation of the 1, 1-dihydroxyethane, the oxygen not being added to the aldehyde but serving as a hydrogenacceptor:

.

CH3 C-OH → → CH3 C=O + H2 OH OH The argument for this view is based on the fact that acetic acid is formed when palladium black is added to a water solution of aldehyde in the absence of free oxygen or of any oxidising agent. 

Since palladium contains no oxygen, it cannot give oxygen to the aldehyde but it does have the power of taking up hydrogen. If, after the palladium has taken up what hydrogen it can, air is admitted, this hydrogen is oxidised. The palladium then takes up more hydrogen and so on until all of the aldehyde is oxidised to

OXO DERIVATIVES 

197 acetic acid. Aldehyde is readily oxidised and therefore it is a strong reducing agent. It reduces silver ions to atoms and cupric ions to cuprous ions. The reducing power of aldehydes is used commercially for silvering mirrors and scientifically for the detection and estimation of aldehydes. 

Tollens'¹ reagent is prepared by mixing equal volumes of a 10 per cent solution of silver nitrate and a 10 per cent solution of caustic soda and adding just enough ammonia to dissolve the silver oxide. The addition of a dilute solution of aldehyde to this causes the deposition of a silver mirror in the cold. 

Fehling's2 solution (Chapter XXII) in which copper oxide is held in alkaline solution in the presence of alkali salts of tartaric acid, can be used to detect aldehydes in extremely dilute solution, down to one part in a million. The same solution is used for the quantitative estimation of aldehydes. 

Schiff's³ reagent, which is a solution of rosaniline hydrochloride decolorized by sulphur dioxide, has its color restored by the addition of an aldehyde. This is the most used qualitative test. 

20. Chlorine and bromine replace the hydrogen atoms of the methyl group:

CH3-CHO + 3Cl2 → CClg -CHO + 3HCl Chloral

This reaction goes far more readily than the halogenation of methane. The -CHO group seems to facilitate the substitution.

Aldehyde has been taken up first, since it is the best known of the aldehydes and the most typical of the whole group. 189. Formation of Formaldehyde. Formaldehyde is produced when methanol vapor is passed over heated copper: CH3OH→ H2CO + H2 

Methanol Formaldehyde

31,100 cal.

The hydrogen is taken care of by causing it to combine with oxygen. Platinum sponge glows in a mixture of methanol vapor and air and produces formaldehyde. Commercially, air is saturated with methanol vapor by bubbling it through methanol kept at 40° to 50° and passed over copper or silver gauze which is maintained in a glowing condition by the heat of the reaction: CH3OH + O2 → HCHO + H2O + 36,900 cal. 170,900 Formaldehyde 134,000

The gauze has to be heated to start the reaction. The evolution of the hydrogen according to the first reaction is endothermic and can be carried on only by the addition of heat. When air is introduced the hydrogen burns and gives enough heat to maintain the reaction. The vapors are condensed to a liquid which is sold as formalin and usually contains about 40 per cent formaldehyde, the rest being chiefly water and unoxidised methanol. When this solution is evaporated a white substance melting at 63° is left. 

This has the same empirical formula as formaldehyde but is evidently a polymer. It is called paraformaldehyde or paraform and when heated evolves vapors of formaldehyde. At least four polymers are known and are called a-, 6-, 7-, and &-polyoxymethylenes. 

The molecular weights and structures of none of them are known. 

Some of these exist in formalin in equilibrium with the monomolecular formaldehyde. As this is a mobile equilibrium, the mixture reacts as if it were entirely in the monomolecular form. 

The vapor from heated paraform, passing over drying agents into a very cold vessel, condenses to a liquid which is the monomolecular formaldehyde, H2CO. This boils at -21° and even at that temperature polymerizes in a short time. The most of the syntheses in which formaldehyde is required are carried out with formalin. In case water is objectionable, dried paraform is used

199 or the vapor from heated paraform is passed directly into the reaction mixture.

Many efforts have been made to obtain formaldehyde by the partial burning of carbon compounds, particularly methane. As high as 8 per cent of formaldehyde has actually been obtained from methane: CH4 + O2 → CH2O + H2O + 76,900 cal. 210,900 134,000 The reaction is highly exothermic and is hard to control. The oxidation of ethylene is also of interest: H2C CH2 + O2 → 2H2CO + 63,600 cal. 331,600 268,000

This has been accomplished by the aid of ozone, but not on a commercial scale. Methane may be chlorinated to methylene chloride which reacts with steam:

CH2Cl2 + H2O→ CH2O + 2HC1 190. Reactions of Formaldehyde. Except as noted below, formaldehyde reacts much as does aldehyde. It can be reduced to methanol, adds sodium bisulphite, reacts with hydroxyl-amine and phenylhydrazine and with two molecules of an alcohol or of a mercaptan. With caustic soda it gives equivalent amounts of methyl alcohol and formic acid. While other aldehydes add ammonia, formaldehyde reacts on ammonia with the elimination of water: 

6H CHO+4NH3 (CH2)6N4 + 6H2O The product is called hexamethylene tetramine. It is a white solid which sublimes but does not melt. It is used as a drug under the name of urotropin. 

The polymerization of formaldehyde has already been mentioned. Under the influence of a mild alkali, such as lime water, it polymerizes in a different way to form a mixture of sugars, one of which has beer identified as inactive fructose (355): 

6HCHO C6H12O6 + 131,000 cal. dl-Fructose 

804,000 673,000

The reaction is highly exothermic and may be a source of energy in some plant process. Little is known of the mechanism of this reaction but it must be a case of repeated aldol condensation: H H H H HC+ CO → HC—CO 0 H OH Formaldol

This aldol being an aldehyde may condense with a third molecule of formaldehyde, until there are six carbons in the chain and five hydroxyl groups. This condensation is of the utmost theoretical interest, as it offers a plausible explanation of the processes by which plants build up sugars, starch and cellulose or woody fibre. 

Under the influence of sunlight, carbon dioxide is absorbed by the plant leaf and oxygen is given off. Nothing is known as to how this is accomplished but it can be represented thus: H2O + O CO→ H.CHO +02 

This representation is supported by the fact that this reaction has been found to take place in the laboratory under the influence of light waves of the extreme ultra-violet. Assuming the formation of formaldehyde, the next step would be the polymerization of the formaldehyde into a sugar which can be transported in the sap. 

It has been shown experimentally that formaldehyde fed to a plant is converted to sugar. When the sugar reaches its destination, it is further polymerized into starch and finally into cellulose. 

If this idea is correct, everything that is in the vegetable world is directly or indirectly a polymerization or condensation product of formaldehyde. Water may be eliminated in some of these condensations and nitrogen and sulphur compounds may be brought into some of the reactions. Search has naturally been made for formaldehyde in green leaves, and its presence has been reported by some and denied by others. If it is there, it is present in very small amounts. This does not disprove the above hypothesis, since it is known that formaldehyde is extremely reactive, and it may be that it polymerizes as rapidly as it is formed. Formaldehyde, CH2O, is the first carbohydrate (see Chapter XXV).

Formaldehyde condenses with a great variety of compounds to produce many products. Some of these are comparatively simple and have had their molecular structure determined, while

OXO DERIVATIVES 

201 others are far more complex. The simpler ones are soluble in water, alcohol, and other solvents, while some of the more complex products are hard, resinous substances which are practically insoluble in any ordinary solvent. Bakelite¹ is a well-known substance of this class. It is a complex condensation product of formaldehyde and phenol. 

191. Uses of Formaldehyde. Formaldehyde is a valuable antiseptic and disinfectant. In some cases it is generated as used, by burning methanol in specially designed lamps which do not admit enough air for complete combustion. Anatomical specimens are preserved in formaldehyde solution. It hardens albuminous substances and gelatine, hence is used in tanning and in hardening photographic films. It is condensed with certain compounds to build up dyes and with others to form resins. Formaldehyde and urea give a hard, colorless, transparent resin which is coming into use as a plastic. The manufacture of formaldehyde began in 1893 and the industry has since grown to very large proportions. 

192. Detection and Estimation of Formaldehyde. As formal dehyde has been used so widely as a preservative, its detection is a matter of importance. A number of delicate tests have been discovered. One part of formaldehyde can be detected in 200,000 parts of milk. The details of these tests will be found in books on food analysis. 

In presence of caustic soda it is oxidised quantitatively by hydrogen peroxide to formic acid. This serves as a convenient analytical method, since each molecule of the formic acid that is produced neutralizes one of alkali. A measured amount of standard alkali is added to the sample of formalin, the oxidation is effected and then the alkali that is left over is titrated with standard acid.

THE ALDEHYDE SERIES 

There are many primary alcohols and as a rule they lose hydrogen to form aldehydes when their vapors are passed over hot

As alcohol has given its name to a whole class of substances, so the name aldehyde has become generalized and is applied to every compound which contains the distinctive aldehyde group, -CHO. 

193. Naming Aldehydes. The systematic method and one which is applicable to a great variety of compounds is to name the hydrocarbon and then add the ending -al, eliding the e. Thus aldehyde itself is ethanal. The method is exactly the same as that for alcohols except that al is used instead of ol. H HCHH H HC-CC-COH H HCH H H 

2,2-Dimethyl-butanol-4

HC H HCH HCH HH -C-CO 2,2-Dimethyl-butanal-4

The longest chain that contains the aldehyde group is chosen. 

As the CHO group must be at the end of a chain, it does not always require a numeral. 

The method most commonly used is to name the aldehyde from the acid that is produced by its oxidation. Thus CH3-CHO which was originally named aldehyde becomes acetaldehyde, since on oxidation it gives acetic acid CH3COOH. The next is propionaldehyde, since it is oxidised to propionic acid. There is lack of uniformity in usage in forming the names. One writer will use butyraldehyde and another butyric aldehyde. Sometimes it is convenient to name aldehydes as substitution products of acetaldehyde. Thus (C3H7)2CH·CHO is dipropyl-acetaldehyde. 

194. The Higher Aldehydes. The aldehydes of this series are nearly always made from the corresponding alcohols and therefore their availability has depended on the supply of the alcohols. 

Hence only a few of the lower aldehydes have been investigated to any great extent. None of this series except acetaldehyde and formaldehyde has been of any considerable commercial importance. Butyraldehyde has recently been manufactured for use in

OXO DERIVATIVES 

203 making a rubber accelerator. The other aldehydes have been prepared in the laboratory and used in the building up of organic chemistry. The odors of the lower aldehydes are pungent and unpleasant. With an increasing number of carbon atoms up to 

C10, the odors become more pleasant, after which they fade completely. Some of the higher aldehydes are useful in making perfumes. The reactions of the higher aldehydes so far as known are those given for acetaldehyde. Some of the aldehydes of high molecular weight react less readily. It is to be noted that the aldol condensation may take place between two different aldehydes. This involves the aldehyde group of one and the carbon next to the aldehyde group in the other. From propion-aldehyde the product will be:

ACETONE 

196. Propanol, a primary alcohol, when passed over hot copper, loses two atoms of hydrogen; i-propanol, under the same circumstances, loses the same amount of hydrogen and it is natural to assume that it is given off in the same way:

Instead of passing the vapors of the i-propanol over hot copper, the hydrogen may be removed by various oxidising agents just as in making aldehydes. It is commonly said that the i-propyl alcohol is oxidised to the ketone. It is probable that the oxidising agent serves as a hydrogen acceptor, taking away the hydrogen at a much lower temperature than would otherwise be required. 

Acetone is a pleasant smelling, colorless, mobile liquid, boiling at 56.15°, solidifying at — 94.3°, and having the density 0.790015.

It mixes in all proportions with water, alcohol, ether and hydrocarbons. Analysis and molecular weight determinations show the formula to be C3H6O. Its constitution is shown by its formation from isopropyl alcohol and by the fact that in water solution it is readily reduced by sodium amalgam back to isopropyl alcohol. 

197. Reactions of Acetone. Obviously, reactions that depend on the hydrogen of the -CHO group of the aldehyde cannot be duplicated with acetone, but those that involve the carbonyl group may be expected to take place with acetone as with aldehyde. 

Actually, most of them do, but acetone is usually much less reactive than aldehyde. Following the reactions of aldehyde, as given above, it is found that acetone reacts similarly; it adds hydrogen, water or hydrocyanic acid much as does aldehyde (reactions 1, 2 and 4) and combines with sodium bisulphite, but does not add ammonia or acetanhydride (6 and 7). Aldehyde polymerizes in a number of different ways (reactions 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12), while acetone polymerizes in only one way, that in which aldol is formed (9). A molecule of water is nearly always split off with great ease so that the intermediate addition product is seldom in evidence. 

With hydroxylamine (13) acetoxime is formed, likewise acetonephenylhydrazone (14) with phenylhydrazine. In addition to these, acetone has a number of unique reactions.

198. The Manufacture of Acetone. In Chapter III it was stated that acetone and acetic acid are obtained along with methanol by the destructive distillation of wood. Until the World 

War this was the chief source of acetone, but the insistent demand for acetone for use in the manufacture of smokeless powder brought about the development of the fermentation process, in which acetone and butyl alcohol are produced. Since the war this process has been operated on a large scale. As two products are formed, commercial success has depended on finding uses for both of them. 

Wood distillation has been the source of acetone in a double sense, acetone being obtained directly and also from the acetic acid. The crude distillate is neutralized with lime, purified and evaporated. The residue is largely calcium acetate, which is distilled as described below. Calcium acetate has also been made from the dilute acetic acid obtained by the quick vinegar process. 

Acetone is obtained from calcium acetate by heating the salt

in a steel retort and condensing the vapors by a cooling coil. Acetone goes over and calcium carbonate is left: CH3 COO CH3 Ca→ CO + CaCO3 CH3 CO COO CH3 This process has been used on the large scale for a long time and has yielded thousands of tons of acetone. 

The vapor method, which is a modification of the above method, is sometimes used. If a quantity of calcium carbonate is placed in a tube into which the vapor of acetic acid is passed, calcium acetate will be formed with the liberation of carbon dioxide and water, and on heating the tube, the calcium acetate will decompose into acetone and calcium carbonate. It has been found by experiment that if acetic acid vapor is passed continuously through a tube containing calcium carbonate and heated to about 450°, the products leaving the tube are acetone, carbon dioxide and water. 

It is assumed that the formation and decomposition of calcium acetate go on simultaneously. Carbonates or oxides of manganese, magnesium, zinc, cadmium and iron can be used in place of calcium carbonate. All of these may be supposed to form acetates which are later decomposed. 

Acetone is now being manufactured from i-propyl alcohol by passing its vapor mixed with air over hot brass gauze. 

199. Uses of Acetone. Its principal use depends on its property of dissolving a great variety of organic compounds and many inorganic compounds, either alone or mixed with other solvents. 

It is used as a solvent for cellulose nitrate and acetate, for extracting resins from wood, in paint and varnish removers and for many other purposes. 

THE KETONE SERIES 

200. Naming Ketones. The name ketone comes from acetone

CH3 CO CH3, which was named from acetic acid from which it has long been prepared. In French, ketones are called acetones. 

The common way to name ketones is to give the names of the alkyl groups which are present, naming the smaller group first. 

Thus CH3 CO C2H5 is methyl-ethyl ketone and C2H5 CO C2H5 or CH3 CH2 CO-CH2-CH3 is diethyl ketone. It is obvious that there are two classes, simple and mixed ketones, just as there are

OXO DERIVATIVES 

209 with ethers and sulphides. In the simple or symmetrical ketones, the two alkyl groups are the same while in mixed or unsymmetrical ketones they are different. The systematic names are formed by adding one to the name of the hydrocarbon, eliding the e, just as in naming alcohols and aldehydes. Thus CH3 CH2 CH2.CO CH3 is pentanone. To this a numeral must be added to show the position of the carbonyl group, since there are two pentanones. The one above is pentanone-2. Formerly the prefix keto with a numeral was used instead of the ending -one, according to which this compound would be called 2-keto-pentane. The student should practice naming ketones according to all of these systems. 

201. The Higher Ketones. These have been prepared in great numbers and varieties. The calcium salt of any acid of the acetic acid series (Chapter XIV) gives a ketone on distillation:

The higher acids, such as stearic and arachidic (214) are converted into ketones by heating with iron turnings to 370°. The dehydrogenation, or oxidation, of secondary alcohols is a useful method of making ketones. This may be accomplished by passing the alcohol vapor with or without air, over heated copper or copper-zinc gauze. The reactions of the higher ketones call for little comment except to say that they are similar to those of acetone, although usually the higher ketones react more slowly and less completely. Many of them do not react with sodium bisulphite (5). Ketones are readily halogenated, the hydrogen of the carbon next to the carbonyl group being substituted.

213 The 1,1-dihydroxy-ethane was discussed in Chapter XIII as the hypothetical addition product of aldehyde and water. It loses a molecule of water to give oxo-ethane or aldehyde. The trihydroxyethane, also called ortho-acetic acid, has never been isolated, but is believed to exist in water solution in equilibrium with acetic acid. The equilibrium is far to one side, only a small proportion of the trihydroxy-ethane being in equilibrium with large proportion of the dehydrated form. In other words, the 1,1,1-trihydroxy-ethane loses a molecule of water, as would be expected from the conduct of 1,1-dihydroxy-ethane, to give 1,1-oxohydroxy-ethane, which, as will be seen later, is acetic acid. In carrying out the last of the three reactions above an excess of sodium hydroxide is used and sodium acetate is obtained instead of the free acid as written.

Monohydroxy-ethane can be dehydrogenated as shown in Chapter XIII; 1,1-dihydroxy-ethane might be similarly dehydrogenated:

It has long been known that aldehyde is readily oxidised to acetic acid, but it is only recently that the reaction has become of commercial importance. 

204. Structure of an Acid. According to the above, acetic acid is: (1) either ethane in which one of the methyl groups has had two hydrogens replaced by an oxygen atom, and the other hydrogen replaced by a hydroxyl group; or (2) alcohol in which the two hydrogens of the -CH2OH group have been substituted by an oxygen atom; or (3) aldehyde in which the hydrogen of the -CHO group has been replaced by hydroxyl. There are two kinds of substituents in the same methyl group. At first sight it might be expected that the resulting compound would show the properties

of alcohol and also those of aldehyde, but the presence of each of these substituents influences the reactions of the other. The ionization of alcohol is extremely low, comparable to that of water, while that of acetic acid is considerably higher. Contrasting nitrous and hypochlorous acids with nitric and chloric acids, it is seen that the addition of oxygen greatly increases the ionization of the hydrogen of the hydroxyl: ON OH O₂N OH Cl.OH O2C1.OH 

In each case a weak acid becomes a strong one. Contrasting alcohol with acetic acid it is found that the same change is brought about by the substitution of oxygen for hydrogen: CH3 C.OH H2 CH3 C.OH Since the concurrent action of the oxo- and the hydroxyl groups is required to give acetic acid its characteristic properties, it is customary to regard them as making up a special group OH which is commonly written -CO OH or -COOH and called carboxyl. Taking this group as a substituent, acetic acid may be called carboxy-methane, just as methanol is hydroxy-methane: HC-COOH HC-OH Whenever the hydroxyl group is substituted in a paraffin hydrocarbon (Chapter IX), the compound is an alcohol. Likewise when the carboxyl group is present, the compound is an acid. There are a few, but very few organic acids, which do not contain this group. 

Acids form a large and important class of carbon compounds. 

Thousands of them are known. Many are found in natural products, sometimes free, as citric acid in lemons, sometimes in salts, as tartaric acid in cream of tartar from grapes, and sometimes combined with alcohols in esters, as salicylic acid in oil of wintergreen. For this reason scores of acids have proper names which indicate their origin, as tartaric, citric, malic, suberic, palmitic, butyric, capric, lauric, cinnamic, stearic, lactic and benzoic.

ACIDS 

215 

ACETIC ACID 

205. This is the most common organic acid and the one longest known. Dilute acetic acid as vinegar was the only acid known to the ancients, who ascribed to it remarkable dissolving power. 

Our word acid is from the Latin acidus, which means vinegar. 

Cider, wine, and similar dilute solutions of alcohol turn sour when exposed to the air, although pure alcohol in pure water will not undergo this change. There must be present small amounts of compounds of nitrogen and of other elements, such as are found in natural fruit juices. The change is brought about by an organism, micoderma aceti, masses of which settle out of vinegar and are popularly known as "mother of vinegar." As the process involves oxidation, air is necessary for its continuance. In a barrel of cider, where the necessary oxygen has to diffuse through a great depth of liquid, this process is very slow. 

Vinegar contains 4 to 6 per cent of acetic acid. This is its characteristic constituent, to which its sour taste is chiefly due. 

The special flavor and aroma of any particular variety of vinegar depend upon the presence of other substances derived from the materials from which it was made. Cider vinegar is the most highly esteemed. White vinegar or spirit vinegar contains little else than acetic acid and water and is lacking in flavor. 

206. Properties of Acetic Acid. It melts at 16.6° and boils at 

118.1°, and has the density 1.0492220. This is increased by the addition of water until the density is 1.0748 and 22 per cent of water is present. Further addition of water lowers the density down to that of pure water. The maximum density corresponds very nearly to the composition C2H4O2-H2O. Some consider this water combined with it to form ortho acetic acid, CH3C(OH)3. 

Acetic acid mixes in all proportions with water, alcohol, ether and most organic liquids. It is an excellent solvent for many organic substances and is frequently used in the laboratory as a solvent for recrystallizing such substances. Its odor is distinctive and penetrating. In concentrated form it blisters the skin. 

207. Salts of Acetic Acid. Acetic acid is a monobasic acid and forms salts with all bases. Practically all of these acetates are

soluble in water, although some basic acetates are not. The sodium salt, CH¿CO₂Na·3H2O, crystallizes well. The potassium salt, CH3CO2K, is anhydrous. The calcium salt is Ca(C2H3O2)2· 

2H2O. Lead acetate, (CH3CO2)2Pb. 3H2O, or sugar of lead, is well known. It is made by dissolving litharge in acetic acid. It is very soluble in water and crystallizes well. Several basic lead salts are known. Verdigris (CH3COO)2Cu Cu(OH)2, is a basic acetate of copper. Paris green, Cu3 (AsO3)2 · Cu(C2H3O)2, is a mixed acetate and arsenite of copper. Aluminum and iron acetates are used as mordants in dyeing. When a solution of ferric acetate is heated, a basic iron acetate is precipitated. This fact is used in qualitative analysis to separate ferric salts from those of other metals. In the manufacture of white lead, coils of sheet lead are exposed to the vapor of acetic acid, air and carbon dioxide and the lead acetate first formed is converted into basic lead carbonate. 

The reactions in water solution of the salts of acetic acid are those that are to be expected, considering that acetic acid is weakly ionized and very soluble. Strong acids set acetic acid free; from very concentrated solutions this free acid may be distilled. Thus acetic acid is obtained commercially by the action of acids on calcium or sodium acetate: (CH3COO)2Ca + H2SO4 → CaSO4 + 2CH3COOH Calcium acetate is manufactured on the large scale by neutralizing the distillate from wood (Chapter III) with lime, and evaporating it to dryness. The dilute acetic acid obtained in the "quick vinegar" process is similarly converted into calcium acetate.

209. The Manufacture of Acetic Acid. Three methods have been used to a great extent in industry. The formation of acetic acid from dilute alcohol has been mentioned above. In order to hasten this reaction the “ quick vinegar process" has been devised.

Tall casks are filled with beech-wood shavings which are covered with a layer of mother of vinegar by steeping in vinegar. A weak alcohol solution is allowed to trickle over the shavings. In this way a large surface is exposed to the air, so that the oxidation is comparatively rapid, but even then eight to twelve days are required. The optimum temperature for the process is 30°. To facilitate the reaction air is circulated upward through the casks. 

During the World War this process was carried out on an enormous scale. Thousands of tons of acetic acid were thus made from alcohol obtained by the fermentation of molasses. 

Acetic acid is obtained in large quantities from the distillation of wood (Chapter III). The wood distillate is neutralized with lime and the methyl alcohol and acetone distilled off. By evaporating the remaining solution to dryness "gray acetate of lime " is obtained. The color is due to by-products of the wood distillation. This is the starting point for the manufacture of acetic acid. 

It is distilled in copper vessels with concentrated hydrochloric acid. The distillate is somewhat colored by impurities and contains about half its weight of acetic acid. The impurities are destroyed by potassium permanganate and the acid redistilled. A more nearly anhydrous acid is obtained by distilling anhydrous sodium acetate with concentrated sulphuric acid. To obtain the purest acid, a very strong acid is partially solidified by strong cooling and the part remaining liquid poured off. The solid acid

is melted and again partially frozen. This is repeated until the melting point is no longer raised. An acid that is strong enough to freeze readily is called "glacial" acetic acid. When water is the only impurity present, its amount may be judged from the freezing point, which is lowered 2.16° for each per cent of water present. Instead of converting the acid into acetate of lime it may be extracted from the water solution with ether. This is now being used commercially.

A method of manufacture, which was begun on the large scale during the World War, is the oxidation of acetaldehyde by air under pressure in the presence of oxides of vanadium and cerium as catalysts. The yield of pure acid from the aldehyde is nearly quantitative. At the present time this is being used in a number of plants and is expected to supplant other processes, except so far as wood distillation is kept up by the demand for charcoal, methanol and acetone. 

210. Uses of Acetic Acid. Acetic acid is an important chemical material. It is a useful reagent and solvent in the laboratory. 

Acetates of lead, copper, aluminum and iron are manufactured on a large scale. Much acetic acid is used in the synthesis of dyes and still larger amounts are consumed by the textile and papermaking industries. The demand for cellulose-acetate is increasing greatly. Enormous quantities are being made into ethyl acetate, butyl acetate and other esters for solvents in the lacquer industry.

OTHER ACIDS 

211. Formic Acid. The first member of the series, like that of the aldehydes, is quite different from the other members, so different in fact that it does not appear to belong to the series. 

Formic acid gets its name from the Latin formica, which means ant, since this acid can be obtained by distilling ants. It occurs in nettles, honey, some fruits, perspiration and wine. Formic acid is believed to be the effective agent in the liquid injected by bees, wasps and other insects when they sting.

Formic acid can be obtained by the oxidation of methanol, or of formaldehyde, but this method is not used on account of the

ACIDS 

221 cost. In the laboratory it is made by heating oxalic acid, C2H2O4, with glycerine (291):

COOH COOH COOH →HCOOH + CO2 An ester of glycerine is formed as an intermediate product, but as it decomposes with the regeneration of glycerine, glycerine may be omitted from the equation.

The structure of formic acid is best known by its preparation from chloroform by heating with alkali: CI NaOH CI HCCl + NaOH → 3NaCl + HC-OH → HC NaOH OH OH OH 

Formic acid

Its reactions agree with this structure. A comparison of its formula with that of acetic acid shows why the two differ so markedly: H.CO.OH 

Formic acid

CH3.CO OH 

Acetic acid

In acetic acid the carboxyl group is substituted for a hydrogen of a hydrocarbon, while in formic acid this group is combined with hydrogen. Formic acid contains no organic radical and like carbonic acid is more allied to inorganic compounds. It is a much stronger acid than acetic or any other of the acetic acid series. It forms water soluble salts with all bases. Those of lead and copper crystallize particularly well. 

212. Properties of Formic Acid. Formic acid is a liquid which solidifies at 8.35°, boils at 100.47°, and has the density 1.217820.

It mixes with water, alcohol, ether and many other solvents in all proportions. With water it forms a constant boiling mixture, which contains 77.5 per cent of the acid and boils at 107.1°. The strong acid blisters the skin. 

213. Reactions of Formic Acid. Carbonic and formic acids both lose water:

HO.COOHH2O + CO2 HCOOH → H2O + CO - 4,200 cal. 67,000 62,800

The first reaction is reversible and proceeds readily in either direction. The second reaction is not reversible and does not take place readily without a catalyst but does take place when formic acid is warmed with sulphuric acid or with certain metallic oxides. A water solution of carbon monoxide is not acid to indicators, as is one of carbon dioxide. Silicon dioxide, although the anhydride of an acid, does not give an acid reaction with water but does react with heated caustic soda. Sodium formate is manufactured by heating caustic soda to about 200° in carbon monoxide under a pressure of 8 atmospheres or more:

CO + NaOH → H COONa This resembles the union of caustic soda with carbon dioxide which takes place far more easily: CO₂+ NaOH→ HO.CO.ONa 

Comparing the formulae above for sodium formate and sodium. bicarbonate, it appears that they differ by one atom of oxygen. 

When sodium bicarbonate is heated to 70° with hydrogen under high pressure, reduction to sodium formate takes place very slowly. The reaction is greatly accelerated by the presence of a catalyst such as palladium black. Conversely, formic acid is readily oxidised to carbonic acid. This leads to its use as a reducing agent.

Instead of giving carbon monoxide and water, formic acid can decompose into carbon dioxide and hydrogen: 

H CO-OH→→ CO2 + H2 − 5,200 cal. 62,800 68,000

From the thermal data it appears that formic acid decomposes into water and carbon monoxide, or into hydrogen and carbon dioxide with the absorption of the same amounts of heat. The presence of a dehydrating agent favors the first reaction, while a hydrogenating catalyst favors the second. This reaction takes place when the acid is heated alone to 160°, or when catalysts such as finely divided rhodium or palladium are added to it at room temperature. Formic acid is obtained commercially by distilling a mixture of the sodium salt and sulphurie seid.

214. The Acetic Acid Series. Of the great number and variety of acids only one series, that of the normal acids, can be considered here. By this term is meant those containing a straight carbon chain with the active group at the end. Of the first ten all are found in natural products, while of the second ten only those containing an even number of carbon atoms are produced by nature. Many of these acids are found in fats, and therefore the series is known as the fatty acids series. Each acid in this series can be made by the oxidation of the corresponding alcohol in the series in Chapter IX. The properties are given in the table below.

215. Individual Acids. The acids from propionic on up the series are true homologs of acetic acid. They are all of nearly the same degree of ionization and all have the same reactions. In the table above the progressive changes in boiling points, melting points and densities can be followed. Formic, acetic and propionic acids mix with water in all proportions. The solubilities of the others decrease as the number of carbons increase, 100 cc. of water dissolves 5.61 g. butyric at - 1º, 3.9 g. n-valeric at 16°, 0.4 g. caproic, 0.24 g. heptoic at 15°, 0.25 g. caprylic at 100° and only 

0.034 g. stearic. Pelargonic and those below it are liquids at ordinary temperatures; the higher acids are waxy solids. Acetic acid has a sour but agreeable odor. The odor of propionic is less pleasant, while that of butyric and valeric are disagreeable, suggesting rancid butter. The odors become less as the vapor pressures diminish; the higher acids such as palmitic have practically no odor. The acids below heptoic are readily volatile with steam (14), those up to lauric go over slowly with steam, while palmitic and those above it are non-volatile. On this fact is based a practical method of detecting the adulteration of fats. It will appear later that the fats consist of the fatty acids combined with glycerine. Each fat yields a complex mixture of acids. It is practically

ACIDS 

225 impossible to separate these mixtures into their components but it is easy to determine the ratio of volatile to nonvolatile acids. 

This ratio has different values for different fats. 

Stearic and palmitic acids practically always occur together and are found in enormous amounts. They make up a large part of fats (Chapter XXVII) and are hence important constituents of foods and of many manufactured substances, as, for example, soap. 

In fats they are found in combination with glycerine.

The univalent CH3 CH2— group is called ethyl, and given the symbol Et; the univalent CH3.CO— group is named acetyl and is represented by the symbol Ac. As alcohol may be regarded as water in which one hydrogen has been replaced by ethyl, so acetic acid is water for one hydrogen of which acetyl has been substituted. These may be spoken of as ethyl-water or ethyl hydroxide and acetyl-water or acetyl hydroxide and acetyl chloride. 

217. Acetyl Bromide, Iodide, and Fluoride. These are of little importance as compared with acetyl chloride. Acetyl bromide is made from acetic acid and phosphorus tribromide. Acetyl iodide is usually prepared from acetyl chloride and calcium iodide. 

Acetyl flouride is obtained from acetyl chloride and zinc or silver fluoride.

In the ether (Chapter X) two alkyl radicals are joined by oxygen. 

The combination is broken up with difficulty, only by heating with an acid as hydrobromic, or with water at a high temperature. 

The acid anhydride contains two acyl radicals held together by an oxygen atom and reacts with water in a few minutes even in the cold, to form two molecules of acetic acid. The bond between carbon and oxygen in alcohol or ether is very stable, but the presence of the carbonyl oxygen loosens the bond between it and a second oxygen atom. 229

In structure the ester is intermediate between the ether and the acid anhydride, having an alkyl on one side of the central oxygen atom and an acyl group on the other. The bond between this central oxygen atom and the alkyl should be very stable and the one between it and the acyl group comparatively labile. An ester reacts with water much more rapidly than an ether but far more slowly than an acid anhydride. 

The structure of an ether resembles a metal oxide in which two electro-positive atoms are held together by oxygen, and the acetanhydride is much like an anhydride of an inorganic acid in which two oxidised non-metallic atoms are joined by oxygen. In a typical salt of an oxygen acid a metal atom and a non-metallic atom carrying oxygen are connected by an oxygen atom: Ag.O.Ag Base

For this reason esters have frequently been called ethereal salts. 

Misconceptions have arisen from this designation. In structure esters do resemble salts but there are great differences in properties, particularly in that esters are not ionized in water solution. 221. Esterification. When acetic acid is mixed with alcohol there is a slow loss of acidity, as may be shown by taking out 1 cc. of the mixture from time to time and neutralizing it with standard alkali. If the mixture is kept at room temperature, this diminution of acidity goes on for many months, the differences becoming less and less as time goes on until the acidity becomes constant. 

A mixture of equivalent amounts of acetic acid and ethyl alcohol, 60.04 g. to 46.06 g. was kept for 10 years, and at the end of that time 65.2 per cent of the acid had disappeared. Ethyl acetate and water are formed in this reaction: CH3COOH + HOC2H5→ CH3 COOC2H5 + H2O + 1,100 cal.

At 100° the reaction goes much faster. In one experiment 65.6 per cent of the acid disappeared in 200 hours. Longer heating did not cause further change in the mixture. On the other hand, a

231 mixture of 88.06 g. ethyl acetate and 18.02 g. of water, that is, two neutral substances which give a neutral mixture, gradually develops acidity, until finally this mixture has exactly the same strength as the one made from acid and alcohol.

The ester has been hydrolyzed, that is, decomposed by water: CH3 COOC2H5 + H2O→ CH3 COOH + C2H5OH 

Starting with 100 moles of acetic acid and 100 moles of alcohol or with 100 moles of ethyl acetate and 100 moles of water the result is the same, 67 moles of ester, 67 moles of water, 33 moles of acetic acid, and 33 moles of alcohol.

The mechanism of esterification is not definitely known. It appears to be molecular rather than ionic. Acetic acid is believed to add water (Chapter XIV). Addition of alcohol also seems to take place:

222. The Mass Action Law. Esterification presents one of the best examples of the working of the mass action law. A large proportion of the known chemical reactions are reversible. The mass law has been constructed as a means of calculating equilibria in reversible reactions. It is a mathematical statement suggested by common-sense reasoning and verified by many careful quantitative experiments. Two substances, A and B, react to give C and D, but C and D also react to give A and B. The reaction is written: A+B C+D In all such cases experiments show that the equilibrium state is the same regardless of whether A and B or C and D are originally present. When the equilibrium is reached, there is not necessarily a cessation of chemical action. A and B react with each other whenever they are present in the same mixture; they are in this mixture at equilibrium and must continue to react with each other, as their nature has not changed. The equilibrium is dynamic rather than static; the opposing reactions continue to go on but at equal rates. Two near-by cities may remain of the same relative size, although train-loads of people continually pass from one to the other.

ESTERS 

233 It is a common experience that the more of a reagent that is put into a mixture, the faster it acts. How fast it can react must depend also on the amount there is present of the substance on which it is reacting. Stating this more exactly, the mass law results: the velocity of a reaction is proportional to the amounts of the reactants present in a unit volume. The amount of A in a unit volume is the concentration of A which is written [A], which means the number of gram moles per liter. This is a conventional symbol which is read "concentration of A." It should be noted that the units are the gram molecule, or mole, and the liter. The above statement translated into symbols becomes: v α [A] X [B] In this v is the reaction velocity. This may be written:

v = k[A] X [B] In this k is a constant for the particular reaction under consideration at a given temperature. For the reverse reaction between 

C and D the expression is similar: v' = k'[C] X [D] When the reaction mixture containing A, B, C and D has come to equilibrium, the velocities of the two opposing reactions are equal, v equals v' and therefore: k[A] [B] 

From this is derived: 

As the ratio of the velocity constants k and k' is constant, it may be represented by K, which is the equilibrium constant. The magnitude of this constant, K, shows which substances will predominate when the equilibrium is reached. If K is large, the product [C] X [D] is large as compared with [A] X [B], which means that A and B react to a large extent to form C and D, or if the reaction is started with C and D, they will disappear to only a small extent. If K is small, the reverse will be true, while if K has a medium value, considerable concentrations of all four reactants will co-exist.

The mass action law may be applied to the esterification experiments mentioned above. To state the concentrations properly the volume of the reaction mixture would have to be known, but as all of the components are in the same volume the molecular percentages may be used: 

[Ester] [Water] [Acid]. [Alcohol] 

66.5 X 66.5 = K = 

33.5 X 33.5 = 3.91

It is customary to take this K as equal to 4. This numerical value of K is for acetic acid and ethyl alcohol; for other reactants K has other values. From the experiments with equivalent quantities, the amount of ester that will be produced from any other proportion of acid and alcohol may be calculated. If instead of 100 moles, 200 or 500 moles of alcohol to 100 moles of acid is used, what will be the amounts of ester formed? Let the amount of ester be x, then the water formed is also x, and the acid remaining is 100-x. In one case the alcohol left over is 200-x and in the other it is 500X. 

The equations are: x2 x2 

4 and (100 — x) (200 — x) 

(100 — x) (500 — x) Solving these, x is found to be 85 moles in one case and 94 moles in the other. Each of these quadratic equations gives two values for x which satisfy the equation but one is thrown out as unreasonable. Thus doubling the amount of alcohol causes 85 per cent of the acid to go into ester and increasing it five times raises this to 94 per cent. It is possible to reverse the proportions and esterify 85 per cent of the alcohol by using two equivalents of acid. It is obvious that the complete esterification of a given amount of acid or alcohol cannot be attained, no matter what excess of the other is used. Practically an excess of a cheap alcohol, such as ethyl, is taken to esterify an expensive acid and vice versa. The ease of purifying the product and possibility of recovering the unreacted alcohol or acid are also considered.

The mass action law applies to the substances that co-exist in one homogeneous solution. In case one of the reactants or products escapes from the solution the equilibrium is readjusted accord-

ESTERS 

235 ingly. If alcohol is added to a dilute solution of acetic acid, only a small amount of ethyl acetate can be formed, as the large amount of water opposes the esterification; but if the ester is removed, as it is produced, more will be formed. As a matter of fact it is possible to obtain a high yield of ethyl acetate from acetic acid that is less than 10 per cent. In esterifying high molecular weight alcohols and acids which dissolve little water, the water that is formed by the esterification separates as a layer and may be removed. When a mixture of equivalent amounts of glycerol and a non-volatile acid such as stearic is heated to 150° or 200° under reduced pressure or with a current of inert gas bubbling through it, the water is removed as it is formed and the esterification goes to completion.

224. Change of Equilibrium Constant with Temperature. The change of the equilibrium constant, K, with the temperature is given by the equation: 

dinK ΔΗ dT RT2 In this InK is the natural logarithm of the equilibrium constant, T is the absolute temperature, R is the gas constant, and AH is the heat given off or taken up in the reaction. In the esterification equation given above, the heat evolved in the reaction is only 500 calories. Compared to the heats of many chemical reactions, this is a very small figure, which means that the esterification equilibrium will change very slightly with the temperature.

200° 67.3 66 225. Catalytic Esterification. As stated above, acetic acid and alcohol react with each other at an extremely low rate at room temperature. However, if to such a mixture a small amount, 1 to 

3 per cent, of hydrogen chloride or of concentrated sulphuric acid is added, esterification goes on rapidly, as much ethyl acetate being formed in an hour as would normally be produced in months.

ESTERS 

237 The percentage of ester formed is the same whether the reaction is hastened by the catalyst or not. If hydrogen chloride is passed into a mixture of ethyl acetate and water, the decomposition of the ester is hastened to a similar extent, but hydrolysis ceases just where it would without the hydrochloric acid. The hydrochloric acid acts as a catalyst and hastens the reaction, but does not change the nature or the relative amounts of the products. 

The velocity of the reaction, either esterification or hydrolysis, is roughly proportional (for small concentrations of hydrochloric acid) to the amount of acid added. When equivalent amounts of various acids are added to the acetic acid-alcohol mixture, the effects are approximately proportional to their degrees of ionization. All the evidence points to the conclusion that it is the hydrogen ion that is the catalyst. There is not space here to go into the explanations that have been proposed for this effect. An enormous amount of work has been put on this problem and hundreds of articles have been published in support of one theory or another, but just how the hydrogen ion acts is not yet clearly understood. It appears to add to one or more of the kinds of molecules that participate in the reaction to form complexes that have enhanced reactivity. 

226. Vapor Phase Esterification. A mixture of acetic acid and alcohol vapors may be heated to a high temperature for many hours without an appreciable amount of ester being found. Similarly, hydrolysis of ethyl acetate vapor by water vapor does not appear to take place to any considerable extent. However, when the mixed vapors are passed over certain oxides at high temperature these reactions take place with extreme rapidity. Titania and thoria have been largely used at 150° to 300°. Silica gel appears to be the most efficient catalyst for this reaction under these conditions. As shown above, a mixture of equivalent amounts of alcohol and acetic acid reaches equilibrium at about 67 per cent in the liquid phase; the same mixture passed over silica gel gave the following figures: 

At 150° 

84.7 per cent 200° 83.3 66 250° 78.3 300° 74.9

It is to be noted that in the vapor phase the equilibrium shifts with the temperature. 

227. Preparation of Esters. For low-boiling alcohols and acids hydrogen chloride or sulphuric acid are used as catalysts, the mixture of alcohol, acid and catalyst being warmed for some hours. 

The product is shaken with water to free it from the mineral acid, and with soda solution to take out the remaining organic acid. 

It is then dried and fractionated. For many acids and alcohols that boil above 150° a mixture of equivalent amounts of the acid and alcohol may be heated under reflux to 150° or above while a slow stream of inert gas is passed in to carry off the water that is produced. Practically complete esterification may be thus effected. 

228. Reactions of Esters. The most characteristic reactions are those in which the -OR group is exchanged for some other group, as -OH, -OR', -NH2. 

1. The exchange of OR for -OH is simply the reversal of the reaction by which an ester is formed from an acid and an alcohol and is called hydrolysis:

CH3COOC2H5 + HOH→ CH3COOH + HOC2H5 This may be accomplished by heating an ester with water, a large amount of water being necessary to displace the equilibrium to the right. Catalysts facilitate the decomposition just as they do the formation of esters and are useful in shortening the reaction time.

When alkali is added to the water the reaction is commonly called saponification. The making of soap (Chapter XXVII) is a useful application of this reaction. The alkali serves two purposes, as it greatly hastens the reaction and also combines with the acid that is set free so that the reaction goes to completion. It is better to regard saponification as hydrolysis followed by the neutralization of the acid, but it is commonly written: CH3COOC2H5 + NaOH → CH3COONa + HOC2H5 This reaction is quantitative, either all of the alkali being used up if the ester is in excess, or all of the ester disappearing if the alkali is in excess.

ESTERS 

239 

2. The exchange of -OR for -OR' is known as alcoholysis. 

When methyl acetate is dissolved in ethyl alcohol, no change seems to take place at room temperature, but if the mixture is heated to 100° for some days, or to 180° or 200° for a few hours, the ethyl alcohol displaces a part of the methyl alcohol:

CH3CO OCH3+HOC2H5 381,200 328,000

CH3CO OC2H5+HOCH3-200 cal. 538,500 170,900 The result is a mixture of methyl and ethyl acetates and methyl and ethyl alcohols. The reaction is reversible and comes to an equilibrium in accordance with the mass action law. The heat of reaction is extremely small, as in direct esterification. In the liquid phase, to which these figures apply, the equilibrium should not change with the temperature. Any alcohol will replace any other, the extent of the action depending on the relative amounts of the alcohols and on a constant peculiar to the two alcohols which oppose each other. This constant may be calculated from the esterification constants for the two alcohols. How two alcohols will compete with each other can be judged by the way in which they compete with water in esterification. This reaction can be speeded up greatly by hydrochloric or any other strong acid and still further by sodium ethylate or any other sodium alkoxide. A slightly volatile alcohol may drive out a volatile one, provided the temperature and pressure are such that the volatile alcohol escapes. 

3. The replacement of OR by -NH2 is a common method for the preparation of amides (Chapter XVI): CH3COOC2H5 + NH3 → CH3CONH2 + HOC2H5 Obviously an acid cannot be employed to catalyze this reaction in the forward direction, but it does accelerate its reversal, the formation of an ester from an amide and an alcohol. As the acid combines with the ammonia, an excess of acid causes the complete esterification of an amide. 

4. In the condensation of esters the -OR group may be said to be exchanged for another group, although in a peculiar way. 

An ester condenses with another, a ketone or a nitrile (Chapter XVI):

CH3COOC2H5 + HCH2COOC2H5 → CH3CO CH2COOC2H5 + HOC2H5
