100 From the table the influence of structure on the properties can be traced. Reading diagonally as from hexyl formate to methyl hexoate gives the members of a group of isomeric esters. In each of these the end members have the highest boiling points. 

The lowest boiling ester in a group is the one that has alkyl groups of nearly the same size, as ethyl propionate, C2H5CO-OC2H5, ethyl butyrate, C3H7CO-OC2H5, propyl butyrate, C3H7CO· 300 2 

OCTATES HEPTATES HEXOATES VALERATES BUTYRATES PROPIONATES ACETATES FORMATES BOILING POINTS OF ESTERS AGAINST NUMBER OF CARBONS NUMBER OF CARBONS FIG. 15.-Boiling Points of Some Esters. 

OC3H7, and amyl valerate, C4H9CO-OC5H11. The formates boil lower than the alcohols from which they are derived. The acetates boil very close to the corresponding alcohols for the lower members of the series but somewhat higher for the others. The butyl esters boil just a little higher than the acids from which they are derived. These figures indicate that the esters are less associated than the alcohols or the acids. 

230. Identification and Estimation of Esters. Esters are fre quently found in natural products and their identification is important. In many cases an ester is the valuable constituent in an essential oil and in such a case the price of the oil may depend

on its ester content. Fats and many vegetable oils (291) are esters. Hence the quantitative estimation of esters is of great importance.

A few esters can be identified by their melting points. Boiling points are useful as indications but are not conclusive. Thus an ester, boiling at 145-146°, might be either butyl propionate (b.p. 145.4°) or ethyl valerate (b.p. 145.5°) or a slightly impure pentyl acetate (b.p. 147.6°). It is difficult to purify esters and other liquids to such an extent that their boiling points can be depended on for identification. The boiling point is useful, as it confines the search to a limited group. 

As an ester is derived from an alcohol and an acid, it is positively identified when the alcohol and the acid concerned are determined. The first step is to hydrolyze the ester, which is usually done by heating with alkali: CH3COOC4H9 + KOH → CH3COOK + C4H9OH A volatile alcohol thus produced may be distilled over, along with some water, concentrated or collected by any appropriate means and identified. A non-volatile alcohol is extracted with an appropriate solvent. The acid is left in the form of an alkali salt from which it is set free, collected and identified. 

The same reaction serves as a basis for the estimation of the amount of an ester present in a mixture. The saponification is simply carried out with a weighed sample of the mixture containing the ester and a measured volume of a caustic potash solution of known strength. Alcoholic potash is employed for the double purpose of providing a solvent for the ester and for excluding carbonates, as phenolphthalein is the proper indicator for organic acids. An excess of the alkali is used and the excess determined by finding the volume of a standard acid solution used to bring the mixture to neutrality. From the figures obtained, the amount of ester is calculated. It is evident that this method gives the number of equivalents of ester present instead of the weight of the ester. If the nature of the ester present is known, its weight may be calculated from the data. In the case of an essential oil, the ester is frequently calculated in terms of the ester that is the valuable constituent, regardless of the fact that other esters may be present. In the case of a fat which is a mixture of esters, the result is stated as the "saponification number," which is defined

ESTERS 

243 as the numbers of milligrams of potassium hydroxide required to saponify 1 gram of the fat. This figure is a characteristic constant of a particular natural fat. 

231. Occurrence and Uses of Esters. A great number and variety of esters are found in plants, particularly in fruits and flowers, which owe their flavor and taste largely to them. Esters are manufactured and used in rather large quantities for making artificial fruit flavors. Still greater quantities are used as solvents for nitro-cellulose and other materials in the making of lacquers. 

In the choice of solvents the volatility is of prime importance. If the solvent is too volatile, the lacquer becomes too thick before it can be applied properly; while a solvent that is not volatile enough lingers and makes the coating sticky. Usually a mixture of several solvents of different boiling points is used. Among the many esters one can be found of almost any degree of volatility. 

Naturally, the availability of the alcohols and acids determines which esters will be used most. Ethyl, methyl, butyl, isoamyl, isobutyl and propyl alcohols are the most plentiful alcohols. Their esters are largely used, the acetates being the most common, since acetic acid is the cheapest of the low boiling acids except formic acid. The esters of formic acid are not of much service because they are comparatively readily hydrolyzed by water. Ethyl, isopropyl, butyl and mixed amyl acetates are produced in the greatest quantities, the United States producing 6,000,000 gallons of butyl acetate in 1928. PROBLEMS 

1. Acetic acid is heated in a sealed tube with its own weight of 95 per cent alcohol. What per cent of it should be converted to ester? 

2. Butyl alcohol and water form a constant boiling mixture at 92.5°. If acetic acid, and an excess of butyl alcohol are heated under a fractionating column, what fractions should be taken off and at what temperatures? 

3. A pure ester was saponified; 0.3416 g. of it required 29.41 cc. of 0.1 N alcoholic potash. What was its molecular weight? The silver salt from the acid of the ester was found to contain 59.63 per cent of silver. What was the ester? 

4. A sample of commerical ethyl acetate weighting 0.4952 g. was boiled with 

30 cc. of 0.2 N alcoholic potash. For back titration 15.0 cc. of 0.1 N acid was required. What was the percentage of ester? 

5. A mixture of butyl alcohol and octane was acetylated. The product was freed from excess of acetanhydride and dried. It was found to contain 38.4 per cent of butyl acetate. What was the percentage of butyl alcohol in the original mixture?

CHAPTER XVI SOME NITROGEN COMPOUNDS NITRILES 

232. Compounds of carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen are not only numerous but belong to many different classes and present many interesting characteristics. The amines, RNH2, R2NH, etc., have already been discussed. Several other classes will be taken up in this chapter. Nitrogen compounds differ greatly among themselves in properties; some of them are among the most stable organic compounds known, while others are violently explosive; some are the most important constituents of foods, while others are violent poisons. Nitrogen compounds are formed in a wide variety of ways and undergo diverse reactions. Only the simpler compounds can be taken up here. 

233. Cyanides. When nitrogen is brought in contact with sodium, carbon and iron at high temperatures, sodium cyanide, NaCN, is formed, the iron appearing to act as a catalyst. The sodium and carbon seem to unite to form sodium carbide, which then reacts with the nitrogen. It is simpler to use sodium carbonate, carbon and iron turnings heated to 800-1000° in a current of nitrogen:

Na2CO3 + 4C + N2 → 2NaCN + 3C0 This is the Bucher process. It has been operated on a large scale, but has not yet been commercially successful on account of difficulties with materials for the furnaces and in the purification of the product.

In the Castner process, which has been used extensively since 1900, sodamide is prepared by the action of ammonia on sodium: 2NH3+2Na→ 2NaNH2 + H2 244

NITROGEN COMPOUNDS 

245 This is mixed with carbon and heated first to 500-600° to form sodium cyanamide, and then the temperature is raised to 800°: 2NaNH2 + C→ Na2N2C + 2H2 Na2N2CC→2NaCN Sodium cyanamide Sodium cyanide In another method calcium cyanamide is fused at 750° with carbon and sodium chloride or carbonate:

Ca(CN)2+ C + 2NaCl → CaCl2 + 2NaCN. 

From the sodium salt, cyanides of other metals are readily formed by double decomposition. These cyanides are noted for the ready formation of complex salts.

When potassium cyanide is added to a ferrous salt, ferrous cyanide is precipitated but redissolves in excess: 2KCN + FeCl2 → 2KCl + Fe(CN)2 4KCN+Fe(CN)2 → K4Fe(CN)6 This salt has long been made by fusing potassium carbonate, iron and animal matter, such as horns and hoofs. A water solution of potassium ferrocyanide, K4Fe(CN)6 does not contain appreciable amounts of ferrous or cyanogen ions, as this salt dissociates into potassium ions and the complex ferrocyanide ion, Fe(CN)6. There are many other double cyanides. These differ considerably in their ionization, some, like the ferrocyanides, give only the complex negative ions, while the water solutions of others contain the cyanide ion, CN, as well. Only those salts that give cyanide ions yield hydrocyanic acid when treated with dilute acids. Potassium cyanide was formerly made by heating potassium ferrocyanide: K4Fe(CN)64KCN + 2C + N₂+ Fe N2 By adding sodium the yield of cyanide was increased:

K4Fe(CN)6 + 2Na→ 4KCN + 2NaCN + Fe Since the cyanogen was the important part, this mixture was marketed as 109 per cent "potassium " cyanide. 

234. Hydrocyanic Acid. This acid is volatile and therefore is readily driven out of its salts by other acids: NaCN+ HCl → NaCl + HCN

A convenient method is to add a 50 per cent solution of sulphuric acid to a sodium cyanide solution of equal strength, preferably at room temperature and under reduced pressure. The evolved gas is dried with calcium chloride and liquefied. 

Hydrocyanic acid is formed in many ways: from ammonia and active carbon, from carbon monoxide and ammonia passed over thoria at 400-450°, and from acetylene and nitrogen, in an electric discharge, or from hydrogen and nitrogen if the discharge is between carbon poles. Coke oven gas contains as much as 50 g. per 1000 cu. ft. of it or a pound per ton of coal used. When amygdaline, a complex substance found in bitter almonds, peach kernels, and in some other plant substances, is hydrolyzed this acid is one of the products. The leaves of cherry-laurel contain 

0.20 to 0.46 per cent of it. 

Hydrocyanic acid, sometimes called prussic acid from its connection with Prussian blue, is a colorless mobile liquid, boiling at 

25.6°, solidifying at - 11.4° and having the density 0.696918. Its critical temperature and pressure are 183.5° and 50 at. It mixes with water, alcohol, ether, and with most other organic solvents. 

It is extremely toxic, but in spite of this it proved a disappointment as a lethal gas in the World War. The reason was that its effects are not cumulative; a concentration below that necessary to kill produces no serious effects even when encountered frequently. It was abandoned in favor of gases that are cumulative and produce effects on long exposure to low concentration. Hydrocyanic acid is employed on a large scale to rid ships of vermin and to destroy pests on fruit trees. In this case a tent is placed over the tree and the desired amount of the liquid is sprayed into the tent. Sodium cyanide and other soluble cyanides are likewise toxic. Potassium ferrocyanide is not toxic, as its solution does not contain cyanide ions. 

235. Cyanogen Chloride. By the action of chlorine on a water solution of hydrocyanic acid or on sodium cyanide under carefully controlled conditions, cyanogen chloride is obtained: Cl2 + NaCN→ CICN+ NaCl →CICN+NaCl 

This is a poisonous liquid solidifying at 6°, boiling at 13.8°, and having the density 1.186. Cyanogen bromide is similarly pre-

NITROGEN COMPOUNDS 

247 pared. It melts at 52°, boils at 61.6°, and is also toxic. Both of these were used to a small extent as war gases in the World War. 

236. Cyanamide. Ammonia and cyanogen chloride react to form cyanamide: NCCIHNH2→N C. NH2 + HCl Cyanamide According to this formation it should be amino-hydrocyanic acid and most of its reactions are in accord with this formula, but others are best explained by writing it as HN: C: NH. There is no sure way of deciding between the two; perhaps it may pass readily from one to the other (see tautomerism in Chapter XXIV).

Sodium cyanamide, Na₂N CN, was mentioned above as an intermediate product in the Castner process. Calcium cyanamide is manufactured on a large scale by the reaction of nitrogen on calcium carbide:

CaC₂+N2 → CaCN2 + C + 97,800 cal. 

Nitrogen is passed over finely ground calcium carbide. This is heated in one spot to about 1000° to start the reaction, which then continues without further heating. The sintered mass is cooled and ground. The crude material runs about 58 per cent calcium cyanamide, the rest being carbon that was set free and impurities from the calcium carbide. The crude material is treated with enough water to decompose any calcium carbide that may be left and is then a useful ingredient of manufactured fertilizers. 

Cyanamide can be prepared by adding cold 20 per cent sulphuric acid to a cold filtered solution of one part of calcium cyanamide in 10 parts of water. The filtrate from this is evaporated in a vacuum and the separated cyanamide taken up in ether. It is a white solid very soluble in water and ether, melting at 44° and boiling with some decomposition at 140° under 19 mm. pressure. 

It behaves as a weak dibasic acid, its soluble alkali salts being hydrolyzed to acid salts and free base. The neutral heavy metal salts are insoluble in water and are useful for analytical purposes.

When mercuric cyanide is heated, cyanogen is evolved: Hg(CN)2- →Hg (CN)2 Cupric cyanide, like cupric iodide, is unstable and decomposes into cuprous cyanide and cyanogen: 

CuSO4 + 2NaCN → Na2SO4 + Cu(CN)2 2Cu(CN)2 →2CuCN+ (CN)2 

Cyanogen is a colorless gas at ordinary temperature, but liquefies at 20.5° and solidifies at 27.90°. Its vapor density shows it has the molecular weight 52, which corresponds to C2N2 and not to CN. Its formula is commonly written (CN)2 to show its analogy to Cl2. The molecule of chlorine contains two chlorine atoms and the molecule of cyanogen has two of the compound atoms, or radicals. The CN group was early recognized as a radical. The constitution of cyanogen is shown by the fact that it takes up water to form oxamide and then ammonium oxalate: CN CN Cyanogen

The fact that addition takes place to both the carbon and nitrogen indicates that they are joined by more than one bond. The facts that nitrogen is usually trivalent except in salts of the ammonium type, and that carbon is almost always quadrivalent, justifies the writing of three bonds between the carbon and nitrogen atoms. The view is generally held that hydrocyanic acid is a mixture of two isomeric substances having the formulae, HC; N and H-N: C, but that the proportion of the one corresponding to the second formula is extremely small.

Acetonitrile is a mobile, non-poisonous liquid with a pleasant odor. It freezes at 41°, boils at 81.60°, and has the density

239. Structure of Acetonitrile. In ethyl amine and in acetic acid the two carbon atoms are known to be joined together, and it is fair to assume that they are still united in acetonitrile. The fact that these reactions are reversible strengthens this view. As carbon is usually quadrivalent and nitrogen trivalent the carbon and nitrogen are represented as being held together by three bonds: -C N or -C=N.

This method of writing has the additional advantage of indicating that addition reactions can take place without severing the carbon and the nitrogen. It is important to note that hydrogen adds in equal amounts to the carbon and the nitrogen. When water is added the bivalent oxygen atom goes to the carbon and the two hydrogens to the nitrogen. In terms of electrons the formula indicates that six valence electrons are employed in holding the carbon and nitrogen atoms together. This does not say that the orbits of all six are packed between the two atoms. 

Some of the orbits may extend to quite a distance and set up fields of force around the molecule. This may be regarded as an explanation of why addition reactions take place so readily.

One carbon atom cannot hold more than one hydroxyl group and it does not usually keep more than one amino group. The trihydroxy compound loses water to give acetic acid and the other loses two molecules of ammonia to form acetonitrile.

244. If in place of potassium cyanide silver cyanide be heated with methyl iodide, the liquid which is obtained has the composition C2H3N, although a part of it boils at 59.6° instead of 81.6° and has a fearful odor. The compound boiling at 59.6° is called methyl isocyanide. When methyl amine is mixed with chloroform and alkali added, the same compound is produced: CH3NH2 + Cl3HC→ CH3NC + 3HC1

The alkali combines with the hydrochloric acid, which for clearness is represented as being set free. The molecular weights of both methyl cyanide and isocyanide are the same and correspond to the formula C2H3N. As the methyl group is present in both the isomerism must be due to differences in the CN group. Two arrangements appear to be possible: 

CH3 CN or CH3 C N and CH3 NC 

or CH3 NC 

The first of these has been found to agree with the reactions of inethyl cyanide or acetonitrile, so the second is assigned to the isonitrile. The question has been whether to put two bonds between the nitrogen and carbon, regarding the one as trivalent and the other as bivalent, or write four bonds, the nitrogen being pentavalent and the carbon having its usual valence of four. 

Most chemists prefer the first view. This agrees well with the fact that sulphur is readily taken up to form a mustard oil:

CH3NC+S→ CH3NCS By catalytic hydrogenation 4 atoms of hydrogen are added but only one of these goes to the nitrogen while three are taken up by the carbon:

CH3NC + 4H→ CH3·NH CH3 This is in sharp contrast with the conduct of methyl cyanide under the same circumstances. The product is dimethylamine, in which the nitrogen atom is between the two carbon atoms as it is represented to be in the formula CH3 NC. On account of the fact that methyl isocyanide combines readily with hydrochloric and other acids, it was for a time regarded as a base and called methyl carbylamine. The products formed do not appear to be salts and this idea has been given up. Methyl isocyanide is converted to methyl cyanide by heating to about 250°. The cyanide is stable even at much higher temperatures. This is another difference between the two.

251. Fulminic Acid. This is an unstable volatile compound resembling hydrocyanic acid in odor and in toxicity. It is believed to have the formula C: N.OH 

Its mercury and silver salts are obtained when alcohol is added, under the proper conditions, to solutions of these metals in strong nitric acid. These salts explode by percussion. Mercury fulminate is extensively used in percussion caps to set off other explosives.

If ammonium acetate is heated in a sealed tube or in an autoclave to 200° for 24 hours, about 75 per cent of it is changed to acetamide, which analysis and molecular weight determinations show to be C2H5ON. The structure of this compound is best shown by its formation from acetyl chloride and ammonia: CH3CO CI+HNH2 → CH3CONH2 + HCl Acetamide

An excess of ammonia is actually used which converts the liberated acetic acid into its ammonium salt. 

The formation of acetamide by heating ammonium acetate may be written so as to show its analogy to the esterification of acetic acid by alcohol:

CH3COOH + HOC2H5 CH3COOC2H5 + HOH CH3COOH + H NH2CH3CONH2 + HOH The two reactions are alike in that they are both reversible, the limits, 67 per cent and 75 per cent, being of the same order. They both take place with somewhat similar velocities under the same circumstances. It may be objected that acetic acid and ammonia form ammonium acetate when they are brought together, but at high temperatures this compound is largely dissociated. 

Acetamide may also be prepared from ethyl acetate by mixing it with two volumes of strong ammonia water and letting the mixture stand for several days, when it becomes homogeneous: 

CH3COOC2H5 + H NH2CH3CONH2 + HOC2H5 In this the equilibrium is far to the right, but if dry hydrogen chloride be passed into an alcoholic solution of acetamide, the acid combines with the ammonia. This removal of one of the reactants upsets the equilibrium and if an excess of hydrogen chloride is used all of the amide is converted into the ester in time. 

Acetamide is a white solid which dissolves in about its own weight of water at room temperature and in less than half that amount of hot water. The usual form melts at 81°, an unstable form at 69.40°, and boils at 222°. Its water solution is neutral and does not show the presence of ions. When this solution is boiled, the acetamide is very slowly hydrolyzed to acetic acid and ammonia. In the presence of either hydrogen or hydroxyl ions this reaction goes on rapidly. It is complete if excess of acid or

alkali is used, since the ammonia combines with the acid in the one case and the acetic acid with the alkali in the other. The rate of hydrolysis is nearly, but not quite, proportional to the concentration of the hydrogen ions that brings it about. There is a similar proportionality with hydroxyl ions, but the rate with a given concentration of hydrogen ions is not the same as with an equivalent concentration of hydroxyl ions. In the case of esterification either the formation or the decomposition of an ester can be accelerated by the addition of an acid, but the reaction of ammonia and acetic acid cannot be thus hastened, since the strong acid would combine with the ammonia and prevent any other reaction.

From the above reactions, it appears that the structure of acetamide differs from that of acetic acid by having the -NH2 group in place of the OH group of the acid: 

CH3 C OH and CH3.C.NH2 

Acetic acid

Acetamide

The difference is the same as between an alcohol and a primary amine: 

CH3 C OH and CH3.C. NH2 H2 H2

Contrasting these formulae it appears that replacing the hydrogen on the carbon atom next to the hydroxyl group changes the nearly neutral alcohol into a decidedly acid substance, acetic acid. The same change in structure converts the basic ethyl amine into the neutral acetamide. The acidic influence of the CH3 CO- group is balanced by the basic influence of the -NH2 group. In the absence of water strong acids combine with acetamide to form salts, but these are hydrolyzed readily on contact with water. On the other hand, acetamide acts as an acid and forms salts in which one of its hydrogen atoms is replaced by a metal.

NITRO-PARAFFINS 

257. In Chapter XI it was shown that the mono- and di-alkyl derivatives of hydrogen sulphide are oxidised to mono- and di-alkyl derivatives of hexavalent sulphur. The alkyl phosphines and arsines are similarly oxidised. Were nitrogen readily oxidisable, a similar reaction would take place:

C2H5N + 30 → C2H5NK In fact this reaction can be carried out, although it is difficult and is not used for preparation purposes. The reverse of this, the reduction of the nitro compounds, goes easily and is the simplest way of obtaining a primary amine provided the nitro derivative is available.

Nitro derivatives of the paraffins can be made by direct action of nitric acid on the hydrocarbons. Representing the hydrocarbon by R H this becomes:

R.H+HONO2 → R. NO2 + H2O 

At least some of the paraffin hydrocarbons can be nitrated but with difficulty. The hydrocarbon is sealed up in a tube with dilute nitric acid and is heated for many hours to about 110°. 

When ethyl iodide is added to silver nitrite at -10°, a vigorous reaction takes place:

C2H5I + AgNO2 →C2H5NO2 + AgI On investigation the product proves to be a mixture of two liquids which are easily separated, as one boils at 17° and the other at 114.8°. Both have been found to have the composition and the molecular weight corresponding to the formula C2H5NO2. The low boiling liquid is readily decomposed by caustic soda, alcohol and sodium nitrite being formed:

C2H5NO2 + NaOH → C2H5OH + NaONO This, and the fact that it is identical with the product from alcohol and nitrous acid, show that it is ethyl nitrite, the ester of nitrous acid, having the constitution:

C2H5O N 0 The liquid, boiling at 114.

8°, proves to be nitro-ethane and is iden-

tical with that obtained by the oxidation of ethyl amine. Other alkyl iodides react with silver nitrite to give analogous mixtures. 

It is in this way that most nitro-paraffins have been prepared.

259. When ethyl iodide is heated with granular zinc in a flask connected with a reflux condenser, it boils as any other liquid would do, but after a time it is observed that the vapors no longer come up in the condenser. The ethyl iodide combines with the zinc:

C2H5I + Zn → C2H5ZnI The structure of the resulting compound is written C2H5ZnI in agreement with the usual valencies of zinc and iodine. A similar reaction takes place with methyl iodide and with a number of other alkyl iodides, but not so well with alkyl bromides. It is greatly aided by the presence of copper in the zinc. 

If the flask containing the ethyl zinc iodide is heated more strongly, a mobile liquid distils off. It boils at 118° and by vapor density determination and analysis has been shown to have the molecular formula C4H10Zn, which is written (C2H5)2Zn, since ethyl iodide was used in its preparation. It is called zinc di-ethyl. 

The reaction appears to be: 2C2H5ZnI → (C2H5)2Zn + ZnI2 It ignites on contact with air and burns with a bright flame with a characteristic green tinge which gives off zinc oxide fumes. The other alkyl zinc iodides give the corresponding zinc alkyls. Those containing the higher alkyls are not so inflammable.

260. Grignard Reaction. In 1899 Barbier¹ discovered a reaction which Grignard2 developed into one of the most useful in synthetic organic chemistry. Probably no other reaction has had so many applications, or has resulted in the preparation of so many new compounds. 

261. Formation of the Grignard Reagent. Magnesium is not easily attacked by ethyl iodide under the conditions given above for zinc, but does react with it in anhydrous ether solution. The reaction may be written:

C2H5I + Mg→ → C2H5MgI As in the case of zinc, it is written according to the usual valencies of the elements present. The compound C2H5MgI, which is ) is known for his work on the chemistry of aromatic perfumes and natural terpenes. He has been Professor at the University of Lyons since 1881.

267 known as the Grignard reagent, remains in solution in the ether. 

If this solution is evaporated at moderate temperatures the residue is found to contain ether which can be driven off only by heating it strongly. Quantitative experiments indicate that there are two molecules of ether for one of the magnesium-ethyl iodide complex, so the formula of the reagent is more correctly written: C2H5MgI· 

2(C2H5)2O. There has been much discussion as to the function of this ether. It has been regarded by some as analogous to the water of crystallization of salts, while others consider one, at least, of the ether molecules as a constituent part of the Grignard reagent. 

The oxygen atom of the ether may be functioning as quadrivalent, as in the addition compound of ether and hydrogen chloride. It is possible to prepare the reagent with only one molecule of ether. 

The fact that the formation of the reagent does not readily take place except in ether indicates that the ether has some important function in the reagent. In discussing the reactions of be left out of consideration,

An analogous reaction takes place with almost all alkyl halides, chlorides and bromides, as well as iodides. The product is always known as the Grignard reagent and is commonly written RMgX, in which R is any alkyl and X is chlorine, bromine or iodine. The wide usefulness of the reaction is due to two facts: that the reagent can be formed from so many compounds and that it is so reactive after it is formed. On account of the great reactivity of the Grignard reagent, water must be scrupulously excluded from all the materials used in preparing the reagent and air and carbon dioxide kept out of the apparatus as far as possible. 

262. Reactions of the Reagent. Magnesium has tremendous affinity for oxygen, as is shown by its burning in an atmosphere of carbon dioxide. The bond between magnesium and carbon is readily broken. From these two facts the reactions of the Grignard reagent may be predicted. It reacts by double decomposition and also by addition. 

1. Water reacts by double decomposition: 

C2H5 MgBr + HOH → C2H5H + Mg(OH)Br

The organic product is ethane, the hydrocarbon from which the ethyl bromide is derived. Thus, by causing ethyl bromide to react with magnesium and adding water, the alkyl bromide is changed to the corresponding hydrocarbon, the net result being the replacement of the halogen by hydrogen. The reaction is complete and may be used as a method of quantitative analysis. 

If an excess of water be added to a solution containing the Grignard reagent, the volume of the ethane evolved will correspond to the amount of the reagent present. Conversely, the amount of water present in a mixture can be deduced from the volume of the gas evolved when an excess of ethyl magnesium bromide is added. 

2. Alcohols, mercaptans, amines and other compounds containing active hydrogen react similarly. Hence the Grignard reagent may be used for the detection and estimation of such substances:

C2H5MgBr + HOC3H7 → C2H6 + C3H7OMgBr For simplicity in writing the equation the magnesium is shown on the right as the mixed alcoholate and bromide; it is more accurate to double the quantities and write the products (C3H7O)2Mg and MgBr2, but the point is to represent the relation of the ethane formed to the active hydrogen present:

C2H5MgBr+HN(C3H7)2 → C2H6 + (C3H7)2NMgBr 2C2H5MgBr + H₂NC3H7 →2C2H6 + C3H7NMg + MgBr2 This method of estimating active hydrogen was preposed by Chugaeff. 

3. An alkyl halide produces a hydrocarbon, but the reaction is unsatisfactory for preparation purposes except in special cases: C2H5MgBr + BrC2H5→ C2H5 C2H5 + MgBr2 As during the preparation of the reagent some of the reagent is present along with some of the alkyl halide from which it is being made, there is always an opportunity for this reaction to take place. In some cases it interferes seriously with the preparation of the reagent.

264. These are of the two classes represented by the formulae (CH3)2Hg and CH3HgI. Accordingly, the mercury compounds correspond to the zinc compounds in formulae and in many of their reactions. of mercury compounds in contact with water and air; in the variety of reactions by which they are produced and in the monoalkyl mercury compounds almost any anion can serve in place of the iodine. Only a few of the mercury compounds are noted here and for these only a few of their reactions.

CHAPTER XVIII THE ONE CARBON GROUP 

268. Many of the substitution products of methane have already been considered; that is, halogen substitution products in 

Chapters II and VII, methanol in Chapter III, methyl ether, mer captan and amines in Chapters X, XI, and XII, formaldehyde in Chapter XIII and formic acid in Chapter XIV. In several places it has been pointed out that the methane derivatives have special properties and differ markedly from the higher members of any series, as formaldehyde and formic acid. Some valuable comparisons can be made by bringing together the various substitution products of methane.

A tertiary carbon, as in isobutane, (CH3)3CH, carries only one hydrogen atom, so substitution on this carbon is limited to one univalent element, such as chlorine. A secondary carbon atom, for example, the middle atom in propane, has two hydrogens for which two univalent atoms or a bivalent atom may be substituted: CH3 CH2 CH3 CH3 CC12 CH3 CH3 CO CH3 There are more possibilities in the case of a primary carbon with its three hydrogens, as:

CH3 CH CH3 C-H Cl Cl CI OH OC2H5 CH3 C-Cl CI SC2H5 CH3C CH3C CH3C CH3C CH3.C=N 

A carbon atom that has four hydrogen atoms offers a still greater variety of substitution products. One, two, three or four of the hydrogens may be replaced by univalent atoms, two by a bivalent or four by two bivalent. Many combinations of different elements, univalent, bivalent, and trivalent are possible. 275

SH Thiocyanic acid 269. Carbonic Acid. The free acid, its salts and its anhydride, carbon dioxide, may be said to belong to inorganic chemistry, but its esters are typical organic compounds. Urea and guanidine are of great interest physiologically. 

270. Carbonyl Chloride. This is the acid chloride that corresponds to carbonic acid, but it cannot be made from that acid, as anhydrous carbonic acid, H2CO3, is unobtainable. It is produced by the direct union of carbon monoxide and chlorine: CO + Cl2 → COCl2 ->

ONE CARBON GROUP 

279 This reaction takes place under the influence of light or of activated charcoal. In actual practice, the mixture of the two gases is passed through a layer of activated charcoal. 

Carbonyl chloride, which is also called phosgene, is a gas under ordinary conditions, which boils at 8.3° C. and melts at -104° C. It has a stifling odor and is very toxic. Much use of it as a weapon was made during the World War. Its effects are cumulative and serious injury results from long exposure to low concentrations. Next to chlorine, phosgene is the easiest absorbed of the war gases and is readily taken care of by a mask. 

Phosgene reacts similarly to acetyl chloride, though by no means as rapidly, with water, alcohols, amines, etc., which contain active hydrogen. With water carbonic acid is formed and with alkali a carbonate:

OCC12 + 2HOH → OC(OH)2 + 2HCl OCCl2 + 4NaOH → OC(ONa)2 + 2NaCl

Phenyl-urethane Urethane, a white solid which melts at 52° and boils at 180°, is a half-way product between ethyl carbonate and urea. It is used to some extent as a soporific and anesthetic. All urethanes have hypnotic properties, particularly those containing a tertiary alkyl.

Phenyl-urethane results when aniline is substituted for the ammonia. It was shown in Chapter IX that derivatives of this class are used for the identification of alcohols. They are commonly prepared by the addition of phenyl isocyanate to the alcohol: HOC2H5 OC NC6H5 

Phenyl isocyanate

Phenyl urethane 271. Sulphur Derivatives of Carbonic Acid. It appears from the formulae above that a number of these derivatives are possible. 

The free acids are unstable, as would be expected, but the ethyl esters of all of them are known. The materials for making these are phosgene, thiophosgene, CSCl2, ethyl chlorocarbonate, ethyl thiol-chlorocarbonate, carbon bisulphide, alcohol and mercaptan.

The student can work out ways of combining these. 

272. Xanthic Acid. The free acid is unstable but its salts are readily formed and are important. Sodium alcoholate and carbon bisulphide combine:

ONE CARBON GROUP 

281 + Na OC2H5 SNa \OC2H5 

Sodium xanthate

The reaction takes place with great ease when the two substances are brought together, even when caustic soda and alcohol are used. 

The name comes from the Greek word for yellow. The alkali salts are slightly yellow and the copper salt is decidedly yellow. The formation of sodium xanthate is so easy and the copper salt is so characteristic that minute traces of carbon bisulphide in gases are readily detected by this reaction. Sodium xanthate is used on a large scale in flotation. The xanthate reaction is a general one for alcohols and takes place even with cellulose (375). 

273. Carbamic Acid. This is not known in the free state but the union of dry carbon dioxide and ammonia gives ammonium carbamate. Urethane (see above) is the ethyl ester of carbamic acid. 

274. Urea. The amide of carbamic acid, carbamide or urea, was discovered in the urine in 1773; it is a white solid, melting at 

132°. Its synthesis by Wöhler in 1828 has already been mentioned. It is found in many of the fluids of the animal body and is secreted in the urine of mammals. A human adult excretes about 30 g. per day. It is the chief nitrogenous end-product of the metabolism of proteins and is the form in which most of the nitrogen is eliminated. As it is very soluble in water, neutral and odorless, it is well adapted to this purpose. 

Two methods for the formation of urea have been given; from phosgene and ammonia and by the hydrolysis of cyanamide (236). 

One other method might be included, the reaction of ammonia with carbon dioxide under pressure at 140°. Many specific conditions have been suggested in patents. 

The best-known reaction of urea is its hydrolysis to ammonium carbonate:

CO(NH2)2 + 2H2O → CO(ONH4)2 

When urea is heated alone to 150-170° it loses ammonia:

H2N-CO NHH+H2NCO.NH,−HN, CO NH.CONH,+NH3 Biuret

Although urea is practically neutral it combines with strong nitric acid to form urea nitrate, CO(NH2)2 HNO3, which is sparingly soluble and separates out when this acid is added to a concentrated solution of urea. This is a useful method of obtaining urea. The urea nitrate is mixed with barium carbonate, which liberates the urea.

The estimation of urea is of importance. It is readily accomplished by mixing the urea solution with nitrous acid or with sodium hypochlorite or hypobromite:

CO(NH2)2 + 2HONO→ CO2 + 2N2 + 3H2O The nitrogen is caught and measured over caustic alkali solution. 

275. Guanidine. This may be regarded as urea in which the -O is replaced by the imino group, NH, or as tetra-aminomethane which has lost a molecule of ammonia. It is found in the sugar beet and in some other plants. It dissolves readily in water to give a strongly alkaline solution and forms salts with acids, even with a weak acid such as carbonic acid. BOILING POINTS 

277. The property that varies most regularly with the molecular weight is the boiling point. The boiling points of the members of a number of series are given in Table XLIII and the same data

are plotted in Fig. 16 against the number of carbon atoms. The data included are restricted to the normal hydrocarbons and their substitution products in which the substituent is on the end carbon atom.

In all cases the data give smooth curves. The elevation of the boiling point from one member to the next becomes steadily less as the number of carbons increases. Each of these curves may be regarded as a characteristic of the series, just as the boiling point is a characteristic of a particular compound. 

There are two things to compare: the relative positions and the shapes of the curves. The hydrocarbon curve is the lowest; the substitution of any atom or group, even fluorine, for hydrogen increases the molecular weight and raises the boiling point of the product. Comparing substituents of the same kind, the halogens, for instance, it is seen that the curve nearest the hydrocarbon curve is that of the fluorides; above it are those for chlorides, bromides and iodides. When the substituents are of different kinds, the elevations of the boiling points which they cause may be in a different order from that of their weights. Thus methyl alcohol boils at 64.6° and methyl mercaptan at 5.8°. Oxygen has an effect about equal to that of chlorine, while the entry of the hydroxyl group raises the boiling point of methane more than the substitution of bromine or even iodine. This asso- Some of the curves are quite different in shape from the others. 

Those for the alkyl halides closely resemble the hydrocarbon curve. 

The curves for acids, alcohols and aldehydes are much higher than would be expected, particularly for the lower members of the series. 

Measurements of surface tension and other properties of these oxygenated compounds indicate association in the liquid state. 

This would explain their relatively high boiling points. ciation seems to decrease as the hydrocarbon chain lengthens. 

The curves approach the hydrocarbon curve more and more as the number of carbons increases. The alcohol curve has quite a different slope from the others. Methyl alcohol boils considerably above methyl iodide, propyl alcohol a little below propyl iodide, while heptyl alcohol boils lower than heptyl bromide. The boiling points of the acids do not seem to fall on a smooth curve but appear to alternate slightly.

CHAPTER XX POLYHALOGEN AND POLYHYDROXY COMPOUNDS 

284. The reactions of halogen and hydroxyl derivatives of the hydrocarbons are fundamentally the same whether only one or several of these groups are present in the molecule. In many cases the halogens or hydroxyls react independently and the reactions of the mono-derivatives can be written for the poly- but there are cases where the presence of two or more similar groups, particularly in certain relations to each other, leads to peculiar reactions.

Contrasting these with tetramethylene and pentamethylene oxides, it is noticed that the rings containing an oxygen atom and two or three carbons are difficult to form and easy to decompose, while the rings with five or six members are readily formed and are stable. 291. Glycerol. The third member of the above series is glycerine, a compound of great importance. As it is a hydroxyl compound, many prefer to call it glycerol, which shows its relationship with methanol and glycol. Fats (Chapter XXVII), which are found abundantly both in animals and plants, are esters in which glycerine is the alcoholic constituent. This is combined with a number of acids, the three most common being stearic, palmitic, and oleic. Two of these, stearic, C17H35COOH, and palmitic, C15H31 COOH, have already been described, the third oleic, C17H33COOH, will be taken up in Chapter XXVII. Stearin, palmitin and olein, the chief constituents of fats, are glycerol esters.

The naming of esters of glycerol is peculiar and is illustrated with the above examples. The names of the tri-esters are made by adding"-in" to the distinctive part of the name; that is, butyrin, palmitin, and stearin. Frequently, the prefix "tri" is used with these. The ethers of glycerol are sometimes similarly named, as triethylin for the triethyl ether.

Glycerol, discovered by Scheele in 1779, is a viscous liquid having a sweet taste, the name coming from a Greek word meaning "sweet." At low temperatures it freezes, although not readily, because of its great tendency to supercool. It melts at 18.07°, boils at 290° and has the density of 1.260420.

Glyceric acid Tartronic acid 293. The Manufacture of Glycerol. This has been an important adjunct of the soap industry, for until recently fats have been the only practicable source of glycerol, which is obtained by their saponification or hydrolysis. Using stearin as an example, the three common methods are represented below: 

1. By saponification with caustic soda or potash: (C17H35COO)3C3H5 + зNaOH →3C17H35COONa + C3H5(OH)3 2. By heating with water containing sulphuric acid as a catalyst and the "Twitchell reagent" which is an emulsifying agent: (C17H35COO)3C3H5 + 3H2O → 3C17H35COOH + C3H5(OH)3 

3. By heating with lime: 2(C17H35COO)3C3H5 + 3Ca(OH)2 →→ 3(C17H35COO)2Ca + 2C3H5(OH)3 In the first reaction the alkali used is equivalent to the acid in

POLYHALOGEN, POLYHYDROXY COMPOUNDS 

307 the fat or is in excess. The resulting sodium salt is very soluble in hot water and moderately soluble in cold, but is practically insoluble in a water solution of caustic soda or of sodium chloride. 

After the reaction is complete either alkali or sodium chloride is added, which causes the sodium stearate to separate as a layer on top of the water solution. This layer is oily when hot and solid when cold. The glycerine remains in the water layer. In the acid saponification, equation 2, the free fatty acid which is obtained is insoluble in water and separates as a top layer which solidifies on cooling. The glycerine remains in the water layer. 

In the lime process which is usually carried on in a closed vessel at a high temperature, less lime is used than is called for by the equation. One-third of this amount is sufficient at 170° and onetenth at 190°. The calcium stearate is insoluble in water and is separated along with the free stearic acid from the water solution of the glycerol, which is the other product of the reaction. The calcium stearate is decomposed by warming with dilute sulphuric acid. The advantage of this process is that the glycerol is obtained unmixed with anything but water, while the mother liquor in the first process contains either salt or sodium hydroxide along with the glycerol, and in the second, sulphuric acid and the “reagent." 

The presence of these substances in the mother liquor makes the recovery of the glycerol more difficult. For the sake of simplicity, only stearic acid has been mentioned in the saponification of fats.

Similar equations can be written for the decomposition of glycerol palmitate and oleate, the other chief constituents of fats. 

The next step is recovering the glycerine from the water solution, which contains various impurities in addition to the inorganic substances mentioned. The bulk of the water is removed by evaporation at reduced pressure. The separation of the glycerol is accomplished by steam distillation at a low pressure. As the vapor tension of glycerol at 100° is only 0.05 mm., it would take 

3 kg. of steam to carry over 1 g. of glycerol, if this operation were conducted simply by blowing steam through the solution under ordinary conditions. The vapor pressure of the glycerol is raised by working at a higher temperature and the proportion of steam is kept down by maintaining a low total pressure in the system. 

The vapors pass through a warm condenser which separates the glycerol and then into a cold condenser where steam is liquefied.

294. Glycerol by Fermentation. In the usual alcoholic fermentation process, some glycerol is produced. The distillation residue usually contains about 3 per cent of glycerol, but this is not enough to pay for its recovery. By a special fermentation process in which the alkalinity is kept within certain limits, the yield of glycerol is increased to 20 to 30 per cent of the sugar present in the molasses. The alcohol, which is also produced, is distilled off, the residue partially evaporated and the glycerol separated from the remainder by the aid of superheated steam. This process has recently been put into operation in the United States. 

295. Uses of Glycerol. The chief use of glycerol is in making nitro-glycerine. Other large uses are in the manufacture of cellophane (Chapter XXV), which remains pliable when it contains 10 to 15 per cent glycerine and of glyptal resins. As glycerol has a sweet taste and is an excellent solvent and harmless, it finds many applications in pharmacy and in the preparation of cosmetics. It does not evaporate and is hygroscopic; therefore, it is useful wherever it is desirable to maintain anything in a moist, plastic condition. It finds many uses in textiles, inks, soaps and lotions. 

296. Nitroglycerine. This compound, which is not a nitro compound but the trinitrate of glycerine, has long been of the greatest importance. It is readily made by dissolving glycerine in "mixed acid," which is a mixture of nitric and sulphuric acids. 

One function of the sulphuric acid is to take up the water that is formed by the action of the nitric acid:

Nitroglycerine, or glycerol trinitrate, is an oily liquid almost insoluble in water, having the density 1.6009 at 15°. It crystallizes in two forms, one of which melts at 2.9° and the other at 13.2°.

When detonated by a shock of sufficient intensity, it explodes with

POLYHALOGEN, POLYHYDROXY COMPOUNDS 

309 terrific violence and is therefore used in shooting oil wells. As it is difficult to handle a liquid, nitroglycerine is made into a solid called dynamite by incorporating it with a porous solid. At first inert material was used for this purpose, but later gun cotton or another solid explosive was substituted. 

The trichlorate of glycerol is twice as powerful an explosive as nitroglycerine. The choice of an explosive depends on the safety of handling as well as on the powerfulness of an explosive. Nitroglycerine, particularly when mixed with other materials, as in dynamite and smokeless powder, combines the two advantages. PROBLEMS 1. If both alcohol groups are oxidised simultaneously, a double aldehyde, glyoxal, is the intermediate product. This illustrates the complexities that are possible when compounds containing several hydroxyls are oxidised, glycol being the simplest example. 

Any compound containing two carboxyl groups will be a dibasic acid and will have the properties peculiar to dibasic acids, particularly the ability to form acid salts. Each carboxyl group may be expected to act independently, but each will influence the other to a greater or less extent. 

Carbonic acid, the derivatives of which have been discussed in Chapter XVIII, is the simplest dibasic acid containing carbon, but it does not belong to the class that will be considered in this chapter, since it does not contain two carboxyl groups. The simplest possible acid of this class is oxalic acid. 

This consists only of two carboxyl groups joined together, so it is different from the higher members of the series in which the carboxyls are substituted in a hydrocarbon. An organic acid is usually defined as a hydrocarbon in which the carboxyl group has been substituted for a hydrogen atom; neither formic nor oxalic acid complies with this definition. It is found in a number of plants, usually as the acid potassium or the calcium salt. Calcium oxalate frequently separates from urine as a crystalline sediment, and when much is present, the condition is called oxaluria. Ammonium oxalate is found in guano. Oxalic acid is formed as an endproduct when sugars, starch and cellulose are oxidised by strong nitric acid. It may be obtained by gently heating sugar with an excess of concentrated nitric acid. A cheaper method is to heat sawdust with caustic potash or soda to above 200°. The product is extracted with water, and from this solution calcium oxalate is precipitated by the addition of lime. This is filtered off, washed and treated with sulphuric acid, which sets free the oxalic acid. 

A high yield of oxalic acid can be obtained by oxidising corn cobs with nitric acid in the presence of a catalyst. 

The constitution of oxalic acid is shown by the fact that it is obtained by the oxidation of glycol. Cyanogen in aqueous solution is slowly converted to ammonium oxalate: CN + H2O CN + H2O

301. Salts of Oxalic Acid. A large number of these salts are known. Oxalates of only the alkali metals and ammonium are soluble in water. In quantitative analyses calcium is regularly precipitated as the oxalate. Oxalic acid and its salts are somewhat poisonous. The acid and its salts find many minor uses in the arts.

305. Malonic Ester Synthesis. Diethyl malonate is the starting point in a most interesting and important synthetic method which has served for the synthesis of a large number of acids. 

The method is typical of synthetic organic chemistry and merits close study. Diethyl malonate, which is commonly known as malonic ester, manifests slight acidic properties. Its solution in water does not show any appreciable conductivity or acidity, but the pure ester does dissolve sodium to form a sodium salt. When the ester is added to a solution of sodium ethylate in absolute alcohol, this same sodium salt is formed. As ethyl acetate, CH3COOC2H5, does not form a sodium salt, the reaction does not seem to concern the group -COOC2H5, which is common to both. 

The conclusion is that the -CH2- group which joins the two carboxyls is responsible for the salt formation. 

The sodium salt is commonly written: Na CO⚫OC2H5 CO-OC2H5 Hydrogen joined to carbon is not usually replaceable by metals but the influence of the two adjacent carboxyl groups is sufficient to loosen the hydrogen of this -CH2- group. The acidifying influence of the carbonyl group, -CO-, has been noted (204) in contrasting the acidic strength of ethyl alcohol, CH3 CH2 OH, with that of acetic acid, CH3.CO.OH. An alternative formula for sodium malonic ester, and one which is probably more correct, will be given when aceto-acetic ester is discussed (344), but the one above is convenient for representing its reactions. 

Heating this sodium compound with an alkyl halide replaces the metal by the alkyl:

Na C2H5I + COOC2H5 C2H5 → NaI + COOC2H5 COOC2H5 COOC2H5 The product is ethyl-malonic ester; that is, the diethyl ester of ethyl-malonic acid. As methyl, ethyl, propyl, butyl and other

307. The Alpha Omega Series of Dibasic Acids. The best known series of dibasic acids is that in which the two carboxyls are joined to the end carbon atoms of normal hydrocarbons. The first and last positions in such a chain are called alpha and omega. 

Most of these are prepared by special methods which need not be given here. General methods would be the oxidation of the polymethylene glycols (287) or converting these glycols into dibromides and then into dicyanides. The same phenomenon is noticed here; the melting points of the dibasic acids fall on two curves, those of the acids containing an even number of carbon atoms being on the higher curve. The solubilities in water are also found to alternate, the acids with an odd number of carbon atoms being more soluble than the adjacent even numbered acids. The acids containing an even number of carbon atoms appear more stable towards oxidation and are produced by further oxidation of even or odd dibasic acids. All of these acids crystallize well, oxalic with two molecules of water, the others without water.

308. In Chapters VIII, IX, and XX it has been shown that compounds containing one or more hydroxyl groups have certain properties and in Chapters XIV and XXI it has been shown that acids owe their properties to the presence of one or more carboxyl groups. Many compounds are known which have both of these in one and the same molecule, either one hydroxyl and one carboxyl group, or more than one of both of these groups. Such compounds are both alcohols and acids and may be called carboxyalcohols or hydroxy-acids, but the latter name is used since the acid properties are more pronounced than the alcoholic. Many hydroxy-acids are produced in life processes and are found in plant and animal products. To synthesize a hydroxy-acid, the hydroxyl group may be introduced into an acid by any of the usual methods for making alcohols, or the carboxyl group may be put into an alcohol.

In these mixed compounds each group reacts more or less independently of the others, so that the one compound has two sets of chemical properties. The reactivity, however, of either group may be modified by the other. Thus hydroxy-acetic acid is more strongly dissociated than acetic acid, the influence of the hydroxyl group being, in this case, similar to that of the chlorine in chloracetic acid, although less pronounced: 

Acetic acid... 

Hydroxy-acetic acid.

0.18 X 10-4 1.52 X 10-4 

15.55 × 10-4 

Chlor-acetic acid......... K

As the introduction of either the hydroxyl or the carboxyl group into a hydrocarbon increases the solubility in water, compounds containing two or more of these groups may be expected to be very soluble. This is true of the lower members of the series, although the higher members are less soluble. 322

HYDROXYL AND CARBOXYL-HYDROXY-ACIDS 323 

Methane boils at 161.4°, methanol at 64.5°, and acetic acid at 118.1°, from which it appears that the introduction of the hydroxyl group into methane raises the boiling point 225.9°, while the carboxyl group raises it 279.5°. Hence, HO CH2.COOH, hydroxy-carboxy-methane would be expected to boil only at a very high temperature. As a matter of fact, it cannot be distilled under atmospheric pressure without decomposition. Only a few of the lower members of the series can be distilled even in a vacuum.

310. Hydroxy-Propionic Acid. A glance at the formula of propionic acid shows the possibility of two acids, the hydroxyl being attached to either the alpha or the beta carbon atom:

311. Lactic Acid. This acid, which is a-hydroxy-propionic acid, is produced when milk sours, this change being due to the action of an enzyme on the milk sugar of the sweet milk. It was isolated from sour milk by Scheele in 1870. It is present in sourkraut and silage and is found in the human stomach and muscles. 

Lactic acid is produced in the muscles during exercise and consequently is in normal human blood, the average amount being 11 mg. per 100 cc., although after heavy exercise this may rise to 

70 mg.

It may be prepared by fermenting a 15 per cent solution of glucose containing milk and some old cheese, the solution being kept neutral by the addition of zinc oxide or calcium carbonate. 

On a large scale raw beet juice is fermented in vats, air being blown in and lime added to keep down acidity. The calcium lactate formed is only slightly soluble in water and separates from the solution. This is filtered off and treated with the calculated amount of sulphuric acid in the presence of some water, giving a solution containing 40 to 50 per cent of lactic acid. When this is evaporated at atmospheric pressure, dehydration of the lactic acid begins before all the water is gone. The pure acid can be separated by fractionation under reduced pressure. It boils at 83° at 

1 mm. or at 119° at 12 mm. pressure and melts at 18°, but is rarely obtained as a solid since it is very deliquescent. 

The relation of lactic acid to propionic acid is shown by heating it with concentrated hydriodic acid, which reduces it to propionic acid. When a salt of a-bromo-propionic acid is boiled in water solution, lactic acid is formed:

CH3-CHBr.COONa + H2O → CH3•CH(OH)-COOH 

When it is heated with dilute sulphuric acid to 130°, it is split into aldehyde and formic acid:

CH3-CH(OH).COOH → CH3-CHO + HCOOH

It is oxidised by chromic acid to acetic acid and carbon dioxide:

CH3 CH(OH)·COOH + 20 → CH3 COOH + CO2 + H2O The products of each of these reactions contains a methyl group which could not have been produced in either reaction; hence lactic acid contains a methyl group and therefore must be ahydroxy-propionic acid. 

The central carbon atom in lactic acid is combined with four different groups and thus is an asymmetric carbon atom. Hence there is a possibility of optical isomers. The lactic acid obtained as above described and also that found in milk, are optically inactive, but the lactic acid found in flesh is dextrorotatory. This d-lactic acid was formerly called sarco-lactic acid or para-lactic acid. When the inactive lactic acid is exposed to the action of 

Penicillium glaucum, the laevo form is consumed and the dextro remains. The laevo form may be obtained by the fermentation of sugar with a special bacillus. The two acids, d-lactic and l-lactic, are identical in all of their chemical and physical properties and differ only in their effect on a beam of polarized light. Both rotate the plane of polarization to the same degree but in opposite directions. This statement can be made of each one of the salts of the two, except salts with active bases. The active acids melt at 27° while the racemic melts at 18°. The dl-lactic acid appears to be some sort of a combination of the dextro and laevo forms rather than a simple mixture of the two. The salts of the active acids differ in solubility, in water of crystallization and in other properties from the corresponding salts of the racemic acid; for instance, the zinc salt of either of the active acids is readily soluble in water and crystallizes with two molecules of water, while that of the inactive acid has four molecules of water and is only slightly soluble. 

Lactic acid imitates glycollic acid in the ways in which it loses water. Lactid, a double ester corresponding to diglycollid, is formed by heating lactic acid under diminished pressure. It melts at 125°, boils at 255°, and has the structure: CH3 CH.O.CO OĆ.0.HC

This compound is called butyrolactone, and all internal esters of this class are known as lactones. Hydroxy-acids in which the hydroxyl is further from the carboxyl than the delta position seldom form lactones. 

The gamma and delta lactones are five and six-membered rings. 

Rings containing five or six members are the most frequently encountered among the compounds of carbon.

314. Glyceric Acid. This acid, which contains two hydroxyl groups, is obtained by the careful oxidation of glycerine. As only a primary alcohol group can be oxidised to a carboxyl without breaking the carbon chain, the only possible way to represent the reaction is:

HOCH2CH(OH). CH2OH → → HOCH2 CH(OH). COOH Glycerol dl-Glyceric acid

Glyceric acid is a thick syrup which mixes with water and alcohol but is insoluble in ether. It is of little importance and has not been thoroughly studied. The central carbon atom is asymmetric and it is known that a solution of one of its salts becomes optically active after it has been acted upon by penicillium glaucum, which destroys one of the optical isomers, leaving the other. 

There are many polyhydroxy alcohols, some of which were mentioned in Chapter XX (287). These may be oxidised to give polyhydroxy-acids after the order of glyceric acid. Where there are two primary alcohol groups, careful oxidation gives a monobasic acid and stronger oxidation a dibasic acid. On account of the possibility of a large number of optically active modifications of the higher alcohols, the number of these acids is very large.

316. Malic Acid. This important and widely distributed fruit acid was isolated by Scheele in 1785 from unripe apples (L. malum, apple). It is the characteristic acid in apples, cherries, gooseberries, raspberries, strawberries, currants and other acid fruits.

It is frequently found in the roots, stems, leaves or seeds of

plants. If the unripe berries of the mountain ash are macerated with water, the filtered solution neutralized with lime and evaporated, crystals of calcium malate will form. From a solution of this salt, the free acid is obtained by adding the exact amount of sulphuric acid required, filtering off the calcium sulphate and evaporating the filtrate. 

Malic acid is a deliquescent solid melting at 100°. It is very soluble in water but less so in alcohol and ether. The constitution of the acid is shown by the fact that it is an intermediate product in the reduction of tartaric acid by hydriodic acid to succinic acid:

Malic acid, as obtained from plants, is optically active but in a curious way. In concentrated solution it rotates toward the right, but in dilute solutions toward the left, while at a point between it does not rotate at all. The racemic acid, which melts at 130°, can be obtained by appropriate synthetic methods. It can be resolved into the two optically active forms by means of the cinchonine salt. 

317. The Walden Inversion. When one group in an organic molecule is replaced by another, as when a bromide is made from an alcohol, it is naturally assumed that the exact position occupied by the original group is taken by the one entering. When an optically active compound is subjected to any drastic treatment, such as heating to a high temperature or boiling with strong acids or alkalies it is commonly racemized. The groups may be supposed to have been momentarily detached and reunited in a helterskelter fashion. If drastic conditions are avoided, an optically active compound may be put through a series of reactions and brought back to its original state with very little loss of optical

HYDROXYL AND CARBOXYL-HYDROXY-ACIDS 331 

activity. Walden discovered a remarkable inversion which has never been satisfactorily explained; in some cases the optically active compound is regenerated with practically undiminished rotation, but the direction of the rotation has been reversed. In some cases the same active compound can be converted into compounds of opposite configuration. Thus l-chlorosuccinic acid gives l-malic acid or d-malic acid, according to whether silver hydroxide or potassium hydroxide is used to remove the halogen: COOH HCH нсон COOH with AgOH COOH 1-Malic acid HCH HCCI COOH with KOH 

1-Chloro-succinic acid

COOH HCH HOCH COOH COOH d-Malic acid It is possible to go completely around the circle:

COOH COOH HCH with AgOH HCH HCCI HCOH Соон COOH 

1-Chloro-succinic acid ↑ with PCl5 COOH HCH HOCH with KOH

COOH d-Malic acid COOH 1-Malic acid ↓ with PCl5 COOH HCH CICH CICH Соон COOH d-Chlorosuccinic acid

Since the original discovery in 1895 a great many transformations of this sort have been discovered. The Walden inversion gives a valuable method of converting one optical isomer into the other. 

318. Tartaric Acid. HOOC CH(OH)·CH(OH) COOH. This acid, or more properly the group of four tartaric acids, is of great importance. The investigation of these acids by Pasteur was a brilliant chapter in the history of organic chemistry and led to a great advance in the understanding of optical activity. d-Tartaric acid is found in many vegetable products, sometimes as the free acid but more commonly as the acid potassium or calcium salt. Grapes contain a large proportion of the acid potassium salt. This salt is only sparingly soluble in water and less soluble when alcohol is present. Hence a large proportion of it separates when alcohol is formed during the fermentation of grape juice. The sediment that forms in a wine vat hardens to a crust which is known as argol or tartar. The argol is mainly acid potassium tartrate, but contains various other substances, including some coloring matter. It is dissolved in hot water, the solution decolorized with animal charcoal, filtered, and cooled or evaporated. The purified salt is known as cream of tartar. Or the acid potassium tartrate may be converted into the neutral calcium salt CaC4H406·4H2O, of which only 0.016 g. is soluble in 100 cc. of water at 15°: and 2KHC4H4O6+ Ca(OH)2 → K2C4H4O6 + CaC4H406 K2C4H4O6+ CaCl2 → CaC4H4O6 + 2KCI The calcium salt is collected and decomposed with the calculated amount of dilute sulphuric acid. The calcium sulphate is filtered off and the filtrate evaporated in lead-lined pans under reduced pressure. The free acid is very soluble in water, 343 g. per 100 cc. at 100° and 115 g. at 0°. It melts at 180° but cannot be distilled, as at a little above its melting point it begins to lose water and yield anhydrides which differ with conditions. Heated higher it turns brown and finally chars, with the formation of a variety of products, among them pyruvic (340) and pyro-tartaric acids.

Heated to 175° with a small proportion of water, it is transformed

HYDROXYL AND CARBOXYL-HYDROXY-ACIDS 333 

largely into racemic acid and to a less extent into meso-tartaric acid. 

319. Salts of Tartaric Acid. The acid potassium tartrate, or cream of tartar, has already been mentioned. It is only slightly soluble in cold water, 0.60 g. in 100 cc. of water at 20°, but much more so in hot water, 6.95 g. at 100°. It is used on a very large scale for making the cream of tartar baking powders. Sodium potassium tartrate, KNaC4H4O6-4H2O, formed by the action of acid potassium tartrate on soda, is known as Rochelle salt. It crystallizes well and is readily obtained in pure condition. Tartar emetic, which is potassium antimonyl tartrate, K(SbO) C4H4O6 H2O, has been used in medicine and as a mordant in dyeing. A baking powder contains sodium bicarbonate mixed with a solid acid or a solid which may function as an acid. When water is added to the mixture, solution takes place followed by the evolution of carbon dioxide. While soda is used in all powders, many different acids have been employed. The sodium salt of the acid must be non-toxic, as it remains in the bread. The acid must not be deliquescent, else it would attract moisture and react prematurely with the soda Tartaric acid fails in the latter respect. 

Cream of tartar, in spite of the fact that it is already half neutralized, has been extensively employed:

KHC4H4O6+ NaHCO3 188 84

KNаC406H4 + H2O + CO2 210 18 44

A popular mixture is two pounds of cream of tartar to one of baking soda, which corresponds very well with the above equation. 

A baking powder keeps better if some dry inert material is mixed with the active constituents. Some variety of starch is commonly added, the amount being adjusted so that the carbon dioxide evolved will be about 13 per cent by weight. 

320. Racemic Acid. This acid is sometimes found with tartaric acid in grapes. Acid potassium racemate is more soluble than the corresponding tartrate and can be obtained from the argol mother liquor. Racemic acid can be synthetically made in various ways as well as by heating tartaric acid. It crystallizes with one molecule of water which is driven off at about 110°, the

anhydrous acid melting at 206°. It is optically inactive and differs markedly from tartaric acid in its physical properties. Its salts differ in solubility and in other physical properties from those of tartaric acid. Yet all the reactions of racemic acid are identical with those of tartaric acid and all the methods of synthesis of the two acids point to the same structural formula for racemic and for the tartaric acids. In 1848 Pasteur, while investigating the crystalline form of the salts of racemic acid, observed that its sodium ammonium salt, on spontaneous evaporation, gave two kinds of crystals. The crystals of the two kinds had the same faces and angles but differed in the arrangement of these, a crystal of the one sort being a mirror image of one of the other. Pasteur separated the two varieties of crystals and found that a solution of the one turned the plane of polarized light to the right and a solution of the other to the left. From these two salts the free acids were obtained. One of these turned out to be d-tartaric acid, identical in every respect with the natural acid, while the other was a new acid having exactly the same chemical and physical properties as d-tartaric acid but being laevo-rotatory and hence called l-tartaric acid. The rotations of the two are equal in amount but opposite in direction. When penicillium glaucum is grown in a solution containing racemic acid, l-tartaric acid is left unconsumed. 

When equal amounts of d-tartaric and l-tartaric acid are dissolved in water and the solutions mixed, racemic acid crystallizes from the solution. It appears that racemic acid is not simply a mixture of the two active tartaric acids, but rather some sort of molecular combination of the two. Yet observations on the water solutions of racemic acid indicate that its molecule corresponds to C4H6О6. The vapors of its esters have molecular weights corresponding to the unimolecular form. The salts of l-tartaric acid are exactly like those of d-tartaric acid in all respects, except in their action on polarized light. When a solution of a salt of d-tartaric acid is mixed with a solution of an equal amount of the corresponding salt of l-tartaric acid, a salt of racemic acid is produced. 

Racemic acid, being the first inactive compound to be resolved into two active components, has given its name to the inactive mixtures of optically active compounds. Such a mixture is said to be racemic. A compound is said to exist in a racemic and two active modifications as d-tartaric acid, l-tartaric acid, and racemic

HYDROXYL AND CARBOXYL-HYDROXY-ACIDS 335 

acid, which has been written r-tartaric acid but is preferably written dl-tartaric acid. In place of racemic the word "inactive" has been frequently used, but this is not accurate in all cases, since, as will appear in the section below, there are inactive compounds which are inactive by internal compensation and consequently incapable of resolution. When a racemic compound is separated into two active compounds, it is said to be resolved into its optical antipodes. 

321. The Separation of Racemic Mixtures into Active Com ponents. Pasteur devised three methods for separating racemic acid into active tartaric acids: (1) mechanical, (2) salts with active bases, (3) biochemical. These three methods have been standard ever since and have been successfully applied to many racemic mixtures. 

1. Mechanical method. This is the method by which the first separation was made, as was described above. It is applicable only in the rare cases in which the components of a racemic mixture crystallize separately in well-formed distinguishable crystals. 

Below 27°, sodium ammonium racemate separates in right- and left-handed forms, but above that temperature a mixed salt is obtained. The zinc ammonium salt of dl-lactic acid crystallizes in two forms which can be separated. From these d-lactic and 

7-lactic acids have been isolated. 

2. Salts with active bases. This is the method that has the most general application and is the one commonly used. Optically active bases, such as quinine, brucine and cinchonine are known. d-Tartaric acid has exactly the same physical properties, including solubilities in various solvents, as l-tartaric acid. Similarly d-quinine has exactly the same physical properties, except direction of optical rotation, as l-quinine. The salts, d-quinine d-tartrate and l-quinine l-tartrate, have the same solubilities and other physical properties, except direction of rotation, but l-quinine d-tartrate is quite different from l-quinine l-tartrate. When l-quinine, the ordinary form of this base, is added to a solution of racemic acid, these two salts are formed. The l-quinine d-tartrate is less soluble in water than the other salt and may be obtained pure by recrystallization. From this salt pure d-tartaric acid can be separated. It has been found that d-cinchonine l-tartrate is less soluble in water

than d-cinchonine d-tartrate and crystallizes out when this base is added to a solution of racemic acid of the proper strength. By recrystallization this salt may be obtained pure and l-tartaric acid prepared from it. dl-Lactic acid was first resolved into its optically active components by combining it with strychnine, an active base. Conversely, this method may be used for the resolution of a racemic mixture of the two forms of an active base. 

3. The biochemical method. It was known before Pasteur's time that tartaric acid is destroyed by certain ferments. He found that a green mould, Penicillium, when grown in ammonium racemate, destroys the salt of the dextro acid and leaves ammonium l-tartrate in solution, from which it may be obtained by evaporation. It has been found in many cases that fungi and bacteria, or the enzymes from them, destroy one optical modification and do not touch the other. Thus d-glucose is readily fermented by yeast but l-glucose is not. If dl-glucose is subjected to fermentation l-glucose is left and may be isolated. The active form that is found in natural products is the one that is most readily attacked by enzymes. This method has given good service in many cases but is limited in its application, and has this serious disadvantage one of the modifications is lost in the process. 

322. Meso-Tartaric Acid. i-Tartaric acid, or meso-tartaric acid, is formed by certain synthetic methods and by heating tartaric acid as stated above. Analysis shows it to have the same composition as the other tartaric acids and it has the same molecular weight. It is produced by the same synthetical methods that yield the other tartaric acids, and its reactions show that it must have the same structural formula, notwithstanding the fact that it melts much lower than the other acids and that its acid potassium salt is readily soluble in water. 

It has been found to be impossible to resolve i-tartaric acid into two active components. The explanation now given is that it is internally compensated. The molecule of tartaric acid consists of two halves which contain exactly the same groups. If the groups in these two halves are so arranged that the action of the two halves on a beam of light are opposite, the one neutralizes the other and the effect of the whole molecule is nil. Since the two halves are rigidly bound together, no process that does not destroy

HYDROXYL AND CARBOXYL-HYDROXY-ACIDS 337 

the molecule can separate them, so there can be no resolution into optically active components. It is assumed that the two halves of the molecule of either of the active tartaric acids rotate the plane of the polarized light in the same direction. 

323. The Configuration of the Tartaric Acids. Since the groups are supposed to be arranged around the two central carbon atoms in space of three dimensions, the molecules cannot be properly represented in a diagram on a plane surface. Models are useful in making these relations clear. They may be constructed by the student from corks and bits of wire. By agreeing that certain arrangements of the atomic symbols on paper stand for certain groupings in space, printed diagrams can take the place of the models. The two active acids and meso-tartaric acid are represented thus in print: COOH

H-C-OH HO-C-H COOH d-Tartaric acid COOH

HO-C-H H-C-OH COOH 

1-Tartaric acid COOH

H-C-OH H-C-OH COOH 

Meso-tartaric acid 

Racemic acid

The two asymmetric carbon atoms of each acid are printed in heavy type. If the first of these is imagined to be a model suspended by the upper asymmetric carbon atom, the three groups, -H, -COOH and -OH, will take their positions in a plane somewhat below the lower asymmetric carbon atom. Looking down on these three groups they appear to be in clockwise sequence. 

If the same model is suspended by the lower asymmetric carbon so that the other carbon and its groups hang down, these groups will be found to be in the same clockwise sequence. If one-half of the molecule is dextro, the other half is also. These diagrams are conventional and either one may be assigned to d-tartaric acid, but when this is done the other must represent the laevo acid. 

Taking the second formula, the same relationships are observed, except that the sequence of the groups is just opposite. In the model of inactive or meso-tartaric acid it is observed that the

sequence of the groups in one end is contrary to that in the other end of the chain. Whatever effect one end may have on a beam of light, the other end will have the opposite effect. In this case the upper half is a mirror image of the lower, just as the right hand is of the left. The one cannot be made to coincide with the other by superposition. As all of the molecules of meso-tartaric acid are of the same kind, there can be no separation into dextro and laevo. The first and second formulae are mirror images of each other and if a beam of light is acted upon by the molecules represented by both of them, the effect of one will be neutralized by the other. Light passed through a solution containing equal numbers of dextro and laevo molecules is not affected. Such a mixture is inactive by external compensation, but when the oppositely acting parts are both in the same molecule, it is called internal compensation. The racemic acid is a mixture of equal numbers of dextro and laevo molecules and may be separated into two active substances.
