326. Citric Acid. This acid was discovered in lemons by

Scheele in 1784 and was shown by Liebig to be a tribasic acid, since it forms three sodium or potassium salts. With ethyl alcohol it forms an ester which contains three ethyl groups. This ester can be acetylated, showing the presence of a hydroxyl group. 

The structure of citric acid is shown by its synthesis. Hydrocyanic acid is added to sym-dichloracetone (I). The cyanide (II) is hydrolyzed into the product (III), which is heated with potassium cyanide to form the double cyanide (IV), and this is hydrolyzed to citric acid (V).

CH2Cl II CH2Cl 

CH2Cl CH2CN CH2COOH OH OH OH OH CO CN COOH COOH CH2Cl CH2Cl CH2Cl CH2CN COOH CH2COOH 

Citric acid

Citric acid is very soluble in water, 207 g. in 100 cc. at 25°, less soluble in alcohol, 116 g. in 100 cc. at 25° and only slightly in ether. It forms rhombic prisms which contain one molecule of water. The hydrated acid melts at about 100°, loses water by 130° and then melts at 153°. Many of its salts are employed in medicine. The free acid is used in soft drinks and in calico printing. 

The juice of unripe lemons contains as high as 6 per cent of citric acid. For its isolation advantage is taken of the fact that calcium citrate is readily soluble in cold water but only slightly so in boiling water. The lemon juice is neutralized with calcium carbonate, the filtered solution boiled and filtered hot. The precipitated calcium citrate so obtained is dissolved in water and the calculated amount of sulphuric acid added. The solution of citric acid is filtered from the gypsum and evaporated. A ton of lemons contains about 70 pounds of citric acid, of which about 85 per cent is in the expressed juice. Citric acid is found in many other fruits and even in milk, which contains 0.16 to 0.2 per cent of it. 

By the use of the proper ferments citric acid is obtained, on a commercial scale, by the fermentation of beet juice and other sugar solutions. PROBLEMS 1. Give the equations for the preparation of lactic acid from (a) acetaldehyde, (b) propionic acid.

332. Proteins. Of all classes of organic compounds the proteins are probably the most important, since they are closely connected with life processes and are the chief constituents of living cells. Proteins are by far the most essential food materials and are the chief factors of life, growth and health. Digestion and assimilation are largely concerned with pulling to pieces the protein molecules and building others from their fragments. There are many individual proteins. These are not sharply characterized by melting points, boiling points, densities and other physical properties, as are the hydrocarbons, alcohols, esters and other compounds which have been considered in previous chapters. 

Instead of melting they decompose on heating and cannot be volatilized even in the most perfect vacuum. They are insoluble in such solvents as ether, benzene, aliphatic hydrocarbons and strong alcohol. In water some of them are readily soluble, some less so and some insoluble. Some that are readily soluble, as egg albumin, are precipitated by heating. Those that are soluble are precipitated from their water solutions by various substances. In some cases this is a mere salting out similar to the precipitation of sodium chloride from its water solution when concentrated hydrochloric acid is added. The salts used for this purpose are sodium chloride, ammonium, magnesium and zinc sulphates. Individual proteins are sometimes characterized in terms of the concentrations of ammonium sulphate at which the precipitation begins and at which it is complete. Other precipitants such as phosphotungstic acid, phosphomolybdic acid, picric acid and tannic acid form more or less definite compounds with proteins. Salts of the heavy metals, such as copper acetate, mercuric chloride and lead acetate precipitate most proteins. In the absence of melting points or of crystalline derivatives of the proteins, they are characterized by their solubility in water and in salt solutions or in acids or alkalies. 

Proteins in water solution depress the freezing point of water very slightly, so slightly that molecular weights calculated from the depressions by the freezing point method are far from accurate. 

Yet the conclusion is certain that the molecular weights are very large. Various determinations have given molecular weights from 

500 to 15,000. The simpler proteins are probably present in true solution, while some of the more complex proteins may be in colloidal condition. This is indicated by their precipitation with

electrolytes. An idea of the minimum molecular weight may be obtained from the percentages of sulphur and phosphorus present. 

Sulphur appears to be a constant constituent rather than an accidental contamination of most of the proteins. In some of them the percentage is very low; for instance, zein, a protein from maize, contains 0.60 per cent of sulphur. If the molecule contains one atom of sulphur, the molecular weight is found by the proportion: 

0.6 100 :: 32: x

This gives x 5333. Some other proteins contain still less sulphur and must have even larger molecular weights. The actual molecules may be multiples of the minimum or empirical formula. 

These molecules are probably more or less grouped together as colloidal particles. 

333. Classification of Proteins. Three classes are recognized: 

Class I.-Simple proteins. 

Class II.-Simple proteins combined with more or less complex molecules of non-protein nature. It is usually possible to break this union by comparatively simple chemical treatment. 

Class III.-Derived proteins comprising those formed from the above classes by action of reagents or heat. The following subdivisions of these three classes have been adopted by the American Society of Biological Chemists. Inspection of these will show that they are not based on differences of constitution, but rather on superficial physical properties. The members of Class II are subdivided according to the non-protein substance present. 

I. SIMPLE PROTEINS. Protein substances which yield only a-amino-acids or their derivatives on hydrolysis. The various groups of simple proteins are designated as follows: (a) Albumins. Simple proteins soluble in pure water and coagulated by heat. (b) Globulins. Simple proteins insoluble in pure water, but soluble in neutral solutions of salts of strong bases with strong acids. (c) Glutelins. Simple proteins insoluble in all neutral solvents but readily soluble in very dilute acids and alkalies. (d) Alcohol-soluble Proteins. Prolamins. Simple proteins soluble in relatively strong alcohol (70-80 per cent), but insoluble in water, absolute alcohol, and other neutral solvents.

(e) Albuminoids. Simple proteins which possess essentially the same chemical structure as the other proteins, but are characterized by great insolubility in all neutral solvents. (f) Histones. Soluble in water and insoluble in very dilute ammonia and in the absence of ammonium salts, insoluble even in an excess of ammonia; yield precipitates with solutions of other proteins and a coagulum on heating, which is easily soluble in very diltue acids. On hydrolysis they yield a large number of amino-acids, in which the basic ones predominate. (g) Protamines. Simpler polypeptids than the proteins included_in the preceding groups. They are soluble in water, uncoagulated by heat, have the property of precipitating aqueous solutions of other proteins, possess strong basic properties, and form stable salts with strong mineral acids. They yield comparatively few amino-acids, among which the basic amino-acids predominate. 

II. CONJUGATED PROTEINS. Substances which contain the protein molecule united to some other molecule or molecules otherwise than as a salt. (a) Nucleoproteins. Compounds of one or more protein molecules with nucleic acid. (b) Glycoproteins. Compounds of the protein molecule with a substance or substances containing a carbohydrate group other than a nucleic acid. (c) Phosphoproteins, Compounds of the protein molecule with some, as yet undefined, phosphorus containing substance other than a nucleic acid or lecithins. (d) Haemoglobins. Compounds of the protein molecule with hematin or some similar substance. (e) Lecithoproteins. Compounds of the protein molecule with lecithins (lecithans, phosphatids).

III. DERIVED PROTEINS. 

1. Primary Protein Derivatives. Derivatives of the protein molecule apparently formed through hydrolytic changes which involve only slight alterations of the protein molecule. (a) Proteins. Insoluble products which apparently result from the incipient action of water, very dilute acids, or enzymes. (b) Metaproteins. Products of the further action of acids and alkali whereby the molecule is so far altered as to form products soluble in very weak acids, and alkalies but insoluble in neutral fluids. This group includes what are ordinarily called acid albuminates and alkali albuminates, but does not include the salts of proteins with acids.

(c) Coagulated Proteins. Insoluble products which result from the action of heat on their solution, or the action of alcohols on the proteins. 

2. Secondary Protein Derivatives. Products of the further hydrolytic cleavage of the protein molecule. (a) Proteoses. Soluble in water, uncoagulated by heat, and precipitated by saturating their solutions with ammonium sulphate or zinc sulphate. (b) Peptones. Soluble in water, uncoagulated by heat, but not precipitated by saturating their solutions with ammonium sulphate. (c) Peptids. Definitely characterized combinations of two or more amino-acids, the carboxyl group of one being united with the amino group of the other with the elimination of a molecule of water.

335. Estimation of Proteins in Foods. Foodstuffs have long been classified according to their content of proteins, their most valuable constituents, but it can be readily seen that it would be

difficult to separate the proteins quantitatively from a piece of meat or a sample of cattle food, and even more troublesome to get them into a condition suitable for accurate weighing. The element nitrogen is the characteristic element of the proteins, and since it is readily determined, it is used as the basis of the estimation of protein. Two assumptions, neither of which is strictly correct, are made: first, that protein is the only nitrogenous substance present and, second, that it contains 16 per cent of nitrogen. The nitrogen is determined, usually by the Kjeldahl method and the per cent found is multiplied by the factor 6.25 (100 per cent ÷ 16 per cent 

6.25). If the source of the food is known, a factor other than 6.25 may be used according to the nitrogen content of the protein present. All natural foods contain proteins, fats or carbohydrates. 

Usually the protein is the only nitrogen bearing material present in any considerable amount. The protein is the body building part of the food while the fats and carbohydrates are mainly energy producers. Foods have commonly been rated on their content of these three. It is now known that proteins have unequal food values and certain accessory substances which do not belong to these three classes must be present in a complete diet. A high protein content does not necessarily mean a high nutritive value, but if the protein is low, the food value cannot be high. 

335a. Hydrolysis of Proteins. When any protein is heated with moderately concentrated hydrochloric or sulphuric acid or with alkali, it is broken down into a number of parts which prove to be amino acids. Enzymes may effect the same disintegration. 

These facts have long been known and many special processes have been developed for isolating particular products from hydrolyzed proteins. The most thorough and general method of working up this mixture was devised by Emil Fischer.1 The amino-acids, resulting from the hydrolysis of a protein are converted into their methyl esters which are separated by fractional distillation at a very low pressure. 337. The Constitution of Proteins. While it is possible to take a protein to pieces and identify all of the parts, it is not yet possible to reconstruct the protein from these parts. Yet these parts can be coupled together to build up molecules that resemble the proteins and very probable surmises have been made as to how the parts are put together in natural proteins. As proteins are not salts they cannot be produced by the simple union of an acid and a base as ammonium acetate, otherwise they would break up when dissolved in water. It withstands boiling in water, but when heated with an acid or a base it is readily hydrolyzed. Nitrous acid reacts in a characteristic way with ammonia or with primary amines, evolving gaseous nitrogen (177). This reaction is so complete that it is used for the quantitative determination of ammonia and the amino group. A sample of a protein when treated with nitrous acid liberates only a trifling amount of nitrogen which shows that it does not contain amino groups, but if the same amount of the same material is boiled with acid for a time and then similarly treated, there will be a large evolution of nitrogen. Similarly proteins do not show acid properties and hence do not contain carboxyl groups, or at most a very small proportion of such groups, but after hydrolysis with strong acid carboxyl groups are present. Carboxyl and primary amino groups, -NH2, are simultaneously produced in the hydroly-

This contains the link -CONH- and on hydrolysis would give two molecules of glycine. It is possible to carry this method of synthesis a step further and prepare glycyl-glycyl-glycine. In fact this process may be repeated a number of times so as to link together a large number of glycine molecules. A similar chain may be built up, using a single amino-acid or several different ones. In

The molecular weight of this is 1212. In properties it resembled one of the simpler proteins. Substances of this class are known as polypeptides. There is little doubt that the natural proteins are composed of amino-acid residues, by which are meant the acids, less the -OH of the carboxyl and one -H of the amino group, coupled together. They are in fact substituted amides. The molecule of a natural protein may contain a hundred or more amino-acid residues and these may be of a dozen different kinds. In the illustration above the simplest of the amino-acids have been used. With the more complicated ones branched chains or ring structures may be derived. A little contemplation will show that it would be possible to build an inconceivably large number of hypothetical protein molecules. If only six groups, two of each of three kinds, which may be called a, b and c, are taken there result: aabbcc, ababcc, abcabc, bcaacb, cabcab, cabacb and so on. 

With a hundred simple amino-acids of ten different kinds the number of possible arrangements approximates the number of post-war marks and roubles. While the way to the synthesis of proteins appears to be known, there seem to be insuperable difficulties in the way of duplicating any particular protein. It may well be that what is now considered a single protein, egg-albumin, for instance, may be simply a class of proteins numbering thousands or millions of individual proteins. It is even possible that each egg contains a slightly different protein. What has been said above has to do with proteins having the polypeptide structure. This appears to be the structure of the simpler proteins and is possibly the prevailing structure among the others, but some at least may have other structures.

When a protein is eaten, it is taken apart in the processes of digestion and assimilation and the resulting amino-acids used to build up proteins suited to the needs of the organism. The actual digestion of proteins is taken care of by special digestive enzymes. 

Pepsin, found in the gastric juice, splits proteins into proteoses and peptones. Trypsin, in the pancreatic juice, splits proteins into proteoses, peptones and amino-acids. Erepsin splits peptones into amino-acids and ammonia. To be a proper food for a particular animal the protein must furnish all of the kinds of amino-acids required by that animal. Articles of diet must be selected so as to

provide essential amino-acids that the body is unable to build. particularly tryptophane, cystine, lysine and histidine. 

338. Vitamins. When foods were first studied chemically, three classes of food constituents were recognized: proteins, fats and carbohydrates. For many years foods were rated according to their content of these three. It was believed that the food requirements of man and of other animals could be met by a proper supply of these together with small amounts of mineral salts. In recent years it has become evident that animals do not thrive on diets which do not include uncooked fruits, vegetables and milk. 

These substances contain some things in addition to sugars, fats and proteins which are necessary for good health. Certain diseases, as the beri-beri, are known to be due to deficiencies in these food accessories. The accessories have been named vitamins. This name came from the idea that vitamins might be amino compounds, more or less connected with the proteins. 

A vast amount of work has been done on vitamins; and their importance has been demonstrated. Vitamins A, B, C, D and E are recognized as being present in certain foods. They may be highly concentrated or even isolated but there is nothing definitely established as to their chemical constitution. Vitamin D, the antirachitic principle, is formed when ergosterol, a sterol related to cholesterol, which latter is the common sterol in mammalian tissues, is irradiated with ultra violet rays. Ergosterol is present in fungi generally, and is now readily prepared from either the oil of ergot or from yeast. PROBLEMS 1. CHAPTER XXIV OXO-ACIDS ALDEHYDE-ACIDS AND KETO-ACIDS 

339. The acids to be considered in this chapter contain a carbonyl group -CO- as well as the carboxyl group. Naturally they fall into two classes according to whether this group is at one end, as in HCO CH2 CH2. COOH or somewhere along the chain, as in CH3 CO-CH2-CH2-COOH. The first of these is evidently an aldehyde-acid while the other is a keto-acid. The general properties of the two classes can be predicted from a knowledge of aldehydes and ketones and of acids. As acids they will form salts, amides and esters, while the presence of the carbonyl group will manifest itself in ways characteristic of aldehydes and ketones. In the oxo-acids the two groups do not react with each other as the carboxyl does with an amino or hydroxyl group in the amino and hydroxy acids, but each group influences the reactions of the other. 

The amount and character of this influence depends on the distances between the groups.

When dibrom-acetic acid is heated with water, the bromine atoms are replaced by hydroxyl groups:

Acidification with acetic acid gives an oil which is ethyl acetoacetate, CH3 CO. CH2 · COOC2H5, and is commonly spoken of as aceto-acetic ester. In old chemical literature it is "aceto-acetic ether," esters being formerly called ethers in English as they still are in French. The reaction is known as the aceto-acetic ester condensation. The mechanism of this condensation is not yet clearly understood, although it has been the subject of many investigations.

In general this type of reaction is called a “condensation," since the result is the condensing of two molecules into one by union of the carbon atoms. The term " condensation " is usually reserved for those reactions by which carbon is made to combine with carbon to form a longer carbon chain than was originally present. 

¹ Anton Geuther (1833-1889), Professor at Jena 1863–1878, worked on sulphur compounds and derivatives of aceto-acetic ester.

Aceto-acetic ester is a somewhat oily liquid which has the density 1.021225, and boils at 180°. As it decomposes somewhat when boiled under atmospheric pressure, it is usually distilled at reduced pressure.

The property of this ester that adapts it to the synthesis of organic compounds is that it readily forms salts. When the ester is added to an equivalent amount of sodium in absolute alcohol, a mono-sodium salt of aceto-acetic ester is formed. This can be isolated by evaporating off the alcohol in a vacuum but the salt is always used in the alcohol solution just as it is formed. The same salt is produced by dissolving sodium in the ester, either pure or dissolved in a non-aqueous solvent. The sodium salt is completely hydrolyzed when put into water, which shows that the acid in it is extremely weak. The aceto-acetic ester salts of cobalt and copper are so very insoluble that they are precipitated when acetoacetic ester is added to water solutions of the acetates of these metals. The question arises as to which of the hydrogens in acetoacetic ester, CH3 CO CH2 CO-OC2H5, is replaced by the metal in its salts. There are three groups of hydrogen atoms, those in the methyl group, those in the ethyl and lastly those in the methylene group, -CH2-, in the middle of the molecule. In ethyl acetate, CH3 CO-OC2H5, methyl and ethyl groups are similarly placed but there is no salt formation. This fact points to the methylene group -CH2- as the location of the replaceable hydrogen. As there are two hydrogen atoms in this group which appear to be equivalent, aceto-acetic ester might be expected to function as a dibasic acid, but considering the fact that the monosodium salt is so readily hydrolyzed, the disodium salt would not be readily formed. Under ordinary conditions only one of these hydrogen atoms is replaceable by metals but when the place of this one is taken by an alkyl group, the second becomes replaceable. 

It will be recalled that the hydrogens of the methylene group in malonic ester are similarly reactive. The two compounds are much alike in constitution and also in their reactions: CO.OC2H5 H2C CO-OC2H5

342. The Tautomerism of Aceto-acetic Ester. This ester is the oldest and most famous example of tautomerism. It reacts with various compounds in the manner characteristic of ketones. 

Its physical properties agree with the ketone formula. Yet it gives a color with ferric chloride and dissolves sodium readily, both of which reactions indicate the presence of a hydroxyl group. Two different formulae have been proposed for this one compound: CH3.C.CH2.CO.OC2H5 and CH3 C-CH.CO.OC2H5 

Keto formula OH 

Enol formula

The designation enol is made up of the syllable, -en- which, as will be discussed more fully later (Chapter XXVI), designates a double bond between two carbon atoms, and the ending -ol which denotes a hydroxyl group. For some years there was a great deal of argument between the advocates of the two views. The suggestion was made that both formulae may be correct, the compound shifting from one to the other according to circumstances, somewhat as an actor may play different rôles at different times, appearing and acting quite differently according to the part. This phenomenon has been given the name of tautomerism, the word being compounded from the Greek words meaning "the same parts." Many similar cases have been discovered and are now included in the same class. Tautomerism is to be distinguished from isomerism in which there are two distinct substances to each of which a definite formula can be assigned. In both cases there are "the same parts." The possibility of isomers is due to the

stability of the arrangements of the atoms in the molecules of carbon compounds, but even this is relative rather than absolute and there are many degrees of stability. Usually the carbon to carbon linkages are the most permanent but cases are known where even these are shifted. The hydrogen to carbon linkage is usually quite stable in hydrocarbons, except at high temperatures, but as shown above the hydrogen becomes loosened under some circumstances. 

The transformation of propyl bromide into isopropyl bromide by contact with aluminum bromide has already been considered: CH, CH, CH2Br → CHg•CHBr-CH3 n-Propyl bromide i-Propyl bromide

In this reaction a bromine atom changes its attachment from one carbon atom to another and a hydrogen atom moves in the opposite direction. The n-propyl bromide and i-propyl bromide are wellknown substances, distinct from each other and having entirely different properties. A catalyst causes the n-propyl bromide to rearrange into the iso-propyl bromide but no way is known of bringing about the reverse change. Corresponding to the lightness of the hydrogen atom, to its ready dissociation as in the ionization of acids and to the high migration velocity of the hydrogen ion, many cases have been found in which a hydrogen atom shifts its position in a molecule with comparative ease. Tautomerism may be limited to the shifting of a hydrogen atom from one position to another. In case there is a double bond, as there is in the C=0 group in aceto-acetic ester, there is a readjustment of the bonds to compensate for the change of linkage of the hydrogen atoms and only one atom moves. In terms of electrons, probably the only thing that really migrates is the proton of the hydrogen; the electron which it leaves would move in between the two carbon atoms, causing a readjustment of the valence electrons of the other carbon atom, the result being that the oxygen atom acquires an electron and is left in the state in which it exists in the hydroxyl group. 

There are cases of isomerization in which only one hydrogen atom moves but tautomerism is distinguished by the ready reversibility of the process, the two forms coexisting in what appears to be a single substance. These two forms are called tautomers; sometimes the one is called a tautomer of the other just as i-propyl bromide is an isomer of n-propyl bromide.

OXO-ACIDS 

363 According to the conception of tautomerism, the liquid which is prepared in the laboratory and which is known as aceto-acetic ester is actually a mixture of the two kinds of molecules which are represented by the two formulae above. These are in dynamic equilibrium with each other; if in some reaction the keto molecules are used up, the enol molecules at once rearrange into keto to restore the equilibrium, this process continuing until complete transformation has taken place. If sodium ethylate is added to aceto-acetic ester, it is the enol form that reacts to form the sodium salt. As the enol molecules are used up some of the keto molecules change to enol. If an excess of sodium ethylate is added all of the keto molecules disappear and the final product is the sodium salt of the enol form. This is very similar to the equilibrium between molecular and ionized acetic acid in water solution. If hydroxyl ions are added, the hydrogen ions are used up until there is complete dissociation of the acetic acid, but if the acetic acid molecules are extracted with ether more molecules are formed by recombination of the ions. 

In 1911, after forty-five years of discussion and supposition, the above view of the aceto-acetic ester tautomerism was verified by the isolation of the keto and enol forms. Aceto-acetic ester largely solidifies when it is cooled in a bath of solid carbon dioxide and ether. At that temperature the velocity of the transformation of the one form into the other is extremely slow and the liquid form is not transformed to the solid. The solid form which melts at-39°, has been shown to be the keto form. By treating the solid sodium compound of aceto-acetic ester with dry hydrogen chloride the aceto-acetic ester that is set free is largely the enol form. The two forms differ from each other in density, refractive index, boiling point and solidification point. Either of them is transformed into the ordinary equilibrium mixture, slowly at low temperatures and rapidly at high temperatures. Various substances, particularly acids and alkalies hasten this change; even contact with ordinary glass is sufficient to bring about the change. 

The proportion in which the two forms are present in any mixture can be estimated by determining the amount of bromine taken up, since only the enol form adds bromine. In pure aceto-acetic ester that has come to equilibrium at room temperature there is about 93 per cent of the keto form and about 7 per cent of the enol form.

Besides aceto-acetic ester many other examples of tautomerism have been found. In a very few cases it is possible to separate the two forms; in many more cases, estimates can be reached as to the relative amounts of the two forms that are present. The evidence for the coexistence of the two forms is so clear in the case of acetoacetic ester that it is generally believed that the corresponding forms exist in many cases in which their separation has not been accomplished.2 

343. The Reactions of the Sodium Salt of Aceto-acetic Ester. 

As will appear below, this sodium salt is used extensively in syntheses. In all the syntheses, so far considered, in which a sodium salt is used with an alkyl halide as in the preparation of ethers, it has been assumed that the alkyl enters the place in the molecule from which the sodium has been removed; that is, that the structure of the alkyl derivative and of the sodium compound are identical. As a matter of experience, the alkyl in the product obtained by the reaction of an alkyl halide on the sodium salt of aceto-acetic ester is joined to the carbon atom of the -CH2group and not to the oxygen as would be expected from the enol formula of the sodium salt. To account for this, the reaction with the alkyl halide is represented as taking place by the addition of the parts of the latter to the two sides of the double bond: ONa CH3 C=CH-CO-OC2H5→ CH3C-CH-COOC2H5 ONa I-C2H5 C2H5

CHAPTER XXV OXO-ALCOHOLS CARBOHYDRATES OR SACCHARIDES 

348. From several standpoints this group of compounds is of the greatest interest. In the growth of plants carbohydrates are of the utmost importance. Sugars which are in the sap of plants, starches which the plants store up in such quantities and cellulose from which they construct their framework, all belong to this class. 

Sugars and starches are important as food materials while cellulose in myriad forms of paper, cotton thread and cloth, and wood products makes up a large part of the wares of commerce. quest of the sugars, that is the determination of their constitutions and the tracing of their intricate relationships leading up to the synthesis of the simple sugars, is regarded as the most brilliant achievement of organic chemistry. It is largely due to the genius and industry of Emil Fischer. The con- The name carbohydrates has been given to the group, since all but a few of them contain just twice as many atoms of hydrogen as of oxygen. Some of the best known are dextrose, C6H12O6, levulose, C6H12O6, sucrose, C12H22O11, and lactose, C12H22O11. 

Considering the composition only, these can be written C6-6(H2O) and C12 11(H2O). This is not to be taken as meaning that they can be produced by bringing carbon in contact with water. There are a few compounds which belong to the group which do not have exactly this composition and some substances such as acetic and lactic acids, C2H4O2 and C3H6O3, which have carbohydrate formulae but none of their other characteristics. This name is going out of use since it is derived from a non-essential characteristic of only a part of the class. The designation saccharides is from the fact that all the sugars belong to this group. The saccharides are divided into mono-, di- (including several tri- and tetra-) and polysaccharides, or monoses, dioses and polyoses respec- 370

OXO-ALCOHOLS 

371 tively for those containing one, two, or several simple sugars. 

Starch and cellulose, which in their physical properties seem quite unlike the sugars, are put in this class since they can be transformed into sugars by simple treatment.

As in the case of the oxo-acids they are divided into two great classes, aldoses and ketoses, depending upon whether the carbonyl group is at the end of the chain or in some other position. In the longer chains it is conceivable that there might be several ketoses since the keto-group might be in either position 2, 3 or 4, etc. However, only the ketoses with the carbonyl group in the 2 position are of any interest, so only these will be considered.

Of all the groups, the hexoses overshadow all the others. The pentoses are next in importance. 

The other groups are largely synthetic compounds which are of scientific interest, as they are required for completing the system. 

All the monosaccharides, or simple sugars, have been found to be straight chain compounds. This has been proved by reducing various ones to known straight chain compounds and further verified by passing from one member of a series to the next higher by reactions which are known to add a carbon atom at the end of the chain. The reactions of any one sugar are of two classes, those due to the hydroxyl groups and those characteristic of the carbonyl group. The characteristic reactions of the hydroxyl groups are esterification and etherification. Thus acetates and other esters are readily formed, one acid radical entering the molecule for each hydroxyl group present. This is a method for determining the number of hydroxyl groups present in a sugar. For example, dextrose forms a pentacetate, hence it contains five alcoholic hydroxyls. Diazo-methane and other methylating agents convert the hydroxyl groups into methoxyls, -OCH3. This has been of great use in the study of the structure of the sugars. 

With some reagents a hydroxyl group reacts more readily than the group which it is desired to attack. In such cases the hydroxyl

OXO-ALCOHOLS 

373 is rendered inactive or "protected" by methylation. Methylation of the hydroxyl groups in a sugar renders it less soluble in water and more soluble in organic solvents, which is sometimes an advantage in making separations. Of the hydroxyl groups present in an aldose one is primary and the others are secondary. In a ketose there are two primary hydroxyls, of which the one adjoining the keto group is the more reactive and the more readily oxidised. 

The carbonyl group reacts readily with hydroxyl amine and with phenyl-hydrazine, C6H5NH NH2 (Chapter XXXII). The latter reagent has been spoken of as the "key to the sugars." The aldoses, as is to be expected, are readily oxidised to the corresponding hydroxy-acids. As there is a primary alcohol group at the other end of the carbon chain, the oxidation goes further to give a hydroxy-dibasic acid. The aldoses add hydrocyanic acid readily to form cyanhydrines which readily yield acids. This is an important method of lengthening the carbon chain. 

351. Glucose. Of all the monoses this is the most abundant in natural products and the most widely distributed. It is found free in many fruits, particularly in grapes, from which fact it is called grape sugar. It is regularly found in the blood and urine although in very small amounts. In diabetes mellitus the amount in the urine may rise as high as 12 per cent corresponding to the excretion of 500 to 1000 g. per day. Scores of natural products, such as indican, tannin, and amygdalin give glucose as one product of hydrolysis either by the action of enzymes or on heating with dilute mineral acid. Such substances are known as glucosides. 

In each case some other substance is formed in addition to the glucose. Thus indican is split into glucose and indigo, tannin into glucose and gallic acid and amygdalin into glucose, benzaldehyde and hydrocyanic acid. Among the polysaccharides many glucosides are found, the best known being sucrose, ordinary sugar, which splits into equal parts of glucose and levulose: C12H22O11+ H2O → C6H12O6 + C6H12O6 Sucrose Glucose Levulose

The best laboratory method for the preparation of glucose is the hydrolysis of cane sugar by hydrochloric acid. It is separated from the levulose by crystallization from alcohol. Commercially, glucose is made on an enormous scale by the hydrolysis of stareh

by hydrochloric acid in an autoclave, the closed vessel being used so that the solution may be heated above its normal boiling point. 

In order to make corn syrup for use on the table and in the making of confectionery, the hydrolysis is not carried to completion, as it is for glucose that is to be fermented. 

Glucose, which is commonly called d-glucose since it rotates the plane of polarized light to the right, can be obtained in two forms known as a- and B-d-glucose. When d-glucose crystallizes from a water solution in the cold, the a-form is obtained as the hydrate, C6H12O6+ H2O. From boiling alcohol it separates anhydrous. 

It crystallizes in prisms which melt at 146°. In 100 g. of water 

32.3 g. glucose dissolves at 0° and 82 g. at 25°. When a glucose solution is evaporated to dryness at 110°, the residue dissolved in its own volume of water and alcohol added with stirring, B-d-glucose is precipitated. The two differ from each other in rotation, the specific rotation of the a-form being +111.2° and that of the ẞform +17.5°. These values are for freshly made solutions. 

Slowly in pure water, more rapidly in dilute acid or alkali, both of them change until they have the value +52.3°. This phenomenon is known as mutarotation and is shown by some other sugars. It is believed that each of the two modifications is transformed into the other until an equilibrium is reached, the final value of the rotation being the average rotation of the constituents of the mixture. d-Glucose is readily fermented by yeast, or zymase, to alcohol and carbon dioxide:

C6H12O62C2H5OH + 2CO2 d-Glucose

Alcohol l-Glucose, which can be obtained in various ways, resembles d-glucose in all of its physical properties even appearing in a- and B-forms, the rotations of which are equal in magnitude but opposite in sign to those of the corresponding forms of d-glucose. They show mutarotation in the same manner. There is one striking difference; l-glucose is not fermented by yeast or zymase. If yeast is put into dl-glucose, the d-glucose is fermented and the l-glucose remains.

The aldehyde form of glucose is represented as being in dynamic equilibrium with the two modifications a-glucose and B-glucose. 

Some chemists prefer to regard alpha and beta-glucose as passing directly, the one into the other, without the aldehyde form acting as an intermediate. They assume that this takes place by the loss of a molecule of water from one of the modifications to give an unsaturated form which adds a molecule of water to give the other modification. The difference between alpha and betaglucose is believed to be due to the difference in spatial arrangements of the hydrogen and hydroxyl on the aldehyde carbon atom. 

In the aldehyde form this carbon is not asymmetric but it becomes so when the oxide ring is closed. In solution all three forms coexist. When a-glucose is dissolved in water, some of it passes into the beta form until the equilibrium is established and vice versa when the beta form is dissolved. As the equilibrium is mobile all of the glucose present in a solution may separate from a solution either as the a- or B-form, or it may react as if it were entirely the aldehyde. This is what takes place when a reagent is added which reacts with the aldehyde form and withdraws it from the solution.

This series of reactions is outstanding in its importance since by its aid the carbon chain of a sugar can be lengthened. By its use glucose has been converted into an aldo-heptose, an aldo-octose, an aldo-nonose, and finally into an aldo-decose. A pentose and then a hexose may be obtained by applying this reaction to a tetrose. By identifying the pentose and hexose formed from a given tetrose the genetic relationships of the pentoses and hexoses can be determined.

Attention must be called to the fact that lengthening the carbon chain brings in another asymmetric carbon atom, which means that two gluco-heptoses are obtained from the one glucose. These two heptoses have exactly the same structure as glucose, as far as the fifth carbon atom starting with the primary alcohol group, and differ from each other in the arrangement of the groups around the sixth carbon atom.

In a similar manner each aldose can be characterized and changed into a ketose. The result is that each aldose is linked up with a particular ketose, as d-glucose with d'-fructose. The only way to effect the reverse change is to reduce the ketose to the hexahydric alcohol, which can be oxidised to the aldohexose. 

355. Fructose. It has been mentioned that the hydrolysis of sucrose gives one molecule of d-glucose and one molecule of d'-fructose. These two sugars are found together in the juices of fruits. Inulin, a poly-saccharide, yields only d'-fructose on hydrolysis. d'-Fructose is much sweeter than glucose. It does not crystallize as well as glucose and is thus harder to isolate. From the fact that it turns the plane of rotation of polarized light to the left it is commonly called levulose, but in spite of this it is written d'-fructose to show its close relationship to d-glucose. The prime shows that its actual rotation is in the contrary direction. 

The structure of d'-fructose has been deduced from its reactions and from its formation from glucosozone, as described above. It can be acetylated and methylated and its ketone group reacts with the usual ketone reagents. Oxidation by means of mercuric oxide breaks the molecule into two parts, as is to be expected of a ketone, the products being glycollic and trihydroxy-butyric acids:

356. Mannose. This sugar is not found as such, but is found in many plants in the form of mannosans, which are condensation products of mannose, and are converted into mannose by hydrolysis with acids. Vegetable ivory nuts, from which buttons are commonly made, is a convenient source of mannose. Mannose has a sweet taste with a slightly bitter after-taste. It exists in alpha and beta forms and shows mutarotation. 

357. Galactose. The name indicates a relationship to lactose from which it is obtained by hydrolysis. In the form of galactan, its polymer, galactose is found in many gums and in pectins. It is a constituent of several complex substances that are found in the brain. Galactose exists in the alpha and beta forms and shows mutarotation. It is fermented by some yeasts. 

358. Configuration of the Monoses. By configuration is meant the arrangement of the groups around the asymmetric carbon atoms. The working out of the complicated relationships in the sugar groups has required an enormous amount of difficult experimentation and of keen reasoning. In Chapter IX optical activity has been considered. The use of models to show the arrangement of the atoms in three dimensional space was recommended. As the pictures of such models are difficult to draw on a blackboard and take up much space on a printed page, conventional representations that are readily written or printed have been devised to take their place. These are called projection formulae and may be derived from the shadows of the models. In this conventional system the formulae of the dextro- and levo-aldotrioses may be written:

CHO 

B CHO 

G HOCH

HCOH CH2OH CH2OH l-Aldotriose

d-Aldotriose

As these are conventional representations either may be called the dextro or levo form, and are merely symbols arranged in different orders to represent two substances which differ only in the arrangement of their parts. As the formulae are printed, the groups -CHO, -OH, -CH2OH amd H surround the asymmetric carbon atom in formula A in a certain sequence and are oppositely arranged in formula B. With reference to a plane MN, the one formula is a mirror image of the other; if one of them is taken to represent d-aldotriose the other will be assigned to l-aldotriose. 

A short-hand representation of these may be used. If it is agreed that in writing the structural formulae the primary alcohol group is always at the lower end of the chain, represented by a circle, and the aldehyde group at the upper end, represented by a triangle, the carbon chain may be represented by a vertical line. 

The hydroxyl group is designated by a short horizontal line and the hydrogen is simply understood to be opposite this. The above formulae then become: l-Aldotriose a-Aldotriose 

359. Number of Optical Isomers. When there is one asym metric carbon atom there will be one pair of isomers, a dextro and a levo form. This number will double every time an asymmetric carbon is added. Aldotriose exists in two forms, aldotetroses in four forms, aldopentoses in eight forms, and aldohexoses in sixteen forms. Of the sixteen aldohexoses, eight will be dextro and eight levo, each one of the dextro corresponding to one of the levo, the two having identical physical properties, except optical rotations which are numerically equal but have opposite signs. 

The diagram on next page represents the working out of the possible aldoses starting with the two aldotrioses and using the shorthand symbols. Hydrocyanic acid may be considered to be added to each of the two aldotrioses. As this introduces another asymmetric carbon atom, each one of the aldotrioses gives a mixture of two cyanhydrines, which by hydrolysis, lactone formation and reduction passes into a mixture of two aldotetroses. A separation

OXO-ALCOHOLS 

385 is supposed to be effected at one of these stages. Thus the two aldotrioses yield four aldotetroses. By a repetition of these processes, eight aldopentoses and sixteen aldohexoses should be obtained. Starting with d-aldotriose two aldotetroses are obtained, 1 and 2. In these the configuration of the lower asymmetric carbon atoms are the same as in the parent aldotriose, but the configurations around the upper carbons are reversed. From

HEXOSES ALDO- PENTOSES ALDO TETROSES ALDO TRIOSES FIG. 28.-The l- and d-Families of the Aldoses. 

aldotetrose 1, two aldopentoses, 1 and 2 are derived. The configurations around the two lower asymmetric carbons in these are identical with those of the parent tetrose 1, but the configurations around the upper carbons are reversed. From aldopentose 1, two aldohexoses, 1 and 2 are derived by reversing the configurations around the upper asymmetric carbon atom. Similar relationships can be traced up and down in all of the other groups. It is to be observed that the whole number of the aldoses can be divided into two groups called the d-sugars and the l-sugars, according to their relationships to d-aldotriose and l-aldotriose. The configuration

around the lower asymmetric carbon atom in any d-sugar is identical with that in d-aldotriose, and the same is true for the l-family. 

It is to be noticed that for each sugar in the d-family there is one exactly opposite in the l-family. Thus 1 is the mirror image of 1', 2 of 2', etc. Whatever rotation is shown by 1, will be equal in amount but opposite in sign to that of 1'. Sugars 1 and 1' will be identical in all other physical properties, such as solubility and melting point, and identical in reactivity with chemical reagents. 

The same can be said of any other pair. These statements hold equally well for pairs of tetroses, pentoses or hexoses and for the one pair of aldotrioses. So far as the heptoses and higher sugars have been investigated, the same is true of them. 

360. Determination of Configuration. The diagram above con tains all of the possible configurations for the aldoses up to six carbon atoms. Four pairs of aldopentoses are known. Fifteen aldohexoses have been discovered or prepared, of which fourteen are in pairs. As one member of each pair is the exact opposite of the other in rotation, only one need be studied. The discussion will be limited to the d-family. There are four d-aldopentoses: d-arabinose, d-ribose, d-lyxose and d-xylose. The problem is to assign the proper one of the four formulae, 1, 2, 3 and 4, in the diagram above to each of these. 

When treated with phenylhydrazine, d-arabinose and d-ribose give identical osazones, which shows that they differ only in the configuration around the carbon next to the aldehyde group. This shows that these two sugars are either the pair 1 and 2 or the pair 3 and 4. On oxidation arabinose gives an optically active dibasic acid and so does lyxose, while ribose and xylose give dibasic acids that are optically inactive and that cannot be resolved into active acids, which shows that they are internally compensated. These two acids have different properties, the one from xylose melting at 152° and that from ribose being converted into a lactone on heating. Inspection of the diagram shows that the pentoses having formulae 1 and 3 should give internally compensated acids, while those having formulae 2 and 4 should give optically active dibasic acids. Hence formulae 2 and 4 belong to arabinose and lyxose and 1 and 3 to ribose and xylose. It is necessary to decide which of the formulae 2 and 4 belongs to arabinose and which to

361. The Rotations of the Sugars of the d-Family. It has been considered of more importance to show the interrelations of the sugars than to tell the sign of the actual rotation. Hence all of the sugars of this group are given the prefix d- to show that they belong to the same group as d-glucose. As a matter of fact, the gulose, idose, xylose and threose which are put in the d-family on account of their genetic relationships to the other d-sugars, rotate the plane of polarized light to the left. In order to indicate that their rotation is opposite to that indicated by the prefix, they are written d'-gulose, d'-idose, etc. Conversely, l'-gulose belongs to the l-family but rotates to the right. 

362. The Configuration of the Ketoses. The configuration of any ketose follows immediately from that of the aldose with which it is connected through the osazone. As there can be only half as many keto hexoses as there are aldohexoses, a pair of aldoses corresponds to each ketose. As d-glucose and d-mannose differ only

in the configuration around the carbon atom next to the aldehyde group, both of them correspond to d'-fructose. The three form a group:

Nothing need be said here about the keto-pentoses and ketotetroses. 

363. The Pentoses. Two of these, l-arabinose and d'-xylose, are widely distributed in nature in polymeric forms called pentosans but are not found as the simple sugars. Xylose is obtained from straw, oat hulls and most woods, and l-arabinose from gums such as cherry gum and gum-arabic. d-Arabinose is also found in plants. d-Ribose is a product of the plant nucleic acids and appears to be the only pentose present in them. 

The pentosans, which are high molecular weight polymers of the pentoses, appear to be chiefly structural materials in plants. 

They are not hydrolyzed by enzymes and are not readily utilized by animals as food. The reactions of the pentoses are the same as those given above for glucose, so need not be repeated here.

THE CARBOHYDRATE ACIDS 

366. These are of two classes, monobasic and dibasic. The monobasic acids, known as tetronic, pentonic, and hexonic, correspond exactly to the aldoses, differing only in the oxidation of the aldehyde group to the carboxyl. 

The dibasic acids correspond in number and configuration to the carbohydrate alcohols above, from which they can be obtained

by oxidation. As mentioned many times in connection with the determination of configurations, they are obtained by the oxidation of the aldoses. Only two need be mentioned. d-Saccharic acid has long been known, since it is obtained by oxidation of sucrose by nitric acid. The acid is a syrup which gradually changes to a crystalline lactone. 

Mucic acid, which is inactive by internal compensation, is obtained by the oxidation of either of the two galactoses or of milk sugar. It has been made for industrial purposes by the oxidation of galactose extracted from larchwood. 

DISACCHARIDES 

367. These are numerous and several of them are of great importance. All of them are glucosides in the sense that they contain glucose united with something else, the second constituent being in this class another sugar. They are subdivided into two classes, 1, those which contain a potential aldehyde group and hence have more or less reducing properties, and, 2, those in which there is no aldehyde group and hence no reducing power.

The three, sucrose, maltose, and lactose, are the most widely distributed and most thoroughly studied. 

Much has been learned about the disaccharides, but more remains to be found out. By hydrolysis it is possible to separate

OXO-ALCOHOLS 

395 them into monoses which can be identified. By a study of their reactions it is sometimes possible to determine which form of glucose, alpha or beta, is involved. The conclusions of such studies are indicated by the a- and ẞ- in the table above. The chief difficulty is in deciding which groups of the constituent monoses are concerned in the linking together of the two parts. The union of the two is believed to be always of the ether or acetal type, but as there are a number of hydroxyl groups present in each of the monoses and a carbonyl group in each, it is extremely difficult to localize the union. It is comparatively easy to pull a disaccharide apart, but to put the parts together again is more difficult, and to get them linked up just as they were originally is the most difficult of all.

In the disaccharides of type 1 the aldehyde or keto group of one of the sugars takes part in the union and is thereby deprived of any reactivity, but the carbonyl group on the other constituent remains much as it was in the monose. Hence these disaccharides show mutarotation, exist in the ring forms, reduce Fehling's solution, react with phenylhydrazine, add hydrocyanic acid and otherwise react similarly to glucose.

In the formation of disaccharides of class 2, the active aldehyde or keto groups of both constituent monoses seem to be concerned in holding the two together and both thereby have their activity suppressed. Hence these disaccharides do not show the reactions that are characteristic of these groups, they are not reducing and do not react with phenylhydrazine. They do not show mutarotation. Disaccharides of both classes show the presence of hydroxyl groups by undergoing methylation, acetylation and nitration. 

368. Sucrose. This is the best-known and most plentiful of all the sugars. Unlike most of the sugars it crystallizes readily, which indicates that it is a single pure substance and not a mixture of alpha and beta isomers. Sucrose has a rotation of +66.5°, but on hydrolysis changes to a mixture of d-glucose and d'-fructose, the latter rotating to the left more strongly than d-glucose does to the right, so that the rotation of the mixture is 20°. Since the sign of the rotation changes in this process, it is called inversion and the mixture d-glucose and d'-fructose is known as invert sugar. 

---

The constitution of sucrose is not known with certainty, but is supposed to be:

CH2 (OH) CH(OH) · CH(CHOH)2CH Glucose -H2O CH2(OH). CH(OH) CH(OH)·CH-C-CH2OH Fructose. The glucose seems to be in the butylene oxide form and the fructose in the ethylene oxide form. Sucrose can be methylated, acetylated and nitrated, eight hydroxyl groups being in evidence.

POLYSACCHARIDES 

370. Polysaccharides are found in plants in great variety and in enormous quantities. In fact, the chief business of a plant consists in building sugar molecules, particularly d-glucose, out of

OXO-ALCOHOLS 

397 carbon dioxide and water, possibly through formaldehyde (190) and then coupling these sugar molecules in more complicated structures. Some of these, as starch, are stored temporarily and later pulled apart by means of enzymes, transported to other parts of the plant and built into cellulose, of which the permanent woody framework is constructed. Asparagus tips contain sugar and starch, which become woody fiber as the plant matures. Mannosans and pentosans have already been mentioned. More abundant and important than these are starch and cellulose. 

371. Starch. Whether starch is an individual compound or a class of substances is hard to say. Starches are found in many forms and in many parts of plants, usually as tiny grains. Under the microscope it is easy to recognize by their structure the grains of starch from any particular plant, but starch is not crystalline and has no melting point or other physical property by which its varieties can be distinguished.

Starch is manufactured on a large scale from corn and potatoes. 

As it is stored more or less loosely in grains in the cells of the potato or corn, its separation is purely a mechanical process. The plant structure is thoroughly broken down and the starch grains washed out with water which is passed through fine sieves to hold back fibrous materials. It is then passed into settling tanks, where the starch is deposited.

Starch is insoluble in cold water but forms a paste with hot water. Its most characteristic reaction is the formation of a blue color with iodine, but whether this is chemical or physical is not certainly known. When starch is heated with dilute acids, it is partially hydrolyzed into a gummy material known as dextrine and then completely broken down into d-glucose. Dextrine, known as British gum, ‚" is manufactured on a considerable scale for use as an adhesive and in calico printing. 

Starch contains no aldehyde groups, as it has no reducing power and does not react with phenylhydrazine, but does contain hydroxyl groups which react with acids. Nitrostarch, more properly starch nitrate, has been used as an explosive to a limited extent.

372. Cellulose. This is the most complex and most resistant polysaccharide that is built up in the plant, and forms the cell

walls of all plants. Cellulose is the chief constituent of wood, cotton fiber, flax, hemp, and such materials. The residue obtained by treating wood pulp or cotton with dilute alkali, dilute acid, water and organic solvents, everything that can be removed having been thus eliminated, is called cellulose. As is to be expected, somewhat different products are obtained from different starting materials, but cellulose from various sources is much the same. 

The composition of cellulose approximates the formula (C6H1005). 

The molecular weight has been believed to be large, but recent X-ray pictures indicate much smaller values for n than the 34 which was formerly given. 

Cellulose is insoluble in water but swells to some extent in water. It dissolves, at least colloidally, in water solutions of various salts, as in Schweizer's reagent, a solution of copper oxide in ammonia, or in 10 per cent caustic soda at -10°. Hydrolysis with acids splits the cellulose molecules into smaller parts, among which dextrines appear. Cellobiose, or cellose, a glucose-6-glucoside, is the simplest product obtained before d-glucose is reached. 

The final product is d-glucose. Cellulose appears to be built up entirely of glucose units, as from cotton cellulose 90 per cent of the glucose, calculated on this assumption, has been obtained in crystalline form.

How the glucose units are put together in cellulose is not known fully, but the aldehyde groups must be involved, since their reactivity is completely suppressed. The hydroxyl groups, or at least a part of them, are still free to react. The maximum number of reactive hydroxyls in the unit (C6H10O5) is three. The products obtained by nitrating, acetylating, methylating, etc., are more or less amorphous and are difficult to separate from unreacted cellulose or from over-treated portions. Analyses of such products give averages only. 

373. Nitrocellulose. Cellulose is readily nitrated by a mixture of nitric and sulphuric acid. There is little change in appearance of the material but a marked difference in properties. Here, as in the case of nitroglycerine, the product is really nitrate of cellulose in which the O.NO2 group takes the place of each reacting hydroxyl. The number of nitrate groups introduced varies from

399 1 to 3 for the C6H10O5 unit, according to the thoroughness of the treatment. The properties of the product vary continuously with the extent of the nitration. The different grades of nitrocellulose are distinguished by the percentage of nitrogen. 

374. Uses of Nitrocellulose. The higher nitrated product, 13.2 per cent of nitrogen approximating [C6H7O2(ONO2)3]n, is known as gun cotton and is a most useful explosive. It explodes only when detonated. Cartridges for blasting and torpedoes are filled with compressed nitrocellulose. Nitrocellulose in its ordinary state explodes too suddenly for use in guns, but it has been found that it swells and loses its structure when treated with an amount of a solvent, such as acetone, insufficient for solution. When the solvent is removed, the nitrocellulose is left as an amorphous horny mass of the same composition as before the treatment, but having entirely different properties. In this mass the explosive wave travels much more slowly, so that this gelatinized nitrocellulose can be used as a propellant in guns. This is the basis of smokeless powder, which is now in use in all ammunition of all nations. Different substances, such as nitroglycerine, may be incorporated in the gelatinized nitrocellulose to modify the powders.

Nitrocellulose of lower nitrogen content, about 11.2 per cent, is manufactured in enormous quantities for use in plastics and lacquers. Such nitrocellulose is soluble in a mixture of alcohol and ether and this solution is known as collodion. For fabrikoid and other artificial leathers, cloth is coated with a nitrocellulose solution containing pigments. Automobile finishes, such as "Duco," are solutions of nitrocellulose containing pigments and other materials. Softeners which are nonvolatile solvents for nitrocellulose are added to maintain the softness of the film. 

For making plastics, such as celluloid or pyralin, nitrocellulose is incorporated with camphor or a similar material in the presence of a small amount of a mutual solvent. 

Cellulose acetate is prepared by acetylating cellulose with acetanhydride in the presence of some sulphuric acid. This is a valuable material and is used for plastics and also in one variety of rayon.

Sodium cellulose xanthate 376. Rayon. In recent times the manufacture of rayon, formerly called artificial silk on account of its appearance, has become an important industry. Three processes are used in large-scale production, the viscose, cuproammonium and acetate processes, while another, the nitrocellulose process, is now of historical interest only. In the viscose process, cellulose, either purified woodpulp or cotton linters (the short fiber removed from cottonseed), is steeped in strong caustic soda solution, the excess of which is pressed out. The alkali cellulose, which is written above as 

NaO Cel, and which may or may not be a definite compound, is comminuted, stored at a definite temperature for a certain time, and then exposed to carbon bisulphide vapor in a rotating drum. 

A reaction takes place and the whole mass becomes an ambercolored transparent viscous mass, called viscose. This is aged under experimentally determined conditions, filtered and forced through fine holes into an acid solution. Cellulose xanthic acid is precipitated as a fine thread. This decomposes rapidly, regenerating cellulose as a fine thread. This is the viscose method of making rayon. This has grown to be an immense industry. Cellophane is made by forcing viscose through a narrow slot into an acid bath, washing and drying the resulting sheet. The first artificial silk was made by extruding a solution of nitrocellulose through fine holes, forming threads of nitrocellulose. This material was too inflammable, but this difficulty was overcome by denitrating the thread, which left it nearly pure cellulose. The cuproammonium process differs from the viscose in that the cellu-

OXO-ALCOHOLS 

401 lose is brought into solution in an ammoniacal solution of copper oxide.

Cellulose acetate dissolved in a volatile solvent may be forced through fine holes. The solvent evaporates, leaving fine threads of cellulose acetate. The thread remains cellulose acetate and cloth made from it is liable to dissolve if it comes in contact with an organic liquid. The threads obtained by the other processes have nearly the composition and properties of pure cellulose. PROBLEMS 1. 377. In Chapter XIII it was shown that alcohol in which an oxygen atom is bound to carbon by a single bond loses two atoms of hydrogen, one from the oxygen and the other from the adjacent carbon: 

CH3CH O CH3CH: 0 + H2 20,500 cal.

Instead of writing CH3.CH-O and assuming a change in valence of the carbon and oxygen, it is customary to write CH3 CH : 0, placing a double bond between the carbon and oxygen atoms. The most characteristic reaction of aldehydes is the addition of hydrogen and various substances to the two doubly bound atoms, so that they may revert to the singly bound condition. 

When propane, or any other paraffin, is heated to a high temperature, hydrogen is given off, one atom from each of two adjacent carbon atoms: 

CH3CH CH2CH3CH: CH2 + H2 − 31,700 cal.

Propene 

H H Propane 526,300 490,000 68,000

For similar reasons a double bond is written between the two atoms that have suffered the loss of hydrogen. The most characteristic reaction of hydrocarbons such as this is the addition of hydrogen and various other things to the two doubly bound atoms, so that they may revert to the singly bound condition. The heat changes incident to the loss of the hydrogen are comparable; both reactions being endothermic and taking place only at high temperatures. 

Alcohol is a saturated compound, all its atoms being held together by single bonds, and therefore there is no opportunity for 402

ETHYLENE HYDROCARBONS 

403 anything to be added. In the reactions of alcohol something is exchanged for an atom or a group already in the alcohol, or something is taken away. Likewise, propane is a saturated compound, all its atoms being held together by single bonds. It can react only by exchanging an atom for something or by the loss of something. Aldehyde and propene are unsaturated compounds and react preferably by addition. In French, propene and others of its class are aptly called incomplete hydrocarbons.

380. The Structure of Ethylene. Two carbons and four hydro gens can be arranged in several ways:

H H (2) HC-C- H H (3) HC–CH HH H H (4) HC=CH (5) HC–CH

In (1) a quadrivalent carbon and a bivalent carbon are represented and addition would take place by the second carbon changing its valence. In (2) both carbons are quadrivalent but one of them

has two free valencies. The difference between these two is largely a matter of words and definitions. In both cases the chlorine addition product would be represented by CH3. CHC12. 

As was stated in Chapter XIII, aldehyde reacts with phosphorus pentachloride to give 1,1-dichlorethane CH3 CHC12, which boils at 57.3°. The addition product of chlorine and ethylene boils at 

83.7° and must have the symmetrical formula CH2C1 CH2Cl. 

The other formulae, (3), (4), and (5), represent ethylene as symmetrical and account for the formation of 1,2-dichlorethane.

Which of these representations is to be preferred depends on definitions and conceptions of the nature of valence. Compounds which are believed to contain trivalent carbon are known, but they have strongly marked properties which are decidedly different from those of ethylene. The choice seems to be between (3) and (4), and chemists generally use formula (4), since it is difficult to form a satisfactory picture of the free bonds postulated in (3), while compounds with double bonds, as in Ca-0, 0-C-0, and O=S=0 are quite familiar. In all of these compounds there is more or less tendency towards addition. Writing ethylene 

H2C-CH2 allies it with other substances which have double bonds and aids in correlating its reactions. However, the double bond must not be taken too literally; it does not mean that the two carbons in ethylene are held together twice as firmly as the two carbons in ethane. Thermochemical measurements show that this is not the case. It is frequently said that a double bond is the weak point in a molecule. The explanation of the breaking of a molecule at a double bond is usually that addition takes place on both sides of this bond and that the two carbons thus loaded may part more readily.

In terms of electrons, if a single bond consists of a pair of electrons with their orbits between the two atoms which they hold together, then a double bond must involve four such electrons. 

These electrons repel each other so that their orbits must be distorted. It is quite possible that the orbits of two of them may be so altered and shifted that they no longer lie between the two atoms which they hold together. This might approach a condition represented by formula (3) above and would explain the readiness with which ethylene reacts by addition. Probably it is best to think of ethylene as being something between the structures

ETHYLENE HYDROCARBONS 

407 represented by (3) and (4). As a matter of fact, some ethylene derivatives take up bromine and similar substances with great avidity, while others can hardly be made to add bromine. In those which readily take part in addition reactions, the orbits of the electrons corresponding to the second bond may be pushed far out, so that these electrons may be readily attracted by other atoms. 1 Baeyer's ¹ strain theory, which was brought out in 1885, before electrons were discovered, explained the reactivity of the double bond in different terms. According to the tetrahedral model of the carbon atom, each of the four valencies of carbon is at an angle of 109° 28′ to the others. In the case of ethylene two of the valencies of each of the carbons must be distorted from their natural positions. This imposes a strain on the structure which makes it less stable, that is, more reactive. This theory will be mentioned again in Chapter XXX, when cyclic compounds are taken up.

Ethylene when heated to 300° or above in contact with iron or with various other substances is polymerized, that it, it is converted into substances of the same composition but of much higher molecular weight. 382. The Manufacture and Uses of Ethylene. Ethylene has been produced in the United States by the dehydration of alcohol, using two methods. Alcohol vapor is passed through a heated tower filled with coke moistened with phosphoric acid. For the large amounts of ethylene required for mustard gas during the World War the alcohol vapor was passed through heated tubes containing a variety of kaolin. In the natural gas region propane is cracked by passing it through heated tubes. 

Ethylene burns in oxygen with an intensely hot flame and has in recent years come into large use for cutting and welding. For this purpose it has partially supplanted acetylene. Ethylene is inferior to acetylene in the temperature of its flame, but it has a great advantage over the latter in that it can be stored and transported in cylinders at high pressure without danger of explosion. 

Large amounts of ethylene are consumed in the manufacture

ETHYLENE HYDROCARBONS 

411 of ethylene chlorohydrine, ethylene chloride and other compounds. 

In recent years it has come to be widely used as an anesthetic in place of ether. One very remarkable property is its action in the ripening of fruits, for which it is now extensively used. 

383. The Homologs of Ethylene. The general formula for a paraffin hydrocarbon is CH2n+2. The presence of a double bond means two hydrogen atoms less, hence the general formula for ethylene and its homologs is CH₂n. The possible number of unsaturated hydrocarbons is many times that of the saturated. 

Thus it is evident that while there is only one normal heptane, there are three unsaturated hydrocarbons, all having this same skeleton: CH3 CH2 CH2 CH2 CH2 CH2 CH3 n-Heptane

While a large number of unsaturated hydrocarbons have been studied, the knowledge of this class is far more incomplete than that of the paraffins. 

384. Naming Ethylene Hydrocarbons. The official method in naming these is to change the vowel " a " in the ending of the name of the saturated hydrocarbon to "e" for the unsaturated. Thus ethane becomes ethene. With the longer chains it is necessary to specify the position of the double bond by adding a numeral. 

This is the smaller of the two numerals which designate the two carbons between which the double bond is located. In numbering the carbons of a chain the double bond takes the smallest number possible, having precedence over all substituents. In a branched hydrocarbon the longest chain that contains the double bond gives the stem name even if there is a longer chain. Several examples will illustrate these rules:

A system formerly much in vogue used the Greek A with a numeral as a prefix, 43-octene for octene (3). It is frequently convenient to consider unsaturated compounds as derived from ethylene, prefixing s-(sym-) or u-(uns-) according to whether the groups named are joined to different carbons or to the same carbon atom in the ethylene. According to this plan the octene (2) above is s-methylbutyl-ethylene, the 7-methyl-octane (2) becomes s-methyl-isohexylethylene, and the 2-propyl-hexene (1) is u-propyl-butyl-ethylene. 

Older names which are commonly used for the best-known unsaturated hydrocarbons end in "-ylene" as ethylene, propylene and butylene.

These methods are readily extended in naming compounds which have more than one double bond:

413 385. Reactions of the Homologs of Ethylene. These may be predicted from those of ethylene, that is, both polymerization and addition reactions take place, but the speed of such reactions varies greatly with the structure of the unsaturated hydrocarbon, particularly as related to the substituents near the double bond. 

According to Markownikow's rule, when a halide acid is added, the halogen goes to the carbon which carries the least number of hydrogens:

CH3 CH CH2 + HCl → CH3CHCI-CH3 Bromine chloride gives a mixture of products, but for the most part acts like hydrogen chloride: 

CH3 CH CH2 + BrCl CH3 CHC1 CH2Br 

CH3 CHBrCH2C1 . 

Hypochlorous acid, HOCl, adds as does hydrogen chloride:

CH3 CH: CH2 + HOCI→ CH3 CHOH CH2Cl 

When a halogen is attached to one of the carbon atoms adjoining the double bond, the halogen of a halogen acid adds to that carbon. In case there are different alkyl groups on the two sides of the bond, the halogen goes to the carbon with the lower alkyl: CH3-CH, CH:CH-CH3 + HBr → CH3-CH, CH, CHBr-CH3 The addition of sulphuric acid takes place much more readily with some of the higher unsaturated hydrocarbons than with ethylene; thus, propylene is absorbed by 85 per cent sulphuric acid, while ethylene requires fuming acid. In the case of many of the more complicated hydrocarbons, addition of sulphuric acid and decomposition of the alkyl sulphuric acid go on under the same conditions, so that shaking the unsaturated hydrocarbon with dilute, even 10 or 20 per cent sulphuric acid, converts it to the alcohol.

386. Dienes and Trienes. As an alcohol loses water to give an ethylene derivative, so a glycol can split off two molecules of water, leaving a hydrocarbon which has two double bonds. A dihalogen derivative may lose two molecules of the halide acid with the formation of a doubly unsaturated hydrocarbon. It is possible to extend these reactions to produce compounds which

ETHYLENE HYDROCARBONS 

415 contain three or even more double bonds, but such compounds need not be considered here. The reactions of the hydrocarbons containing two or three double bonds are very similar to those of ethylene and its homologs. They differ quantitatively in that they take up two or three times as much bromine, etc., as do those having one double bond. Dienes have the general formula CnH2n-2.

388. Rubber. The sap of the rubber tree, known as latex, contains a hydrocarbon in colloidal suspension. For a long time the natives of Brazil collected this sap and evaporated it over a smoky fire until masses of rubber mingled with soot and other materials were obtained. This was sold as crude rubber. from the state of Para in Brazil was known as para rubber. That

The composition of rubber has been found to be represented by the empirical formula C5Н8, but all efforts to get its molecular weight have failed, so the molecular formula has to be written (C5H8). Freezing point determinations on solutions of rubber give no reliable figures, but recent X-ray pictures indicate 8 as a probable value for n. Attention is called to the fact that the percentage composition of rubber is the same as that of the terpenes, such as pinene and limonene, C₁0H16 (Chapter XXX). 

Rubber is not volatile without decomposition, but on heating

decomposes into a large number of hydrocarbons, the most of which are unsaturated and of comparatively low molecular weight. 

The one hydrocarbon that is formed in the largest amount, although its percentage is small, is isoprene, which has been shown to be 2-methyl-butadiene(1,3). It has been found that isoprene besides showing the appropriate addition reactions, polymerizes on long standing to an elastic mass more or less like rubber. It was discovered that this polymerization can be hastened by heating with acetic acid, or better, with sodium metal. The material thus obtained can be vulcanized and used in the manufacture of articles that are commonly made of rubber. Butadiene, CH2: CH·CH: CH2, 2,3-dimethyl-butadiene, and other similar hydrocarbons give more or less similar polymerization products. 

The polymerization product from isoprene is called artificial rubber and has been used on a considerable scale for making rubber articles, including automobile tires. The rubber molecule breaks up into isoprene units and these can be made to reunite, but it is highly unlikely that the new structure would duplicate the original. 

Much time and money have been spent on the problem of artificial rubber and there is no doubt that useful materials can be obtained by the polymerization of isoprene and allied substances. The question of the future of such efforts comes down to competition in price. At the time this investigation was started the uses of rubber were multiplying and automobile tires were beginning to consume enormous quantities; the supply of wild rubber could not be greatly increased and a rubber shortage with consequent high prices seemed imminent. Such conditions would certainly have led to the development of a large synthetic rubber industry. In 

1890 the cultivation of rubber trees was begun in Ceylon and elsewhere and the product from such trees, collected and cured under scientific conditions, has come on the market as plantation rubber. The production of this has expanded rapidly and has kept pace with the rapidly increasing demand for rubber. Wild rubber has not been able to compete with plantation rubber and its supply has declined.
