CHAPTER XXVII DERIVATIVES OF THE ETHYLENIC HYDROCARBONS 

390. In Chapter XXVI hydrocarbons containing an ethylene grouping have been considered. In this chapter compounds will be considered which contain this grouping along with some other active group, such as the hydroxyl, the aldehyde or carboxyl group. Such compounds will have two sets of properties; that is, the capability of combining directly with halides, halide acids, sulphuric acid, etc., and the properties characteristic of the other active group.

Of course the presence of each group will modify the reactivity of the other to a certain extent. To a remarkable degree the influence of the ethylene grouping depends on its position with reference to the group affected. 

The presence of the double bond is the basis of geometric isomerism in which the isomers differ markedly in physical properties instead of in optical rotation. This manifests itself particularly well in the unsaturated acids.

In the addition of halogen acid, the halogen adds to the carbon that has the least hydrogen.

Vinyl chloride polymerizes in sunlight and under the influence of catalysts to a solid which may be somewhat soft and soluble in some organic solvents, or hard and insoluble, according to the conditions of polymerization. The polymerized material is find ing industrial application as a plastic. Vinyl bromide polymerizes under the same conditions to a white solid which is insoluble in organic solvents. These polymers do not show unsaturation. 

The unreactivity of the halogen in these vinyl halides is remarkable. Vinyl chloride or bromide may be heated with a sodium salt without any reaction. They are indifferent to magnesium in contrast to the corresponding ethyl compounds.

The name allyl comes from the Latin word for garlic, since allyl sulphide is found in garlic and in onions. Allyl alcohol, CH2 CH CH2OH, is a liquid boiling at 96.69°, melting at -129°, and having a density 0.846725. The corresponding data for propyl alcohol are 97.17°, -127° and 0.799825. The difference of two hydrogen atoms has little effect on the boiling or melting points, but affects the density considerably. Unlike the saturated alcohols, allyl alcohol has a penetrating, somewhat disagreeable odor.

396. Other Unsaturated Alcohols. 

When the double bond is in the second position there is greatly enhanced reactivity, as in

allyl alcohol. Crotonyl alcohol, CH3-CH: CH CH2OH, resembles allyl so closely that one might be mistaken for the other except for the differences in boiling points. When the double bond is further removed, it scarcely influences the alcohol group. 

Some of the higher unsaturated alcohols are of great interest to the perfumer. Two of these, geraniol and citronellol, occur together in attar of roses and in oil of geranium. Citronella oil contains about 80 per cent of geraniol and some citronellal, the aldehyde corresponding to citronellol. Lemongrass oil contains geraniol and its aldehyde, citral. Both of these alcohols, as well as linalool, which is the chief constituent of linaloe oil, have the same carbon skeleton. Linalyl acetate is an important constituent of bergamot and of lavender oils.

CH3 CH3 CH2 C CH2 CH2 CH2 C: CH CH2OH

Linalool, 2,6-dimethyl-octa dien (1,7) ol-6

All of these are written with a double bond between carbons 1 and 2, but this double bond may be between carbons 2 and 3. There is some evidence that there are two varieties of each, differing in the position of this double bond. Geraniol and citronellol are primary alcohols and can be oxidised to the corresponding aldehydes and acids. They differ from each other in that geraniol has two double bonds while citronellol has only one. Linalool is isomeric with geraniol but is a tertiary alcohol. All of them take up halogens, halogen acids, and act in other ways as unsaturated compounds. 

397. Naming Unsaturated Alcohols. An alcohol derived from a saturated hydrocarbon is named by adding -ol to the name of

ETHYLENE DERIVATIVES 

427 the hydrocarbon. The same rule applies to the unsaturated alcohols. The hydrocarbon must end in -ene or -diene and the location of the double bond must be specified. Allyl alcohol is propenol or more exactly propen (1)ol(3). Citronellol is 2,6-dimethyl-octen (1)ol(8) and geraniol is 2,6-dimethyl-octadiene(1,6)ol(8).

The same rules apply to the naming of aldehydes and ketones, the endings -al and -one being used.

401. In acrolein and crotonaldehyde the presence of a double bond near the carbonyl group makes for increased activity. 404. Acrylic and Crotonic Acids. These have already been mentioned in Chapter XXII as being formed by loss of water from 

B-hydroxy acids. Acrylic acid melts at 12.3°, boils at 141.9°, has the density 1.062116, and mixes with water in all proportions.

405. Oleic Acid. This is one of the three acids of the glycerides which make up the bulk of the fats. The liquid fats, such as olive oil and cottonseed oil, contain relatively large amounts of the glycerol esters of oleic acid.

Oleic acid is best prepared from olive oil. The oil is saponified by heating with caustic soda, which liberates the glycerine and gives the sodium salts of the acids present. The water soluble sodium salts are converted into the insoluble lead salts by double decomposition with lead acetate or nitrate. This gives a mixture of the lead salts. Advantage is taken of the fact that lead oleate is a liquid and is soluble in ether, while the lead salts of the saturated acids are insoluble in this medium. Treatment of the lead oleate with hot dilute mineral acids liberates the oleic acid, which is readily separated. Oleic acid is a liquid melting at 14°, boiling at 286° at 100 mm. and having the density 0.893848, and is insoluble in water but readily soluble in alcohol and ether. As an acid it forms salts and esters in the usual way. It is readily hydrogenated to stearic acid and takes up Br2 or Cl₂ to form dibromoor dichloro-stearic acid. Its conversion to stearic acid shows that its skeleton is a straight chain of carbon atoms and its addition reactions reveal the presence of one ethylene grouping. The remaining question is the location of this double bond. Shaking with cold dilute potassium permanganate solution gives a mixture of pelargonic acid and azelaic acid. This locates the double bond in the middle of the molecule:

CH3(CH2)7CH: CH(CH2)7COOH

CH3(CH2)-COOH + HOOC(CH2),COOH

406. Sorbic Acid. As there can be two or more hydroxyls or carboxyls in a molecule, so there can be two or more ethylene bonds. Sorbic acid which is found in the juice of the unripe sorb apples, adds four atoms of bromine to form tetrabromo-caproic acid or two molecules of hydrobromic acid, giving dibromo-caproic acid. It can be hydrogenated to hexoic acid. The two double bonds which have been located as shown can be hydrogenated: 

CH3 CH: CH CH: CH COOH

407. Linolic Acid. This is the most important acid having two double bonds. Its name is due to the fact that its glyceride is found in linseed oil. Cottonseed oil and many other oils also contain it. The properties of linolic acid are not accurately known, as it is difficult to separate in pure form. The hydrogenation of linolic acid to stearic acid takes place readily, and during the hydrogenation oleic acid appears to be formed as an intermediate product. It adds four atoms of bromine, forming tetrabromostearic acid. These facts agree with the formula that is generally accepted: 

CH3(CH2)5CH: CH·CH: CH(CH2)7COOH 

Linolic acid 408. Linolenic Acid. This acid is still more difficult to obtain in pure form than linolic, from which it differs in composition by having two less hydrogen atoms. Its glyceride is found along with that of linolic acid in linseed oil and in other "drying" oils. It is brominated to hexabromo-stearic acid or hydrogenated to stearic acid. These facts agree with the generally accepted formula: CH3(CH2)3CH: CH·CH: CH·CH: CH(CH2)7COOH 

Linolenic acid

There are other polyethylenic acids; some are isomeric with these and others contain four and even more double bonds, but their properties are about what would be expected from a consideration of those mentioned. 

409. Fats. In plants and in animals great quantities of fats are found in both solid and liquid form. In plants the fats are commonly concentrated in the seeds but are present, in traces at least, in almost all other parts. Animals store fats in all parts of their bodies, but especially just under the skin. Fats appear to be largely reserve material to be drawn upon to supply energy when needed, as in the hibernation of a bear. 

It is generally believed that fats are produced by the organism from carbohydrates, but nothing is known as to the mechanism of this process. It is interesting that the chief acids in the fats have eighteen carbons in their chains, while the chief carbohydrates have six. Fats, proteins and carbohydrates are the three great classes of foods. Of all of these, fats have the highest fuel value, a gram of fat giving more than twice as many calories as a gram of sugar or starch. Fats pass through the stomach unchanged but are hydrolyzed by the pancreatic juice; some of the products of hydrolysis are used to build up other fats, but the most of them are burned to carbon dioxide and water. In the oxidation of the fatty acids in the body the attack is on the beta carbon atom, so that two carbons of the chain are cut off at each step. This may have something to do with the fact that the carbon chains in the fatty acids found in natural products differ from each other by two carbon atoms.

Physically fats vary considerably, including many solids such as tallow, some pasty materials, such as shea butter, and many liquid fats, such as olive oil and cottonseed oil. Chemically fats are esters, the alcoholic part of which is always glycerine. This is combined with many acids, the chief of which are stearic, palmitic and oleic. Besides these there are the saturated acids, containing an even number of carbons, butyric, caproic, caprylic, capric, lauric, and myristic, and the unsaturated acids containing 18 carbon atoms, linoleic and linolenic acids. Acids, both saturated and unsaturated, containing longer carbon chains, C20, C22

ETHYLENE DERIVATIVES 

435 and C24 are present in many fats but usually in insignificant amounts.

These compounds are readily prepared by heating to 150° to 200° equivalent amounts of the desired acid and glycerine. As the water that is formed is volatile at that temperature and escapes, the reaction goes to completion. Mono- and di- esters can be made in which the acids are joined either to an end or a middle carbon of the glycerol. 

It is evident that a very large number of mixed glycerides is possible provided different acids are used to esterify the three hydroxyls of the glycerine. Laborious synthetic methods are required to build up molecules having different acid radicals in known positions, but a number of such have been prepared. It is probable that natural fats are partly, at least, mixed glycerides rather than a mixture of single glycerides. As all of these glycerides have much the same solubilities, it is impossible to separate them from a mixture in pure condition so as to identify them properly. By saponifying a fat, a mixture of fatty acids is obtained. Thus it is possible to determine what acids are present in a given fat and in what relative amounts, but no one can say in just what arrangement they were in the original fat.

411. Soap. When a fat is heated with caustic soda, hydrolysis of the ester takes place. Taking glyceryl stearate as an example, the reaction is: 

H2C O CO C17H35

H2COH 

HC.O.CO.C17H35 + 3NaOH → HCOH + 3C17H35 COONa H2C.O.CO.C17H35 

H2COH 

Sodium stearate Stearin

Any natural fat is a mixture, consequently the soap made from it is a mixture. If caustic soda is used the product is a mixture of sodium stearate, sodium palmitate and sodium oleate, not to mention the sodium salts of other acids that may have been present in smaller amounts. If sodium stearate predominates, the soap is hard and relatively insoluble, while if sodium oleate is the chief constituent, the soap is soft and relatively soluble in water. If caustic potash is used instead of caustic soda, a much softer soap

ETHYLENE DERIVATIVES 

437 is obtained from any given fat. By choosing the fats and by using a mixture of sodium and potassium hydroxides, the soap maker can produce a product that has the desired characteristics. 

Soap may be made in a number of different ways. In the so-called cold process the fat is emulsified with the calculated amount of strong alkali and the mixture is warmed and then let stand until saponification is complete. In this process the glycerine remains in the soap. The mixture of free acids obtained by the acid hydrolysis of a fat or the decomposition of a fat by the lime process is warmed with a solution of the proper amount of alkali. The product formed is a soap. Rosin is nearly pure abietic acid, C20H3002, the alkali salts of which are similar to those of the fatty acids and are largely used in soaps. When soap is dissolved in alcohol and the alcohol evaporated off, the soap is left as a jelly which when dried is transparent soap.

When a dilute water solution of a sodium or potassium soap is added to a solution of a calcium or magnesium salt, the corresponding calcium or magnesium soap is precipitated. Waters which cause such precipitation are called "hard" waters. 

412. The Hardening of Fats. The glycerides of the saturated acids melt much higher than those of the unsaturated acids, tristearin melting at 72.2°, tripalmitin at 65.5°, and triolein at −5°.

Fats, such as tallow, which contain large proportions of the glycerides of stearic and palmitic acids, are solids at ordinary temperature, while those in which oleic, linoleic and linolenic acids predominate, such as cottonseed oil, are liquid. For some purposes, such as shortening pastry and making soap, solid fats are more desirable than the liquid. This has led to the hardening of fats by catalytic hydrogenation. Hydrogen is pumped into the oil heated to about 180°, containing a nickel catalyst in suspension. 

Triolein is hydrogenated to tristearin: H2C.O.CO.C17H33 H2C.O.CO.C17H35

Tristearin Except for special purposes the hydrogenation is not carried to

complete saturation, but only far enough to secure the desired consistency of the product. Glycerides of linolenic and other unsaturated acids are similarly hydrogenated. Cottonseed oil is hydrogenated to about the consistency of lard, and this material is now largely used in place of lard. 

413. Drying Oils. Linseed oil may be taken as the type of these. When a film of linseed oil is spread upon a surface and left exposed to the air, a noteworthy change takes place; in the course of a few hours the film becomes more and more viscous and finally hardens. This is called "drying," although it is very different from drying by the evaporation of a volatile liquid. The "dry" film of linseed oil has not lost anything. On the contrary it has gained somewhat in weight. It can be shown that oxygen from the air is taken up in the process. It was once thought that simple oxidation had taken place with the addition of two hydroxyl groups at each double bond to form a polyhydroxy-stearic acid. It is still believed that this is partly true, but there appears to be polymerization as well as oxidation. In some unknown way the two processes seem to influence each other. To hasten the drying of linseed oil, it is heated with small amounts of various oxides, particularly those of lead and manganese. The product is known. as boiled linseed oil and dries more rapidly than the raw oil. These oxides appear to form soaps with the acids. These soaps are soluble in the oil and are thought to act as catalysts in its oxidation. 

The processes involved in the drying of an oil are complex and are far from being understood, although they have been studied by many chemists over a long period of years. Practically the drying of linseed oil is of great importance. If a pigment is mixed with water or other volatile liquid and the mixture spread on a surface, the liquid evaporates and the pigment falls off, but if a mixture of linseed oil and pigment is spread on a surface, the oil liquid film hardens to a solid which holds the embedded pigment. 

A paint in its simplest form is a pigment ground up with linseed oil. There are other drying oils which may be used either alone or with linseed oil.

GEOMETRIC ISOMERISM 

415. The theory that the valencies of a carbon atom are directed toward the vertices of a regular tetrahedron has particularly strong confirmation in the isomerism of the sugars. It may be regarded as one of the facts of organic chemistry. According to this the two carbons of ethane are represented in Fig. 26a below. There is freedom of rotation around the point of union so that any one of the groups A, B and C which are joined to one carbon can be brought opposite or near any one of the groups D, E, and F on the other carbon. Two carbons joined by a double bond are to be represented as in Fig. 266, in which the two tetrahedral models are joined at two vertices and there can no longer be free rotation. 

Group C is opposite A and can be made to approach A, the side that is common to the two tetrahedrons serving as a hinge, but the group D cannot approach A. In Fig. 26c, the groups C and D XX XX B 

FIG. 26.-Single and Double Bonded Carbon Atoms.

ETHYLENE DERIVATIVES 

441 are oppositely arranged, with the result that A and D or B and C can be brought together. In terms of the electron theory, when two carbon atoms are held together by a single pair of valence electrons, they can rotate on the line which joins their centers, but when two pairs of valence electrons are concerned in the union the system does not permit rotation.

If C and D are the same, the differences between the two models disappear. A number of pairs of isomers have been discovered in which the differences are to be explained by this theory. The most striking case is that of fumaric and maleic acids.

CHAPTER XXVIII ACETYLENE HYDROCARBONS AND DERIVATIVES 

421. In the last two chapters unsaturated compounds in which two carbon atoms are held together by a double bond have been considered. Unsaturation can go still further. Ethane, when heated to a high temperature, changes to ethylene with loss of hydrogen: 

CH3 CH3CH2 CH2 + H2 . Ethane Ethylene

At higher temperatures ethylene may lose a part of its hydrogen: CH2 CH2 →CH CH + H2 Ethylene Acetylene

To make the formulae conform to the usual quadrivalency of carbon, a triple bond is written in acetylene as it is in acetonitrile. 

Unsaturation manifests itself with acetylene as it does with ethylene, only to a greater degree; acetylene combines with the same things that ethylene does, but with twice the amount. Acetylene as well as ethylene can be obtained by the complete elimination of halogen acid from a halogenated hydrocarbon: and

CH3-CHBr →CH2; CHBr + HBr CH3 CHBг2 → CH CH + 2HBr -> In addition to the property of unsaturation, acetylene has some peculiar properties, such as salt formation, that could not be predicted from its analogy to ethylene. 

422. Acetylene. Acetylene is formed directly from the elements when an electric arc is passed between carbon electrodes in an atmosphere of hydrogen. It is frequently found among the products when carbon compounds are decomposed by heat; thus coal gas contains about 0.06 per cent. When a Bunsen burner 445

strikes back, the issuing gases contain up to 0.8 per cent of acetylene. This was the source of supply of acetylene for the older experiments. When lime and powdered coke are heated in an electric furnace, calcium carbide is formed: CaO + 3C → CaC2 + CO -> This reacts with water to give acetylene:

CaC2 + 2HOH → →Ca(OH)2 + C2H2 As both lime and coke contain appreciable quantities of compounds of nitrogen, phosphorus and sulphur, the crude acetylene is contaminated with small amounts of ammonia, phosphine and hydrogen sulphide and has an unpleasant odor. 

Pure acetylene is a gas of slight ethereal odor. It is soluble in its own volume of water at 0°, that is, four times as soluble as ethylene. It is very soluble in alcohol, ether and other organic solvents. Acetone dissolves 25 volumes of acetylene at 15°. 

Acetylene melts at -81.8° and boils at -83.6°, which means that, like carbon dioxide, it passes directly from the solid to the vapor unless it is under a pressure greater than that of one atmosphere. 

At 0° it liquefies under a pressure of 26 atmospheres. Acetylene is explosive, particularly in the liquid state. For that reason liquefied acetylene is not used commercially. Its solution under pressure in acetone can be shipped and handled without danger, and it is in this form that acetylene is employed industrially. 

Acetylene burns with an intense heat and therefore is used in the oxy-acetylene torch, which has found great use in cutting and welding steel and other metals. In air acetylene burns with a sooty flame unless special burners are used, but under the proper conditions its flame is intensely brilliant. It was extensively used for illumination before electricity became so widely available. 

For this purpose acetylene is either drawn from a tank in which it is stored under pressure in solution in acetone or some other solvent, or else it is generated as it is consumed by the reaction of water and calcium carbide. Much heat is generated in this reaction, hence in large generators it is customary to drop the carbide into a large volume of water, while in a small unit, such as that in a bicycle lamp, this is reversed.

ACETYLENE HYDROCARBONS 

447 423. The Structure of Acetylene. Two formulae have been considered: 

HC CH and H2C-C

Since the addition of chlorine or bromine to acetylene to form Cl₂CH CHC12 or Br₂CH CHBr2 takes place symmetrically the first formula is preferred. 

The arguments for a double bond between the two carbon atoms in ethylene may be used in favor of writing a triple bond in the case of acetylene. The chemical behavior of acetylene can be readily interpreted in terms of this representation. The double bond in ethylene (as was stated in Chapter XXVI) does not mean that the two carbon atoms are held together twice as strongly as the carbons in ethane. The triple bond in acetylene is far from being three times a single bond. 

From heats of combustion the following thermal values, in calories per gram atom, have been calculated for the various bonds:

C-H 87,000

C-C 70,000

C-C 118,000

C=C 170,000

The values for the double and triple bonds are far less than the corresponding multiples of 70,000. Ethane contains six carbonhydrogen linkages, so its heat of formation is found by adding 6 X 87,000 to 70,000. The heats of formation of these hydrocarbons come out: Ethane 591,000 Ethylene 466,000 Acetylene 344,000

These heats of formation are based on the assumption that the carbon and hydrogen are in the atomic state and to find the heats of formation of these gases from hydrogen gas and solid carbon the energy necessary to dissociate hydrogen and to vaporize and dissociate carbon must be subtracted from the above figures. The quantities of energy required by the carbon are certainly large, although their values are not known very exactly. When they are subtracted, the heat of formation of acetylene may actually be negative. The facts that compressed acetylene is explosive and that acetylene is formed in the electric arc, as is nitric oxide, seem to show that its formation is endothermic.

424. The Reactions of Acetylene. 1. Besides the addition reactions which can be predicted from its unsaturation, acetylene has one peculiarity which distinguishes it sharply from other hydrocarbons; it forms salts with metals. When the gas is passed over molten sodium, reaction takes place: HC CH+Na→ HC CNa + H This sodium compound is best prepared by passing acetylene into a solution of sodamide in ammonia: HC CH+NaNH2 → HC CNa + NH3 When the monosodium derivative is heated to 200°, it goes into the disodium salt and acetylene: 2HC CNa→ NaC CNa + HC CH Both of these salts are hydrolyzed instantly on contact with water. The silver and cuprous salts, Ag2C2 and Cu2C2, are so insoluble that they are precipitated when acetylene is passed into an ammoniacal solution containing silver or cuprous ions. These salts are decomposed by dilute acids with the evolution of acetylene. Before the days of the electric furnace, acetylene was commonly prepared from the cuprous salt produced by passing gases containing acetylene through a cuprous chloride solution. The silver, copper and other heavy metal salts of acetylene are extremely explosive and are dangerous to handle in the dry condition. Explosions are commonly thought of as due to the sudden evolution of a large volume of gas. This cannot apply to the decomposition of copper acetylide, C2Cu2, which gives two solids, copper and carbon. An explosion is due to the sudden conversion of a large amount of latent energy into kinetic energy. Usually this kinetic energy is applied to surrounding objects through the intermediary of expanding gases, as in gunpowder. The mechanism by which the energy is applied is incidental; the important thing is that a large amount of potential energy suddenly becomes kinetic energy. The formation of metallic derivatives is peculiar to acetylene and its mono-alkyl derivatives and may be used as a means of showing their presence.

ACETYLENE HYDROCARBONS

2C2H2 + S→ C4H4S Thiophene One theory of the formation of petroleum is that acetylene, resulting from the action of water on quantities of metal carbides

ACETYLENE HYDROCARBONS 

451 down in the earth, has been polymerized by coming in contact with heated metals, such as nickel and iron. If hydrogen had been mixed with the acetylene before it reached the catalytic metals, more or less hydrogenation would have taken place along with the polymerization. The two processes would go on at different rates in different localities. This would account for the wide range in composition of petroleums, varying all the way from aromatics to the paraffins. 

425. Homologs of Acetylene. These are divided into two distinct classes, mono-alkyl such as methyl-acetylene, CH3.C: CH, and di-alkyl such as dimethyl-acetylene, CH3 C C-CH3. Both classes show the addition reactions of acetylene, but only the mono-derivatives form metal salts. These are obtained under the same conditions as the corresponding salts of acetylene. They differ from acetylene compounds in containing only one equivalent of the metal. Thus, methyl ethyl acetylene, CH3-C; C·C2H5, does not form salts, but from methyl acetylene, CH3 C CH, the silver and copper salts, CH3 C CAg and CH3-C CCu, are obtained by precipitation and the sodium salt, CH3-C CNa, by the action of sodium metal. As the homologs of acetylene contain four hydrogen atoms less than the paraffins, their general formula is C₂H2-2. It is important to note that they are isomeric with the di-enes. 

426. Naming Acetylene Hydrocarbons. The systematic names of acetylene homologs are those of the paraffins of the same number of carbon atoms except that -ane is changed to -ine, which is pronounced as in wine. According to a recent agreement this ending is -yne. For the three carbon groups the names are: CH3 CH2 CH3 Propane 

CH3 CH CH2 CH3 C CH 

Propene Propine

The position of the triple bond is shown by a numeral. The more common names are those which regard them as substitution products of acetylene, propyne being methyl-acetylene. As in the case of the derivatives of other hydrocarbons, the alcohols, aldehydes, ketones and acids derived from the acetylene hydrocarbons are named by adding the proper ending, -ol, -al, -one, etc., to the name

of the hydrocarbon.

Thus, CH3C C-CH2-CH2-CHO is hexyn- (2)al(6) and CH3C CCH2 CH2. CO-CH3 is heptyn (2)one (6). If the compound CH3 C C CH₂CH: CH·CH2·CH: CH·CH2· 

CHO is ever prepared, it will be called undecadien (5,8)yn(2)al(11). 

427. Preparation. Acetylene homologs are not readily prepared and the yields are low. Acetylene hydrocarbons may be regarded as the anhydrides of aldehydes and ketones, but they cannot be prepared directly from these by the abstraction of water from the corresponding aldehyde or ketone.

428. Reactions of Acetylene Homologs. All of the addition reactions resemble those of acetylene. The halogens and hydrogen halides are readily taken up. Water adds to form a ketone even when the acetylene group is at the end of the molecule which gives a methyl ketone. For the reactions of acetylene which depend on the active hydrogens, only the mono-derivatives need be considered. The reactions of the sodium salt are of interest, as they lead to the synthesis of a variety of acetylene derivatives: CH3(CH2)4 C CNa + C1-CO-OCH3 → → C5H11 C C·COOCH3 Heptyne-sodium Methyl chloro-formate Methyl heptyne-carboxylate The product is the methyl ester of heptine-carboxylic acid. It has an odor resembling violets and is sold as methyl heptinecarbonate.

A mono-alkyl-acetylene reacts with the Grignard reagent as does acetylene:

C3H7C CH + C2H5MgBr→ C3H7C CMgBr + C2H6 The product is a Grignard reagent in which an acetylene radical

ACETYLENE HYDROCARBONS 

455 has taken the place of the ethyl group. Its reactions are the same as those of the usual Grignard reagent. It reacts with aldehydes, ketones and other compounds and may be used in the synthesis of a variety of compounds, each of which will contain the acetylene grouping.

The sodium derivative of an acetylene hydrocarbon may be regarded as the Grignard reagent, in which the usual univalent group -MgBr is replaced by the sodium atom. It reacts with carbon dioxide, aldehydes, ketones, etc., to give the same products as are obtained from the alkyl-acetylene Grignard reagent described in the last paragraph:

C3H7C CNa + CO2 → C3H7C C-COONa Sodium pentyne-carboxylate

PURINES 

438. Uric Acid. This acid was discovered by Scheele in 1776 in urinary calculi and in urine. The nitrogenous part of the excrement of birds and reptiles is chiefly ammonium urate. Mammals excrete about one per cent of their waste nitrogen as uric acid and allantoin. With man there is only a trace of allantoin, while with most other mammals the allantoin predominates. There seems to be a special enzyme present in most mammals but absent in man which oxidises uric acid to allantoïn. Uric acid is a white crystalline powder, insoluble in alcohol and ether and nearly insoluble in cold water, 0.00645 g. in 100 cc. at 37°. It is a dibasic acid; the acid salts of the alkali metals are very slightly soluble and the neutral salts still less soluble. 

The structure of uric acid was not known for a long time. The oxidation of uric acid by alkaline permanganate gives allantoïn and moderate oxidation by nitric acid gives alloxan:

Xanthine, hypoxanthine, adenine and guanine are prominent among the hydrolytic products of nuclein, the chief constituent of animal and plant cells, and are, therefore, closely associated with the processes of life.

Xanthine can be obtained by the reduction of uric acid with sodium amalgam or by the action of nitrous acid on guanine. It is a white amorphous mass only slightly soluble in water, 1 part in 14,000, and is both acidic and basic. Hypoxanthine is similar to xanthine, but less acidic. It can be prepared from 2,6,8trichloro-purine, by partial hydrolysis with alkali to 6-hydroxydichloro-purine from which the halogen is removed by reduction. 

Theobromine, found in cocoa beans, is a crystalline powder having a bitter taste. It is amphoteric and has been made by heating the lead salt of xanthine with methyl iodide. Theophylline is associated with caffeine in tea. 

Caffeine occurs to an extent of 1 to 4.5 per cent in tea leaves and 1 per cent in coffee beans and is the stimulating agent in beverages made from these. It is used in medicine as a heart stimulant. As methyl groups are introduced into xanthine, the diuretic action decreases and the stimulating effect increases. Theobromine and caffeine are manufactured from uric acid. PROBLEMS

CHAPTER XXX CARBO-CYCLIC COMPOUNDS 

441. The y-lactones of Chapter XXII, the y-lactams of Chapter XXIII, the anhydride, and the imide of succinic acid, have cyclic structures:

CH2 CO CH2 CO CH2 CO CH2 CO NH NH

CH2 CH2 .

CH2 CH2 Y-Lactone y-Lactam

CH2 CO Succinicanhydride

CH2 CO Succinimide

In each of these an oxygen or a nitrogen atom is one member of the ring. All of these compounds behave much like the corresponding open-chain compounds. It was shown that the ease of formation of these cyclic structures depends on the number of carbon atoms between the groups which cooperate to close the ring. It was found that the lactones and lactams are not formed from a-hydroxy- or amino-acids and rarely from the beta, but are formed very readily when the hydroxy- or amino-groups are in the gamma or delta positions and less readily when the number of intervening carbon atoms is larger. Comparatively little is known about the corresponding cyclic compounds in which the rings are much larger, although the odorous constituent of natural musk appears to be a lactone in which there are fifteen carbon atoms in the ring. Recent work has led to the preparation of compounds containing as many as thirty atoms in the ring. 

442. Cyclo Propane and Butane. It has been shown in Chapter XIII that straight chain ketones are formed by heating calcium salts. If the di-carboxy-acids are used, the five or six membered cyclic compounds are formed. These will be considered in detail below. However, other methods must be used to obtain the threeand four-membered cyclic compounds, as the calcium salts of succinic and glutaric acids do not give ketones when they are heated. 465

1,3-Dibromo-propane reacts with sodium as in the Wurtz synthesis to give cyclopropane: CH2Br CH2 CH2 CH2Br +2Na → CH2 | +2NaBr CH2 Cyclopropane Cyclopropane reacts with bromine to give 1,3-dibromo-propane, which is called trimethylene bromide, but the reaction goes less energetically than the union of the isomeric propylene with bromine.

Cyclobutane has been obtained through a long series of reactions, starting with trimethylene bromide and sodium malonic ester:

CH₂ COOEt CH2 COOH CH2 → CH2 CH2 COOEt CH2 COOH CH2 CH2 CH2 → CH2 CH2 COOH CH2 CONH2 CH2 CH₂ →CH2 →CH2 CH2 NH2

CH2 N(CH3)3OH CH2 CH2 →CH2 CH → CH2 CH2 CH CH2 Cyclobutene Cyclobutane 443. Baeyer's Strain Theory. This theory was proposed to explain the ease of formation of five and six-membered rings and the relative instability of rings with higher or lower numbers of carbon atoms. There is much evidence to show that the four valencies of a carbon atom are directed toward the vertices of a regular tetrahedron. This gives 109° 28′ as the angle between the directions of any two of these valencies. When any number of carbon atoms form a ring, as in cyclopropane, these valencies must be more or less displaced from their normal angle. If all the members of a ring are assumed to be in a plane, the angles of displacement can be calculated. Thus in cyclopropane the angles

CARBO-CYCLIC COMPOUNDS 

467 between the valencies of any one carbon are 60° instead of 109° 28′. 

In the figure the normal directions of the valencies are represented 24°44' 60° 444 by the dotted lines. 

The direction of each valency is 24° 44' away from the normal position. According to Baeyer's theory this distortion sets up a strain which accounts for the instability of cyclopropane. The greater this distortion, the greater the strain and the greater the instability of the structure. 

The displacements are readily calculated for other rings. 

Ethylene may be brought into this comparison by considering it a ring compound.

0° 44' +5° 16' + 9° 33' + 12° 46' It appears from this that in the cyclopentane ring the valencies may be in practically their normal positions. In cyclohexane the distortion is very slight and is in the opposite direction. The very great distortion in ethylene is supposed to be connected with the strong tendencies of ethylene derivatives to undergo addition

reactions by which this strain is relieved. When more than three carbons are in the ring they are probably not all in the same plane yet the stability of the rings of various sizes up to six members is remarkably well indicated by the figures in the above table. 

The members of larger rings may be so arranged in more than one plane so as to give strainless rings of almost any size.

CARBO-CYCLIC COMPOUNDS 

469 it its attendant groups. In course of time all possible rotations will take place. Starting with the five carbons in the zigzag arrangement a, if the third carbon rotates through 180°, the arrangement b results. If the fourth carbon rotates 180°, the arrangement c will result, bringing the terminal carbons near together. If at this instant the halogens should be removed, carbons 1 and 5 would probably unite. With six carbon chains the terminal carbons may approach each other in the same way. 

With carbon chains of greater lengths it will be rare that the terminal carbons happen to approach each other, although it is possible for them to do so. The terminal atoms of shorter chains do not normally come close together, but may do so on account of distortion caused by collision. Large rings, as shown by recent work, may be as stable as small ones. The fact that they are obtained in such extremely poor yields seems due to the slight probability of the terminal atoms coming within reacting distance at the moment of reaction.

The electron theory, even in its present incomplete state, gives a basis for a more concrete explanation of strains set up in rings. 

In methane the orbits of the pairs of valence electrons take up the most stable positions with reference to each other and to the carbon nucleus. Each pair of electrons would be as far as possible from the other three pairs, that is, in the direction of the vertices of the regular tetrahedron, as seen from the carbon nucleus. When rings are formed, these valence electron orbits must be forced out of their normal positions and will be crowded together and hence set up strains.

Following the name cyclopentanone, the hydrocarbon is called cyclopentane. Cyclopentane has the composition C5H10 and is isomeric with pentene but has no double bond in its formula, does not decolorize bromine water or have any of the other reactions which are characteristic of pentene. It is a fully saturated hydrocarbon, which is not attacked by ordinary chemical agents except the halogens and is relatively stable to heat.

From the halides, the cyclic hydrocarbons are obtained by reduction. All of them have proven to be much like cyclopentane in their properties. They have the general formula C₂H₂n, which makes them isomeric with the ethylenes, although they are saturated and have the chemical properties of the paraffins. Only the five and six-membered rings are at all well known. Cyclohexane and its derivatives will be singled out for further consideration.

Some petroleums, particularly some of those from Russia and California (Chapter V) contain large proportions of cyclic hydrocarbons, such as cyclopentane, cyclohexane and their alkyl derivatives. These are called naphthenes. Little is known as to the identity of the individual hydrocarbons that are present. Some of the high-boiling, lubricating oils appear to contain more than one ring. The composition of some of these hydrocarbons is represented by such formulae as CnH2n-8 and yet they show little if any absorption of iodine, which may mean that they have double bonds that are somewhat inactive or that they have a number of rings.

Hence they are sometimes called polymethylenes, the several members being trimethylene, tetramethylene, pentamethylene and hexamethylene.

The use of these names may lead to confusion and is to be discouraged. Instead of the endings -one and -ol, the prefixes keto- and hydroxy- may be used.

475 It is assumed that carbon atoms 

452. Cis and Trans Forms. 

joined by a double bond are not free to rotate, and this is put forward as the explanation of the existence of isomers such as fumaric and maleic acids. A carbon atom that is a part of a ring is likewise not free to rotate. Of the two groups which such a carbon carries one must be above and the other below the plane of the ring. When two carbons in the ring hold substituents, there are two possibilities: either both of the substituents are on one side of the ring or one is on one side and the other on the other. The situation is represented diagrammatically in the figure: HO cis-Quinitol

OH OH trans-Quinitol The carbon atoms may be supposed to be in the plane of the paper. 

The groups above the carbons are above this plane and the others below. In the left-hand figure the two hydroxyl groups are on the same side of the plane, giving what is called the cis form, while on the right they are on opposite sides, which is described by the prefix trans. Quinitol, the 1,4-dihydroxy-cyclo-hexane, or 1,4cyclohexandiol, does exist in two forms which differ in properties. 

This theory does not demand that all of the carbon atoms in the ring are in the same plane. The only thing postulated is that the carbons in the ring cannot rotate.

TERPENES 

453. The name terpene is applied to an important class of hydrocarbons which are found widely distributed in plants. The most abundant is pinene, or turpentine, which is of great commercial importance. The name terpene is sometimes limited to compounds having the formula C10H16, but it is convenient to consider with these some related substances which have the formulae C10H18 and C10H20. The oxygenated derivatives of the terpenes are sometimes called camphors, after the best-known member of the group. In this discussion the oxygenated derivatives will be included under the general name terpenes. 

Closely connected with the terpenes are the sesquiterpenes,

C15H24, diterpenes, C20H32, and polyterpenes, (C10H16), but these cannot be considered here. 

The terpenes, C10H16, and derivatives are divided into three classes, depending on the absence of a ring or the presence of one or two rings. Of the first class, the straight chain terpenes, the most important members are geraniol, citronellol, and their aldehydes, citral and citronellal, and linalool, which have already been considered (Chapter XXVII). 

454. Monocyclic Terpenes. These are derivatives of cyclohexane, cyclohexene or cyclohexadiene. Practically all of them have methyl and isopropyl groups in the 1 and 4 positions.

On further oxidation B-methyl-adipic acid is the end-product.

457. Bicyclic Terpenes. In menthane there is one ring; other hydrocarbons are known in which there are two or even more rings. Three of these belong to the terpene group and are closely allied to the monocyclic terpenes which have been described above. 

As in the case of the monocyclic, the saturated hydrocarbons are given first as reference compounds, although they are not natural products and are not interesting in themselves. All three of them may be regarded as made from menthane by joining the central carbon (8) of the isopropyl group to one of the other carbons of the ring, making a sort of bridge across the ring. One end of this bridge is in all cases at carbon 4, while the other end is at 3 in carane, at 2 in pinane and at 1 in camphane. Carane and its derivatives are of little importance and need not be further considered. Pinane can be prepared by hydrogenating pinene, which has a double bond between carbons 6 and 1 of the above formula. Pinene, probably the most abundant of all the terpenes, is the chief constituent of oil of turpentine and is found in a large number of other essential oils. It is optically active, occurring in American turpentine as the dextro modification and in French as the levo. It is widely used as a solvent for resins in varnishes and as a thinner in paints.

481 Pinene, being unsaturated, readily takes up halogen, halide acids, etc. Its most striking reaction is the addition of hydrogen chloride. When this gas is led into well-cooled pinene, a solid is formed which melts at 127-128°. In odor and appearance it closely resembles camphor, for which reason it is frequently called "artificial camphor." The name is confusing, as camphor, identical with natural camphor in all respects except in optical activity, is manufactured on a large scale and may also be called artificial camphor. The hydrogen chloride adds at the double bond, but the addition product first formed isomerizes at once, so that the pinene hydrochloride that is obtained is actually isobornyl chloride: HC CH3 CH CCI CCH CH CCH HC CHCI HC.C⋅CH₂ HC.C.CH HC.C.CH

This remarkable isomerization by which a derivative of pinene goes into one of camphane gave chemists a great deal of trouble in assigning the proper formulae to camphor and to the other compounds of this group.

Borneol, a secondary alcohol, is a natural product, being found in small quantity in various oils, particularly in pine oil. It is readily oxidised to camphor:

CH CH₂ HC CHOH HC Co HCCCH, HC.C.CH

HC CH₂ HC CH CH Borneol Camphor

Camphor, sometimes called Japanese camphor, is obtained from the camphor tree, Laurus camphor, which grows in Japan and China. The wood is distilled with steam. The camphor which passes over is purified by sublimation. It melts at 179° and boils at 209.1°, and is only slightly soluble in water, 0.08 g. in 100 cc.,

but dissolves in less than its own weight of alcohol. Its ketone character is evidenced by the formation of an oxime and other ketone reactions. It is dextro-rotatory. Its antipode l-camphor is found in Matricaria parthenium. The two forms are identical in every respect except optical rotation and give the inactive dl-camphor when they are mixed. Camphor is used as a drug but on a far larger scale as a constituent of celluloid and other plastics. 

As the supply of the natural product is not sufficient for the demand, synthetic camphor takes its place for industrial uses. 

It is made from a-pinene, which is obtained by the close fractionation of oil of turpentine. There are various ways of converting pinene into camphor, a typical method being: pinene → pinene hydrochloride bornyl chloride → isobornyl acetate →isoborneol (by oxidation) → camphor. 

Isobornyl chloride and isoborneol are believed to be stereoisomers of borneol and bornyl chloride.

CHAPTER XXXI BENZENE 

460. When cyclohexane is passed over catalytically active nickel at 300°, hydrogen is liberated and a hydrocarbon called benzene is produced:

C6H12 C6H6 + 3H2 This reaction is reversible; thus, benzene and hydrogen passed over nickel at 200° unite to give cyclohexane. Lower temperatures and high pressure of hydrogen favor the formation of cyclohexane. 

Platinum and palladium bring about the union of benzene and hydrogen at still lower temperatures. 

The reversibility of the reaction and the fact that hydroxybenzene and amino-benzene can be hydrogenated under similar conditions to hydroxy-cyclohexane and amino-cyclohexane, argue strongly for the presence of a six-carbon ring in benzene, as in cyclohexane. As cyclohexene, C6H10, and cyclohexadiene, C¿Hs, are known it is natural to assume that benzene is cyclohexatriene: HC HC CHE CH₂ HC CH₂ CH₂ Cyclohexane

To a certain extent the properties of benzene agree with this. 

As already stated, it takes up six hydrogen atoms to form cyclohexane. Under the influence of light it adds six chlorines to give 

C6H6Cle, benzene hexachloride, or less readily, six bromines to produce C6H6Bг6, benzene hexabromide. While the quantities of these elements taken up correspond to the presence of three double bonds, the reactions do not take place with the ease that would be expected. Cyclohexene decolorizes bromine water instantly when the two are shaken together. Its reaction with dilute potas- 484

BENZENE 

485 sium permanganate solution is also prompt. Cyclohexadiene exhibits these properties to a greater extent than cyclohexene, but benzene shows a marked difference. It may be boiled for hours with permanganate solution without decolorization. While cyclohexene and cyclohexadiene act as typical unsaturated hydrocarbons, benzene which contains still less hydrogen reacts with most reagents as if it were saturated. In the presence of traces of catalysts, such as ferric or aluminum chlorides, chlorine and bromine react readily with benzene, but give substitution products instead of addition products. Not only with chlorine and bromine but with almost all reagents, benzene gives substitution products rather than addition products. More than one bromine or chlorine may be substituted:

Benzene was discovered by Faraday 2 in 1825 in a condensate from illuminating gas which had been made by heating oil. It was made from benzoic acid by Mitscherlich 3 in 1834 and identified in coal tar by A. W. Hofmann in 1845. The molecular formula of ben-

zene was early shown to be C6H6, but chemists had no idea of the constitution of benzene or of the many substances which were recognized as related to it, until the cyclohexatriene formula given above was suggested by Kekulé ¹ in 1865. The publication of the article giving this formula is regarded as one of the greatest events in the history of chemistry, and its twenty-fifth anniversary was celebrated in Berlin by an assemblage of chemists from all parts of the world who met at the invitation of the German Chemical Society. 

462. Benzene readily undergoes a number of substitution reactions similar to those mentioned above. The variety of such reactions, the ease with which they can be controlled, and the usefulness of many of the reaction products have led to an enormous development of the chemistry of benzene and its homologs. On account of the pleasant odors of certain benzene derivatives, benzene and its derivatives were given the name "aromatic." In order to set them off from this group, the straight chain hydrocarbons and their derivatives are called aliphatic, from a Greek word meaning fat, since the fats belong to that class. The cyclic compounds other than those related to benzene are called alicyclic. 

While benzene is like methane, ethane and other paraffin hydrocarbons in reacting with chlorine and some other reagents by substitution, it is quite unlike them in the ease with which these reactions can be carried out. While the paraffin hydrocarbons are found in petroleum in enormous quantities, they have been utilized to only a very small extent in chemical manufacture. The manufacture of the chloropentanes was mentioned in Chapter VII as a recent achievement. On the contrary, benzene and its homologs are used as starting materials for great industries, the most noteworthy of which is that of synthetic dyes. So great has been the development of aromatic chemistry that at the present time probably two-thirds of the organic compounds known belong to this 'class. This is a justification for the separate consideration of aromatic compounds.

Ghent and the University of Bonn. He was noted for working out the quadrivalence of carbon and the benzene theory. He was in London from 1854-56, where he worked under Stenhouse. Here he discovered thioacetic acid.

Claus-Thompson

Armstrong and Baeyer

The diagram labeled Claus¹ and Thompson2 really represents two formulae which are quite different, but which look alike when projected on a plane surface. Claus conceived of the six carbons as being symmetrically placed on the surface of a sphere, opposite carbons being joined by the three long diagonal bonds and adjacent ones by the six ordinary bonds. Thompson's representation, which does not involve the sphere, was based on the fact that the heat of formation of benzene corresponds to nine single bonds rather than to three single and three double, as postulated by Kekulé. These diagonals suggest the bridge bond of borneol and camphor.

Thiele's 3 formula was an extension of his ideas on conjugatea double bonds. It has been frequently observed with compounds having conjugated double bonds, that is, double bonds alternating with single, that addition takes place to carbons 1 and 4 rather than to 1 and 2 or to 3 and 4: 1 2 3 X2C CH-CH: CX2 + Br2 → X2BrC CH: CH.CBrX2 

Thiele's explanation for this is that the second bond in the double bond does not use up the affinities of the two carbon atoms, 1 Adolf Claus (1840-1900) was Professor at the University of Freiburg in Baden.

so-called residual affinities being left to attract other atoms. 

These residual affinities of adjacent carbon atoms are supposed to neutralize each other and leave the residual valencies of the end carbons active.

Partial valencies

X2C-CH-CH=CX2 Conjugated double bonds with partial valencies

The double bonds assumed in the Kekulé formula are all conjugated and the residual valencies are supposed to be neutralized. 

Partial valencies may be interpreted in terms of the electron conception of valence by assuming some kind of displacement of the orbits of the extra valence electrons. 

The Ladenburg 1 formula is quite different in that it represents the six carbon atoms at the corners of the triangular prism. It has failed of acceptance for two reasons. It represents each carbon atom as being adjacent to three others, while, as will appear later, each carbon in benzene appears to be near only two others. 

Difficulties are encountered in representing what takes place when benzene is hydrogenated to cyclohexane. In this transition three bonds must be broken, one of the vertical and two of the horizontal, and consequently a disubstituted benzene should produce a mixture when hydrogenated. Thus, if there are methyl groups joined to carbons 1 and 2, the hydrogenated dimethyl-benzene might be a mixture of 1,4and 1,2-dimethyl-cyclohexane, depending on whether the 1-2 bond or one of the other vertical bonds breaks.

The fourth formula was proposed by Armstrong² in England and advocated by Baeyer of Germany. It is commonly called the centric formula. It differs from Thompson's in that the diagonal bonds do not reach all the way, but are simply directed toward the center of gravity of the ring. If two hydrogen atoms are added to benzene, this arrangement would be disturbed and two double ¹ Albert Ladenburg (1842-1911) worked on the synthesis of alkaloids and the constitution of benzene. He was appointed Professor in the University of Kiel in 1874 and in the University of Breslau in 1889. 

Henry E. Armstrong, an English chemist and writer, was Professor in the City and Guildhall Technical College, London.

489 bonds formed, which would account for the striking difference between benzene and cyclohexadiene: HC HC CH₂ + 2H - HC CH HC Benzene Dihydro-benzene, cyclohexadiene The advantage of the centric formula is that it uses different representations for benzene and for cyclohexadiene, two hydrocarbons which are strikingly different. Its weakness is that the idea of these bonds being simply directed toward the center is hard to grasp.

As valence forces are believed to involve electrons, the structure of benzene must depend on the arrangement of electrons that hold the six carbons together. Some regard the bonds between the carbons as polar, one carbon taking an electron from another. 

This would make the carbons alternately positive and negative. 

Others believe that the bonds are non-polar, each bond being a pair of electrons held jointly by the two carbons. An extension of this adapts it to the partial valence theory by assuming three electrons between each two carbons, according to which the six carbons would be held together by six sesqui bonds instead of by three single and three double as postulated by Kekulé. It has been suggested that there are both polar and non-polar bonds in benzene. 

As the electrons are in motion, it may be that their positions correspond at one time to one formula and to another an instant later; that is, that any given formula is to be regarded as a sort of instantaneous view. Kekulé assumed that the double bonds were all the time shifting, being between carbons 1 and 2, 3 and 4, and 

5 and 6 at one instant and between 2 and 3, 4 and 5, and 6 and 1 at the next. Otherwise the relationship of carbon 1 to carbon 2 would be different from that of carbon 2 to carbon 3. 

For practical purposes questions as to the superiority of one formula or another are avoided by using a simple hexagon to represent benzene, it being understood that a hydrogen is to be assumed as present at each vertex unless replaced by some other atom or group.

464. Substitution Products of Benzene. Cyclohexane gives only one mono-substitution product. The same may be said of benzene and with far greater certainty, since an enormous amount of time and energy has been devoted to its study. In spite of all efforts to prepare more than one variety, any mono substitution product produced is always the same substance with unvarying properties. Starting with nitrobenzene, C6H5NO2, in which the substitutent may be said to be at a, aminobenzene, C6H5NH2, can be made in which the amino group is at a. This can be nitrated giving a nitro-amino-benzene, NH2 C6H4 NO2, in which the nitro group must be in some other position, as b. The amino group in this case can be replaced by bromine, which gives bromo-nitrobenzene, C6H4 Br(a)NO2(b), in which the bromine is at a and the .

NO2 ΝΗΣ NH₂ Br NH₂ 0-0-0-0-0 nitro group at b. These reactions have been carried out and the two amino-benzenes having the amino groups at a and b have been proved to be identical in all respects. This process has been extended until a given group has been made to occupy all six of the possible positions and the six products found to be identical in all respects. The complete symmetry of benzene can be regarded as one of the most thoroughly established facts of science. 

465. Polysubstitution Products. When there are more than one substituent, there are isomers, the number of which can be readily predicted. Two substituents give three isomers: 1,2 Ortho, o- 1,3 Meta, m- 1,4 Para, p- The number of isomers here is the same whether the two substituents are the same or different. The 1,2-grouping is called ortho," the 1,3- "meta," and the 1,4- "para," from Greek words meaning" straight,' ""beyond," and "alongside of," as in

BENZENE 

491 Ortho applies to any two and 3,5 as well as 1,3 are orthodox, metaphysics and paradox. adjacent positions, as 2,3 or 4,5; 2,4 meta; while 2,5 and 3,6 are para. Applied to benzene derivatives these prefixes are not descriptive and are to be regarded simply as tags. These are abbreviated to the prefixes o-, m-, and p-. Corresponding to the theory there are actually known three dichlorobenzenes, three dibromo-benzenes, three dinitro-benzenes, and so on for a great number of different substituents, the three isomers of each kind differing among themselves in all physical properties, such as density, melting point and boiling point. Similarly, there are three nitro-chloro-benzenes, three nitro-bromo-benzenes, and so on for many pairs of substituents. The isomers in each case are distinguished by their physical properties.

When there are three similar substituents, there are three isomers, and if the substituents are different, the number of isomers increases. Four groups of the same kind give three isomers, and five of a kind only one. 1,2,3

Symmetrical, s For three substituents, the various forms are called vicinal, unsymmetrical and symmetrical, which are abbreviated to the prefixes, v-, u-, and s-. There are many groups of three isomers known, although in general the tri-substitution products have not been so thoroughly investigated as the di-substitution products. 

466. Naming Benzene Compounds. The system of numbering that is used for cyclohexane applies also to benzene; the six carbon atoms of the ring are numbered 1 to 6. When there are groups of more than one kind substituted, the numbering starts at the smallest group, thus: CH3 

2 CHS NO₂ NH₂ ΕΝΟ

Groups such as -NO2, -OH and SH are rated on the atomic weights of the atoms which are joined to the ring, preference being given to the lighter one. When the atoms joined to the ring are the same, as in-NH2, -NO and -NO2, the weight and number of the other atoms are taken into account. Where there are two or more groups of the smallest size, the formula is written so as to give these the smallest possible numbers. Thus if in the 1-methyl- 

2-ethyl-benzene above, a second methyl group were introduced at 5, the product would be called 1,3-dimethyl-6-ethyl-benzene. 

Mono-substitution products are frequently named by calling the group C6H5-phenyl. Thus chlorobenzene, bromobenzene and iodobenzene become phenyl chloride, phenyl bromide and phenyl iodide. Phenyl and other aromatic radicals are called aryl, which corresponds to alkyl among the aliphatics. Sometimes 

C6H4 is called phenylene and o-diamino-benzene becomes o-phenylene diamine. 

467. Orientation. From Kekulé's benzene formula it was seen that there should be three dichloro-benzenes and it was decided to call these ortho, meta and para. By various methods three isomeric substances of the formula C6H4Cl₂ were obtained. These have the following properties, (a) m. p. -17.6°, b. p. 179°, (b) m. p. - 24.8°, b. p. 173°, and (c) m. p. 52.9°, b. p. 173°. The problem which puzzled chemists from 1865 to 1872 was to fit the three substances to the three formulae, that is, to ascertain which of them is ortho, meta and para. Griess¹ in 1872 settled the question by a study of the dinitro- and diamino-benzoic acids. 

He found it possible to prepare six different dinitro-benzoic acids, which he characterized by their melting points, solubilities, etc. 

A study of the formulae shows that six are predicted by Kekulé's theory. At higher temperatures the tendency to dehydrogenation is greater but this may be overcome by increased pressure; benzene is rapidly hydrogenated at 300° under 20 atmospheres pressure. The only serious difficulty in the hydrogenation of benzene is the presence in commercial benzene of thiophene (Chapter XXXVIII), a sulphur compound, which poisons the catalyst. The hydrogenation of benzene derivatives, phenol, aniline, etc., can be effected under the same conditions as that of benzene.

470. Place of Entry of the Second Substituent. In the halo genation of benzene the dihalogen product is almost entirely the para isomer; the halogen of the first formed mono-halogen compound directs the second halogen to the para and ortho positions. 

When benzene is nitrated or sulphonated, the dinitro-benzene and the disulphonic acid are chiefly the meta isomers. It has been found that the chlorine in mono-chlorobenzene directs not only a halogen but any other entering group chiefly to the para and ortho positions. Thus the bromination, nitration and sulphonation of chlorobenzene give chiefly p-chlorobromobenzene, p-nitrochlorobenzene and p-chlorobenzene sulphonic acid along with considerable amounts of the corresponding ortho derivatives with very little of the meta. A similar statement can be made about the nitro and sulphonic acid groups. The nature of the group already in the benzene ring is the dominant factor and determines whether the product will be chiefly a mixture of the para and ortho isomerides or the meta isomer. The nature of the entering group, temperature, solvent, or catalyst are of less importance, but do influence the proportions of the isomers produced. 

The groups that may be present in benzene may be divided into two classes: one class comprises those, which like the halogens, direct an entering group chiefly to the para and ortho positions, while in the other class are those that favor meta substitution.

471. A closer examination of the proportions of isomers shows that there is a sort of gradation in the amount of meta isomer formed as the character of the directing group changes. Instead of saying that the groups in Class 1 direct the entering group to the ortho and para positions and those of Class 2 direct it to the meta position, it may be better to think of all the groups in both classes as influencing the ortho and para positions. In 

Class 1 are found groups which facilitate substitution in these positions; phenol and aniline are nitrated or chlorinated in dilute solution in the cold while benzene requires much more drastic treatment. The groups in Class 2 may simply prevent substitution in the ortho and para positions, so that substitution would have to take place in the meta position, if at all. Nitrobenzene and benzoic acid are more difficult to chlorinate or nitrate than benzene.

472. Commercial Production of Benzene. Benzene is one of the products commonly obtained when organic substances are

BENZENE 

501 highly heated. In the heating of coal for the purpose of making coke and illuminating gas relatively small quantities of organic liquids are obtained as by-products. When the coal is heated at 

600° under reduced pressure, the organic part of the distillate is about 1 per cent of the weight of the coal and is chiefly aliphatic hydrocarbons, but under the usual conditions for making coke and illuminating gas (a temperature up to 1000° and atmospheric pressure), the condensable organic distillate is only 0.4 to 0.5 per cent and consists almost entirely of aromatic compounds. The aromatic hydrocarbons probably result from the effect of the high temperature on the primary aliphatic compounds. 

The coal is heated in retorts and the issuing gases led through chambers where the coal-tar is condensed. The gas is washed with water or dilute sulphuric acid to obtain the ammonia which it contains. As benzene has an appreciable vapor pressure at ordinary temperature a considerable amount of it is carried off by the gas and is largely responsible for the illuminating power of ordinary coal gas. The benzene can be abstracted from the gas by scrubbing it with heavy oil or passing it through active charcoal or silica gel.

The coal-tar is fractionated from large steel stills, being thus separated into three or four distillates and the residue. The residue is coal-tar pitch and is used as a binder in briquet and road making and for roofing materials. The lower boiling part of the distillate up to 140°, called "light oil," is washed with alkali and with dilute acid and refractionated through an efficient column whereby pure benzene is obtained. Some homologs of benzene, as toluene and xylene, are obtained along with the benzene. For a long time the tar produced in coal-gas plants was sufficient to supply the demands. For making coke, of which enormous quantities are required for steel making and other purposes, coal was until recent times heated in beehive ovens and the gases produced allowed to burn. The increasing demand for benzene and other substances which are obtained from coal-tar caused a gradual shifting of coke production from the beehive ovens to modern by-product ovens which save the gas, tar, and ammonia. 

Germany, where the industries depending on coal-tar are the most highly developed, was the first country to abandon the beehive ovens. England and the United States have followed.

473. Uses of Benzene. These may be divided into three groups: in the chemical industries, for making dyes, drugs and perfume materials; as a solvent in lacquers, automobile finishes and the like, and in blended motor fuel because of its anti-knock value. CHAPTER XXXII  

474. The chemical industries that make use of benzene and its homologs are very complex. From benzene to a dye or a pharmaceutical requires a long succession of chemical reactions. A few compounds are made directly from benzene and these serve as intermediates for the preparation of a larger number of compounds. 

Many millions of dollars and many years of the lives of a host of the best-trained chemists have been spent in working out all of these reactions. The three fundamental reactions for making the primary intermediates are chlorination, nitration and sulphonation which were discussed in Chapter XXXI.

Chlorobenzene and bromobenzene, or phenyl chloride and bromide, are far less reactive than ethyl chloride and bromide and consequently are not so readily used for synthetic purposes. In reactivity of the halogens they resemble vinyl chloride and bromide, as should be the case according to the Kekulé formula. 

Recently it has been found that chlorobenzene reacts satisfactorily with certain reagents at a high temperature under pressure. 

Phenol and aniline are now being manufactured from chlorobenzene in this way: + NaOH + NaCl Phenol NH₂ + HCI + NHs Aniline

476. Phenol. Coal tar contains large quantities of phenol, C6H5OH, the mono-hydroxy derivative of benzene. The part of the distillate from coal tar which boils from 170° to 230° is extracted with caustic soda solution from which the phenol is liberated by passing in carbon dioxide. This phenol is collected and purified by fractionation. Phenol is a solid melting at 41° and boiling at 

182°. At 20°, 100 cc. of water dissolves 9.05 g. of phenol, but at 

67.5° phenol and water mix in all proportions. It is extremely soluble in alcohol and in ether.

The constitution of phenol is shown by its reaction with phosphorus pentachloride which gives chlorobenzene:

C6H5OH + PC15 → C6H5Cl + POCl3 + HCI Phenol Chlorobenzene

In constitution phenol, the hydroxyl derivative of benzene, resembles alcohol, C2H5OH, but in properties the two differ considerably. 

Phenol is to be classed with the tertiary alcohols since the carbon atom that carries the hydroxyl does not have a hydrogen. 

Whether or not this carbon is to be considered as joined to three other carbon atoms, as in a tertiary alcohol depends on the benzene formula adopted, but it is certain that three of its valencies are used in holding it in its place in the ring structure. Although metal alcoholates are known, the acidic power of the alcohols is very slight, while that of phenol is decided, as is evidenced by its popular name "carbolic acid."

478. The Manufacture and Uses of Phenol. It has been indicated above that large amounts of phenol are obtained from coal tar. It has long been manufactured by fusing benzene sulphonic acid with caustic soda:

C6H5SOзNa + NaOH→ C&H OH + Na2SO3 Recently it has been produced on a large scale from chlorobenzene and caustic soda in the presence of phenyl oxide: C6H5Cl + NaOH→ C6H5OH + NaCl Phenol has been used largely as a disinfectant and germicide, for which it is the accepted standard. A germicide is rated by its phenol coefficient, which is of the ratio of its killing power for organisms to that of phenol. Large quantities of phenol are used in the manufacture of resins and plastics. Bakelite is a condensation product of phenol and formaldehyde. 

479. Amino-phenols. These are obtained by the reduction of the nitro-phenols. The acid character of phenol practically vanishes with the introduction of the amino group. The aminophenols are relatively unstable and decompose on exposure to moist air and light, but their salts crystallize well and are more stable.

Certain of their derivatives are of more interest than the aminophenols themselves. By nitrating anisol and phenetol and reducing, the anisidines and phenetidines are obtained. As the nitration gives a mixture of ortho and para compounds, the ortho and para anisidines and phenetidines are the most readily obtained. The para compounds are most useful in the preparation of dyes. Aceto-

phenetidine is known as phenacetine and is an extensively used anti-pyretic drug: NH₂ NH₂ NH.CO.CH,

481. Hexahydroxy-benzene. The potassium salt of this is of interest on account of the remarkable reaction by which it is formed from carbon monoxide and heated potassium: 6CO + 6K C606K6 It is difficult to imagine the formation of a six-carbon ring from six molecules of carbon monoxide. This potassium compound, which becomes explosive when exposed to the air, is believed to be the chief constituent of a by-product in the old method of preparing potassium by heating charcoal with potassium carbonate. 

When the potassium compound is treated with dilute acid in the absence of air, the hexahydroxy-benzene is obtained as long needles which darken at 200° but do not melt. 

482. Thiophenol. This compound, C6H5SH, the sulphur analog of phenol, is obtained, among other products, by the action of sulphur on benzene:

C6H6 + S→ C6H5SH

It is a liquid boiling at 172.5° and resembling phenol in many of its reactions. Oxidation converts it to a disulphide and then to benzene sulphonic acid: 2C6H5SH + O→ C6H5S SC6H5 C6H5SH + 30 → C6H5SO2. OH 

483. Nitrobenzene. As stated above, one of the characteristic reactions of benzene and of other aromatic hydrocarbons is the ease of nitration. Nitrobenzene is manufactured on an enormous scale as a starting substance in making benzene derivatives. It is always made by the nitration of benzene. It is an oil which melts at 5.67°, boils at 210.85°, and has the density 1.1986725. It is only slightly soluble in water, 0.19 g. at 20° and 0.8 g. at 80° in 

100 cc. of water. It has a pleasant odor and is called essence of mirbane, but is not used in perfumery, since its vapor is somewhat toxic. 

484. Reactions of Nitrobenzene. 1. The reduction of nitro benzene can yield a number of different products according to the reducing agent and the conditions, the most important being aniline, which is obtained by the use of metals in acid solution: C6H5NO2 + 6H→ C6H5NH2 + 2H2O Aniline

With tin and zinc an excess of acid has to be used, but with iron a small percentage of that called for by the stoichiometric equation suffices. The explanation seems to be that the acid present dissolves some of the iron to form the salt which is hydrolyzed, setting free the acid which, in turn, dissolves more iron and so on. The iron is converted to ferrous hydroxide: C6H5NO2 + 3Fe + 4H2O → C6H5NH2 + 3Fe(OH)2 Commercially the nitrobenzene is warmed with iron turnings and water, with the addition of a small amount of hydrochloric acid. 

The aniline is recovered from the reaction mixture by steam distillation. 

2. In neutral solution, buffered with ammonium chloride, nitrobenzene is reduced to phenyl hydroxylamine: C6H5NO₂+2Zn + 3H2O→ C6H5NHOH + 2Zn(OH)2 Phenyl hydroxylamine

This phenyl hydroxylamine is a white solid, melting at 82° and dissolving in 50 parts of water at 20° and in 10 parts at 100°. 

3. With reducing agents it gives aniline, while with strong oxidising agents it goes to nitrosobenzene: C6H5NHOH + O→ C6H5NO + H₂O Nitrosobenzene

Nitrosobenzene crystallizes in colorless needles, which melt at 68° and volatilize at 59° at 17 mm. It is an emerald-green in color, either when it is melted or in solution. It is readily reduced to aniline and can be oxidised to nitrobenzene. 

4. Nitrobenzene is reduced by sodium methylate in boiling methyl alcohol solution to azoxybenzene:

HN NH₂ Benzidine 485. Aniline. The starting point for the manufacture of a large number of valuable products is aniline. It has been manufactured on a large scale by the reduction of nitrobenzene as mentioned above and also by the action of ammonia on chlorobenzene. 

Aniline is aminobenzene but as an ammonia derivative it is phenyl amine and has the reactions of a primary amine. As a substituted ammonia it forms salts, as does ammonia, but these salts are less stable, as aniline is a weaker base than ammonia. Phenyl hydrox-

ide is more acidic than ethyl hydroxide and phenyl amine is a weaker base than ethyl amine. Salts are formed from ammonia by the direct addition of an acid or more strictly by the neutralization of ammonium hydroxide which must exist in water solution. 

The salts of aniline are similarly formed. Phenyl ammonium hydroxide must be formed, to some extent at least, from aniline and water and must be present in a water solution of aniline, in which it would ionize into phenyl ammonium and hydroxyl ions: 

C6H5NH2 + HCl → C6H5NH3Cl Aniline Aniline hydrochloride C6H5NH2 + HOH → C6H5NH3OH 

Phenyl amine 

Phenyl ammonium hydroxide

C6H5NH3OH + HCl → C6H5NHзCl + H₂O 

Phenyl ammonium chloride

Ammonia is NH3 while NH4Cl is ammonium chloride. The naming of the salts formed from aniline is neither logical nor consistent. The salt above is commonly called aniline hydrochloride and its formula is frequently written C6H5NH2 HCl, but C6H5NH2 H2SO4, or C6H5NH3SO4H is known as aniline sulphate, and C6H5NH3NO3 is aniline nitrate. It would be more logical to say anilinium hydroxide and chloride for C6H5NH3OH and C6H5NHзCl. The salts of aniline are usually soluble in water, the hydrochloride very soluble and the sulphate only slightly soluble. 

Its salts with weak acids are hydrolyzed by water. These salts are formed by dissolving aniline in dry benzene or in dry ether and adding a solution of the acid, such as acetic acid, in the same solvent. The salt is formed immediately and precipitates.

From the name of the first of the class they are called phenyl urethanes. When a new alcohol is prepared and described, its boiling point, density, and the melting point of its phenyl urethane are the data usually given for its characterization.

5. Like phenol, aniline undergoes substitution with great ease, the para and ortho hydrogens being exchanged for the entering group. The halogens especially react with aniline to form mono-, di- and tri-halogen anilines. The preparation of tribrom-aniline is used for the identification and estimation of aniline. This reaction takes place at such extreme dilution that it has been found practicable to obtain bromine from sea water by its aid. Just enough chlorine is mixed with the sea water to liberate the bromine which it contains and the required amount of aniline is added; tribrom-aniline is formed and filtered off. This was shown to be a practical process by the voyage of the good ship "Ethyl.”¹ 

6. The sulphonation of aniline takes place readily when aniline sulphate with excess of sulphuric acid is heated to 180° for several hours. The sulphonic acid group enters the para position in the aniline:

HN Aniline HO SO,H HN SO,H + HO 

Sulphanilic acid

The product is called sulphanilic acid. It crystallizes with two molecules of water. It is but slightly soluble in water, one part in 93 of water at 20° and only slightly soluble in alcohol or ether. 

It is probably an inner salt, the sulphonic group neutralizing the amino group of the same or of another molecule. It is largely used as a starting point in the manufacture of dyes.

With the substitution of a second phenyl group the basic power almost completely disappears. Diphenyl amine forms a hydrochloride but it is hydrolyzed on contact with water.
