It is sensitive to oxidation, the product being tetraphenyl-hydrazine: +0 2(C6H5)2NH + O→ (C6H5)2N⚫N(C6H5)2 + H2O Diphenyl amine is used in nitroglycerine mixtures as a stabilizer. 

Nitroglycerine is remarkably stable when entirely pure, but its decomposition once started is autocatalytic since traces of nitric or nitrous acids hasten its decomposition. The theory is that diphenyl amine reacts with these decomposition products of nitroglycerine and thus prevents their causing further decomposition. 

11. With aldehydes aniline reacts to form compounds which are known as Schiff's bases": 66 C6H5NH2 + OCH CH3 → C6H5N: CH-CH3 + H2O OCH·CH3 

Schiff's base

These bases polymerize readily so what is actually obtained is an amorphous mass. 

487. The Diazo Reaction. This is one of the most remarkable and most useful reactions in organic chemistry. It was discovered

in 1860 by Griess. A salt of aniline is treated with nitrous acid: Hoi + ON CI NEN بش 2 HO 

Benzene diazonium chloride 2 The reaction product like the aniline hydrochloride is colorless, very soluble in water and highly ionized, one ion being the chloride ion. The migration velocity of the ion C6H5N₂ is comparable to that of quaternary ammonium ions. These facts and others point to the presence of pentavalent nitrogen. For this reason the compound is called benzene diazonium chloride. For a long time it was called diazobenzene chloride and represented by the formula: N:N-CI مس If this were correct, the compound should be more like azobenzene, which is highly colored and insoluble in water and does not resemble ammonium salts.¹

Other salts of aniline react similarly to give the corresponding diazonium salts. These salts are all soluble in water and nearly all are extremely unstable. Most of them can be kept in water solution only at low temperatures, usually below 5°. By diazotizing in alcohol solution with amyl nitrite or by passing in nitrogen trioxide the diazonium salts can be made in alcohol solution from which they can be precipitated by the addition of ether. They separate as solids which usually decompose in a short time. Most of them are highly explosive; some detonate at the slightest touch. 

On account of the difficulties and danger involved in obtaining and handling the solid diazonium compounds they are seldom isolated. 

Instead they are used in solution immediately after their formation. 'Arthur Hantzsch (1857- ), Professor at the Universities of Wurzburg and Leipzig, has worked extensively on the structure of the diazo compounds and is well known for his studies on the relation between color and chemical constitution.

The azo dyes, which are the most numerous and varied of all classes of dyes, are made directly from the solution and so are most of the other derivatives.

The reactions of benzene diazonium chloride are many. Nitrogen is frequently eliminated. With water it gives phenol, nitrogen and hydrochloric acid. This is what takes place when aniline is diazotized and the solution allowed to warm up: C6H5N₂Cl + H2O → C6H5OH + N2 + HCI This reaction is seldom used to prepare phenol itself but is frequently employed for replacing the amino group in derivatives of benzene by the hydroxyl, that is, for obtaining substituted phenols. 

As diazotization is usually carried on in water solution this phenol reaction almost always takes place to a greater or less extent; phenol is usually a by-product when any compound is prepared by the aid of this reaction.

In alcohol solution two different reactions may occur, the alcohol may function as the water in the above or the alcohol may be dehydrogenated to the aldehyde, the hydrogen going to form hydrogen chloride and the hydrocarbon:

C6H5N₂Cl + HOCH3 → C6H5OCH3 + N2 + HCl 

Methyl phenyl ether

N2 C6H5N₂Cl + HOCH2-CH3 → C6H5H + N₂ + HCl + CH3.CHO Benzene

In many cases these reactions take place concurrently, the first one predominating when the simpler diazonium compounds are warmed in solution in the lower alcohols. When more complicated amines are diazotized in the higher alcohols, the aldehyde and hydrocarbon are the chief products. The latter reaction is frequently useful for replacing an amino group by hydrogen. 

Benzene diazonium iodide, in water solution, decomposes in two ways:

C6H5N₂I+HOH → C6H5OH + N₂+ HI C6H5N₂I→ C6H5I + N2 These reactions go on simultaneously but the latter reaction predominates to a sufficient extent to make this a satisfactory method of preparing phenyl iodide.

In the case of phenyl diazonium chloride and bromide the reaction with water to form phenol takes place to the exclusion of the other unless cuprous salts, or finely divided copper, are present. 

Sandmeyer,¹ for whom this reaction is named, discovered that cuprous salts speed up the formation of phenyl chloride and bromide to such an extent that satisfactory yields are obtained although some phenol is always formed also. Phenyl cyanide is similarly obtained. In the presence of cuprous salts, the reactions are: C6H5N2C1→ C6H5Cl + N₂ C6H5N₂Br→ C6H5Br + N₂ C6H5N₂CN → C6H5CN + N2 These are useful preparation methods, particularly for the substituted phenyl chlorides, bromides and iodides. Gattermann 2 later found that finely divided copper may be used instead of cuprous salts.

490. The Theory of Colored Compounds. This is involved and not fully understood but for practical purposes several conceptions are commonly used. A chromophor, or color-bringer, is a grouping that is associated with color. Azobenzene is red and other compounds containing the group -N: N-, particularly

if it is between two benzene rings, are also colored. Hence this is called a chromophor. The substitution of any group in either ring of azobenzene will change its color more or less, shifting the color either toward the red or toward the violet end of the spectrum and either weakening or intensifying the color. An auxochrome group is one which intensifies the color. The chief groups of this class are the hydroxyl and amino groups in the para or ortho position relative to the -N: N-group. Either of these intensifies the color of azobenzene enormously. Azobenzene is red but if it is ground up with several parts of chalk the mixture is a pale pink. 

One part of either p-hydroxy-azobenzene or p-amino-azobenzene will dye a hundred times its weight of wool an intense color. Both of these groups are salt forming. The substitution of a methyl, or other radical, for the phenolic hydrogen destroys its effectiveness as an auxochrome but substitutions in the amino group only modify the color.

It is a notable fact that chromophor groups contain conjugated double bonds and, as in the examples given below, the alternation of double and single bonds goes around the molecule or some distance in it. According to the Kekulé formula benzene contains three double bonds, all conjugated. Benzene appears colorless since it has no absorption band in the visible spectrum but it does have such a band in the ultraviolet. In quinone there are four conjugated double bonds and seven in azobenzene: Benzene 0: Quinone

ON:NO 

N:N Azobenzene

The color is certainly due to selective absorption of light of particular wave lengths by the molecule or by some of its parts which are capable of vibrating at periods corresponding to the wave lengths which are absorbed. The vibration periods of the grosser parts of the molecule would be too low for visible light and those of the regular valence electrons too high. The three extra bonds which have given so much trouble in constructing benzene formulae are, in modern parlance, six valence electrons which are not required in holding the atoms of the ring together. These six and those corresponding to the other conjugated double bonds in the molecule may be held less rigidly than the regular valence elec-

trons and be more liable to go from one energy level to another with the absorption or emission of smaller amounts of energy. 

The frequencies of these energy transitions might be comparable to those of visible light. In all colored substances these semi-bound electrons are rather numerous and are arranged systematically around the molecule. Some sort of resonance effect is developed. 

The remarkable intensification of the color by the hydroxyl or amino group in certain positions may be due to the introduction of an intense localized electric field which might greatly increase the probability of the transfer of electrons from one energy level to another. 

491. Benzene Sulphonic Acids. One of the characteristic reactions of benzene is its sulphonation. Benzene dissolves in concentrated or fuming sulphuric acid with the production of benzene sulphonic acid:

C6H5H+HO SO2 OH→ C6H5SO2 OH + H2O As in nitration the reaction comes to a standstill when the acid is diluted to a certain extent by the water which is formed. The benzene sulphonic acid is obtained mixed with the excess of sulphuric acid. Both acids are extremely soluble in water but may be separated by taking advantage of the fact that the lead, barium and calcium salts of benzene sulphonic acid are very soluble in water while the sulphates of these metals are insoluble. The barium ions can be removed from a solution of barium benzene sulphonate by the addition of exactly the right amount of sulphuric acid. When the solution so obtained is evaporated, benzene sulphonic acid is deposited as colorless crystals containing one molecule of water and melting at 46°. The water can be driven off and the benzene sulphonic acid can be distilled but only in vacuum. It is deliquescent and extremely soluble in water, very soluble in alcohol but insoluble in ether. It is a very strong acid, comparable with hydrochloric and hydrobromic acid and forms salts with all inorganic and organic bases. All of these are soluble in water. In all respects it closely resembles the sulphonic acids of the aliphatic series, such as ethyl sulphonic acid. 

The free acid is seldom prepared, the sodium salt being the form in which it is commonly used.

While benzene sulphonic acid is very soluble in water, it is only slightly soluble in concentrated sulphuric acid. By properly adjusting the proportions of benzene and sulphuric acid the benzene sulphonic acid may be made to separate from the sulphonation mixture directly. Sodium benzene sulphonate is very soluble in pure water but only slightly so in concentrated sodium chloride or sulphate solution, so this salt may be precipitated when the sulphonation mixture is poured into a strong brine or sodium sulphate solution:

C6H5SOзH+NaCl → C6H5SOзNa + HCl Benzene sulphonic acid can be decomposed by superheated steam:

C6H5SO2 OH + HOH→ C6H6 + H2SO4 Industrially, the most important reaction of benzene sulphonic acid is its conversion into phenol by fusion with caustic soda: 

C6H5SO₂ONa + NaOH → C6H5OH + Na2SO3 It is to be noted that the by-product is sodium sulphite, a derivtive of tetravalent sulphur.

Phosphorus pentachloride reacts with the sodium salt of benzene sulphonic acid to give benzene sulphone chloride: 

C6H5SO₂ONa+ PCl5 → C6H5SO₂Cl + POCl3 + NaCl 

Benzene sulphone chloride

This acid chloride melts at 14.5°, boils at 247° and has the reactions of an acid chloride, but is so insoluble in water that it reacts very slowly with it and may be washed with water with but little action.

With ammonia it forms the amide: 

C6H5SO2Cl + HNH2 2 → C6H5SO2NH2 + HCl 

Benzene sulphone amide

This amide is a crystalline solid which melts at 156°, is soluble in 230 parts of cold water and considerably more so in hot. It is easily prepared, can be readily purified by recrystallization from hot water and has a convenient melting point. For these reasons, it is used as a means of identifying benzene sulphonic acid and

indirectly for identifying benzene. A hydrocarbon supposed to be benzene is sulphonated and the amide made by the above reactions. By the same reaction related hydrocarbons give amides of other melting points characteristic of the hydrocarbons from which they are derived.

Benzene sulphonic acid cannot be reduced but the sulphone chloride can be:

C6H5SO2C1 + 6H → C6H5SH + 2H2O + HCl Thiophenol

Not only benzene but its many derivatives can be sulphonated. 

Sulphonation is frequently employed to render azo dyes soluble in water, the sodium salt of the sulphonated compound being used as the dye. The sulphonic acid group may be introduced in one of the components out of which an azo dye is prepared. Thus sulphanilic acid, aniline p-sulphonic acid, can be diazotized and coupled with a phenol or an aromatic amine and the resulting azo dye will contain the sulphonic acid group.

CHAPTER XXXIII HOMOLOGS OF BENZENE AND SOME DERIVATIVES 

493. The alkyl derivatives of benzene are numerous and some of them are very important. Many of them are produced along with benzene when coal is heated, and are found with it in coal tar from which they can be obtained by fractionation. Benzene and methyl-benzene can be separated pure in this way; but the dimethyl-benzenes have to be taken out together as their boiling points, 144°, 139° and 137.7°, are too close for separation by fractionation from each other and from ethylbenzene which boils at 136.1°. The same is true of other groups of isomers. 

Some of the homologs of benzene have proper names, particularly those that were well known before their relationships to benzene were determined. Thus methylbenzene is toluene and the dimethylbenzenes are xylenes. Cumene is isopropyl-benzene while pseudocumene is the isomeric 1,2,4-trimethyl-benzene.

Mesitylene is s-trimethyl-benzene. Cymene is p-methyl-isopropylbenzene while durene is 1,2,4,5-tetra-methyl-benzene and isodurene and prehnitene are the 1,2,3,5and the 1,2,3,4-isomers.

The general formula for all of these is CnH2n-6. The properties of some benzene homologs are shown in the tables below.

In the ethylation of benzene some hexaethyl-benzene is frequently formed before all of the benzene has been converted to monoethyl-benzene. A still greater difficulty lies in the fact that the reaction is reversible so that groups are removed as well as introduced, and groups originally present are shifted. Thus, if methylbenzene is ethylated the product may contain benzene, methyl-ethylbenzene, dimethyl- and diethylbenzenes as well as products containing three or more of these groups. In this reaction the aluminum chloride may be considered a catalyst, since a small amount of it brings about the reaction between large amounts of the other reactants. Its catalytic action is usually explained by assuming that an addition compound of benzene and aluminum chloride is more reactive than benzene alone. There is considerable evidence that such addition compounds are formed, but whether or not they are responsible for the enhanced reactivity is not certain. In some cases the aluminum chloride isomerizes the alkyl halide which is being used. Thus benzene, aluminum chloride and n-propyl chloride give isopropyl-benzene instead of n-propylbenzene.

496. Reactions of the Alkyl Benzenes. An alkyl benzene, such as toluene or ethylbenzene, is made up of two parts, one a phenyl group and the other an aliphatic radical. Each of these parts shows its characteristic reactions although the reactions of each group are somewhat modified by the presence of the other group. 

The case of toluene, C6H5 CHз, is typical of all the others. The typical reactions of benzene, sulphonation, nitration and chlorination or bromination in presence of a carrier, take place with toluene as with benzene, only somewhat more readily. With benzene the limit of nitration is two nitro groups, but with toluene three nitro groups may be introduced without difficulty. Methane is indifferent to nitric and sulphuric acids and in the nitration and sulphonation of toluene the methyl group is not affected. Benzene is halogenated in the presence of a carrier while methane is chlorinated under the influence of light. Toluene may be halogenated either in the ring or in the side chain, that is, in the methyl group, depending on the conditions used; in the dark with a carrier the halogen enters the ring, while in sunlight halogenation takes place in the side chain. Even at the temperature of 0° toluene is chlorinated with extreme rapidity in the side chain. In this reaction heating has the same effect as sunlight. CH3 CI CH3 CH3 CI CI

Without a carrier but at higher temperatures or in sunlight:

0-0-0-0 Benzylchloride Benzalchloride Benzotrichloride

The chlorinated products are divided into two classes which have very different properties. When the halogen is in the ring, the compounds resemble chlorobenzene in physical properties and in indifference to reagents. When the halogen is in the side chain, the compounds are reactive and thus resemble the corresponding aliphatic halogen derivatives. In fact the presence of the phenyl group seems to loosen the chlorine atoms; benzyl chloride and bromide react many times more rapidly than methyl chloride or bromide. This recalls the fact that the double bond in vinyl chloride suppresses the reactivity of the halogen in vinyl chloride but enhances it when the chlorine is separated from it by -CH½as in allyl chloride. The compounds having the halogen in the methyl group are unusual in that they are extremely irritating to the eyes. Benzyl bromide was used to some extent as a lachrymator during the war as was also the corresponding bromine derivative of xylene.

498. Nitrotoluenes. Under the same conditions toluene is nitrated somewhat more readily than benzene. erties. The relatively low melting point of trinitro-toluene, 80.7°, compared with picric acid, 121.8°, the fact that it does not have acid properties, and is insoluble in water, are advantages for its use in bare steel shells.

CHAPTER XXXIV  ALDEHYDES, KETONES AND QUINONES 

505. Many aliphatic alcohols are found in natural products or are easily produced from them. Aliphatic aldehydes are usually made from the alcohols and are of subordinate interest. 

In the aromatic series the relationship is reversed; that is, the aldehydes are of much greater importance than the alcohols and are more abundant in natural products. Frequently, the alcohols are made from the aldehydes.

As the benzene ring consists of=CH groups which contain one hydrogen each, there is no possibility of substituting a bivalent atom in the nucleus; that is, as long as it retains its aromatic character. The typical aldehyde group —CHO is univalent and can be substituted for a hydrogen of the benzene ring. The simplest possible aromatic aldehyde is C6H5 CHO, called benzaldehyde, which is an oxo derivative of toluene:

CH₂ میں C:O Toluene Benzaldehyde

The homologs of benzene with longer side chains offer opportunities for a variety of oxo derivatives, both aldehydes and ketones. 

A distinction must be made between the aldehydes in which the -CHO group is substituted for a hydrogen of the nucleus and those in which this group is separated from the ring by one or more carbon atoms. Only the former are strictly aromatic aldehydes; the others more closely resemble the aliphatic aldehydes. 

506. Benzaldehyde. This may be considered as phenylformaldehyde. The introduction of a phenyl group into methyl chloride modifies the reactivity of the chlorine greatly, phenyl- 548

methyl chloride, or benzyl chloride, being far more reactive than methyl chloride. Phenyl-formaldehyde is quite different from formaldehyde, but in this case the influence of the phenyl group is to decrease the reactivity of the aldehyde so that it is not nearly as reactive as formaldehyde or even acetaldehyde although it shows many of the same reactions. The constitution of benzaldehyde is easily derived from its preparation from benzal chloride. As benzal chloride gives benzoic acid by oxidation, its two chlorine atoms must be in the methyl group of the toluene from which it is made. It follows that the oxygen atom which replaces them must also be in the same position. 

Benzaldehyde is found in oil of bitter almonds as a constituent of the glucoside amygdalin from which it was first obtained. One of the most famous articles in chemical history is that by Liebig and Wöhler published in 1832 on the oil of bitter almonds. This was long before Kekulé's benzene theory, but these chemists isolated and purified benzaldehyde and determined its composition. 

They made from it benzoic acid, benzoyl chloride and other compounds, all of which they recognized as containing a common group. 

This introduced into organic chemistry the idea of a "radical " or "compound element." Benzaldehyde melts at -56.0°, boils at 179.5° and has the density 1.050415. It is soluble in about 300 parts of water and mixes in all proportions with alcohol, ether and most other organic solvents. It is manufactured from benzal chloride as already mentioned. In the chlorination of toluene to benzal chloride, no matter what precautions are taken a small amount of the chlorine goes into the phenyl group, and therefore it is difficult to obtain it free from chlorine. For use in perfumery the highest possible grade of benzaldehyde is demanded. This is usually made by the oxidation of toluene, which may be effected in various ways, such as by manganese dioxide and moderately concentrated sulphuric acid. If benzyl alcohol were more readily prepared, benzaldehyde might be obtained by its dehydrogenation. 

Aromatic aldehydes can be prepared from the corresponding acid chlorides by catalytic hydrogenation: 

C6H5COCl + H2 → C6H5CHO + HCl

512. Reactions of Aromatic Ketones. The reactions of these ketones offer nothing new. Those in which phenyl is next to the carbonyl group do not combine with bisulphite even when the radical on the other side is methyl. Thus, acetophenone does not give this reaction while methyl-benzyl ketone, C6H5CH2COCH3, does. With strong oxidising agents these ketones are oxidised to two acids, one of which is always benzoic acid.

515. Oximes. Aromatic aldehydes and ketones react with hydroxylamine:

Benzophenone oxime ¹ Wilhelm Michler (1846-1889), Professor in the Polytechnic School in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, from 1882 to 1889, carried out numerous investigations on the reactions of substituted ureas.

In the case of aldehydes and of unsymmetrical ketones it is sometimes possible to isolate two isomeric oximes from the same aldehyde or ketone. This is explained by assuming that the possibility of the two isomers is due to stereo-isomerism similar to that of compounds containing two carbons joined by a double bond. This assumes that the valencies of a trivalent nitrogen atom are not in a plane but extend into space like three edges of a regular triangular pyramid. The two oximes from benzaldehyde will then be represented: C6H5.C.H C6H5.C.H and N.OH C6H5.C ||| + H2O HO.N anti-Benzaldoxime 

M. P. 35° syn-Benzaldoxime 

M. P. 130°

The oximes from an unsymmetrical ketone would be: BrC6H4 C C6H5 HO.N

BrC6H4 C C6H5 and 1.OH N.OH

In the case of the aldoximes it is easy to decide which of the two is to be given the syn formula, since water is readily split off from one and not from the other. There is no correspondingly simple way to decide the formulae of ketoximes. Dependence is usually put on the Beckmann rearrangement, but it is a complicated reaction and the results obtained with it are variously interpreted. Stereoisomerism should be manifested by aliphatic aldehydes and ketones but it is much easier to isolate the higher melting and slower reacting aromatic oximes. 

516. The Beckmann Rearrangement. When a ketoxime is treated with certain reagents among which are phosphorus pentachloride and concentrated sulphuric acid, a rearrangement takes place, the final product being a substituted amide: a0-0:0 NOH NH

Although many theories have been advanced to explain this rearrangement, no definite conclusions have been reached. It has usually been assumed that the radical on the same side of the mole-

cule as the double bond is the one that appears joined to nitrogen in the amide.

The representation of quinone gave chemists a great deal of trouble. 

The formula, as written above, apparently violated Kekulé's dictum that only univalent atoms or groups can be substituted in a benzene ring. Apparently, the most satisfactory solution of the difficulty is to write quinone as a diketo-hexadiene and regard it as derived from dihydro-benzene or cyclohexadiene: он OH Hydroquinone Quinone

Cyclohexadiene (1,4)

That it is a ketone is shown by the fact that it reacts with hydroxylamine in two stages to form a mono- and a dioxime. It shows its unsaturation by combining directly with either one or two molecules of chlorine or bromine. It forms addition compounds with phenols and with other substances.

When phenol reacts with nitrous acid, p-nitrosophenol is formed. The surprising thing is that this and the mono-oxime of quinone turn out to be identical:

OH NO p-Nitrosophenol

In accordance with the first formula is the fact that it can be oxidised to p-nitrophenol; in support of the second is the fact that it reacts with hydroxylamine to form a di-oxime. It is probable that the substance is a mixture of the two tautomeric forms but their proportions are not known.

Quinone crystallizes in yellow needles which melt at 115.7°. It is slightly soluble in hot water and very soluble in alcohol and ether. It is volatile with steam and has a strong odor. It is obtained by the oxidation of a number of benzene derivatives particularly those which contain amino and hydroxyl groups. It is best prepared by the oxidation of aniline at low temperatures. 

When benzene and air are passed over certain catalysts at high temperatures, some quinone is formed. The fact that quinone is colored while hydroquinone is colorless is regarded as having great significance. On it has been based the quinoid theory of color which will be discussed in connection with indicators and triphenylmethane dyes.

CHAPTER XXXV AROMATIC ACIDS 

520. These acids constitute a numerous and important class of organic compounds. The oxidation of toluene to benzoic acid has already been mentioned. Substituted toluenes are oxidised to the corresponding substituted benzoic acids unless the substituent is sensitive to oxidation. Thus p-nitrotoluene and p-bromotoluene yield p-nitrobenzoic acid and p-bromobenzoic acid, while p-aminotoluene goes to other products, the amino group being the point of attack. There is little difference between aromatic acids and aliphatic acids; their reactions are quite similar. With the same alcohols the esterification limits for benzoic and acetic acids are practically identical. This is also true for the limit of amide formation, but with benzoic acid at a given temperature a much longer time is required to reach these limits. At 0° benzoyl chloride dissolved in excess of absolute ethyl alcohol requires four hours for complete reaction, while acetyl chloride reacts in a few seconds.

As in the case of the aromatic aldehydes, there is a distinction between the acids in which the carboxyl group is joined directly to the benzene ring and those in which it is in a side chain. The former are more strictly aromatic in character, while the latter are more like aliphatic acids.

Substituents enter toluene in the ortho and para positions, seldom in the meta position. Hence ortho and para substituted toluenes are readily available for oxidation to ortho and para substituted benzoic acids. Meta substituted benzoic acids must usually be obtained by other methods. Substituents usually enter benzoic acid in the position meta to the carboxyl group, thus giving rise to many meta substituted benzoic acids. 

521. Benzoic Acid. This acid has been known for about three centuries as it is obtained from gum benzoin by sublimation. Its 562

AROMATIC ACIDS 

563 composition was determined in 1832 by Liebig and Wöhler. As benzoic acid contains a phenyl group it is subject to the reactions of benzene. It can be nitrated, sulphonated, chlorinated and brominated although not so readily as benzene. The reactions which depend on the carboxyl group duplicate the corresponding reactions of acetic acid. In order to convert it into benzoyl chloride, it is necessary to use phosphorus pentachloride as the trichloride is not effective:

When a soluble acid is added to a concentrated cold water solution of sodium benzoate, the acid is precipitated. Benzoic acid is manufactured on a considerable scale from toluene either through benzotrichloride or by direct oxidation. Its sodium salt has been largely used as a food preservative but such use is regulated by the "Pure Food Law." The benzoates of many phenols and the benzoyl derivatives of many amines are crystalline solids with definite melting points. These are made by the action of benzoyl chloride on the phenol or amine:

525. Nitrobenzoic Acids. By the direct nitration of benzoic acid about 74 per cent of the meta acid is obtained along with 20 per cent ortho and 2 per cent para. It is quite unusual to obtain the ortho and meta derivatives together. Substitution reactions which give meta products rarely give more than small amounts of ortho forms. The p-nitrobenzoic acid is readily made by the oxidation of p-nitrotoluene. Further nitration of m-nitrobenzoic acid gives 3,5-dinitro-benzoic acid. As many of the esters of this acid are solids, their melting points are frequently given as characterizing the alcohols from which they are made. By oxidising trinitro-toluene, 2,4,6-trinitro-benzoic acid is obtained. The carboxyl group is eliminated on fusion or on heating with water. 

This is the best method of obtaining trinitro-benzene. 

526. Hydroxybenzoic Acids. One of these acids, the ortho hydroxybenzoic acid, is of great importance. It is called salicylic acid, the name being from salicin, a glucoside found in willow bark which hydrolyzes into glucose and o-hydroxy-benzyl alcohol. This alcohol yields salicylic acid on oxidation. It is found in many plants. Oil of wintergreen has been proved to be almost pure methyl salicylate.

Salicylic acid is manufactured in large quantities by the Kolbe¹-Schmitt synthesis. Dry sodium phenate is saturated with carbon dioxide under four atmospheres pressure and heated to 140°. The sodium phenyl carbonate which is first formed isomerizes to sodium salicylate: Sodium phenate ONa OCQNa 

Sodium phenyl carbonate

OH CQNa Sodium salicylate

Salicyclic acid is precipitated from a water solution of its sodium salt by the addition of a soluble acid and is purified by sublimation in a current of hot air. It is used as a preservative, as a drug, particularly for rheumatism, and for making artificial oil of wintergreen. The meta and para acids are of little interest. 

527. Derivatives of Salicylic Acid. The phenol group of salicyclic acid is readily acetylated either by acetyl chloride with zinc chloride or by acetanhydride with sodium acetate. The product, acetyl-salicylic acid, is known as aspirin and has come into wide use as a drug. Salol, the phenyl ether of salicylic acid is used to some extent as a drug. 

528. The Aminobenzoic Acids. These can be obtained by the reduction of the corresponding nitroacids. They are of considerable service since they can be diazotized like aniline and thus converted into a great variety of substituted benzoic acids. o-Aminobenzoic acid, called anthranilic acid, since it was first made by fusing indigo with alkali, is of importance and has been manufactured somewhat extensively as an intermediate in one process for making synthetic indigo. One method of producing it, which has been used on the large scale, is by treating phthalimide with sodium hypochlorite (Hofmann reaction Chapter XVI): COOH

It will be noted that substituents other than the methyl group raise the melting point. In any group of isomers the para derivative has the highest melting point and is the least soluble. The influence of a group on the strength of the acid, as shown by the value of K, depends on the nature of the group and on its position, being by far the greatest when the substituent is ortho to the carboxyl group. The nitro group greatly increases the strength while the amino group diminishes it. 

530. Gallic Acid. Tannin and related substances which occur in considerable quantities in many plants yield, on hydrolysis, gallic acid as the chief product. This has been shown to be 3,4,5trihydroxy-benzoic acid. It is commonly prepared from tannin as it is not readily synthesized from cheap materials. но HO но COOH 

Gallic acid

It is soluble in 80 parts of water at 25° or 3 parts at 100°, and quite soluble in cold alcohol but only slightly so in ether. It crystallizes with one molecule of water. At 220° it loses carbon dioxide and is converted into pyrogallol which is v-trihydroxy-benzene. 

In excess of alkali gallic acid readily absorbs oxygen from the air and turns brown, very complicated products being formed. Gallic acid is so readily oxidised that it may be used as a reducing agent to precipitate silver, as in developing pictures. Basic bismuth gallate (HO)3C6H2CO2Bi(OH)2, called bismuth sub-gallate is used as an external and internal antiseptic. 

531. Tannins. There are many tannins differing more or less in properties and in structure. The best known tannin is that called gallo-tannin or tannic acid, which makes up about half of the weight of oak galls and is found in sumach, tea and many other plants. Tannin gives a blue black precipitate with ferric salts. 

From antiquity this has been the basis for an important class of inks. A solution of ferrous sulphate and tannin is only slightly colored, but when this is spread on paper a ferric salt is formed and gives an extremely stable bluish black precipitate which adheres to

AROMATIC ACIDS 

569 the paper. Writing done with iron-tannin inks has endured for thousands of years.

Tannin appears to be penta-digalloyl-glucose. This is analogous to glucose penta-acetate, the five hydroxyls of glucose being esterified by five molecules of digallic acid. Digallic acid is m-galloyl-gallic acid in which one gallic acid molecule is joined to a но HO HQ HO HO COOH 

Digallic acid second, a molecule of water being eliminated between the carboxyl of the one and the meta hydroxyl of the other. The constitution given is apparently true for this tannin but there are other tannins which contain other acids more or less related to digallic acid, and even sugars other than glucose.

571 534. Saccharin.¹ o-Sulphobenzoic acid is dibasic and can form an anhydride and an imide in the same way as succinic acid (441). The imide particularly is readily obtained. In fact it is usually the product that is obtained directly when o-toluene sulphonamide is oxidised. ΝΗ $ 80 o-Sulphobenzoic anhydride 

Benzoic sulphinide, saccharin

Benzoic sulphinide crystallizes from acetone in monoclinic crystals melting at 228° with decomposition. Its solubility in 100 cc. water is 0.43 g. at 25° and 4 g. at 100°. It is remarkable for its extraordinarily sweet taste, being estimated to be 550 times as sweet as cane sugar. Since 1885 it has been manufactured on a considerable scale for sweetening purposes. Its sale has been restricted in most countries by legislation, although extensive feeding experiments have shown that it is harmless in even much larger amounts than would be normally present in foods. In fact it does not appear to be absorbed by the system and is excreted unchanged. As saccharin has no food value it cannot be substituted for sugar where nourishment is required, but for diabetic patients who cannot tolerate sugar and for overweight people who do not desire the nourishment, it is a welcome addition to foods. 

The NH group in benzoic sulphinide is between two acidifying groups -CO- and -SO2-, hence the hydrogen is ionizable. 

In fact the substance is a well defined acid and dissolves in soda solution. As saccharin is inconvenient to use on account of its slight solubility in water, its sodium salt is commonly sold as "saccharin, soluble." Saccharin has the unusual property of triboluminescence; in the dark its crystals glow when rubbed or broken. 

¹ Ira Remsen (1846-1927), the discoverer of saccharin, was the founder of the American Chemical Journal, and was noted as an author and teacher. 

In 1876 he was appointed Professor in the Johns Hopkins University, the first institution for post-graduate work in America. He was President of the University from 1901 to 1913.

535. Phthalic Acids. Of the three dicarboxy acids, all of which are well known, only the ortho derivative is of great importance. 

The ortho derivative is known as phthalic acid and melts at 208°, the meta derivative, called isophthalic acid, melts at 330°, while the para derivative, known as terephthalic acid, sublimes without melting. The solubilities of the three in 100 cc. of water at 25° are 0.62 g., 0.012 g. and 0.0016 g. Phthalic acid gets its name from the fact that it is made by the oxidation of naphthalene. 

The manufacture of phthalic acid, or rather its anhydride, is conducted on a very large scale. Napthalene (561) is always used in starting the synthesis. Since about 1890 this oxidation has been carried on, particularly in Germany, by heating naphthalene with concentrated sulphuric acid in the presence of mercury sulphate as a catalyst. About 1918 the air oxidation process was discovered in the United States. Since then this process has been used exclusively in this country. Naphthalene vapor, mixed with air, is passed over vanadium pentoxide in steel tubes which are kept at the proper temperature. Phthalic anhydride is produced and condensed when the air is cooled: H Naphthalene 

Phthalic anhydride

Phthalimide is readily formed from phthalic anhydride and ammonia. Like saccharin it contains the imino group, NH, joined to two acidifying groups, and consequently acts as an acid, forming well-defined alkali salts which react with alkyl halides to give substituted phthalimides: ---0--0 Phthalimide 

Butyl phthalimide

One of the best ways to obtain a primary amine free from the secondary and tertiary is to prepare the alkyl phthalimide and hydrolyze it. This is Gabriel's synthesis.

AROMATIC ACIDS 

573 Phthalic anhydride combines readily with primary and secondary alcohols to form half esters: + OCH COCH COH Mono-butyl phthalate When a mixture of organic compounds, such as an essential oil, is heated with phthalic anhydride, any primary or secondary alcohol that may be present is converted into the corresponding alkyl phthalate. This is converted into the sodium salt by the addition of a water solution of soda. The non-alcohols in the mixture are removed by ether extraction and the alkyl phthalate saponified to obtain the alcohol. The manganese and cobalt salts of monobutyl phthalate are soluble in oils such as linseed oil and are used as driers. Dibutyl phthalate is used as a softening agent in nitrocellulose lacquers such as "Duco." The U. S. production is about 

5,000,000 lbs. per year. Diethyl phthalate is used as a denaturant for alcohol. Phthalic anhydride is used for making a number of triphenyl-methane dyes such as phenolphthalein and fluorescein. 

A useful resin called glyptal is made by heating phthalic anhydride with glycerine. 

3-Nitrophthalic anhydride combines with alcohols under the same conditions as phthalic anhydride. The 3-nitrophthalic half esters so obtained are useful for the identification of alcohols.

Mellitic acid is found in peat. By various treatments one carboxyl after another can be split off leaving tetrabasic, tribasic, dibasic acids and finally benzoic acid and benzene. The particular interest in the acid is due to the fact that it can be obtained in good yield by oxidising

wood charcoal and graphite. This appears to show the presence of benzene nuclei in charcoal and graphite.

538. Phenyl-alanine. This is an important amino acid that is a constituent of many proteins. It is ẞ-phenyl-a-amino-propionic acid, C6H5 CH2 CH (NH2) · COOH. 539. Cinnamic Acid. This acid is found in many balsams and resins, sometimes free and sometimes combined with various alcohols as cinnamic esters. It is readily obtained from these and has long been known. Its name indicates its connections with cinnamic aldehyde. By heating under the proper conditions it loses carbon dioxide, leaving styrene, which shows it to be a carboxystyrene. On oxidation, it gives benzoic acid from which it can be concluded that the carboxyl group is in the side chain. By hydrogenating it phenyl propionic acid is produced. These facts are accounted for by giving it the formula of B-phenyl-acrylic acid, C6H5CH: CH COOH. It can be nitrated to a mixture of the ortho and para nitro-cinnamic acids. 544. Diphenyl. Benzene, like ethane, gives off hydrogen when highly heated. In the case of ethane the hydrogen comes from adjacent carbons but in the case of benzene one atom of hydrogen is eliminated from each of two molecules of benzene and the two phenyl groups, which probably exist as free radicals for an instant, unite: 2 H₂ + Diphenyl

This reaction takes place when benzene vapor is passed either through a red hot tube or over a heated wire, or when benzene is heated above 500° in a closed vessel. The same product is 577

obtained when phenyl iodide is heated to 220° with copper powder or when bromobenzene is digested with sodium in ether: 2C6H51+2Cu→ C6H5 C6H5+ Cu₂I2 C6H5·C6H5 2C6H5Br+2Na→ C6H5 C6H5 + 2NaBr Considerable diphenyl is formed in the preparation of the Grignard reagent from a phenyl halide:

C6H5MgBr + BrC6H5 →C6H5 C6H5 + MgBr₂ 

Diphenyl melts at 70.5° and boils at 254.93°. It is insoluble in water but dissolves in 10 parts of alcohol at 20°. Obviously many substitution products of diphenyl are possible. It is readily nitrated or halogenated when the substituent enters para or ortho to the point of union of the two rings. Oxidation converts it to benzoic acid, one ring being destroyed.

Eliminating the amino groups, diphenyl is obtained. Benzidine crystallizes in colorless leaflets, melts at 128.7° and boils at 401.7°.

In 100 cc. of water 0.04 g. dissolves at 12° and 0.94 g. at 100°. 

Very large quantities of benzidine are manufactured for use in making azo dyes. Both of its amino groups may be diazotized and coupled with aniline, phenol or their substitution products, as in the case of diazotized aniline. One of the amino groups of benzidine may be diazotized and coupled with one compound and then the other amino group put through the same reactions with another, so that unsymmetrical azo dyes are obtained. Many of the azo dyes obtained from benzidine are direct, or substantive, dyes for cotton; that is, they dye cotton without the assistance of a mordant. This is a valuable property which is shared by few azo dyes outside of the "Congo " class, the name given to azo dyes from benzidine.

548. The Relation of the Quinoid Structure to Color. 4,4′,4"- 

Triamino-triphenyl carbinol, the color base above mentioned, is itself colorless and insoluble in water but its salts are soluble and highly colored. The base, which has the composition, C19H19N3O, dissolves in hydrochloric acid and the product obtained has the composition C19H18N3Cl, a chlorine atom apparently having taken the place of the hydroxyl group. This was at first represented by the equation: (H2NC6H4)3COH + HCl → (H2NC6H4)3CCl + H₂O This represents the change quantitatively but does not account for the properties of the product. Trimethyl carbinol, or t-butyl alcohol, reacts readily with hydrochloric acid: (CH3)3COH + HCl → (CH3)3CCl + H2O In this, as is usually the case, the substitution of a chlorine atom for the hydroxyl group does not introduce color and decreases the solubility in water. Methyl, ethyl, propyl and butyl hydroxides are soluble in water while the corresponding chlorides are nearly insoluble. Phenol is soluble in 11 parts of cold water while phenyl chloride is insoluble. When triamino-triphenyl carbinol dissolves in acid there must be some structural change to account for the production of color. Quinone and its substitution products are colored. The current theory is that there is tautomerism between the two forms indicated below:

Carbinol form of color base, colorless, insoluble, slightly ionized 

Quinoid form of color base, colored, soluble, ionizable

The carbinol and quinoid forms of the base may be considered as in equilibrium with each other. The isomerization appears to involve

POLYPHENYL COMPOUNDS 

583 the migration of the hydroxyl group, but as both forms are dissociated, the quinone form largely so, the actual change is only the transfer of an electron (Chapter XXXI). In neutral solution, the equilibrium will be in favor of the carbinol form in accordance with the general rule that an insoluble or volatile substance will form if possible. In acid solution the hydroxyl ions will be used up, the quinoid form present will ionize and the carbinol form will be converted into the quinoid form. By evaporating an acid solution the salt of the quinoid form is obtained.¹ 

The essential part of quinone is the 41,4-cyclohexadiene structure, not the oxygen atoms. In the above formulae the bivalent groups, NH and =C(C6H4NH2)2, are considered as taking the places of the bivalent oxygen atoms in quinone. For simplicity the structural formulae of the triphenyl-methane dyes which are given below will be written in the carbinol form, it being understood that the actual dyes are salts of the quinoid form. 

549. Triphenyl-methane Dyes. This class of dyes is intermediate between the extremely numerous cheap azo dyes and the comparatively small class of expensive vat dyes. The synthetic dye industry began with an experiment that did not work as anticipated. In 1856 Perkin² oxidised aniline in an attempt to make quinine. Instead of the quinine he obtained a highly colored substance having tinctorial properties. He improved and commercialized the process and called the dye mauve. In 1859 Hofmann produced a dye which he called magenta by the oxidation of aniline, the difference being that he used milder oxidising agents which gave a better product. What was practically the same dye was manufactured in France under the name of fuchsine. All this was before the publication of Kekulé's benzene theory and nothing was known about the chemistry of these processes which had been discovered accidentally and empirically developed. 

1 Julius Oscar Stieglitz (1867- ), Professor at the University of Chicago, has advanced many ideas on the theory of color production. He is especially interested in the mechanism of organic reactions. 

2 William Henry Perkin (1838–1907), received honorary degrees from the 

Universities of Oxford, Heidelberg, Johns Hopkins, and Columbia, the

Hofmann medal from the German Chemical Society and the Lavoisier medal from the French Chemical Society in recognition of his great contributions to the knowledge of dyes.

550. The Structure of Rosaniline. The pure dye that was isolated from the above commercial products was called rosaniline and was found to have the composition, C20H20N3Cl. A similar dye was made from a mixture of aniline and p-toluidine and called pararosaniline. The dye with the longer name turned out to be the simpler substance, C19H18N3Cl, and was studied first. Reduction with zinc dust and acid gave a colorless substance, C19H19N3. 

As it had been made from aniline the presence of amino groups was suspected. Accordingly, it was diazotized and reduced, so as to remove the amino groups, whereby a hydrocarbon, C19H16, was obtained. This hydrocarbon was identified as triphenyl-methane. 

Thus the leuco base of pararosaniline appeared to be triaminotriphenyl-methane. This conclusion was confirmed by nitrating triphenyl-methane and reducing the product. Fortunately three nitro groups were readily introduced and, more fortunately still, they went into the right places, since on reducing to triaminotriphenyl-methane, oxidising to the carbinol and dissolving in hydrochloric acid pararosaniline was obtained. By similar experiments rosaniline was shown to have the same structure as pararosaniline except for the presence of a methyl group in one of the rings. 

The oxidation of a mixture of aniline and p-toluidine to pararosaniline is a remarkable reaction, one that could never have been predicted. It may be represented: +O+H NH₂ HN C-H +0 + NH₂ -> H +O NH₂ OH NH₂ Pararosaniline

It may be supposed that the course of the reaction is by the oxidation of p-toluidine to p-aminobenzaldehyde, which would react with two molecules of aniline: NH₂ HN CH₂- HNK OCH )CHO — HNG CH COH NH NH

585 In preparing pararosaniline two molecules of aniline and one of p-toluidine are used. The aniline used by Perkin had been made from benzene which contained toluene, so the aniline made from it contained ortho and para toluidines. In the reaction above one of the molecules of aniline is replaced by one of o-toluidine and there is consequently a methyl group ortho to the amino group in one of the benzene rings. If the constitution of aniline had been known, no one would have attempted to make quinine by its oxidation, and if the aniline then available had been pure, mauve would not have been discovered. It is fortunate that Perkin followed up an experiment that gave entirely unexpected results. For a long time a mixture of aniline, o-toluidine and p-toluidine was oxidised by heating with arsenic acid. On account of the possibility of arsenic compounds remaining in the dye, nitrobenzene has been substituted for the arsenic acid as an oxidising agent.

When methyl groups are introduced into the amino groups of rosaniline, the red color of this dye is changed toward violet, the shade depending on the number of the methyl groups. Formerly rosaniline was alkylated by heating with methyl iodide and later by methanol and hydrochloric acid to a mixture of tetra-pentaand hexa-methyl-rosanilines, which was known as methyl violet. 

Later this dye was obtained by the oxidation of dimethyl-aniline. 

This was incomprehensible until it was found that the required central carbon atom comes from one of the methyl groups which is separated from one of the nitrogen atoms during the process, the product being penta-methyl-triamino-triphenyl carbinol. Possibly the methyl group is oxidised and this compound rearranged to methyl-amino-benzaldehyde which would couple as in the synthesis of malachite green:

CH CHO CH +20 -OHC CH, CH₂ A benzyl group is sometimes introduced in this dye. Other dyes of this sort contain ethyl groups in place of the methyl groups.

CHAPTER XXXVII FUSED RINGS 

560. In addition to the polycyclic compounds such as were considered in Chapter XXXVI, in which two or more benzene rings are joined together either directly, as in diphenyl, or by one or more connecting atoms, as in triphenyl-methane, there are a number of important hydrocarbons in which the rings may be said to be fused together; that is, two carbon atoms are common to both rings. In some of these one or more of the rings are not aromatic and contain four, five, six or seven carbon atoms, but the most important are those in which all of the rings are six-membered and all have an aromatic character. A number of hydrocarbons of this sort are found in the higher fractions of coal tar. The derivatives of several of these are of importance. 

NAPHTHALENE 

561. When the fraction of coal tar boiling between 170° and 

240° is cooled, crystals are deposited. These are separated and purified by sublimation. Naphthalene sublimes or crystallizes in rhombic leaflets which melt at 80.05° and boil at 217.96°. It is only slightly soluble in water, 0.0030 g. in 100 cc. at 25°, but more soluble in alcohol, 5.29 g. per 100 cc. of absolute alcohol at 15°.

It dissolves readily in ether and in some hydrocarbons, such as benzene and toluene.

The empirical formula of naphthalene was determined in 1826 by Faraday who also prepared and studied its two sulphonic acid derivatives. Forty years later Erlenmeyer ¹ suggested a constitutional formula modeled after Kekulé's benzene formula: Kekulé's benzene formula Erlenmeyer's naphthalene formula 

1 Richard Erlenmeyer (1825-1909), a pupil of Kekulé, was Professor at the University of Heidelberg and the Polytechnic in Munich. 593

Since that time all of the formulae that have been proposed for benzene, have been extended to naphthalene. In fact no benzene formula can gain any acceptance unless it is capable of being adapted to naphthalene. For practical purposes a double hexagon is used for naphthalene just as a single hexagon is used for benzene. The fact that naphthalene is readily oxidised to phthalic anhydride shows that naphthalene contains a benzene ring and that the other part of the molecule is joined to this at two adjacent points. The oxidation is supposed to be similar to that of o-xylene which likewise gives phthalic acid: 

Naphthalene CH -X Phthalic anhydride CH o-Xylene A nitro group in a benzene ring renders it more resistant to oxidation, while the amino group makes it less resistant. When nitronaphthalene is oxidised, nitrophthalic anhydride is obtained. 

When the same nitronaphthalene is reduced to aminonaphthalene and this oxidised, phthalic anhydride is produced. This shows that both the substituted and the unsubstituted sides are benzene rings: NO₂ ---∞ Nitronaphthalene Aminonaphthalene

595 alpha are equivalent; the same can be said of the beta positions 

2, 3, 6 and 7. Faraday showed that there are two mono-sulphonic acids derived from naphthalene. The investigations of a century have added many other pairs of mono derivatives of naphthalene but never more than two of a kind. After the acceptance of Erlermeyer's formula for naphthalene, the next question raised was that of assigning the formulae to the pairs of isomers. This was solved by converting several naphthalene derivatives into benzene derivatives as in the case of nitronaphthalene above. As nitronaphthalene gives the 3-nitrophthalic acid in which the nitro group is adjacent to a carboxyl group, it must be the alpha form. Deciding the question for a-nitronaphthalene settled it for the aminonaphthalene which can be obtained from it and for the many derivatives into which aminonaphthalene can be converted. 

The possibilities of isomerism among naphthalene derivatives is much greater than with benzene. With two substituents of the same kind, ten isomers are possible and this number is increased to fourteen if the groups are different. It has been calculated that if eight different substituents could be introduced into naphthalene there would be the possibility of 10,766,600 isomers. In a few groups of naphthalene derivatives the possibilities of isomerism have been extensively explored. All of the possible dichloronaphthalenes have been prepared, as have the fourteen naphthylamine sulphonic acids and fourteen naphthol sulphonic acids. The positions 1 and 8 are related to each other as ortho groups and can cooperate in forming rings. 

563. The Reactions of Naphthalene. In all of their reactions, naphthalene and its derivatives resemble benzene and its corresponding derivatives, the differences being of degree rather than of kind. Naturally, the naphthyl amines and the naphthols are less volatile than aniline and phenol; they are also less soluble in the same solvents. While the diazonium compounds of benzene are extremely unstable at low temperatures many of the diazonium derivatives of naphthalene are comparatively stable; some can be recrystallized from hot water and stored for months. 

Naphthalene can be hydrogenated in stages, the most inter-

esting products are those in which two, four or ten atoms of hydrogen are added!:

It resembles cyclohexene (Chapter XXX) adding halogens, halogen acids and hypochlorous and hypobromous acids and giving a volatile oxide. 

1,2,3,4-Tetrahydronaphthalene is now manufactured on a considerable scale by the catalytic hydrogenation of naphthalene and sold for use as a solvent under the name of tetralin. Its reactions are those of benzene with aliphatic side chains. The amino and hydroxyl derivatives of naphthalene can be similarly hydrogenated.

Naphthalene is readily halogenated. In this it acts like benzene with an unsaturated side chain, chlorine being added and the halogen acid split off: 1 CHCI CHCI CH CH CH CH CH

The halogen in the mono-derivative of naphthalene is in the alpha, while the dihalogenated compound is a mixture of three isomers. Further halogenation puts four halogens in positions 1, 2, 3 and 4. The halogenation of benzene probably follows the same course, but the intermediate addition products are less stable. By drastic action with a carrier octo-chloronaphthalene may be obtained. The polychloro-naphthalenes have found some use as plastics. Bromine reacts so readily that a convenient laboratory method of making hydrogen bromide is to drop bromine on naphthalene. Naphthalene is readily nitrated, the nitro group entering the alpha position. Further action introduces several nitro groups. Considerable amounts of a-nitro-naphthalene are manufactured for reduction into a-naphthylamine.

Naphthalene is readily sulphonated, the a-sulphonic acid being the chief product when the reaction is carried out at temperatures below 100°, while the beta acid is the main product above 160°.

The a-sulphonic acid is converted into the beta by heating with sulphuric acid. 

564. Naphthols. The naphthols are found in coal tar and can be obtained from the proper fractions of coal tar distillate by extraction with caustic soda and precipitation. The amounts in coal tar are small and are not of sufficient value to warrant extraction from the coal tar. They are manufactured by heating the corresponding naphthalene sulphonic acids with strong caustic soda solution to 300°:

C10H7 SO3Na + 2NaOH → →C10H7ONa + Na2SO3 The naphthols are precipitated from the solutions of their sodium salts by the addition of acid. The naphthols are both solids, the alpha melting at 96° and boiling at 280°, and the beta melting at 122° and boiling at 286°. Both are only slightly soluble in water but readily soluble in alcohol and ether. Chemically, they resemble phenol, being readily soluble in alkali, forming ethers and coupling with diazonium compounds to form dyes. 

565. Naphthol Sulphonic Acids. These are of great technical value for making dyes. The theory calls for fourteen acids containing one hydroxyl and one sulphonic acid group and many more when two or more of each of these groups are present. A large number have been prepared, some of which are manufactured on a large scale for use as dye intermediates. 

Naphthol sulphonic acids are obtained by three methods: 1. partial substitution of sulphonic acid groups by alkali fusion; 

2. sulphonation of alpha and beta naphthols and 3. substitution of the hydroxyl group for the amino group of the amino-sulphonic acids by the diazo reaction. ANTHRACENE AND ANTHRAQUINONE 

569. In the distillation of coal tar, the fraction around 350° partially solidifies. The crude anthracene is separated by a filter press and recrystallized from pyridine, solvent naphtha¹ or furfural. 

Anthracene makes up from 0.25 to 0.4 per cent of coal tar. It was discovered by Dumas and Laurent 2 in 1832, who named it paranaphthalene as they thought it isomeric with naphthalene. 

Anthracene is a solid melting at 218°, boiling at 342° and having the density 1.25. It is difficult to purify completely. Pure anthracene crystallizes in colorless plates and has a blue fluorescence. It is insoluble in water, only slightly soluble in alcohol and ether but readily soluble in hot benzene or toluene.

It was first synthesised by heating benzyl chloride and water to 190°: 2H5C6CH2Cl →C14H10 + 2HCl + H2 Anthracene

This showed the presence of two benzene rings which accounts for 12 of the 14 carbon atoms, its composition being C14H10. It was some time before the positions of the other two carbon atoms were known. The simplest proof of the structure is that dihydro-anthracene is obtained by heating o-bromo-benzyl bromide with sodium: 

CH Br ...+4Na + Br Br + 4 Na Br Dihydro-anthracene ¹ Solvent naphtha is the fraction from coal tar above toluene and includes the xylenes and trimethyl-benzenes. 

2 August Laurent (1807-1853) was a French chemist who opposed the dualistic theory of Berzelius. In 1838 he became Professor in the Academy of Sciences at Bordeaux.

Two atoms of hydrogen are readily removed from this by gentle oxidation:

Dihydro-anthracene Anthracene

There has been much discussion as to the disposition of the remaining bonds of the two connecting carbons. Some have advocated a centric formula, some prefer to put a bond across the central ring, while others advocate the ortho-quinoid formula: Centric

Diagonal bond o-Quinoid

Inspection will show that all three rings cannot have the three double bonds as in the Kekulé formula for benzene. For practical purposes the formula is written without double bonds as is done with benzene and naphthalene: 2 10 The positions 1, 4, 5 and 8 are equivalent and are called alpha, the four positions 2, 3, 6 and 7 are called beta, while 9 and 10 are known as gamma or meso.

Anthracene resembles benzene and naphthalene. It can be sulphonated, halogenated and nitrated; the sulphonic acid group enters one of the outside rings while halogens and the nitro group enter the meso positions. Hydroxy- and amino-anthracenes are known but they are distinctly different from phenol and aniline; for instance, amino-anthracene cannot be diazotized. Their resemblance to phenol and aniline is increased when the connecting

570. Anthraquinone. Anthracene is readily and almost quantitatively oxidised to anthraquinone by boiling with chromate mixture or by passing its vapor mixed with air over a catalyst such as vanadium oxide. Anthraquinone, which melts at 285° and boils at 379.8°, is slightly yellow. Its constitution may be deduced · from that of anthracene and is confirmed by its hydrolysis to benzoic acid on heating with alkali and by its synthesis from o-benzoyl benzoic acid: CONa CONa + 2 NaOH Anthraquinone 

Sodium benzoate COOH... o-Benzoyl-benzoic acid Anthraquinone

At the present time in the United States almost all of the anthraquinone used in the industries is made by this synthesis, which can be equally well adapted to the production of 6-methyl- and B-chloranthraquinone. 

571. The Sulphonation of Anthraquinone. Anthraquinone requires drastic treatment for its sulphonation, that is, heating to

160° for several hours with 40 per cent oleum. The product is the 

B-sulphonic acid, 2,6and 2,7-disulphonic acids and a small amount, 4 or 5 per cent of the a-sulphonic acid. The addition of a small proportion of mercury sulphate to anthraquinone speeds up its sulphonation in the alpha position to such an extent that lower temperatures and weaker oleum may be used. In the presence of the mercury salt the sulphonation products are a-sulphonic acid and 1,5and 1,8-disulphonic acids. These sulphonic acids are valuable as intermediates since nearly all anthraquinone derivatives are made from them by replacing the sulphonic acid groups by other substituents. 

572. Alizarin. The two most valuable dyes, alizarin and indigo, have come down from antiquity. The root of the madder plant contains a glucoside of ruberythric acid which is hydrolyzed by enzymes or by heating with dilute sulphuric acid: C26H28014+2H2O →→→2C6H12O6 + C14H6O2 (OH)2

Benzene, according to the Kekulé formula, is made up of six -CH= groups, each of which is trivalent. Substituting a trivalent nitrogen for one of these gives pyridine, which is a six-membered ring compound. Thiazole is derived from thiophene by a similar substitution of -N- for -CH=. The group -CH: CH— is bivalent and its place can be taken by a bivalent atom, the -S- in thiophene and thiazole,¹ the -0- in furane, and the NH- in pyrrole.

PYRIDINE 

HC CH HC CH 6 2 5 3 576. Of all the heterocyclic compounds, pyridine resembles benzene most closely, even to its formation in pyrogenetic processes, benzene being made from acetylene alone, and pyridine from acetylene and hydrocyanic acid. Its chief source is coal tar in which it is found along with benzene; it is separated from the light distillate by treatment with acids. Pyridine like benzene is very resistant to oxidation; methyl-pyridine is oxidised to pyridinecarboxylic acid, the analog of benzoic acid. The homologs of pyridine are found with it in coal tar and in other sources. Many of the alkaloids are related to pyridine.

THIOPHENE 

HC HC- HC CH 5 2 A n 4 3 580. Commercial benzene contains about 0.5 per cent of thiophene from which it cannot be separated by fractionation, since the boiling point of thiophene, 85°, is near that of benzene. 

Its presence in benzene was not suspected until 1883, when Victor Meyer found that benzene from benzoic acid does not give the indophenine reaction (see below) which had previous to that time been considered characteristic of benzene. 

Thiophene is formed when acetylene and sulphur vapors are passed through a hot tube, and it is formed in small quantities when n-butane is heated with sulphur in a sealed tube. It is prepared by heating sodium succinate with phosphorus trisulphide. 

Thiophene closely resembles benzene in its reactions and even in odor. The most characteristic reaction of thiophene and its homologs is the so-called indophenine reaction, the development of a blue color with sulphuric acid containing a small amount of isatin (585). With halogens, sulphuric acid and nitric acid it reacts by substitution like benzene, but much more readily. The old method of extracting it from benzene consisted in shaking the crude benzene repeatedly with small quantities of concentrated sulphuric acid, which sulphonates thiophene in preference to the benzene. The thiophene sulphonic acid can be broken up by

superheated steam and the thiophene recovered. By preferential mercuration and decomposition of the mercury derivative, the same end may be more efficiently accomplished. Chlorine and bromine react directly with thiophene to give chlorinated thiophenes. Nitrothiophene smells like nitrobenzene. The alpha and beta methyl-thiophenes are found in crude toluene and the dimethyl-thiophenes in crude xylene. There are also sulphur compounds analogous to naphthalene.

586. Indigo. This is probably the oldest dye known and is still one of the most valuable; its antiquity and permanency are attested by the fact that cloth dyed with it and still retaining its color is found in ancient Egyptian tombs. It is produced from a number of plants (the indigofera) which grow in warm countries. 

As stated above, the plants contain indican which is hydrolyzed by enzymes present in the plants. In order to favor the hydrolysis, the plants are placed in water in stone vats and left until the hydrolysis is complete. Water containing the indoxyl is drawn off into other vats where it is agitated vigorously to bring about the oxidation of the indoxyl by the air. The indigo that is thus produced settles out and is collected. This natural indigo contains several other substances. The problem of the synthesis of indigo engaged the attention of a number of the best chemists for many years. The first synthesis by Baeyer in 1870 has been followed by a number of other syntheses, several of which have been operated commercially. The production of artificial indigo has increased steadily while the production of the natural has diminished. At the present time about 90 per cent of that used is the artificial. 

Three methods of synthesizing indigo are of importance, all of them starting with aniline and making indoxyl which is readily oxidised to indigo. In one phenyl-glycine is made from chloracetic acid and aniline and then water is eliminated by heating with sodamide:

587. Dyeing with Indigo. Indigo is the original vat dye; reduction converts it to a colorless form which is soluble in alkali: СОН нос.

Indigo white

In ancient times the reduction was effected by fermentation in the presence of lime or soda. This process is still in use but is being replaced by the use of sodium hydrosulphite, Na2S2O4, and caustic soda. The cloth is first passed through the vat where it adsorbs the indigo white and then is wrung out and exposed to the air which oxidises the soluble indigo white to the insoluble indigo.

590. Carbazole. The anthracene fraction of coal tar contains phenanthrene and carbazole: Phenanthrene Carbazole

It will be observed that the central ring in carbazole is a pyrrole ring instead of the benzene ring in phenanthrene. Carbazole melts at 244.8° and boils at 354.8°. Like pyrrole it forms a potassium salt. It finds some application as a starting point for making dyes.

Furane is a colorless liquid with an odor somewhat like chloroform. It boils at 31°, is very soluble in alcohol and ether but insoluble in water. a-Methyl-furane, also known as sylvane, and dimethyl-furane are found in the tars from pine and beech wood.

Furfural melts at 38.7°, boils at 161.7° and has a sweetish odor. In its reactions it is strikingly like benzaldehyde. It reacts with hydroxylamine, phenylhydrazine, and sodium bisulphite, polymerizes readily and even condenses with dimethyl-aniline to give an analog of malachite green. The large scale manufacture of furfural from oat hulls has recently been taken up.¹ It is a valuable solvent for the purification of anthracene and for other purposes. 

Furfural resins are being developed. 

593. Furoic Acid. This acid, known also as pyromucic, can be obtained by the oxidation of furfural. Furoic acid melts at 133°, is soluble in hot water, forms esters and other acid derivatives, resembles benzoic acid to some extent but is also like an unsaturated aliphatic acid. 

594. Coumarone. The union of a benzene ring with furane gives coumarone:

CH Coumarone

This and some of its methyl derivatives are found in coal tar. It is an indifferent compound which boils at 175° and can be polymerized by strong acids.

PYRAZOLE 

HC HC -NH 5 2N 

595. Pyrazole differs from pyridine as pyrrole does from benzene; that is, it has the NH- group substituted for -CH: CH-. In chemical properties it resembles benzene and pyridine. It is sulphonated and nitrated but not so readily as benzene. Nitropyrazole can be reduced to aminopyrazole, which is readily diazotized and coupled with phenols to give azo dyes. 

5-Hydroxypyrazole has a phenolic character. Homologs of pyrazole are readily oxidised to pyrazole-carboxylic acids. Pyrazole and its homologs resemble pyridine in odor, basicity and in the formation of double salts.

Pyrazole is obtained by the combination of acetylene and diazomethane: HC CH₂ HC CH HC HC NH Pyrazole Diazomethane

It is also formed when hydrazine reacts with the acetal of propargyl aldehyde:

ALKALOIDS 

597. This name is given to a group of organic bases that are found in natural substances, almost all of them in plants. The boundary of the group is indefinite; it is customary not to include the simpler bases and consider only those that contain nitrogen as a member of a heterocyclic ring. About two hundred alkaloids are known, among them there are some of the most violent poisons and some of the bitterest substances, along with some harmless and tasteless compounds. Since antiquity alkaloids have been sought as medicines, at first in the crude drugs as cinchona bark and later as pure preparations such as quinine and morphine. A number of alkaloids are sometimes found in a single plant; opium contains twenty-two known alkaloids. The isolation, determination of structure and syntheses of alkaloids has required the best work of many leaders in organic chemistry. The alkaloids are usually found as salts, sometimes of the usual organic acids and sometimes of special acids. The alkaloids are insoluble, or slightly soluble in water but readily soluble as salts in dilute acids. Hence they are obtained from the plants by extraction with dilute acids, concentration of the acid extract and precipitation with a base. Space permits only a few formulae for the proof of which reference must be made to the literature. 

598. Piperine. This, the alkaloid of pepper, is a substituted amide of piperic acid with piperidine forming the other portion:

HC-O CH:CH•CH:CHCON CH₂ Piperine

Piperonilic acid can be oxidised to the aldehyde piperonal, which is another name for heliotropin. Piperidine gets its name from its connection with this alkaloid. Piperine, which is almost nontoxic, crystallizes in prisms and melts at 129°. 599. Conine. This alkaloid is found in hemlock associated with several related substances, whose structures are:
